paragraphs.text: Translating into action his new ideas regarding history, Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar demonstrates in this book, Histories along the Way Volume One, how the true history of human beings should be written – by reflecting on the weal and woe, the hopes and aspirations, of the common people. The book depicts the living history behind the names of various of the earthʼs towns and villages, and sets down hitherto unwritten lines from the annals of the worldʼs territories, races and languages. In particular, the author has brought to light the neglected, downtrodden and dishonoured communities in society. He has also broken the silence that surrounded the trials, tribulations and sacrifices of hitherto unknown and unsung heroes and heroines, so as to fill human beings with strength to move forward. Finally, the author has provided fascinating anecdotes and descriptions relating to little-known anthropological and archaeological facts. In this manner, he fulfils the primary objective of historical enquiry – to foster the enlightened consciousness of the human family.

He has also broken the silence that surrounded the trials, tribulations and sacrifices of hitherto unknown and unsung heroes and heroines, so as to fill human beings with strength to move forward.

paragraphs.text: Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar had always been a traveller across the length and breadth of India. And for a period of years from 1979 on in particular, he undertook a number of strenuous car journeys during which, when he was not leading the spiritual gatherings that were the primary goal of the trips, he and his entourage would often pass through remote regions and mingle with the simple, common people. At such times he would explain to his companions the history of those places and peoples – a history not to be found in the pages of existing history books. When such tours out from his Kolkata base included the Ananda Marga centre in West Bengalʼs Purulia District, part of the ancient land of Ráŕh, he would seek out and explore the local mountainous areas, river valleys and even caves. In so doing, he came across both rare fossils and human artefacts, the latter including hitherto-undiscovered samples of ancient scripts. Though such palaeological and archaeological research was particularly a feature of his tours in that area, it figured at times during his other tours also. The related pictures of all these are given in the book.

paragraphs.text: In the year 1983, he began giving the series of discourses that would be compiled and published by the end of that year in the book Varńa Vijiṋána (“The Science of Letters”), and at that time his touring such as described above began to diminish, though it did not entirely cease; after a notable tour in 1984, he began to term such tours his “history tours”. In November 1983 he launched the series of discourses that would be published in the eight parts of Varńa Vicitrá (“Various Uses of Letters”), and before the end of 1985 he started the Shabda Cayaniká (“Collection of Words”) discourses. The Varńa Vijiṋána and Varńa Vicitrá discourses involved topics of linguistics, while Shabda Cayaniká had aspects of a general encyclopaedia in addition to a strong aspect of linguistics. None of the three series was formally devoted to history as such, yet in the course of making his other points, the author referred again and again to the cultures and events of different times and places, and thus filled those books with historical information. And much of those historical explanations bore a strong resemblance to the extempore talks he had given to his companions during his extensive tours of India; though in his discourses he sometimes touched on the histories of places far from India as well.

paragraphs.text: In the year 1987, he instructed that all the historical passages from the aforementioned books should be compiled into a new book with the Bengali title Path Calte Itikathá. It was published that same year in six parts. Those six parts contain material from Varńa Vijiṋána, Varńa Vicitrá and the first ten parts of Shabda Cayaniká, since Part 10 was the last that had been published as of that time. Shabda Cayaniká finally extended to twenty-six parts.

paragraphs.text: An updated version of the six parts of Path Calte Itikathá that would include material from the last sixteen parts of Shabda Cayaniká has not yet been published in Bengali; however, the English version of Path Calte Itikathá, which begins with the present book, Histories along the Way Volume One, and will finally include Volume Two, will include material from those eighteen parts. The present book contains large portions from the Bengali Parts 1-5, and also contains material of historical relevance from Shabda Cayaniká Parts 9-26. The remaining portions from Path Calte Itikathá, and further historical material from Shabda Cayaniká Parts 9-26 will constitute Histories along the Way Part Two, to be published in the near future.

paragraphs.text: Due to the aforementioned expansion of the book, it has not been possible to precisely follow the organization that was originally given by the author; hence the responsibility for the present organization and for some of the part titles now lies with the editors. The present book has been divided into six parts and an introduction. Since the author had an original vision and concept regarding the writing of an ideal history, the “Introduction” to the book contains one discourse published in 1970, two discourses published in 1980 and one published in 1983 that express this vision. Part 1 then contains the living history behind different place names. In that chapter, all the excerpts come from Varńa Vijiṋána. Within Parts 2 and 3 we have arranged the authorʼs descriptions of the histories of various of the worldʼs ancient territories, races, languages and scripts, as well as the histories of certain countries and places of the world. From a work published by the author in 1981, some excerpts relevant to the history of ancient Gondwanaland and Ráŕh have also been included. Part 4 contains histories of certain Cities, Towns, Localities of the world. The authorʼs detailed discussions of the histories of different states of India, and of specific sites within each state and histories of different old principalities constitute Part 5 and 6.

paragraphs.text: Many readers are concerned that the authorʼs discourses, as published, should adhere as closely as possible to the precise wording the author used in speaking. For this reason, in the case of discourses given originally in English, the editors do not alter pronouns and other terms which the author in his lifetime considered “common-gender” words. As the author once said, “You know, ‘man’ is not only masculine gender, ‘man’ is common gender also. 'Man is mortalʼ – here ‘man’ means both male and female.”

paragraphs.text: The author used a particular shorthand for explaining the etymologies of words. Under this system, a minus sign (–) follows a prefix, and a plus sign (+) precedes a suffix. Thus ava – tr + ghaiṋ = avatára can be read, “the root tr prefixed by ava and suffixed by ghaiṋ becomes avatára.”

paragraphs.text: Every new book translation starts with a draft by the main translator. It is then reviewed by a “first editor” who compares the English translation with the original Bengali or Hindi. Thereafter it is sent for “second editing” to improve the standard of English. On completion of second editing, it is sent for final verification, which includes one more comparison with the original Hindi or Bengali. Other important functions include the coordination of these different steps and the development and management of a global distribution and sales network.

paragraphs.text: ÁRYABHATTA: A premier mathematician and astronomer born in A.D. 476. He belonged to Kusumpura near Patna in Magadha. He discovered the diurnal motion of the earth causing the division of time into night and day. Long before the time of Copernicus he discovered the truth that the earth moves round the sun. He also knew the real reason for the eclipses of the sun and the moon, that the moon and the other planets have no light of their own and are illuminated with the reflected light of the sun, and that the earth and other planets move round the sun along elliptical orbits. Áryabhatta felt the need for advanced Geometric science in his quest for Astronomy. It has been said that he invented some Geometric principles – especially those related to angles – but no traces of these are available today. Since he had conducted an abundance of research on końas [angles], the pundits of his times decorated him with the title “Kaońika”.
summary: ÁRYABHATTA: A premier mathematician and astronomer born in A.

paragraphs.text: ATIISHA DIPAUṊKARA: A renowned Buddhist monk and scholar. He was born in about A.D. 981 in a well-to-do family of landlords at Vikramanipur village in Dhaka District of Bangladesh. His father was Kalyana Shrii and his mother was Padmaprabha and they gave him the name Chandtragarbha. He acquired such a profound knowledge in Buddhism that Ácárya Shilabhadra of Odantapuri Vihára, where he was studying, conferred on him the title of Diipauṋkara Shriijiṋána. Later on the Tibetans called him Shriijiṋána Atiisha. He was persuaded by the Pala king Nayapala to accept the post of the Chancellor (Kulapati) of the famous Vikramshila Vihára (University) near Antichak village of Bhagalpur District of Bihar. During his time the reputation of the learning in Vikramshila reached to the peak and soon spread far and wide. He was persistently invited by Tibetan kings to go over there and preach Buddhism. He was then sixty years old and made the perilous and hazardous journey from Vikramshila to Tibet. He spent twelve years there and established Buddhism in Tibet and also died there at the age seventy three.
summary: ATIISHA DIPAUṊKARA: A renowned Buddhist monk and scholar.

paragraphs.text: MAHARŚI KAPIL: The first philosopher of the world and the propounder of Sáḿkhya Philosophy. He also discovered the science of angles. He was the first person who observed that the angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees and that the angles of an equiangular triangle measure 60 degrees each. He was a son of the village Pát́i Jháldá on Kangsavati Basin of Ráŕh in Purulia District and born approximately more than 3000 years ago. By the side of Jhalda (a sub-divisional town in the same district), there still stands the Kapila Mountain, where he conducted his meditation and researches on Philosophy simultaneously with Geometry. He got realization there. In the month of January every year local villagers and others organizes a fair there in commemoration of him according to the instructions of the author.

paragraphs.text: MÁYÁN/MAYAN CIVILIZATION: There are various opinions about the exact time period of Mayan civilization in Central America. Historians divided three phases of Mayan civilization – Pre-Classic, Classic and Decline. The classic period is estimated to be 250 C.E. to 900 C.E. In fact, the Mayan civilization is a transplanted Indian civilization. It migrated to Central America during the rule of the Pallavas and Cholas of South India. One should keep in mind that the Sanskrit name for America, Máyádviipa, came from the name of the Mayan civilization. During Indian Middle Ages there was contact between America and India – this was before Columbusʼs discovery of America. Phallic worship was also widely prevalent in Central America, that is, in Mayan civilization and there were abundant signs of this and Shiva temples in the ruins there. Tremendous development occurred in architecture, art, writing, and calendrics in Mayan civilization. At one time, the ancient Mayan civilization of America was more advanced than many other civilizations, but because they lagged behind in the invention of the wheel, they were forced in subsequent times to acknowledge their defeat at the hands of other civilizations. The oldest existing artifacts of the Mayan civilization give evidence to advanced ways of life but no wheel.
summary: MÁYÁN/MAYAN CIVILIZATION: There are various opinions about the exact time period of Mayan civilization in Central America.

chapters.title: Human Society Is One and Indivisible
chapters.partTitle: INTRODUCTION: What Is History?

paragraphs.text: ...Besides language, people have a natural weakness for their glorious national heritage. Every person loves and respects the past national prosperity and the nationʼs glorious traditions. This love for oneʼs glorious heritage is clearly a psychic sentiment. This psychic sentiment can be utilized to consolidate the national unity. Take for instance the Mohangedaro and Harappan civilizations. The glorious heritage of a country should not be kept confined to school curricula or research scholars. Rather, it should be presented to the public. This will create a sense of confidence and glory in the peopleʼs minds and thus strengthen the bonds of fraternity.
summary: Besides language, people have a natural weakness for their glorious national heritage.
Take for instance the Mohangedaro and Harappan civilizations.
This will create a sense of confidence and glory in the peopleʼs minds and thus strengthen the bonds of fraternity.

paragraphs.text: Likewise, the glorious history of a country strengthens the sense of unityecord, but a work of immense educative value. For instance, the Mahábhárata is itihása as it has been a source of inspiration for people since its creation. Even today village people, sitting around a kerosene lamp in the evening, read and discuss the Mahábhárata, each one cherishing a universal attitude of love for the book. The propagation of the Mahábhárata will have a beneficial influence on peopleʼs minds. Many of its passages may be quoted to enlighten people about their glorious past, and offer solutions to their worldly problems. Biographies of great saints, sages and personalities of the past should also be presented to the common people to foster unity in them. There is a subterranean flow of love and devotion in peopleʼs minds for those sages and saints, as those saints rose above narrow sentiments to propagate the ideals of unity and fraternity. Their writings create a stir in peopleʼs minds. So the popularisation of these personalities is essential to inspire unity among the masses.

paragraphs.text: The contemporary leaders do not try to give a practical shape to any of the aforementioned human qualities. They merely deliver high-sounding lectures. Those great personalities of the past provide good opportunities for them to organize bicentennial and anniversary celebrations. They consider that by merely uttering a few well-rehearsed sentences, they are paying a wonderful tribute to those great personalities. These leaders do not realize what an important contribution the great personalities can still give to further the countryʼs welfare. Thus the great ideals are disappearing from social life and disunity is increasing among the people. ( 1 )

chapters.title: What Should History Be Like?
chapters.partTitle: INTRODUCTION: What Is History?

paragraphs.text: Yesterday I said something about history; I said that modern history usually deals with certain very common events such as when a certain king succeeded to the throne, or plundered a neighbouring country, or perpetrated atrocities on his subjects, or died, and so on. What benefit could common people possibly derive from studying such useless information? This is why they have no interest to study this sort of history at all. True history should be a faithful record of the entire human life.

paragraphs.text: That is, history is a resplendent reflection of collective life, whose study will be of immense inspiration for future generations. Iti hasati literally means “the glowing example of glorious human dignity.”

paragraphs.text: Human beings should not be compared to individual flowers, but to an entire flower garden. A flower garden is made up of innumerable varieties of flowers, each with its own fragrance and colours. Human history is like this: the beauty of history lies in its kaleidoscopic variations in spatial, temporal and personal factors. We cannot afford to spoil its characteristics; nor can we forcibly impose a particular type of history on a certain community.
summary: Human beings should not be compared to individual flowers, but to an entire flower garden.
Human history is like this: the beauty of history lies in its kaleidoscopic variations in spatial, temporal and personal factors.
We cannot afford to spoil its characteristics; nor can we forcibly impose a particular type of history on a certain community.

paragraphs.text: Every individual or community will advance by virtue of its own inner vitality and assist in the collective fulfilment of the entire humanity. This is the true spirit of history. While writing history we will have to consider the various spheres of human life and ensure that proper directions are given for the development of each sphere. For instance, history should focus upon the prevalent educational system, cultural standards, thoughts and ideas, dress, the social condition of women, the role of women in the social and economic spheres, and the socio-economic conditions of the weak and backward communities of the society of a particular age, etc. If any of these aspects are omitted while writing history, it will be incomplete.

paragraphs.text: Let us see how people write history or get it written. In most cases history is written in the interest of a particular vested interest. History books are selected in order to establish the glory of a particular era. For example, the heroic tales of the chivalry of the Kśatriya Era, their war-strategies, etc., form the main basis for the writing of the history of the Kśatriya Era. History books are filled with eulogies of the bravery and chivalry of the kśatriya rulers. Similarly, the history of the Vipra era is full of praises for the glorious deeds of the vipra leaders, and the history of the Vaeshya Era contains an abundance of stories about the glories of the vaeshyas. While studying such biased history, the readers lose both interest and patience. Besides that, the study of this sort of so-called history injects some kind of dogma in the readers mind, and consequently chokes the development of a spontaneous human intellect.

, form the main basis for the writing of the history of the Kśatriya Era.
Besides that, the study of this sort of so-called history injects some kind of dogma in the readers mind, and consequently chokes the development of a spontaneous human intellect.

...In the psychic sphere, there are certain factors that serve to unite different linguistic groups of people. For example, all North Indian languages and a few South Indian languages originated and developed from Saḿskrta. These languages have been greatly influenced by Saḿskrta. In such circumstances, the study of Saḿskrta should not be opposed by anybody. This may appear to be a trivial matter, but if it is encouraged it will be a great unifying factor in Indian society.

In some ancient civilizations like the Egyptian civilization and the Mayan civilization, even the remnants of the old customs are now no longer discernible. What was the cause of their downfall? The Mayan civilization lagged behind for one reason: they could not invent the wheel. ... paragraphs.text: Iti + has + ghaiṋ = itihása. The meaning of the root verb has is “to laugh”, “to be expressed in a particular way”. In Sanskrit hasati means “laughing”. It is both spelled and pronounced without a candrabindu. ( 1 ) In Hindi háṋstá háy means “laughing”. It is spelled with a candrabindu, or half-na, and pronounced the same way. In Bengali it is spelled hásche but pronounced háṋsche, that is, it is spelled without the candrabindu, or half-na, but pronounced with it.

paragraphs.text: The etymological meaning of itihása is “that which has been particularly expressed in this way”. I have said before and I will say again that the English synonym for itihása is not “history”, nor is the French synonym histoire. The proper Bengali synonyms for the English word “history” and the French word histoire are itikathá, itivrtta, purákathá, and purávrtta.

paragraphs.text: All those educative subjects that we find in the succession of past events we call aetihásika. It should be borne in mind that something is aetihásika, or about itihása, to the extent that it is educative. That which has less educative value will have to be called itikathá, not itihása, that is, a factual chronicle of events we call itikathá, whether or not it contains something of instructional value. But when we look towards the past and we are unable to discover any continuity of facts, or put together a respectable portrait of reality, then we call it prágaetihásika (prák + aetihásika), or prehistorical or prehistoric. It is also worth remembering here we call prehistoric those temporal events for which we are unable, at present, to discover a historical continuity or common thread due to a lack of adequate research. Yet if in the future, as a result of adequate efforts, we discover that continuity or get hold of the missing link, then we will no longer be able to call them “prehistoric”. They will then pass from prehistory to history.
summary: All those educative subjects that we find in the succession of past events we call aetihásika.

But when we look towards the past and we are unable to discover any continuity of facts, or put together a respectable portrait of reality, then we call it prágaetihásika (prák + aetihásika), or prehistorical or prehistoric.

paragraphs.text: In Sanskrit the word prák is used to mean “pre” in regard to time, and the word uttara is used to mean “post”. For example, that which precedes itihása is prágaetihásika and that which comes after it is itihásottara. In the same way we derive the words prák-baoddha [pre-Buddhist] and Baoddhottara [post-Buddhist].

It is also worth remembering in this case that words formed with the suffix śńik have short i such as aetihásik, kálik [pertaining to time], yántrik [mechanical], and daeshik [pertaining to space]. chapters.title: Bounteous Wisdom–1
chapters.partTitle: PART 1: Bounteous Wisdom on Place Names

paragraphs.text: There is a living history behind the names given to the earthʼs different villages and towns. If the screen hiding that history is removed, then the history of not only the town but indeed of the people as well will be unveiled. If the history of the names of villages and towns of countries that do not have a written history is discovered, then the [real] history of those countries will also come to light. The Indian people have shown a certain apathy towards history since very ancient times; thus they have comparatively little written history. Stone inscriptions, copper inscriptions and coins offer very little help in assessing history; if there is a proper and heartfelt effort to discover the history behind the names given to towns and villages, then that history can be newly explored. The greater portion of history that is presently taught in schools and colleges will have to then be mercilessly discarded. ( 1 )

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Pura/Nagara/Mańd́i
summary: Place-names ending in Pura/Nagara/Mańd́i

paragraphs.text: Many places in India and Southeast Asia have been named with with words such as pura and nagara, etc. added on. In Sanskrit, small cities used to be called pura and large cities were called nagara. (Incidentally, the word pur is actually Farsi). The difference between the two was that a nagara was completely encircled by a wall, which was called nagaraveśt́ańii in Sanskrit. Those who lived within the walls of the nagara were called nágarika. The word used today in English as a synonym for nágarika, “citizen”, bears no relation to the ancient word nágarika. Nágarika means “inhabitant of a nagara”, while “citizen”, as it is used today, refers to any resident of a country, whether they live in a city or in a rural village.
summary: Many places in India and Southeast Asia have been named with with words such as pura and nagara, etc.
The difference between the two was that a nagara was completely encircled by a wall, which was called nagaraveśt́ańii in Sanskrit.
Nágarika means “inhabitant of a nagara”, while “citizen”, as it is used today, refers to any resident of a country, whether they live in a city or in a rural village.

paragraphs.text: Actually the word “citizen” means a resident of this kind of wall-enclosed city. Neither the English “citizen” nor the Bengali nágarika refers to the resident of a particular country. In other words, the pure English expression for the English word “citizen”, as we use it today, as well as for the word nágarika in Bengali, is “bonafide inhabitant”. The Farsi word for this is mulkii.

In other words, the pure English expression for the English word “citizen”, as we use it today, as well as for the word nágarika in Bengali, is “bonafide inhabitant”.
The Farsi word for this is mulkii.

paragraphs.text: This wall-enclosed city used to be called hábelii in Urdu and háolii in Bhojpurii. There is a place in Monghyr District by the name of Habelii Kharagpur. According to the customs of that period, the main gate of the hábelii or nagara used to be closed at nine at night and the key used to remain with the city father or the sheriff.

paragraphs.text: [As mentioned earlier] many places in India and Southeast Asia were named with the words pura, nagara and upanagara, etc. added on. We have taken many of these words from Farsi, for example, the Urdu word mańd́i meaning “marketing centre”; in Sanskrit it is called vipańana kendra or vipańi, that is, “where commodities are taken for the purpose of selling or vipańana”. Many people mistakenly use the word “marketing” to refer to shopping. Actually, “marketing” means selling. The villagers go to the market or bazaar to sell their goods and produce, that is, they go for marketing. We go to the market to buy potatoes or pat́ol [wax gourd], that is, we go for shopping. The pure Bengali word for “marketing centre” or mańd́i is postá. There is a Postá Bazaar in Kolkata. Have you all read the famous poem by Sukumar Ray? Shuńte pelum postá giye / Tomár náki meyer viye [“When I went to market / I heard about your daughterʼs wedding”].
summary: [As mentioned earlier] many places in India and Southeast Asia were named with the words pura, nagara and upanagara, etc.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Gaiṋja
summary: Place-names ending in Gaiṋja

paragraphs.text: If a place has a village and a flourishing market for buying and selling, then it is called a gaiṋja (ganj-a). The British corrupted the pronunciation to ganj (spelled “gunge”). In this manner, the place called Ballygunge came from the name of Mr. Bailey, Tolleygunge from Mr. Tolley, and so on. The actual pronunciation should be Baligaiṋja, T́áligaiṋja. The common people of East Bengal say Náráyańgaiṋja and Munsiigaiṋja. They pronounce these names correctly. Now, if someone persists with a faulty pronunciation, should we follow them blindly or should we open their eyes to this error? You tell me.
summary: If a place has a village and a flourishing market for buying and selling, then it is called a gaiṋja (ganj-a).
The actual pronunciation should be Baligaiṋja, T́áligaiṋja.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Hát́/Ghát́/Kasbá
summary: Place-names ending in Hát́/Ghát́/Kasbá

paragraphs.text: There is another word in Bengali – hát́ [market.] The word hát́ comes from the Sanskrit word hat́t́a. For example, if many hátʼs are strung together [in one area], then it is called hat́t́amálá [garland of markets] in Sanskrit. Certainly many of you have read the story “Hat́t́amálá” (2). In Sanskrit a very large hát́ is called hat́t́ika. Hat́t́a plus the suffix śńik makes hat́t́ika. Although grammatically speaking, the meaning of hat́t́ika should be “small hát́”, in actuality it was used to mean “large hát́”. The Bengali word which is derived from hat́t́a is hát́, for example, rájárhát́, bágerhát́ and májherhát́. The The Bengali word derived from the Sanskrit hat́t́ika is hát́i. For example, naehát́i comes from navahat́t́ika, nalahát́i from nalahat́t́ika, and gaohát́i from guvákahat́t́ika. In south Bengal there was a tendency to pronounce hát́ as hát́á and ghát́ as ghát́á; as a result, we get Páthureghát́á, Beleghát́á, Murgiihát́á, Daramáhát́á and Gariyáhát́á.
summary: There is another word in Bengali – hát́ [market.
Hat́t́a plus the suffix śńik makes hat́t́ika.

paragraphs.text: There is normally a shortage of fodder in the district of Nadia, which is famous for its bumper crop of autumnal paddy. It is bordered by Burdwan, the district for winter paddy. Hay (khaŕ) used to be imported by boat along the Jalangi River to Nadia District from Burdwanʼs Nandanaghát́ (Nádanghát́). At that time, the hay-laden Jalangi River was renamed the Khaŕiyá or Kháre River. In other words, although this tributary of the Padma River was known as the Jalangi River in Murshidabad District, its common name was the Khaŕe River. There was a huge cattle market (garur hát́) near Nadia Districtʼs cow herding centre, Reui village (later Reui village became known as Krishnanagar) – Sanskrit gohat́t́ika > Prákrta gohad́d́ia > Demi-Prákrta gohád́i > old Bengali goháŕi ® modern Bengali goyáŕi. The British made Goyáŕi the headquarters of Nadia District. We still say the two together – Goyáŕi-Krishnanagar.
summary: There is normally a shortage of fodder in the district of Nadia, which is famous for its bumper crop of autumnal paddy.
In other words, although this tributary of the Padma River was known as the Jalangi River in Murshidabad District, its common name was the Khaŕe River.

paragraphs.text: A large centre for buying and selling, whether in a village or city, is called a kasbá in Farsi. There is a place in 24 Paraganas called Kasbá. The old name of Jessore was Kasbá. When Khulna District was created, the real Jessore was included within Khulna District. Khulna is not a very old district. It was formed by piecing together 24 Paraganasʼ Sátkśiirá, Jessoreʼs Khulna and most of Bakharganjʼs Bagerhat. After the place called Jessore was included within Khulna District, there was no purpose in keeping the name Jessore for the remaining portion of the district. Still, the name Jessore continued in use. From then on the people started calling the district headquarters as Kasbá Jessore. When I was a child I have seen the village girls telling the booking clerk when they went to buy tickets: “Sir, would you please give me tickets for Kasbá.” Then the ticket clerk would produce tickets for Jessore and give them to the girls...

paragraphs.text: The British built soldiersʼ barracks at Ghughud́áuṋgá to the north of Kolkata. The incessant firing of weapons there used to make the sound dumdum. It was like a violent boom-boom (damá-dam) on Diipavali night. The village people all around became impatient with the noise and gave the place the name Damdamá [mound for target practice]. Later, when a railway station was built there, it was named Dumdum. The actual name of the place was hence Damdamá. When the local people went to Sealdah station to buy tickets, they would say: “Sir, please give us tickets for Ghughud́áuṋgá,” and the ticket clerk would give them tickets for Dumdum. No one wanted a ticket for Sinthi, perhaps because Sinthi was not as famous as Ghughud́áuṋgá.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Ábád; Aryan Invasions
summary: Place-names ending in Ábád; Aryan Invasions

paragraphs.text: The Aryans established their first colony in northwest India ( 3 ). Later they started slowly advancing eastwards. First they came to the Saptasindhu, now called The Punjab, which means the land of five rivers – the Sutlej, Bias, Ravi, Chenub and Jhelum. Previously the name of this region was the Saptasindhu. Bear in mind here that the Vedic word sindhu means both “sea” and “large river”, as does the Farsi word dariyá. In any case, when the Aryans encountered the Sindhu River they gave this very large river the designation nada [large river] and named it the Sindhu. The Sindhu has six tributaries – the Shatadru, Irávatii, Candrabhágá, Vitastá, Vipáshá and Kábul. Together they formed the Saptasindhu [seven sindhus] of that era, and later it became The Punjab.
summary: The Aryans established their first colony in northwest India ( 3 ).
Bear in mind here that the Vedic word sindhu means both “sea” and “large river”, as does the Farsi word dariyá.
Together they formed the Saptasindhu [seven sindhus] of that era, and later it became The Punjab.

paragraphs.text: When they arrived in The Punjab and discovered an environment eminently suited to farming, they became very happy and began to settle. Their Vedic language underwent transformation and became known as Paeshácii Prákrta in the Saptasindhu. The modern languages descended from Paeshácii Prákrta are Panjabi, Pahari (previously it was called Pahari-Panjabi) and Dogri. The Multani language, being a mixture of Panjabi and Sindhi, shows the influences of both Paeshácii Prákrta and Pahlavii Prákrta. Even today these languages use many words derived from Vedic, for example, ind, pińd́a and pińd́i. The village that was settled by the Rawal Brahmans of south India is Rawalpindi. Although sugar is called khánŕ (which comes from the Vedic word khańd́a) in Panjabi, sugar, especially red sugar, is called sharkará in Vedic and Sanskrit. Since we learned how to make sugar from the Chinese, it was given the name cinii in spoken language. Sharkará is an ancient word from which comes the pure Hindi sakkar, the Marathi sáṋkar, the Tamil sákar, the Latin [saccharum] and the French sucre. The French sucre underwent alteration and became the English “sugar”.
summary: When they arrived in The Punjab and discovered an environment eminently suited to farming, they became very happy and began to settle.
The village that was settled by the Rawal Brahmans of south India is Rawalpindi.
The French sucre underwent alteration and became the English “sugar”.

paragraphs.text: The word khui comes from the Vedic word khud́ikam and it means “well”. The modern Bengali word kúyo comes from the Mágadhii Prákrta word kúa, which comes from the Sanskrit word kúpa. From the Sanskrit word indrakúpa comes the Mágadhii Prákrta word indraua, from that the Demi-Prákrta word indarua, from that indárá, and from that the ultramodern pronunciation inárá. In Sanskrit indra means “best”; thus, a large well, or inárá, is called indrakúpa. In those days the shál tree was considered the best tree. The place that had an abundance of these shál trees or indravrkśa was known as Indrapura > Indpur > Indpur, which is a village in Bankura District. The Pahlavii Prákrta word put́t́ara or put́rá comes from the Sanskrit word puttra. It is the same in modern Sindhi. The Panjabi word dohtar comes from the Sanskrit word daohitra; however, in many areas of north India daohitra is called náti, which comes from the Sanskrit word naptá. Naptá means “that which prevents the fall of a bodiless soul”. According to the social practice of the time, those with whose help one was saved from social downfall during the period of mourning was also called naptá, nápita or nápte. From the Vedic nupta came the Paeshácii Prákrta nutta, in Demi-Prákrta nuta and in modern Panjabi nu, which means “daughter-in-law”. In the rest of north India, however, “daughter-in-law” is called putohu – Sanskrit putravadhú > puttavahu > putohu.
summary: The word khui comes from the Vedic word khud́ikam and it means “well”.
The Pahlavii Prákrta word put́t́ara or put́rá comes from the Sanskrit word puttra.
In the rest of north India, however, “daughter-in-law” is called putohu – Sanskrit putravadhú > puttavahu > putohu.

paragraphs.text: Aryans arrived in Haryana and Ludhiana
summary: Aryans arrived in Haryana and Ludhiana

paragraphs.text: Thereafter, the Aryans advanced further east. The land grew greener and more verdant. They had never seen so much green before. In Vedic dhánya means “green vegetation”, so after crossing the Saptasindhu they named the new land east of it Haritdhánya; this became Hariahánya in Shaorasenii Prákrta, Hariháná in Demi-Shaorasenii, and Hariyáná in modern Hariyánavii (which is a very close relative of Hindi). Similarly, we obtain the word Ludhiyáná. In ancient times the Aryans used to use the pollen from the forest tree flower by the name of lodhra as a cosmetic.
summary: Thereafter, the Aryans advanced further east.

paragraphs.text: Aryans arrived in Prayága or Allahabad; Other names ending in ábád:
summary: Aryans arrived in Prayága or Allahabad; Other names ending in ábád:

paragraphs.text: They advanced even further east [Approximately between ten to seven thousand years from now], travelling from the west towards the eastern sunrise until they came to the region lying between the Ganges and Yamuna rivers, at the point where they are farthest from each other, between Gangotri and Yamunotri. Thereafter the two rivers gradually converged until they merged at Prayága. The area lying between these two rivers was the ancient Brahmávartta or Brahmarśidesha, which later became Shúrasena and still later was given the name Do-áb in Farsi, that is, “the land of two rivers”. The ancient capital of Brahmávartta was Vrśńipura (today Vit́hur near Kanpur). Later, after its name had changed to Shurasena, the capital became Mathura. Before Krśńa, the king of Shurasena was Kaḿsa. His capital was also at Mathura. The Kayasthas of north India, who live in the former Brahmávartta or Shurasena, still call themselves Máthur. Since this latter part of Brahmávartta was eminently suited for living, farming and all sorts of developed undertakings, the Aryans gave it the name Prayága (pra – yaj + ghaiṋ = Prayága). Here ya is in the middle of the word [antahstha ya], so according to the rule – padánte padamadhyasthe “ya”-kára “ia” ucyate – prayága became prayága [with the dot below the letter in Bengali script].
summary: They advanced even further east [Approximately between ten to seven thousand years from now], travelling from the west towards the eastern sunrise until they came to the region lying between the Ganges and Yamuna rivers, at the point where they are farthest from each other, between Gangotri and Yamunotri.
Before Krśńa, the king of Shurasena was Kaḿsa.

Here ya is in the middle of the word [antahstha ya], so according to the rule – padánte padamadhyasthe “ya”-kára “ia” ucyate – prayága became prayága [with the dot below the letter in Bengali script].

paragraphs.text: The meaning of the verbal root yaj in both Sanskrit and Vedic is “to act”. By adding the suffix na to the root yaj we get the word yajiṋa. Yaj + ghaiṋ creates yága. The meaning of both words is “action”. Thus, “the place where action is performed in an excellent manner” is called prayága. The Aryans used to believe that this place was extremely holy. It was their conception that if one took a bath at Prayága then all oneʼs sins would be washed away; hence, even now there is a custom among a certain class of people in India to immerse the remains of the deceased at Prayága. There is a saying in Hindi when a wicked person says something spiritual or righteous – Na sho cuhá khá kar billii calii prayág snán [after swallowing nine hundred mice the cat went for a holy bath in the Prayága]. The words yájaka [officiating priest at a ritual] and yajamán [person for whom the ritual is performed] come from the verbal root yaj.
summary: The meaning of the verbal root yaj in both Sanskrit and Vedic is “to act”.
Thus, “the place where action is performed in an excellent manner” is called prayága.
The words yájaka [officiating priest at a ritual] and yajamán [person for whom the ritual is performed] come from the verbal root yaj.

paragraphs.text: As a result of the Aryans settling down at Prayága, the region became an illustrious centre for learning and culture. Much later, during the Pathan-Mughal era, it grew into a crowded city and became susceptible to flooding during the rainy season. So during the Pathan era, a new city was established not very far away and given the name Álláh-Ábád, or the “abode of Allah”. Later the Shias gave this place, Álláh-Ábád, the name Iláhábád. In modern Hindi it is called Iláhábád. Both names, Álláhábad and Iláhábád, are used in Urdu. One point to keep in mind is that all those cities which have the word ábád added at the end of their names were all named during the Pathan or Mughal era, or else later, for example, Farrukhabad, Muzaffarabad, Alidabad, Jekovabad, Nasirabad (Mymensing), Jahangirabad (Dhaka), Islamabad (Chittagong), Phaejabad (Ayodhya), Shershahabad (Malda) and Sharifabad (Burdwanʼs Paragana). The new name of Burdwan is Vár-e-Dewán and the name of Paragana is Sharifabad. Hence, if we find the word ábád attached, it helps us to determine the history of the city, and we can be certain that the city is no more than seven hundred years old.
summary: As a result of the Aryans settling down at Prayága, the region became an illustrious centre for learning and culture.
In modern Hindi it is called Iláhábád.
Hence, if we find the word ábád attached, it helps us to determine the history of the city, and we can be certain that the city is no more than seven hundred years old.

During the Pathan era [1193-1526] there were three provinces in north India – The Punjab, Hindustan and Bengal. The number of provinces increased during the time of Akbar. The province of Agra was formed from the south, southwest and southeast portions of Hindustan province, and the province of Oudh was formed from the northeastern areas. Thus the people of Bengal and The Punjab still refer to the people of Uttar Pradesh as Hindustanis. Some people wonder why only the people of Uttar Pradesh should be called Hindustanis, if all of India is Hindustan; however, those who call the people of Uttar Pradesh Hindustanis are not entirely incorrect, because Hindustan does not refer to all of India. Though in Urdu poetry and in the spoken language the word Hindustan is used for India, this usage is not a historical fact. Bear in mind that in Farsi the actual word for India is not Hindustan but Hind.

paragraphs.text: Every sound on earth is meaningful, whether or not we are conscious of that meaning. This meaningfulness is bound up with the phonetics and independent pronunciation of the local language. Often we unknowingly forget about the significance of the meaning and we try to forget this local independence of pronunciation as well. Though the error we commit in doing so is pardonable to some extent, it is not completely excusable in all cases.

Often we unknowingly forget about the significance of the meaning and we try to forget this local independence of pronunciation as well.
Though the error we commit in doing so is pardonable to some extent, it is not completely excusable in all cases.

paragraphs.text: The huge city in the south of England used to be called Londres (the French pronunciation was londre) in France, but because the people of Scotland could not pronounce it properly, and for other reasons as well, the city was called Láńd́án. Nowadays the word Láńd́án has changed into London. I am not saying that the city should be called Londre once again, only that there is a definite need to remember the original historical name of the city. If we cannot properly pronounce the name of the city that has for centuries has been called Moscova, and instead pronounce it Moscow, we cannot consider that to be entirely appropriate. Leaving aside English, in Bengali and all other languages of the world there is no difficulty in using the word Moscova. Whether or not Moscova can be said in English is a matter to think over as well.

If we cannot properly pronounce the name of the city that has for centuries has been called Moscova, and instead pronounce it Moscow, we cannot consider that to be entirely appropriate.

paragraphs.text: We have already talked about the word gaiṋja. Now the question arises: What is the philological origin or the original source of the word gaiṋja? There are two opinions regarding this. Some people believe that it is a Farsi word and others say that it is an Indian word. The reason behind this confusion is that in old Farsi we come across the word gaiṋja, while at the same time the word gaiṋja has been used in the spoken languages of north India since ancient times. So we can say that the word gaiṋja is as much Indian as it is Farsi. In the far east of Bengal we have Ashugainj (previous British Tripura District, modern Comilla District) and to the west of Bengal are Hazratgainj and Rahmatgainj.
summary: We have already talked about the word gaiṋja.
Some people believe that it is a Farsi word and others say that it is an Indian word.
In the far east of Bengal we have Ashugainj (previous British Tripura District, modern Comilla District) and to the west of Bengal are Hazratgainj and Rahmatgainj.

paragraphs.text: Like the word gaiṋja, the word luci [a type of fried, unleavened bread] is as much Farsi as it is Panjabi, Kashmiri and Bengali. Even if the word luci has come from Farsi, it is as much at home today in Bengali as any native word. In spoken language luci-nuci and leci-neci are equally correct, so those who claim that leci comes from the Farsi-Urdu word lecchi are perhaps correct. However, in Bengal the word neci with its special characteristics has found its way into our kitchens and pots and pans, rolling pins and mortars. Since ancient times, the city of Burdwan has been influenced by north India, hence some of the residents of Burdwan [Vardhamán] say lei instead of leci or neci. Lei is actually a Hindustani word. The equivalent Sanskrit word for luci is shakkulii or shaḿkulii. Luci and puri are not the same. The Sanskrit synonym for puri is somáliká, which actually means “that which looks like the moon”.

paragraphs.text: Some place-names have been created by blending Sanskrit and foreign words, for example, Jamalpur. Jámál is an Arabic word while pura is a Sanskrit word. When you see such names, you can understand that a cultural blending has taken place.

paragraphs.text: There is another Bengali word – begun [brinjal]. Some people ascribe to it the far-fetched meaning be – guńa, “without quality”. As a joke it can also be translated into English as “dis-qualification”. It is worth mentioning here that the origin of the word begun is not “absence of quality”, that is, it is not “disqualification” at all. Although brinjal does not have much food value, it does stimulate the flow of saliva and it helps in the digestion of other foods. If brinjal is mixed and eaten together with bitter foods (such as neem and ucche), then it counteracts the defects of those foods. The little defect that brinjal does have is that it is classified as an allergic, meaning, if one eats too much of it then it can lead to itching.
summary: There is another Bengali word – begun [brinjal].
It is worth mentioning here that the origin of the word begun is not “absence of quality”, that is, it is not “disqualification” at all.
The little defect that brinjal does have is that it is classified as an allergic, meaning, if one eats too much of it then it can lead to itching.

paragraphs.text: So the word begun is not a combination of the Farsi prefix be [not] and the word guńa. It is a Sanskrit-derived word. The Sanskrit synonyms for beguna are vártáku, vártákii, vártikii, brhatii, vrntáka and vyauṋgana. From the Sanskrit word vyauṋgana come the Bengali words begun, báigun, báigan and the Hindi word veigan.

paragraphs.text: The long pointed brinjal (kulii begun) is called brhatii in Sanskrit. All brinjals come from China, but the brhatii was the last to arrive. At evening time, when the jute factory coolies would return home, they used to enthusiastically buy this kind of brinjal and hence it acquired the name kulii begun. The muktakeshii brinjal [a variety] common in Bengal is called vártáku in Sanskrit. The Sanskrit name for white brinjal which many people consider inedible is vrntáka [white brinjal].

summary: Bahadurabad – a Farsi-Vedic word

paragraphs.text: Another very common word in Bengali is báhádur. Many people think that this word may have come from Farsi. At first glance this seems to be so but actually it has not. There was a common word in Vedic, bhagadhara, which meant “fortunate”. This bhagadhara became bahadara in Prákrta, from that bahádar in Farsi, bahádar in Panjabi, bahádar or bahádur in Urdu, bahadur in Hindi, and in Bengali we clean up this bahádur, dress it in a dhoti and a shawl and set it loose as báhádur.

They like to say árám kedárá for “easy-chair” and jharńá kalam for “fountain pen”; however, both árám and kedárá in the word árám kedárá are foreign words. Árám in Sanskrit means “small house” or “garden house”.

paragraphs.text: Last week we discussed the inclination for creating words. Often when we speak we say things like cá-t́á, cáśá-bhúśá, jal-t́al and nadii-t́adi. When we add a second word whose sound rhymes with the first word, are we doing this in error? Or are these added words completely meaningless?

paragraphs.text: No, they are not meaningless. Human beings try to find rhythm in everything because human life itself is rhythmic. Movement is the natural characteristic of life, so rhythm must exist within human movement. If lifeʼs movement were continuous or linear, then there would be no scope for rhythm, and without rhythm there is also no scope for [the existence of] happiness. So in this universe all movement flows in the waves of systaltic order. It is in this rhythm that one encounters the sweetness inherent in movement. Thus people want rhythm in their actions; they want to enjoy the sweetness of the rhythmicity of movement.
summary: No, they are not meaningless.
If lifeʼs movement were continuous or linear, then there would be no scope for rhythm, and without rhythm there is also no scope for [the existence of] happiness.
Thus people want rhythm in their actions; they want to enjoy the sweetness of the rhythmicity of movement.

paragraphs.text: Human beings also want to preserve this rhythmicity in their language. Mono-syllabic and bi-syllabic words lack rhythm, so in this case an effort is made to introduce some rhythmic order. If one says simply cáśá, cá, jal or nadii, the mind does not feel satisfied due to a lack of rhythm; so instead we say cá-t́á, cál-culo, jal-t́al and cáśá-bhúśo. Granted, it does take more time to pronounce, but it sounds better because one discovers therein a sense of rhythmic order. Thus these kinds of words cannot be considered compound words. Rather they should be considered rhythmic words.
summary: Human beings also want to preserve this rhythmicity in their language.
Granted, it does take more time to pronounce, but it sounds better because one discovers therein a sense of rhythmic order.
Rather they should be considered rhythmic words.

paragraphs.text: The other day I was speaking regarding the inclination for naming different places. That day I discussed how the modern pronunciations of certain historically renowned cities like Londres, Moscova and Roma are distortions of their earlier pronunciations, and that these modern distorted pronunciations are not correct. In the case of these foreign words it is distortion or error. There are also many such errors or distortions in Indian naming. In the case of foreign languages, the proper pronunciation of the capital of France is párii [Paris] because in French a is pronounced like á. Here the “Pa” is pronounced pá, the ri is pronounced rii and the s is silent because there is a rule in French that if any consonant other than “c”, “l”, “f”, or “r” comes at the end of a word then it is silent. Thus the proper pronunciation of “Paris” is párii. However, ninety-nine percent of the people that I have heard pronounce it “Paris” instead of párii. Another mistaken pronunciation that people make is “Chicago”. The proper pronunciation is shikágo. In the European languages “ch” is typically pronounced like sha rather than ca, so in the United States this cityʼs name is pronounced shikágo rather than cikágo.
summary: The other day I was speaking regarding the inclination for naming different places.

Here the “Pa” is pronounced pá, the ri is pronounced rii and the s is silent because there is a rule in French that if any consonant other than “c”, “l”, “f”, or “r” comes at the end of a word then it is silent.
In the European languages “ch” is typically pronounced like sha rather than ca, so in the United States this cityʼs name is pronounced shikágo rather than cikágo.

paragraphs.text: There is a similar tendency in Indiaʼs Assamese language. In Assamese ca is always pronounced like sha. For example, we write tincukiyá but we read it as tinsukiyá. We write cit́ibác but we read it as sit́ibás. Bear in mind that no word on this earth is meaningless. This should be kept in mind in the case of naming. So the distorted or incorrect pronunciation of proper nouns cannot be supported under any circumstances. Proper nouns cannot be changed and must not be changed.
summary: There is a similar tendency in Indiaʼs Assamese language.
Bear in mind that no word on this earth is meaningless.
Proper nouns cannot be changed and must not be changed.

paragraphs.text: At one time all of Vauṋga-D́abák, all of Samatat́-Bágrii, the western portion of Cat́t́al, the southern part of Barendra and eastern Ráŕh, that is, east Midnapore, Hooghly, Howrah, east Burdwan and west Murshidabad, were all under water. Thereafter some land rose from the sea due to the accumulation of silt and sand from the Ganges, the Padma and the rivers of Ráŕh. This kind of silt and sandbank is called dviipa in Sanskrit – that is, “land enclosed by water”. After this alluvial land appeared, groups of people began migrating there from Ráŕh. When Sanskrit words evolve through the Prákrta languages they undergo phonetic changes. According to the style of these phonetic changes, the ka, ta, pa, da in Sanskrit words become a in Prákrta, especially in Mágadhii Prákrta. Thus the Sanskrit dviipa became diia in Prákrta and diiyá or diyá in Bengali. Many settlements have the word diiyá included in their name, for example, Nadiiyá from Navadviipa, Háthiiyá from Hastiidviipa, Shriinivásdiiyá from Shriinivásdviipa; and Májhdiiyá from Madhyadviipa. Since Madhyadviipa became Majjhdiia and then Májhdiiyá, it is spelled with jha and dii. People mistakenly write Májdiyá [a place with a Railway station in Nadia district]. Incidentally, since western Ráŕh was never [submerged] under water, you will not find places in western Ráŕh that have the word diiya included in their name. For the very same reason, there are no villages or cities in the far north of Bengal that have diiyá in their name. On the other hand, there are a plethora of places with diiyá in their name in Hooghly, east Burdwan, Nadia, 24 Paraganas, Jessore, Khulna and Chittagong.
summary: At one time all of Vauṋga-D́abák, all of Samatat́-Bágrii, the western portion of Cat́t́al, the southern part of Barendra and eastern Ráŕh, that is, east Midnapore, Hooghly, Howrah, east Burdwan and west Murshidabad, were all under water.
Thus the Sanskrit dviipa became diia in Prákrta and diiyá or diyá in Bengali.
On the other hand, there are a plethora of places with diiyá in their name in Hooghly, east Burdwan, Nadia, 24 Paraganas, Jessore, Khulna and Chittagong.

paragraphs.text: I should point out one more fact in this regard. Approximately seven hundred or seven hundred and fifty years ago, a terrible ocean storm caused great swells in the waters of the Bay of Bengal. Due to these swells, the water of the Bay of Bengal inundated the coast up to one hundred and fifty miles inland. All settlements in those hundred and fifty miles were wiped out in the blink of an eye. Millions of people, cattle, animals and plants perished in an instant. Gradually the salt waters of the ocean receded and left behind a vast jungle with saline soil. Afterwards the people of western Ráŕh came in groups with their axes and scythes and other implements, cut down the jungle and colonized the area anew. If you look at the bloodlines of the people of 24 Paraganas you will find that they have come predominantly from Midnapore. Their surnames also reflect this. The spoken language of the 24 Parganas region also shows the influence of languages spoken in the Contai and Tamaluk regions.
summary: I should point out one more fact in this regard.
Gradually the salt waters of the ocean receded and left behind a vast jungle with saline soil.
The spoken language of the 24 Parganas region also shows the influence of languages spoken in the Contai and Tamaluk regions.

paragraphs.text: Everything was destroyed up to Ranaghat in Nadia. This jungle became filled with tigers, bears, rhinoceri, huge pythons and king cobras. As recently as a hundred and fifty years ago, huge numbers of rhinoceros could be found in southern Bengal. Acharya Prafulla Chandra Roy wrote in his autobiography that during his childhood their tenants used to bring home rhinoceros meat. P. C. Roy was from Ráŕulii village in Khulna District. This village belongs to Páikgách Tháná. A large portion of this tháná falls within the Sundarbans.
summary: Everything was destroyed up to Ranaghat in Nadia.
Acharya Prafulla Chandra Roy wrote in his autobiography that during his childhood their tenants used to bring home rhinoceros meat.
A large portion of this tháná falls within the Sundarbans.

paragraphs.text: In Sanskrit and Prákrta the suffixes aka, raka and ruka are added to mean “small”. For example, mánava [person] becomes mánavaka [small boy or dwarf]. In English the suffixes “let”, “kin” and “ock” are added as diminutives. For example, “rivulet” comes from “river”, “armlet” from “arm”, “mankin” from “man” and “hillock” from “hill”. In Sanskrit vatsaruka > vaccharua > báchru. From this comes the word báchur [calf]. Go + ruka = goruka > gorua > goru [cow] (thus it is spelled with o – many people incorrectly spell this word garu). Similarly, the suffix raka is added to dviipa to mean “small island”. As such, dviiparaka > diiaraa in Prákrta > diiyárá in Hindi, diiyar in Bhojpurii, dirá in Angika. However, in Angika the word ca-a-r (car) is more common. In the Shershahabad Bengali dialect of Malda District these two words, dirá and car, are used side by side.
summary: In Sanskrit and Prákrta the suffixes aka, raka and ruka are added to mean “small”.
From this comes the word báchur [calf].
In the Shershahabad Bengali dialect of Malda District these two words, dirá and car, are used side by side.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in D́áuṋgá
summary: Place-names ending in D́áuṋgá

paragraphs.text: Be that as it may, we were talking about place-names. In Bengal there are a great many native words used for place-names. One such word is d́áuṋgá. Any settlement which has risen from the sea and which is not very old is called a d́áuṋgá. There are many places in eastern Ráŕh and Bagŕi that include the name d́áuṋgá, for example, Beldáuṋgá. In Kolkata we find Nárkold́áuṋgá. The former name of the place in Kolkata which is presently called College Square was Pat́old́áuṋgá; that is, people used to cultivate pat́ol [wax gourd] in that d́áuṋgá, which had risen from the bosom of the sea. At any rate, if one comes across a settlement with the word d́áuṋgá included in its name, one can be sure that that settlement rose from the depths of the ocean. You will come across the word d́áuṋgá far less in regions that were not under water.
summary: Be that as it may, we were talking about place-names.
There are many places in eastern Ráŕh and Bagŕi that include the name d́áuṋgá, for example, Beldáuṋgá.
You will come across the word d́áuṋgá far less in regions that were not under water.

paragraphs.text: Of course the word d́áuṋgá is also often used to refer to elevated land. In Ráŕh the word d́áuṋgál is used for high land and the word námál is used for low land. There is a locality in Dumka which is called D́áuṋgálpáŕá. The town of Suri also has a locality called D́áuṋgálpáŕá. There is a place near Asansol on dry land called Táld́áuṋgá; however, Bankura Districtʼs Táld́áḿrá does not come from the word d́áuṋgá.
summary: Of course the word d́áuṋgá is also often used to refer to elevated land.
There is a locality in Dumka which is called D́áuṋgálpáŕá.
There is a place near Asansol on dry land called Táld́áuṋgá; however, Bankura Districtʼs Táld́áḿrá does not come from the word d́áuṋgá.

paragraphs.text: In Bengali a very high hill or mountain is called parvata. If it is smaller then it is called páháŕ (hill). If still smaller, then it is called páháŕii (small hill). The station now called Bokaro Steel City was formerly called Mará Páhárii. Many people used to mistakenly pronounce it Márápháŕii. Mará páháŕii means a small hill of mará [dead] stone. I myself have personally crushed and powdered a fistful of stone from this area with my bare hands. For this reason it has been named Mará Páháŕii. Similarly, we have Belpáháŕii, Senpáháŕii, Jhánt́ipáháŕii and Kálipáháŕii (near Asansol). Smaller than a páháŕii is a d́uḿri or d́áḿrá [hillock]. The next smaller is called a t́ilá and even smaller is a d́hibi, for example, ui-d́hibi [anthill]. Naturally, the name Táld́áḿrá comes from the word d́ámrá. Of course, a cluster of palm trees [tál gách] is also called táldáḿrá. In any case it is quite certain that the name is not derived from the word d́áuṋgá. In very old Bengali, a t́ilá used to be called a t́ál. We come across these lines in Bengali of twelve hundred years ago:
summary: In Bengali a very high hill or mountain is called parvata.
For this reason it has been named Mará Páháŕii.
In very old Bengali, a t́ilá used to be called a t́ál.

paragraphs.text: T́álata ghar mor náhi pariveshii,
summary: T́álata ghar mor náhi pariveshii,

I have hardly any neighbours.

paragraphs.text: There is no rice left in the container. I fast almost daily.]

paragraphs.text: Some of the lowlands in the eastern part of Birbhum are called námál, for example, the thánás [Police stations] of Labhpur, Nannur, Mayureshwar, Rampurhat, Nalhati and Murari. In the western region the areas of Dubrajpur, Khayrasol, Suri, Mamudbazaar, Ilembazaar and Rajnagar are d́áuṋgál, while Bolpur and Sainthia are partially d́áuṋgál and partially námál. Námál lands produce a better yield except in the case of paddy, which produces a better yield than d́áuṋgál lands because the soil is clayish. The people of námál lands have the conception that if their girls are given in marriage to d́áuṋgál boys, they will become bored because they are forced to eat so much posta [poppy seed]. So the námál people say “Donʼt give your daughters in marriage there. If you do, they become bored.”
summary: Some of the lowlands in the eastern part of Birbhum are called námál, for example, the thánás [Police stations] of Labhpur, Nannur, Mayureshwar, Rampurhat, Nalhati and Murari.
The people of námál lands have the conception that if their girls are given in marriage to d́áuṋgál boys, they will become bored because they are forced to eat so much posta [poppy seed].
If you do, they become bored.

paragraphs.text: The word d́áuṋgá is a very ancient, prehistoric Austric word. There are many such Austric words used in Bengali and d́áuṋgá is one of them. These Austric words are also plentiful in the Viirhoŕ language. In Santhali Haŕ language, Austric words have undergone some alteration. On the other hand, the Oráonʼs Kuruk language is a Dravidian language. It has very few Austric words. Bengali has many Austric words such as d́áuṋgá, but Kuruk and other Dravidian languages have very few, although we cannot say that they have none at all.
summary: The word d́áuṋgá is a very ancient, prehistoric Austric word.
In Santhali Haŕ language, Austric words have undergone some alteration.
Bengali has many Austric words such as d́áuṋgá, but Kuruk and other Dravidian languages have very few, although we cannot say that they have none at all.

paragraphs.text: The very common Bengali word pallii is originally a Dravidian word. Like Iŕápallii and Tirucirápallii, we also have Bhat́t́apallii and Palliigrám. No matter how much we try to polish and dress up the word pallii in an effort to pretend it is Sanskrit, it is originally Dravidian. Many people believe that the Bengali word páŕá [neighbourhood] is a corruption of the word pallii. In other words, the word Páŕágáoṋ comes from Palliigráma. However this is erroneous. It is true that the word gáoṋ derives from the word gráma [village] but páŕá does not come from pallii. Páŕá is an eastern Indian word which is used extensively in Bengali, Assamese, Oriya, Nagpurii and Chattisgarhii. The Hindustani synonym for páŕá is muhallá. Where we say e páŕáy [in this neighbourhood] in Bengali, we say muhalláme in Hindustani. The word muhallá comes from Farsi. Incidentally, I should point out that in Sanskrit the word pallii does not mean páŕá. In Sanskrit the word pallii means t́ikt́iki [a small house lizard] and krkalása means girgit́i [another variety of lizard]. T́ikt́iki is called chipkalii in Hindi. In Maethilii [Maithili], Magahii and Bhojpurii it is called bichaotii. In Angika it is called t́ikt́ikiyá, and you all know that in English it is called “lizard”.
summary: The very common Bengali word pallii is originally a Dravidian word.
The Hindustani synonym for páŕá is muhallá.
In Angika it is called t́ikt́ikiyá, and you all know that in English it is called “lizard”.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Joŕh
summary: Place-names ending in Joŕh

paragraphs.text: In Sanskrit the word nadii refers to both small and large rivers. However, in the Austric language common in Ráŕh, all rivers except for very large rivers are called joŕ. In the spoken language of the Málpáháŕii community of western Ráŕh, the gods were called mashán. Hence, they named the river, which they considered a holy or divine river, the Mashán-joŕ. We should not imitate others who say másháiṋjoŕ or myáshánjor. As far as I am concerned, one should not say másháiṋjoŕ; one should speak correctly.
summary: In Sanskrit the word nadii refers to both small and large rivers.
Hence, they named the river, which they considered a holy or divine river, the Mashán-joŕ.
As far as I am concerned, one should not say másháiṋjoŕ; one should speak correctly.

paragraphs.text: A similar, well-known word in Ráŕh is haŕká. In the old Austric language it meant “flood”. The common usage of the word haŕká in Ráŕh is for a flood that comes and goes suddenly. The Austric synonym for “bridge” is sáṋko; thus, so the place where there is a sáṋko over a joŕ is called Joŕásáṋko. Similarly there is a Sáṋkomuŕo in Ráŕh.
summary: A similar, well-known word in Ráŕh is haŕká.
The common usage of the word haŕká in Ráŕh is for a flood that comes and goes suddenly.
Similarly there is a Sáṋkomuŕo in Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Sol/Suli
summary: Place-names ending in Sol/Suli

paragraphs.text: Sol and suli are both Austric words. A large village built on high land [t́ilá] is called a sol; if it is small in size, then it is called a suli, for example, Khayrasol. A place where an abundance of khayrá fish (khadirá matsya) can be found in its ponds, pools and creeks is called Khayrásol (a small town on the outskirts of Birbhum). The place that has a lot of sheoŕá trees is Siháŕasol (Burdwan Districtʼs Shiyársol). The sol that was founded by a certain gentleman named Ásán Miian is Asansol (a subdivision town in Burdwan District). It is notable that all three – Asansol, Khayrasol and Siháŕsol – are all near each other. In the western part of Midnapore District there is a village of the Lodhá community called Lodhásuli.
summary: Sol and suli are both Austric words.
The place that has a lot of sheoŕá trees is Siháŕasol (Burdwan Districtʼs Shiyársol).
In the western part of Midnapore District there is a village of the Lodhá community called Lodhásuli.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Sáhii/Sái/Kelá
summary: Place-names ending in Sáhii/Sái/Kelá

paragraphs.text: The villages situated in western Ráŕh and northern Orissa were formerly called sáhii or sái, for example, Bábusáhii and Ciŕimársái (Midnapore). Places or villages encircled on all sides by hills were called kerá or kelá in western Ráŕh and northern Orissa, for example, Seráikelá, Keraikelá and Nandankelá.
summary: The villages situated in western Ráŕh and northern Orissa were formerly called sáhii or sái, for example, Bábusáhii and Ciŕimársái (Midnapore).
Places or villages encircled on all sides by hills were called kerá or kelá in western Ráŕh and northern Orissa, for example, Seráikelá, Keraikelá and Nandankelá.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in D́ihá/D́ihi
summary: Place-names ending in D́ihá/D́ihi

paragraphs.text: If a small village is surrounded by dry fields then it is called d́ihi, for example, Bámund́i, Tentuld́i, Gaoráuṋgad́i, Jaridih and Girid́i. If it is a large village, then it is called d́ihá, for example, Dumka Districtʼs Háṋsd́ihá – that is, the d́ihá where large numbers of swans are taken care of, or that d́ihá whose nearby swamps and pools play host to large numbers of cranes during the winter season. Needless to say, the words d́ihi and d́ihá are both Austric. It should be noted that the villages and towns named d́ihi-d́ihá are not in the rainy part of Bengal (with a few exceptions). They are all located in western Ráŕh because western Ráŕh is a dry land. The localities in east Kolkata named d́ihi were most likely settled at the time by people from Ráŕh who cleared the Sundarbans and used the name d́ihi. Similarly, one does not come across villages or towns in western Ráŕh with the word diiyá in their name, because diiyá is another name for dviipa [island]. Where will you find islands in the dry lands of western Ráŕh? However, the words joŕá or juŕi are used in western Ráŕh in the names of villages or towns encircled by rivers, for example, Jerid́i and Shukjoŕá.
summary: If a small village is surrounded by dry fields then it is called d́ihi, for example, Bámund́i, Tentuld́i, Gaoráuṋgad́i, Jaridih and Girid́i.
They are all located in western Ráŕh because western Ráŕh is a dry land.
However, the words joŕá or juŕi are used in western Ráŕh in the names of villages or towns encircled by rivers, for example, Jerid́i and Shukjoŕá.

paragraphs.text: The word ráŕh comes from the old Austric word ráŕhá or ráŕho, which means “land of red soil”. Viirabhúmi means viirácárińáḿ bhúmi in Sanskrit, and its altered name is Viirabhúma, or Varjyabhúmi in Vedic. Its altered form is Varrabhúmi and also Viirabhúma. Biira means “forest” in Austric language. Biirabhúmi means “land abounding in forests”. If the word is taken to mean “forest”, then undoubtedly this creates an awkward combination because the word biira is Austric and the word bhúmi is Sanskrit. Birbhum was undoubtedly covered with forests at one time. Mamudbazaar Tháná, Rajnagar Tháná, Khayrasol Tháná, southwest Dumka, east Deoghar and west Pakur, which until 1855 was a part of Birbhum, were all heavily forested. The word ráŕhá or ráŕho, which we find in Austric language, means “land of red soil”. Similarly, if we accept the meaning “forest” for the Austric word biira, then it can definitely offer an explanation behind the name Birbhum, Ráŕhʼs own cultural territory. More research is required on this subject.
summary: The word ráŕh comes from the old Austric word ráŕhá or ráŕho, which means “land of red soil”.
If the word is taken to mean “forest”, then undoubtedly this creates an awkward combination because the word biira is Austric and the word bhúmi is Sanskrit.
More research is required on this subject.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Báŕi/Báŕiyá/Beŕe
summary: Place-names ending in Báŕi/Báŕiyá/Beŕe

paragraphs.text: It should be mentioned in this regard that with one or two exceptions, one does not come across any place in the environs of Kolkata with the name d́ihi-d́ihá, but one does come across d́áuṋgá and beŕe. The Bengali word báŕi comes from the Sanskrit word vát́i and the word báŕiyá or beŕe comes from the word vát́iká. Thus baḿshveŕiyá or báṋshbeŕe comes from the Sanskrit vaḿshavát́iká. In north Bengal, báŕiyá has changed into báŕi instead of becoming beŕe, for example, Khaŕibáŕi, Khágaŕábáŕi and Nakasálbáŕi. A reed forest (nalkhágŕá – ikŕá in old Assamese) is called Khágŕábáŕi. Khaŕibáŕi is where there is a jungle of wood suitable for use as fuel (khaŕi means “firewood”). Also there is Bagŕibáŕi (Sanskrit badarii, bagaŕi, meaning “plums”), Sháluniibáŕi (shál tree, in Assamese sháluni) and Nalbáŕi (reed jungle).
summary: It should be mentioned in this regard that with one or two exceptions, one does not come across any place in the environs of Kolkata with the name d́ihi-d́ihá, but one does come across d́áuṋgá and beŕe.
In north Bengal, báŕiyá has changed into báŕi instead of becoming beŕe, for example, Khaŕibáŕi, Khágaŕábáŕi and Nakasálbáŕi.
Also there is Bagŕibáŕi (Sanskrit badarii, bagaŕi, meaning “plums”), Sháluniibáŕi (shál tree, in Assamese sháluni) and Nalbáŕi (reed jungle).

paragraphs.text: In southern Bengal we find places with the suffix beŕe such as Ulubeŕe (Uluberiyá), Cakrabeŕe, Gaoriibeŕe and Láuṋgalbeŕe. ( 7 ) Beŕe has another meaning. Villages surrounded by jungle were named after the predominant tree in that jungle. For example, the village that was surrounded by a gol tree jungle was given the name Golábáŕi. There are still villages by the name Golábáŕi in Howrah and 24 Parganas.
summary: In southern Bengal we find places with the suffix beŕe such as Ulubeŕe (Uluberiyá), Cakrabeŕe, Gaoriibeŕe and Láuṋgalbeŕe.
Villages surrounded by jungle were named after the predominant tree in that jungle.
There are still villages by the name Golábáŕi in Howrah and 24 Parganas.

paragraphs.text: It was mentioned earlier that Kolkata was once submerged under water. After those regions rose up from the water, trees that favoured salty soil began to grow, for example, sundari, hentál [a type of palm], mangrove and báin. Many places, such as Garánhát́á, Hentálii, were named after such jungles. The area of Kolkata known today as Entally was formerly called Hentálii. It was comprised of a jungle of huge hintál trees with thorns. Tigers used to hide in [the trees] hoping to catch deer. In distorted British pronunciation Hentálii became Entally. At that time different varieties of crops grew in different areas of Kolkata. These areas were also named according to the local crop; for example, the area where betel grew was named Guvábágán (the Sanskrit word for “betel” is guváka and from this is derived the Bengali gubá). Similarly we obtain Nebubágán and Hartukiibágán.
summary: It was mentioned earlier that Kolkata was once submerged under water.
Tigers used to hide in [the trees] hoping to catch deer.
Similarly we obtain Nebubágán and Hartukiibágán.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Kháli
summary: Place-names ending in Kháli

paragraphs.text: In southern Bengal there are many places with kháli in their name, for example, Pat́uyákháli, Sandeshkháli, Hánskháli and Dhanekháli. It was Emperor Sher Shah who originally constructed the long road from Dhaka Districtʼs Suvarńagrám to At́t́ak in The Punjab. He did not name the road after himself. It was the people who gave it the name Badshah Road. Later the British extended the road up to Peshawar and renamed it the Grand Trunk Road. It should be mentioned here that the word saraka [road] is not a foreign word. It is actually a Sanskrit word. Sr + ńaka = saraka, that is, “that which exists for moving (sará)”, not for standing, sitting or lying down. Due to mass confusion, the word saraka was replaced by saŕaka. Saŕak in chaste Hindi is a feminine gender word. Many people well-versed in Hindi do not realize that the correct form of the word saŕak is saraka. The words sarańa, sarańii, upasarańii and sáráńa in Ráŕhi Bengali all come from the verbal root sr. Incidentally, it is worth mentioning here that the builder of the Badshah Road, Shershah, came from Sasaram, formerly of Sahabad District and today of Rohatas District. The word śasárám has also undergone distortion. It was named Sahasraráma or Sahasarám after a famous local celebrity (mánuś ( 8 )) named Sahasrarám Singh. The place is still called Sahasarám in local Bhojpuri language.

paragraphs.text: Bear in mind here that the words sará and hat́á are not identical in meaning. The word hat́á or hat́ná in Hindi means “to move from the front” and sará means “to go on moving”, so the work of sará cannot be done by hat́á or hat́ná, although the work of hat́á can be done by sará. Another meaning of the word sará in Bengali is “to bring into use”, for example, ghát́t́á sará hacche ná [the quay is not being used], básant́á sará hacche ná [the container is not being used]. In the domestic life of Bengal, the container or utensil used frequently for regular tasks is called sará in Bengali and not any other word.

paragraphs.text: Southern Bengal did not have sufficient roads for land travel. People used to travel nearly everywhere by water with the exception of a few areas near Tripura. ( 9 ) Imagine, for instance, that someone wants to go to Bhát́igrám in Barishal. First they have to travel some distance by steamer from Khulna. ( 10 ) Thereafter, once the depth of the water decreases, they have to leave the steamer behind and travel by launch boat. ( 11 ) Then, after travelling a little further by boat, they have to continue by footpath to Bhát́igrám. A steamer can travel down a large river or canal but not down a small river or canal; a boat is required to travel down the small rivers and canals. Now, the villages formerly connected to the main waterways through canals (khál) were given the name kháli; examples are Pat́uyákháli, Dhanekháli, Jelekháli and Sandeshkháli. When you see the name kháli, you can assume that there is now or was a canal near the village, and that the canal joined a large waterway.
