paragraphs.text: The name kholá is attached to those villages that have no relation with any khál but have very large trees full of birds, for example, Sharańkholá and Harińkholá. Kholá is a native word that means “bird”. The Sanskrit synonyms for pákhii [bird] are pakśii, vihaga, vihauṋga and vihauṋgama. Similarly, the Sanskrit equivalents for “deer” are kuraga, kurauṋga and kurauṋgama, and for “horse” they are turaga, turauṋga and turauṋgama.

paragraphs.text: The word kholá has other meanings in Bengali. The first is the covering of a fruit or something similar. You must have all seen a kholá ghar [house with a pantile roof] and also used the word. Here also the word kholá means “covering”. Two words are commonly used in Bengali to refer to the covering of a fruit – kholá and khosá. If the covering is hard, then it is called kholá, as in the kholá of a coconut; however, if it is soft, then it is called khosá. For example, a banana has a khosá. However, in Kolkata Bengali a banana skin and a coconut shell are both called kholá. Of course, there is a special word for coconut shell – málá (nárkoler málá).

summary: Place-names ending in Mocá/Muci/Ghát́/Ghát́i

paragraphs.text: Bengali has its own words for “flower” – mocá and muci. The word mocá means “large flower” and muci means “small flower”. Since a banana flower is large in size it is called mocá, but a coconut flower is quite small, so it is called muci. The jackfruit flower is also called muci. In these kinds of philological discussions, one learns not only the history of names but many other things as well, and in this way it becomes easy to demarcate history.

chapters.title: Bounteous Wisdom – 2
chapters.partTitle: PART 1: Bounteous Wisdom on Place Names

paragraphs.text: Place-names linked to English names
summary: Place-names linked to English names

paragraphs.text: The names of specific settlements in this country are inextricably linked to certain English names. After the British occupied India, they imposed the “policy of subsidiary alliance”. As a result of this policy certain kings in the country accepted the authority of the British, for example, the kings of Tripura, Coochbihar and Mayurbhanj. They had a contract with the British. The British took their army into all those kingdoms where the kings or large landowners did not accept their authority. They allowed those who surrendered to them out of fear to keep their zamindarship, but they snatched away the kingdoms of those who did not accept their authority and fought against them. Then they installed their own obedient zamindars in their stead. They managed to find something to name after all those British officers who achieved success in these campaigns. For example, after the kingdom of Palamu was defeated, the district headquarters was named Daltonganj after Mr. Dalton. The Octorloney Monument in Kolkata maidan was built in the name of General Octorloney. Nowadays the Octorloney Monument has been renamed Shahid Minar. This is not proper since it is a distortion of history. Something new should have been dedicated to the memory of the Shahids. Similarly, they have created Pamarganj, Macluskeyganj, Leslieganj, and so on.
summary: The names of specific settlements in this country are inextricably linked to certain English names.
They managed to find something to name after all those British officers who achieved success in these campaigns.
Similarly, they have created Pamarganj, Macluskeyganj, Leslieganj, and so on.

paragraphs.text: Incidentally, it should be pointed out the English word “general” has undergone a distortion of pronunciation to become jáṋdrel in Bengali. We call powerful (jabardast) people jáṋdrel lok. Bear in mind that the word jabardast is Farsi. Dast means “hand”, and if that hand is applied forcibly to something or possesses something forcibly, then it is jabardast. In Panjabi “general” became járńál. If you look around a little, you may able to find a couple of Járnál Singhs present [in the audience].

summary: ‘Mumbai’, not 'Bombayʼ

paragraphs.text: As a result of the Britishersʼ distorted pronunciation the names of many famous cities in this country have become distorted. I have already talked about the distortion of the name Kalikátá (Kolkata) in this regard. A similar situation took place with the city Bombay. Many fishing families were living in the suburbs of the modern city of Bombay. These fishing families were the old inhabitants of the city before it became Bombay. Their traditional deity was the goddess Mumbávatii. Vatii becomes bái in Maharastrii Prákrta, so accordingly Mumbávatii became Mumbábai and, with the passage of time, Mumbái. The word mumbái has been common in both Marathi and Gujarati since that time and remains so today. The British, however, turned Mumbái into Bombay and this “Bombay” became Bombái in Hindi and Bengali. Kothákár jal kotháy ese dáṋŕála [“Where does the water come from; where does it end up?”] ( 1 ). Recently the government of Maharashtra changed the name Bombái to Mumbái. This is a praiseworthy action. Kolkata should promptly be changed to Kalikátá in English. Why should the same proper noun be called differently by different people? This destroys the sense of value of a proper noun. If you ask someone named Sardar Hazara Singh his name, will he reply that his name is “Leader Thousand Lions”? Should we call Krishnanagar “Black City” in English? Someone who gets a kick out of calling Krishnanagar “Black City” should follow suit and call Kolkata “Lime and Rope”. Only then will their penchant for imitation be complete.
summary: As a result of the Britishersʼ distorted pronunciation the names of many famous cities in this country have become distorted.

Since each one of them collects what is due to them, they are called “the twelve ádityas”.

paragraphs.text: However, during the historical time period depicted in this poem, that is, during the era of the king of Magadha, Bimbisar, there was no such rajaniigandhá flower in India. It was only four hundred and fifty years ago that the Portuguese first brought the rajaniigandhá from Mexico and planted it in the garden of their Bandel church. The original home of this flower was Mexico in Central America. Its English name is “tuberose”. Like the shiuili flower [night jasmine], the tuberose is full of fragrant pollen. During the day the breeze becomes light in the heat of the sun. As a result it cannot easily carry the fragrant pollen of the rajaniigandhá. But during the night the breeze becomes strong and easily carries the scent; for this reason the tuberose brought by the Portuguese was given the name rajaniigandhá [literally: night-scent] in Bengali. One can also smell the rajaniigandhá during cloudy days and solar eclipses.

paragraphs.text: Sanskrit influence; Vátávipura is Batavia
summary: Sanskrit influence; Vátávipura is Batavia

paragraphs.text: The bestowing of Sanskrit names is not only confined to India; in many countries outside India the given names show the influence of Sanskrit. At one time the Sanskrit language was used throughout the entire region extending from southern Russia all the way to Suvarńadviipa. The southern region of Russia – what is today Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Tajikistan – was earlier called Shákadviipa [Scythia], and the combined name of India and Afghanistan at that time was Jambudviipa. You must have heard the mantra jambudviipe bháratakhańd́e [In jambudviipa and within the Greater India]. Of course, at that time Afghanistan was a part of India. The name for Burma and all of Southeast Asia was Suvarńadviipa. Sanskrit is still used to speak with the king of Thailand; however, it is pronounced differently. For example, in Thailand ja is pronounced like d́a and ńa is pronounced like d́ha, and both ya and ya [with dot] are pronounced like ya [ja]. The name of the kingdom of Kamboja is pronounced nowadays Kambod́iyá by the people. At that time, the kingdom of Kamboja was much larger than the present Cambodia. At one time a huge Shiva temple existed there called Ouṋkárabhat́t́a. Its modern name is Ouṋkár Bhát́. Today the temple is practically in ruins.
summary: The bestowing of Sanskrit names is not only confined to India; in many countries outside India the given names show the influence of Sanskrit.
Sanskrit is still used to speak with the king of Thailand; however, it is pronounced differently.
Today the temple is practically in ruins.

paragraphs.text: The Sanskrit name for the land we now call Java is Yavadviipa. Its capital was Vátávipura. The modern name Batavia comes from Vátávipura. When the Dutch [Olandáj] came to India in the last part of the Mughal era, they brought a variety of lemon with them from Vátáviipura, which they first planted in the present city of Chinsura [Cuṋcŕo]. ( 2 ) The Dutch had a factory in Chinsura and they christened the city “Chinsura”. The modern Dutch pronunciation was syánsurá, and in Bengali it became cuṋcuŕá, cuṋcŕo in spoken Bengali. When I was staying in Holland, I spoke with a few scholars regarding Cuṋcŕo, and I found that none of them were conversant with Cuṋcŕo. One of them said: “I have never heard anything about Cuṋcŕo in history, but the word cuṋcŕo is from our language.” I have seen a place in Cuṋcŕo called “Dutch Villa”.
summary: The Sanskrit name for the land we now call Java is Yavadviipa.
( 2 ) The Dutch had a factory in Chinsura and they christened the city “Chinsura”.
” I have seen a place in Cuṋcŕo called “Dutch Villa”.

paragraphs.text: The Dutch imported into this country a type of legume from Yavadviipa similar to peas (karáishuṋt́i). In Kolkata Bengali we call mat́arshuṋt́i [peas] as karáishuṋt́i. Although they are not as good as regular peas for making d́ál [pulse], they are quite tasty when eaten fresh in the pod. At one time the village people of Hooghly District used to love eating the pods with puffed rice. They cultivated them as well. They named them oŕandá shuṋt́i (that is, “Dutch peas”). They look somewhat like regular peas.
summary: The Dutch imported into this country a type of legume from Yavadviipa similar to peas (karáishuṋt́i).

paragraphs.text: The Batavia lemon [pomelo] that I mentioned earlier is a well-known name in Bengal nowadays. It does not have any true Sanskrit name; however, the Sanskrit name for the somewhat smaller, sweet and sour lemon already common in this country was mahálauṋga [Citrus grandis]. Today the mahálauṋga has become lost in the abundance of Batavia lemons. The Sanskrit name of the lemon that is somewhat smaller than the mahálauṋga and slightly elongated, and which was already in this country, is jambiira; its modern popular name is jámir, jámerii or jamburá.
summary: The Batavia lemon [pomelo] that I mentioned earlier is a well-known name in Bengal nowadays.
Today the mahálauṋga has become lost in the abundance of Batavia lemons.

The Sanskrit name of the lemon that is somewhat smaller than the mahálauṋga and slightly elongated, and which was already in this country, is jambiira; its modern popular name is jámir, jámerii or jamburá.

paragraphs.text: The jambiira did not come from outside India. It has also become lost nowadays in the crowd of Batavia lemons. Keep in mind that although the Batavia lemon came to this country from Java, it is native to all of Southeast Asia, that is, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines (this countryʼs Sanskrit name is Mahárliká or Mahárliińá). The Sanskrit name shiitanimbu is given to the sweet and juicy lemon called maosambii [sweet lime; Citrus sinensis] in Urdu, and sharvatii in Bengali. It is smaller than the jambiira and quite plentiful in India. Today the name maosambii is more common in Bengali; however, it would not be right to forget the Bengali name, sharvatii nebu. The sharvatii nebu belongs to the nebu family, not the kamalá family. Nebu in English is “lemon”; in Sanskrit it is nimbu; in Hindi niimbu; in Angika nemu; and in Bengali nebu – some people mistakenly say lebu. Kamalá in English is “orange”. In Sanskrit it is kamalá or nágarauṋga, in Urdu náráungi, in Marathi sántará and in Bengali kamalá. The main difference between the nebu family (sharvatii or sweet lemon, jambiira [citrus lemon], mahálauṋga, Batavi or lemon pomelo, páti [lime], kágjii (small, green lime)) and the kamalá family (orange – Sanskrit nágarauṋga group) is that the rind of the nebu is not easily removed. It is cut with a knife. But the skin of the kamalá family (Sylheti kamalá, Assam kamala, Meghalay kamalá, Darjeeling kamalá, Nagpurii kamalá or khokákamalá, gonŕá nebu, gonŕá kamalá) is easily peeled [by hand] and the sections inside come apart. The keno nebu [a kind of lemon], quite common nowadays, is a mix between the lemon and orange families. In those days India was producing less sugar so it was imported from Batavia in Indonesia. Hence, the colloquial name for sugar [ciinii] among the people became bát́á ciinii. (During our young days bát́á ciinii and Barishalʼs bálám rice were very common in Kolkata).
summary: The jambiira did not come from outside India.
Kamalá in English is “orange”.
(During our young days bát́á ciinii and Barishalʼs bálám rice were very common in Kolkata).

paragraphs.text: Shyámdesh is Thailand; Siḿhapur is Singapore; Shákadviipa is Scythia
summary: Shyámdesh is Thailand; Siḿhapur is Singapore; Shákadviipa is Scythia

paragraphs.text: It is said in Thai folk tales that Sahasrarabáhu, the crown prince of Ráŕh, defeated Thailand and gave it the name Shyámadesha [siam]. The land is very green and lush, so the name Shyámadesha [verdant land] is both fitting and beautiful. He established a vast empire in Southeast Asia. At that time the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur. The former name of the place called Siuṋgur in present-day Hooghly District was Siḿhapur. The crown prince, Sahasrarabáhu, founded a city in Southeast Asia and named it after Ráŕhʼs Siḿhapur; its modern name is Singapore. Just as the British established another city called London after going to America, the same practice has occurred many times. There are cities and towns in many places with the same name.
summary: It is said in Thai folk tales that Sahasrarabáhu, the crown prince of Ráŕh, defeated Thailand and gave it the name Shyámadesha [siam].
The former name of the place called Siuṋgur in present-day Hooghly District was Siḿhapur.
There are cities and towns in many places with the same name.

paragraphs.text: We have already mentioned that the Sanskrit name for the southern part of Russia was Shákadviipa. The Greek name for Shákadviipa was Sacdonia. “Alexander” is also a Greek name. Its Arabic equivalent is Sikándár. There is a port in Egypt named Sikandria. Its Greek as well as European name is Alexandria. Alexandria was home to a historically renowned library. The poet, Satyen Datta, has written these lines about the scholar, Acharya Harinath Dey, who was master of many languages:
summary: We have already mentioned that the Sanskrit name for the southern part of Russia was Shákadviipa.
Its Arabic equivalent is Sikándár.
Alexandria was home to a historically renowned library.

paragraphs.text: The people of Shákadviipa were followers of the Árśa religion [religion of the Rśis]. Since they were unwilling to embrace Islam during the age of the first expansion of Islam, they left the region and took shelter in India. In Indian society they became known as the Shákadviipii Brahmans. They mostly kept themselves busy studying astrology and Ayurveda. They used to wear loose pyjama pants with a jacket on their upper body and a Fez cap. Although they were followers of the Rśis, they did not always follow the Vedic customs in their sacrifices and rituals. Furthermore, they were worshippers of the sun god. So the images of the sun god they worshipped that are found in the different sun god temples are also dressed in loose pyjama pants with a Fez cap on the head and a rosary in the hands, which we call jápámálá in Bengali. Thus people say that it is more of a non-Hindu sun god. This kind of sun god temple is found in several places in India. There is a famous temple of this type in Gaya District (present-day Aurangabad District). Today the sun god temple at Końárk is in ruins and its idol has vanished.
summary: The people of Shákadviipa were followers of the Árśa religion [religion of the Rśis].
Furthermore, they were worshippers of the sun god.
Today the sun god temple at Końárk is in ruins and its idol has vanished.

paragraphs.text: The Shákadviipii Brahmans spread (prasár) Ayurveda throughout northern India. ( 3 ) In Bengal, however, there was little use of Ayurveda; rather, the Vaedyaka system was primarily in vogue. In contrast to Ayurveda, the Vaedyaka treatises provided for the dissection of corpses; that is, Bengali physicians did not limit themselves to Ayurvedic theories. They paid attention to the practical side also. Later on, the demonic dogmas of the Shákadviipii Brahmans in north India extended their repressive influence over Vaedyaka physicians as well, and slowly the Vaedyaka practitioners abandoned dissection of cadavers. When Shrii Madhusudhan Gupta began practising western medicine during British rule, the caste injunction against touching dead bodies made him a social outcaste.
summary: The Shákadviipii Brahmans spread (prasár) Ayurveda throughout northern India.
They paid attention to the practical side also.
When Shrii Madhusudhan Gupta began practising western medicine during British rule, the caste injunction against touching dead bodies made him a social outcaste.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Daha
summary: Place-names ending in Daha

paragraphs.text: A large portion of Bengal is watery land. In the areas where big rivers flow, those rivers take a bend at certain places and as a result eddies are created at the bottom of the river near the bend [váṋk]. ( 4 ) Such places are dangerous for boats or ships. There was one such eddy in the Jalangi River where it takes a bend [vánk] (Sanskrit vakra > vaḿka > váṋká) near Krishnanagar. At that time one used to go by water down the Jalangi River from Kolkata to where it met the Padma River and from there to Dhaka [Dacca]. The steamers used to take special care when approaching the eddy. The settlement that sprang up near this eddy [ghurńii] was named Ghurńii. Three places – Ghurńii, Goyári and Krishnanagar – collectively developed into the cultural centre of Bengal at the time, Krishnanagar. During the reign of Maharaja Krishnachandra, some sealing wax artisans were brought from Ilambazaar of Birbhum to reside in Ghurńii. They were the forefathers of Krishnanagarʼs renowned modern-day clay sculptors.
summary: A large portion of Bengal is watery land.
The steamers used to take special care when approaching the eddy.
They were the forefathers of Krishnanagarʼs renowned modern-day clay sculptors.

paragraphs.text: The Bengali name for this whirlpool or eddy at the bottom of the water is daha, so when one hears the word daha in the name of any village or town, one can know that there is or was a large river nearby and that it has or once had a daha or eddy in it.
summary: The Bengali name for this whirlpool or eddy at the bottom of the water is daha, so when one hears the word daha in the name of any village or town, one can know that there is or was a large river nearby and that it has or once had a daha or eddy in it.

paragraphs.text: There was one such eddy in the Mahánandá River also. There are two rivers mentioned in the Atharvaveda called the Paránandá and the Aparánandá. These two rivers joined near Kiśańganj and thereafter became known as the Mahánandá. When the king of the Malla Kśatriyas occupied this region, it was renamed the Máldah. In other words, the kingdom of the Mallas and the nearby Mahánand daha were combined to create the name Máldah. Similarly, in Rajshahi District you find Sardaha. Cákadá in Nadia comes from Cakradaha. At one time the Bhagiirathii River used to flow past Cákdá. At present the Bhagiirathii has moved in a westerly direction.
summary: There was one such eddy in the Mahánandá River also.
In other words, the kingdom of the Mallas and the nearby Mahánand daha were combined to create the name Máldah.
At present the Bhagiirathii has moved in a westerly direction.

paragraphs.text: The Saraswati River passed by Mogra to the west of the Bhagiirathii, and the Yamuna passed by Kalyani. The lands of these three rivers, the Bhagiirathii, Saraswati and Yamuna, is a triveńii [confluence of three streams] – an open triveńii or open stream. In other words, the three rivers flow off in three different directions. The triveńii at Prayág near Allahabad is a closed triveńii or closed stream, because it is at that spot that the three streams coming from different directions unite.
summary: The Saraswati River passed by Mogra to the west of the Bhagiirathii, and the Yamuna passed by Kalyani.
In other words, the three rivers flow off in three different directions.
The triveńii at Prayág near Allahabad is a closed triveńii or closed stream, because it is at that spot that the three streams coming from different directions unite.

paragraphs.text: The open stream of the Yamuna merges into the Ichámatii. At that time the Vidyádharii River used to emerge from the southern outlet of the Yamuna in midcourse; today it flows into the Bay of Bengal after passing the eastern outskirts of Kolkata, south past Canning, then joining with the Bhagiirathiiʼs tributary, the Piyálii, where they assume the name Mátlá and thereafter pass through the Sundarbans. The British had planned to build the port of Canning on the banks of the Mátlá, but the Mátlá is actually no longer actually a river. It is an ordinary estuary [kháŕii]. An estuary is also called a “backwater” in spoken English. Although in Bengali and Oriya kháŕii means “estuary” or “backwater”, in Urdu it means “bay”. For example, the Bay of Bengal is báuṋgál ki kháŕii in Urdu. So seeing that the proposed Canning port was ruined by the flooding of the Mátlá, the plans for the Canning port were abandoned.
summary: The open stream of the Yamuna merges into the Ichámatii.
An estuary is also called a “backwater” in spoken English.
So seeing that the proposed Canning port was ruined by the flooding of the Mátlá, the plans for the Canning port were abandoned.

paragraphs.text: The Vidyádharii that flows from this southern outlet used to change its course practically every year. Later the area turned into a salty swamp so the British named it the Salt Lake area. This area was full of trees and plants that favoured salty soil. There was a jungle of gol, báin [Cynometra polyandra], hintál [marshy date tree; Phoenixar Elate paludosa], mangosteen and mangrove. The salty seawater inundated the area during flood tide and made it even more frightening. There were a number of eddies. Packs of jackals used to roam there in broad daylight. The people used to call the entire area Shiyáldaha [the jackal eddy].
summary: The Vidyádharii that flows from this southern outlet used to change its course practically every year.
The salty seawater inundated the area during flood tide and made it even more frightening.
The people used to call the entire area Shiyáldaha [the jackal eddy].

paragraphs.text: Tales of Kolkata

When the British occupied [India], Kolkata was part of the northern outskirts of the Sundarbans. In order to save Kolkata from the Maratha invasions, they dug a canal to the northeast which was known as the Maratha Ditch. Mr. Tolley joined the Maratha Ditch to the Ádigauṋgá. In olden times the Ádigauṋgá was the original Ganges River and it used to flow past Maháprabhu D́áuṋgá in Báruipur towards Chatrashál. On his way to Shyámpur, Maháprabhu would keep the Bhagiirathii on his right at Khaŕdá, then rest for a little while at the modern Maháprabhu D́áuṋgá in Báruipur, and then cross the Ganges near Chatrashál. From Shyámpur he would take the Gopiivallabhapur road to Puri. This part of the canal was named after Mr. Tolley and part of the Ádigauṋgá as well; it was known as T́alii Nálá [Tolley Canal]. It was an unhealthy saltwater area full of mosquito-infested jungle and undergrowth. Agriculture there was not very successful. Afterwards, when a new settlement was founded there it was named Tolleyganj. It cannot take pride in its antiquity the way in which Behálá and Baŕiśá can.
summary: When the British occupied [India], Kolkata was part of the northern outskirts of the Sundarbans.
This part of the canal was named after Mr.
It cannot take pride in its antiquity the way in which Behálá and Baŕiśá can.

paragraphs.text: If you take a look at a map of Bengal, you will see innumerable estuaries in the south by the Bay of Bengal. They are full of saltwater and are home to ferocious crocodiles. These ferocious crocodiles are called “Crocodile gangelitis” in English. They are not the alligator variety of crocodile. Although the alligator variety of crocodile lives in various regions from the Tropic of Cancer to the equator to the Tropic of Capricorn, their primary home is the Amazon River basin in Brazil. In other words, they are not gangelitis but rather amazonika. At one time there were huge numbers of the gangelitis variety of crocodile on the shoals of the Rupanarayan River basin near Shyámpur, Báganán and Geṋyokháli, especially during wintertime. ( 5 ) During the middle of the day in winter, they would lie on the river shoals with their mouths gaping open, and small birds would enter their mouths to pick out the pieces of meat stuck to their teeth and eat them. There was an unwritten alliance of mutual self-interest and doing each other a good turn between the birds and the crocodiles. The crocodiles used to get their teeth cleaned and the birds found their food there. The crocodile would not close his mouth while the birds were inside.
summary: If you take a look at a map of Bengal, you will see innumerable estuaries in the south by the Bay of Bengal.
In other words, they are not gangelitis but rather amazonika.
The crocodile would not close his mouth while the birds were inside.

paragraphs.text: At that time the Rupanarayan was a huge river. During the rainy season it was full of ilish (hilsa) fish and during the winter it was full of tapse. ( 6 ) The word ilish means “glossy” or “glittering”. In spoken Bengali it is called ilshá or ilshe in some places. The word is derived from Prákrta. If the ilish loses its taste, then it is called viilish [vi-ilish – without ilish]. When the ilish would become separated from the main river and end up in someoneʼs pond or pool due to flooding of the sea or of the Ganges, then they would grow large in size, no doubt, but they would be less tasty because the amount of oil would decrease. This kind of ilish was commonly known as viilish.
summary: At that time the Rupanarayan was a huge river.
The word is derived from Prákrta.
This kind of ilish was commonly known as viilish.

paragraphs.text: When they came to this country for the first time, the British took three settlements from the Nawab for 2700 rupees – Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur. Sutanuti was a village of weavers to the north. ( 7 ) Their trade involved sutá [thread] and nut́i [“bobbin” in English], so naturally the name of the village become Sutanut́i. What is now South-Central Kolkata, from Dalhousie Square to the southern outskirts of the fort field, was Govindapur. ( 8 ) The name Govindapur probably comes from the name of the zamindar Govindaram Basu. Kalighat was to the south of Govindapur.
summary: When they came to this country for the first time, the British took three settlements from the Nawab for 2700 rupees – Kalighat, Sutanuti and Govindapur.
What is now South-Central Kolkata, from Dalhousie Square to the southern outskirts of the fort field, was Govindapur.
Kalighat was to the south of Govindapur.

paragraphs.text: It has been said that Sutanuti was principally a weaversʼ settlement. The old textile merchants of Kolkata used to live in the area between Sutanuti and Govindapur. Now it is known as Baŕabájár. Actually its old Bengali name was Buŕá Bájár – from the local name Buŕo Shiva. The place was probably under the ownership of Baŕiśáʼs Sávarńa Choudurees. They were the forefathers of Baŕabájárʼs merchants. The area beginning where Sutanuti touches the bank of the Ganges straight south up and until the bank of the Ganges to the west of Kalighat was the home of the fisherman community, or jelepáŕá. Jelepáŕá was divided into three localities – Sutanuti, Govindapur and Kalighat. We should keep in mind that this does not mean that the city of Kolkata was formed from only Sutanuti, Govindapur and Kalighat. Kolkata was founded over a vast area to the north and east of these three villages comprising primarily another twenty-seven villages and secondarily thirty-five villages. The villages of Pat́old́áuṋgá, D́ihi, Hentáli (Entally), Citrapur (Chitpur), Hogalkunŕe, Pat́uyápáŕá, Bágmárii, Mogalbágán, Beleghát́á and Táltalá, all became part of Kolkata as well. The neighbourhoods of Garáńahát́á, Áhirit́olá, Mohanbágán, Hartukibágán, Hálsibágán, Hát́kholá, Kumárt́ulii and Shobhábájár were incorporated later; however, they are also not very new.
summary: It has been said that Sutanuti was principally a weaversʼ settlement.
The area beginning where Sutanuti touches the bank of the Ganges straight south up and until the bank of the Ganges to the west of Kalighat was the home of the fisherman community, or jelepáŕá.

The neighbourhoods of Garáńahát́á, Áhirit́olá, Mohanbágán, Hartukibágán, Hálsibágán, Hát́kholá, Kumárt́ulii and Shobhábájár were incorporated later; however, they are also not very new.

paragraphs.text: Kalighat was a small, temple-centred village to the south. A few Brahman families and pat́uyá [painter-caste] families lived there. The pat́uyás were the artists responsible for the renowned Kalighat canvases. It was Jamini Raiṋjan Ray, a resident of Bankuraʼs Beletoŕ, who recognized the excellence of the Kalighat canvases. No written history exists to tell us how old the Kalighat canvases are, but the pat́uyás were living there at the beginning of the Pathan era. They came from the areas of Arambag and Ghatal. In those days the people of Bengal would buy paintings (pat́as) along with other items when they went to market. There used to be an especially brisk trade in the paintings of different Hindu gods and goddesses. The women who worshipped Lakshmi all the year round performed it with paintings. When Durgápúja [worship of Durga] began during the Pathan era, only the zamindars used to make idols for their worship. The middle class people who celebrated Durgápúja at home would use paintings. Those who could not afford to buy paintings would celebrate it with earthen pots. Even as recently as onehundred years ago, worship of Saraswati was performed primarily with earthen pots. The performance of Saraswati pújá with idols was introduced later, with inspiration from the British.
summary: Kalighat was a small, temple-centred village to the south.
There used to be an especially brisk trade in the paintings of different Hindu gods and goddesses.
The performance of Saraswati pújá with idols was introduced later, with inspiration from the British.

paragraphs.text: The temple at Kalighat has been ruined and rebuilt many times. Ultimately a large temple was constructed by the Sávarńa Choudurees. Certain Ráŕhii class Kushárii Brahmans from the Jagannathpur area of Jessore came to Jelepáŕáʼs central area and began living along the banks of the Ganges. They were the forefathers of the renowned Tagore families of Jorasanko and Pathureghata. The fishermen used to call them T́hákur out of respect, and thus they became famous as T́hákurs (Tagore).
summary: The temple at Kalighat has been ruined and rebuilt many times.
Certain Ráŕhii class Kushárii Brahmans from the Jagannathpur area of Jessore came to Jelepáŕáʼs central area and began living along the banks of the Ganges.
The fishermen used to call them T́hákur out of respect, and thus they became famous as T́hákurs (Tagore).

paragraphs.text: At that time Kayasthas lived in the Govindapur area. Later, when the Maratha cavalry invaded Ráŕh, the wealthy Kayasthas of Murshidabad, Birbhum and Dumka districts left and sought shelter with the Datta zamindars of Bhagalpur Districtʼs Dattavat́i, the Ghosh families of Campánagar, and the Ghosh zamindars of Jhauyákut́hi. They began to live in hundreds of villages in Bhagalpur and Monghyr districts. Descendants of Ráŕhii Kayasthas bearing the surnames Ghosh, Mitra, Datta, Das and Singha still live there. They brought with them their own Ráŕhii class Brahman priests as well. During the invasion of the Maratha cavalry, the wealthy Kayasthas of Bankura, Hooghly, Howrah and Burdwan areas sought safe shelter in British Kolkata, the city of officialdom and business. However, for whatever reason, they did not take up residence in Govindapur. They went to Hát́kholá, Shobhábájár, Shyámbájár, Shyámpukur, Kambulit́olá, Kumurt́ulii, and Chitpur.
summary: At that time Kayasthas lived in the Govindapur area.
They brought with them their own Ráŕhii class Brahman priests as well.
They went to Hát́kholá, Shobhábájár, Shyámbájár, Shyámpukur, Kambulit́olá, Kumurt́ulii, and Chitpur.

paragraphs.text: After the fall of Saptagrám port, the Suvarńa bańiks [a business community] and Gandha baniks residing there migrated primarily to Cuncŕo, and secondarily to various cities along the banks of the Bhagiirathii. When the British built up their business interests in Kolkata, many of Cuncŕoʼs Suvarńa bańiks moved there. They started living in the cityʼs western district by the bank of the Bhagiirathii River. In those days Kolkataʼs trade goods were moved principally along the Bhagiirathii. One famous personage of Cuncŕo at that time was Gaorii Sen. He was famous throughout the land for his wealth, his generous heart and his liberality. People still say, “If you need money, Gaorii Sen will give it to you”. These fisher folk, Piráli Brahmans, Kayasthas, weavers, textile merchants and Suvarńa baniks were the old residents of Kolkata.
summary: After the fall of Saptagrám port, the Suvarńa bańiks [a business community] and Gandha baniks residing there migrated primarily to Cuncŕo, and secondarily to various cities along the banks of the Bhagiirathii.
One famous personage of Cuncŕo at that time was Gaorii Sen.
These fisher folk, Piráli Brahmans, Kayasthas, weavers, textile merchants and Suvarńa baniks were the old residents of Kolkata.

paragraphs.text: With the exception of the Piráli Brahmans, many of the other Brahmans who had come to Kolkata at the beginning left for the great Brahman-predominant village of Bálii in Howrah District after the hanging of Maharaja Nandakumar [1775]. ( 9 ) Since a Brahman had been hanged in Kolkata they left for the western bank of the Ganges (“Gauṋgár pashcim kúl varańasii samatul” [the west bank of the Ganges is parallel to Varanasi]); that is, they went to Ráŕh and began living there. Afterwards, although they would still go to Kolkata for work purposes, they would not touch food or water while they were there, nor would they spend the night. They would go in the early morning and return back in the evening.
summary: With the exception of the Piráli Brahmans, many of the other Brahmans who had come to Kolkata at the beginning left for the great Brahman-predominant village of Bálii in Howrah District after the hanging of Maharaja Nandakumar [1775].
Afterwards, although they would still go to Kolkata for work purposes, they would not touch food or water while they were there, nor would they spend the night.
They would go in the early morning and return back in the evening.

paragraphs.text: There was a dense forest between Govindapur and Kalighat. No one dared travel that path alone, even in broad daylight, what to speak of at night. When they would go to perform Kali pújá in the Kali temple they would travel in groups of forty or fifty persons and take their staffs and cudgels with them. Otherwise they would be killed by highwaymen. It is said that the highwaymen used to kill people in broad daylight and hang them from trees. The ashram of Caoraungii Bábá was in the Govindapur area (the Nátha yogi Caoraungiináth). Caoraungii Bábá was pained to see the distress of the pilgrims, so he had his disciples carve out a road through the jungle to Kalighat. For a long time this road was known as Caoraungii Bábáʼs road. I cannot understand why those who have completely or partially changed the name of this road ( 10 ) have done so.
summary: There was a dense forest between Govindapur and Kalighat.
It is said that the highwaymen used to kill people in broad daylight and hang them from trees.
I cannot understand why those who have completely or partially changed the name of this road ( 10 ) have done so.

paragraphs.text: Dharmaráj T́hákurʼs place was slightly to the east of Caoraungii Bábáʼs ashram. Dharmaráj was another name for Buddha. The worship of Dharmaráj or Dharmat́hákur began in Bengal towards the end of the Pál era. There is a Dharmarájtalá or Dharmatalá in Howrahʼs Shálikhá also, as there is in Kolkata. ( 11 ) I also do not understand why the historical name Dharmatala Street in Kolkata has been changed at present to Lenin Sarani. I am unaware of any kind of connection that the noble Lenin had with this part of Kolkata. Would it not have been possible to name a new or non-historical street or park after him? At the end of the Buddhist era in Bengal, the Buddhist followers of Dharmaráj flourished alongside the Nátha cult. It is very likely that the Carak pújá [worship] also began at this time. ( 12 ) There were and are still many Carakd́áuṋgás in our Kolkata. I am waiting for that auspicious day when the name Carakd́áuṋgá will also be changed!
summary: Dharmaráj T́hákurʼs place was slightly to the east of Caoraungii Bábáʼs ashram.
I am unaware of any kind of connection that the noble Lenin had with this part of Kolkata.
I am waiting for that auspicious day when the name Carakd́áuṋgá will also be changed!

paragraphs.text: I was talking about Dharmaráj pújá. Dharmaráj pújá was common to some extent in central Bengal and throughout Ráŕh. In Birbhum and Bankura, Dharmaráj was regarded as non-Brahman and was worshipped as Shiva right from the beginning. In certain parts of eastern Ráŕh and central Bengal, Dharmaráj acquired the appellation Buŕo Shiva. In many villages and towns of this region there is a Buŕo Shivatalá as well as a Dharmarájtalá. The difference was that the majority of worshippers of Dharmaráj were non-Brahmans, that is, people belonging to the ját [original] Bengalees [traditional Bengalees], chiefly Kaevarta and Sadgopa. They were generally known by the name Deváḿshi. The worshippers of Buŕo Shiva, however, were predominantly Buddhist Brahmans with the surname Cakravartii. In subsequent times, this Buŕo Shivaʼs Buddhist colour changed and he was transformed into Paoráńic Shiva.
summary: I was talking about Dharmaráj pújá.
In many villages and towns of this region there is a Buŕo Shivatalá as well as a Dharmarájtalá.
In subsequent times, this Buŕo Shivaʼs Buddhist colour changed and he was transformed into Paoráńic Shiva.

paragraphs.text: Due to the pressure of increasing population in northern Kolkata, a famous local person, Bhavani Prasad Bandopadhyaya, cut down the jungle to the southeast and established a new village. (There is some difference of opinion regarding this.) The Bhawanipur area was built in his name. At that time the ancient Padmapukur of Bhawanipur already had a long history. Towards the end of his life, the poet Hemchandra Bandopadhyaya used to live on Padmapukur Road. You may be familiar with the invitation that he wrote to his son-in-law:
summary: Due to the pressure of increasing population in northern Kolkata, a famous local person, Bhavani Prasad Bandopadhyaya, cut down the jungle to the southeast and established a new village.
) The Bhawanipur area was built in his name.

paragraphs.text: In Bengal there are many places named Gáchá, Gáchi, Gachiyá (Geche). We should know what the origin is of the Bengali word gách [plant, tree]. The Sanskrit synonym for gách is vrkśa. Be that as it may, the Bengali word gách does not come from the Sanskrit word vrkśa. In other words, gách is not originally a Sanskrit word. paragraphs.text: Here also there is no mention of d́ál. The first mention of pulse in Bengali literature comes much later at the beginning of the Pathan era. The Bengalis of that time used to prepare mug-sháuli [one delicious preparation with mung] with mung d́ál. Modern ladies who cook are unfamiliar with the way mug-sháuli was actually prepared, but I would guess that it was prepared by boiling the whole mung in milk after removing the husk and then frying it in a little ghee with cloves, sugar and cassia leaf. Mugkhańd́a was prepared in those days in a similar fashion. The consumption of mung burfi as a sweet had probably not become common yet. Suriʼs artisans began making Suriʼs renowned morabbá [fruits soaked in sugar-cane syrup] approximately four hundred years ago. paragraphs.text: Let us return to the subject of pulse. Whether or not it was used in old Bengal, there is little doubt that pulse was not a favourite food of the people. However, greens [shák] – gacchá in the Bengali of that time – were certainly a favourite. Gimá shák [Hydroctyle rotundifolia], titá shák [a kind of bitter leafy vegetable], heleiṋcá shák [Hingtsha repens] (hiiṋce shák in Kolkata Bengali) were popular foods. Some names of these various greens are Sanskrit-derived and others are native Bengali. Nat́e shák [Petsaii; Brassica chinensis] (tańd́uleraka in Sanskrit; this green grows spontaneously in putrid water left from washing rice, thus the name tańd́uleraka) and d́euṋgo d́áṋt́á (that d́áṋt́á which is cultivated in d́áuṋgá [elevated] land) are native Bengali words. Nálte Shák [jute leaves, a variety of Ipomea reptans] (in Sanskrit nálitá). The name of Nálitábáŕi village in Mymensing District means “where nálte shák can be found in abundance”), punko (a kind of leafy vegetable; Sanskrit puńyaká – the famous sweet greens of Burdwan), hiiṋce [Enhydra fluctuans] (heleiṋcá in Ráŕh, hilamociká in Sanskrit), betho shák [goosefoot; Chenopodium album] (vásttuka in Sanskrit), kalmii [water spinach; Ipomoea reptans] (Sanskrit kalambii), puṋi [Basella lucida] (in Sanskrit putiká, potakii, upadiiká, amrtavallarii; in Vedic: potakyupadiiká svátu mánavamrtavallarii), pálaḿ [Spinacia oleracea] (pálaunkyá in Sanskrit) and shushnii [Belpharis edulis Pers.] (shikhii in Sanskrit), thánakuni [Hydrocotyle Asiatica] (bráhmii in Sanskrit) are all Sanskrit-derived words. Some people believe that pálaḿ shák [spinach] may have come originally from outside India, but that is not correct. Pálaḿ shák is native to India. It is mentioned in old Sanskrit. paragraphs.text: The old Sanskrit for “orange” is nágarauṋga. From this comes the word náráuṋgii, even though the orange is a Mediterranean fruit; that is, it is native to Europe. Nevertheless the English word “orange” is neither originally English nor European. Its origin is the Urdu word náráuṋgii. Ekt́i náráuṋgii in English is “a narangi”. With the passage of time the “n” became displaced. “A narangi” became “an orange,” and through distortion “an orangi” became “an orange”. Similarly “an apkin” became “a napkin” through displacement of the “n”. A gámchá used to be called “an apkin” in old English, not “a napkin”. Its family member, the word “apron”, is still in good health; it has not become “napron”. There are many examples of such changes on this earth, not only in the spelling of words.

paragraphs.text: In certain compositions it can be seen that the outer meaning is not the same as the inner meaning. For example, twelve hundred years ago poetry was written in [the genre of] twilight language. At that time the inner essence of spirituality was not openly stated. For example, in one place Kabir has said kambal varśe bhiuṋge páńi. Here kambal does not mean “a woolen blanket”. One of the many names for water is kambalam. Thus, in this case kambal varśe means “shower of water”, that is, water is seeping from the eyes. And in bhiuṋge páńi, páńi does not mean “water” but rather “palm”. The spiritual aspirant is seated as usual meditating on God, and the flow of tears from their eyes is wetting their palms. Many poems were written in this twilight language in the old Bengali of twelve hundred years ago.

paragraphs.text: Its outer meaning is: “So much milk was obtained by milking a turtle that it could not be carried on the back, and a crocodile is eating the tamarind on the tree.” Needless to say, its inner meaning is different. The rukh here comes from the Sanskrit word vrkśa. Sanskrit vrkśa > rikśa > rukśa > rukh. Generally, whenever r is joined to a consonant in Sanskrit, then in Mágadhii Prákrta it is taken as if the r were not there. For example, nrtya becomes nacca, vrddha becomes vad́hd́ha > vud́d́ha > buŕá > buŕo. If there is only r, then it becomes i in the Yajurvedic style. In the Atharvavedic style it becomes u. For example, rśi becomes isi and rju becomes uju. In the aforementioned verse it would have been more correct had vrkśa been changed into vakśa, but since the pronunciation of antahstha va is akin to a vowel, vrkśa in the Atharvavedic style becomes rukśa and from that comes the old Bengali rukh. Of course, there are also exceptions. For example, the Sanskrit vakśa becomes bukka in Prákrta, and from that buk in modern Bengali. The name of the place where Lord Buddha initiated his first five disciples was Sárauṋganáth; now it has become Sárnath. The sages made a deer park in Sárauṋganáth so the place was renamed in Sanskrit as Rśipattana Mrgadáva, which later became Isipattan Migdába in Prákrta.

paragraphs.text: In any case, we were talking about the names Gách, Gáchá, Gáchiyá, Geche and Gáchi. The name of a place where there is more than one gách [tree] is gratsii in Prákrta, gacchia in Demi-Prákrta, gáchi or gáchiyá in old Bengali, and gáchi or geche in modern Bengali, for example, Belgáchiyá (Kolkata), Kalágáchiyá (Dhaka), Bámungáchi (Howrah), Kánkuŕgáchi (24 Parganas) and Sántarágáchi. To indicate more than one or also a specific one, the words gáchi, gáchá, chaŕá are used in Bengali, for example, hárgáchit́á or háte tule dáo [put the necklace in his hand]. Here both hárgáchá and hárcháŕá can be used. Similarly, the word gáchá is found in village names. For example, Muŕágáchá (Nadia), Muktágáchá (Mymensing) – where there is a collection of objects as valuable as pearls or fit to be welcomed like a pearl, or a golden opportunity for speaking. Gáchi is also added to place-names in the languages of Bihar, such as Nagpurii, Maethilii and Angika. In other words, gáchi is also used to mean “a collection of gách”, for example, Ráńiigáchi (Rátu, Ranchi) and Mańigáchi (Mithila).

paragraphs.text: A small king who is subservient to a greater king is called sámantarájá in Sanskrit. Sámanta rájá > sánotta ráá > sáṋtaráyá in Prákrta > sáṋtará in modern Bengali. Many people in southern Bengal have the surname Sáṋtará. None of them are kings any longer, but they continue to use the surname. The name of a settlement built around a Sámantarájáʼs garden or bágáń (that is, where there are many gách plants) is Sáṋtarágáchi. Sámantarája gratsii > sáṋottaráa gacchia > sáṋtarágáchi. Thus the spelling is Sántarágáchi; Sátrágáchi is an erroneous spelling.

paragraphs.text: There are many villages or places in Bengal as well as in many other parts of India called D́ahari. In old Bengali, the word d́ahar was used to mean “street” or “road”. D́ahar is an Austric word. Betho shák [Chenopodium ambrosioides; a type of leafy green] is found by the side of the road; that is, it is found by the side of the d́ahar, so its name is bethuyád́ahari. ( 15 ) Since buffalo graze by the ponds on both sides of the road, their name is mahiśád́ahari.
summary: There are many villages or places in Bengal as well as in many other parts of India called D́ahari.
D́ahar is an Austric word.
( 15 ) Since buffalo graze by the ponds on both sides of the road, their name is mahiśád́ahari.

paragraphs.text: Nowadays we scarcely use the word d́ahar. It is used a little in certain parts of Bihar. We have abandoned the use of the word d́ahar and accepted the Farsi word rastá in its place. We have not accepted the Farsi word ráha instantly; it has had to travel a long and winding road before being accepted. For example, ráhá-kharac means “expenses for moving along the road”. Someone travelling by road is called ráhii in Hindustani, and a travelling companion is called hamráhii. The descendants of those government officials in Bengal during the Middle Ages who were responsible for supervising the roads (that is, they worked in the Public Works Department) still use the surname Ráhá today. Although the word ráhii is not used much in Bengali, it has been in use for nearly seven hundred years. Of course, the Sanskrit-derived word ráhi means rádhiká > ráhiá > ráhi > rái.
