The famed Indian scientist of the Middle Ages, Áryabhat́t́a, was from Kusumpur.
Pataliputra was destroyed in the floods of the Ganges and Shon rivers, and time and again it was rebuilt.

paragraphs.text: Girivraja or Rajagiri was the capital of Magadha during the time of Bimbisar and before that as well. The place called Rajgir nowadays is the same Girivraja or Rajagiri of that era. Many people think that the word rájgir comes from the word rájagrha, but it does not. The Sanskrit word grha became the word ghar through distortion. If the name of that place had been Rájagrha, then its modern form would have been Rájghar. Actually Rájgir comes from Rájagiri (Royal Mountain). Rájagiri is surrounded by mountains; for that very reason, its name has become Girivraja or Rájagiri.
summary: Girivraja or Rajagiri was the capital of Magadha during the time of Bimbisar and before that as well.
The Sanskrit word grha became the word ghar through distortion.
Rájagiri is surrounded by mountains; for that very reason, its name has become Girivraja or Rájagiri.

paragraphs.text: Magadha never had a city by the name of Rájagrha. The giri has become gir through corruption, so the cityʼs present-day name is Rájgir. Similarly, Mudgagiri was the name of a giri or mountain that looked like mung (mudga > muunga > muḿg > mug), or else the name of a place which was like a mudgar (“club” in English). The name of this place in Angadesh underwent change and became Monghyr. In the Pathan era, its distorted name became Mungher. Monghyr was the last capital of Bengal during the Mughal era. Its nawab was Mirkássim. The fort from those days and the arsenal bazaar originally made for muskets and cannons still exist in Monghyr. There is a Kasimbazar named after the nawab as well as the Kaŕeyá parade grounds for military parades. Rest houses called Sarái could be found throughout the city for travellers. At that time travel lodges, where long-distance travellers would take rest, were called sarái in Farsi. In Indian languages they were called cat́i. It was where long-distance travellers would take rest. In some places the kings or nawabs made arrangements to provide food and in other places almshouses were available. In some places rice, pulse, salt and wood were stored, and the travellers would cook their own food. Sophiyásarái and Púravsarái were near Monghyr and Lakśmiisarái was slightly further away. Burdwan was also the capital of Bengal at one time. Nai-sarái was near Burdwan. At one point Patna was the capital of Bihar province during the reign of Akbar. ( 16 ) Núrsarái and Sohsarái were near Patna and Láheriyásarái was in north Bihar. Earlier I mentioned that sarái is called cat́i in Indian languages. Many villages still exist today along the roads to pilgrimage spots with the name Cat́i, such as Durgácat́i and Niirasácat́i (old Manbhum District and modern Dhanbad District).
summary: Magadha never had a city by the name of Rájagrha.
In Indian languages they were called cat́i.
Many villages still exist today along the roads to pilgrimage spots with the name Cat́i, such as Durgácat́i and Niirasácat́i (old Manbhum District and modern Dhanbad District).

paragraphs.text: So we were talking about Mudgagiri, which was the last capital of Bengal during the era of the Nawabs and the second capital of Anga in olden times. At that time, the Rashtrakuts were a dominant force in western India. They took possession of Monghyr for a short time and they also designated it as their second capital. This was most probably during the time of Mahendra Pal. Monghyrʼs history dates back to the Mahábhárata when Karna was the king of Angadesh. The capital of Angadesh then was Campaknagar (present-day Campánagar near Náthnagar). Although there is no connection between the historical Karna and Monghyrʼs historically famous Karńacúŕá palace, the hillock on which the palace is situated is named after Maharaja Karna. During the time of the Pala kings, Bengalʼs impenetrable fort was on the south side of the Ganges. The fall of Monghyr accelerated the fall of the Pala kings and opened the doors for the Pathan invasion. As a result, the historically renowned Vikramshila University located to the east of Monghyr near Bhagalpur (in nearby Antichak village) was destroyed.
summary: So we were talking about Mudgagiri, which was the last capital of Bengal during the era of the Nawabs and the second capital of Anga in olden times.
The capital of Angadesh then was Campaknagar (present-day Campánagar near Náthnagar).
As a result, the historically renowned Vikramshila University located to the east of Monghyr near Bhagalpur (in nearby Antichak village) was destroyed.

paragraphs.text: With so much going for it, why compare the mountain to mung d́ál? As far as we can tell, mung d́ál was the favourite pulse of people in eastern Bengal. Golden mung has been cultivated in the clayish soil of Central Bengal for a very long time; it is incomparable in taste, aroma and sentience. However there is no way of knowing if the mung mentioned in Bengali literature of the Middle Ages is the śát́há variety of golden mung or some other variety of mung, because in the Ráŕh region ghoŕá mung or gheso mung is cultivated more than golden mung. They grow well even in infertile soil.
summary: With so much going for it, why compare the mountain to mung d́ál?
Golden mung has been cultivated in the clayish soil of Central Bengal for a very long time; it is incomparable in taste, aroma and sentience.
They grow well even in infertile soil.

paragraphs.text: Mung is a pulse of the tropical and equatorial regions. Like lentils and peas, it does not like cold weather, so it is noteworthy that while there are English synonyms for masur and mat́ar (“lentil” and “pea” respectively), there is no proper English synonym for mung. It has been grouped in the gram family. For example, mung is called “green gram”; biri kalái or máś kalái (in Kolkata we say biuli) is black gram; kurthii kalái or kulattha kalái is “horse gram”; cholá is “Bengal gram” (chickpea; buńt́ika or cańaka in Sanskrit; but́ in Ráŕh and Bihar; rahilá in Bhojpuri; cańá in Hindi; harbaŕá in Marathi). The British first came into contact with cholá on both banks of the Kunur River, which begins in the Budbud jungle and merges in the Ajay [River] near Kográm. Since the river was in Burdwan District, they named it “Bengal gram”. Many people mistakenly use the word “gram” only for cholá. “Gram” is the name of a family [of legumes], so if one says “gram” it refers to all grams – biri kalái, mung, cholá, etc. One should use the English synonym “Bengal gram” for cholá.
summary: Mung is a pulse of the tropical and equatorial regions.
The British first came into contact with cholá on both banks of the Kunur River, which begins in the Budbud jungle and merges in the Ajay [River] near Kográm.
One should use the English synonym “Bengal gram” for cholá.

paragraphs.text: Actually [ásale], the common Bengali word cholá is Farsi. And most interestingly, the word ásal [real, actual] is also a Farsi word, and so is nakal [imitation, counterfeit]. Now bal má tárá d́áŕái kothá [“Tell me, mother, where do we stand?”]. Without Farsi there is hardly any scope for moving even a single step. There is no proper English synonym for aŕhar d́ál [pigeon pea; Cajanus cajan, syn. Cajanus indicus; toor d́ál], but in Sanskrit it is kandula. In southern Oriya and in Telugu (Sarkar region Telugu) it is called kandul.
summary: Actually [ásale], the common Bengali word cholá is Farsi.
Without Farsi there is hardly any scope for moving even a single step.
In southern Oriya and in Telugu (Sarkar region Telugu) it is called kandul.

paragraphs.text: A little while ago we were discussing Kusumpur. Girivraja or Rájagiri was the capital of Magadha during the time of Bimbisar, that is, during the age of Buddha. It suffered from a lack of water, so there was need for an ample water supply in the capital. Once Buddha stood at the place where the Ganges and Shone rivers meet and said that if the capital were there, it would be advantageous in every respect. Among the disciples of the Buddha present was a merchant by the name of Pataliputra. At that time there was a synthesis between the matrilineal and patrilineal systems with respect to giving names. The motherʼs name was Rúpasári so the son was named Sáriputta. The motherʼs name was Mahámaodgalii (Mahámaggali), so her son was named Mahámaodagallan Arahań (Mahámaggallan). Similarly, his motherʼs name was Pát́alii so he was named Pát́aliiputra. Pataliputra took on the responsibility of building a city at that spot, and thus the city was named Pataliputra after him. Kusumpur was destroyed and Pataliputra was built in its place. Time and again the Shon changed its course, and time and again Pataliputra was destroyed. When one Pataliputra disappeared, another was founded atop its ruins. As a result of constant reconstruction, the name of the city, which was so often destroyed and rebuilt, became Patná or Pat́ná. ( 17 ) In Bengali and Marathi we write Pát́ná (Pát́ńá in Marathi) but in the local language, Magahii, it is written as Pat́ná. It seems to me that the spelling of Pat́ná is more correct than Pát́ná or Pát́ńá.
summary: A little while ago we were discussing Kusumpur.
Similarly, his motherʼs name was Pát́alii so he was named Pát́aliiputra.
It seems to me that the spelling of Pat́ná is more correct than Pát́ná or Pát́ńá.

paragraphs.text: The flooding of the Shon River is even more destructive than that of the Ganges. This great river takes birth in the Baghelkhandi region of Madhya Pradesh and flows past the borders of the former kingdoms of Kashi and Magadha until it merges in the Ganges. Its waters are golden-coloured like the soń [flax] flower; thus its name is the “Shoń”. Although according to Hindi grammar most rivers are feminine, the Shoń is masculine. For example, Gauṋgá vahatii hae [the Ganges flows] but shon vahatá hae [the Shone flows.]
summary: The flooding of the Shon River is even more destructive than that of the Ganges.
Its waters are golden-coloured like the soń [flax] flower; thus its name is the “Shoń”.
For example, Gauṋgá vahatii hae [the Ganges flows] but shon vahatá hae [the Shone flows.

paragraphs.text: As with Patna there were or now are other cities in India which have risen from the ruins of former cities, for example, Masaliipattanam, Shriirauṋgapattanam, Bhavániipát́ná and Siḿhalapát́an (a small village near Siuṋgur in Hooghly District). At one time the village of Siḿhalapát́an, situated at the confluence of two small rivers, was a port in Ráŕh. It was from this port that the crown prince of Ráŕh, Vijay Siḿha, started his journey towards Siḿhala (its name was Lauṋka at the time).
summary: As with Patna there were or now are other cities in India which have risen from the ruins of former cities, for example, Masaliipattanam, Shriirauṋgapattanam, Bhavániipát́ná and Siḿhalapát́an (a small village near Siuṋgur in Hooghly District).
At one time the village of Siḿhalapát́an, situated at the confluence of two small rivers, was a port in Ráŕh.
It was from this port that the crown prince of Ráŕh, Vijay Siḿha, started his journey towards Siḿhala (its name was Lauṋka at the time).

paragraphs.text: Names and characteristics of rivers
summary: Names and characteristics of rivers

paragraphs.text: In olden times rivers were named according to their special characteristics. For example, the river whose waters were as clear as the eyes of a kapota, or dove, was named Kapotákśa [dove eyes]. The river whose eyes were like those of a peacock was called Mayúrákśii. That river that had fire [dáma] in its belly [udara] was called Dámodar. Since there were charcoal or coal deposits beneath the Damodar, the fire-related word dáma was used. The cruel river that causes terrible harm to a community through sudden flooding is named Kasái (butcher). At present this terrible, cruel-natured Kasái River has been attired as a woman of leisure in a Benares sari and given the name [goddess] Kaḿsávatii. One should bear in mind that there is no relationship between this river and kánsá [bell-metal]. Moreover, the Sanskrit for kánsá is kaḿsya or bharańa, not kaḿsa or kaḿsá.
summary: In olden times rivers were named according to their special characteristics.
Since there were charcoal or coal deposits beneath the Damodar, the fire-related word dáma was used.
Moreover, the Sanskrit for kánsá is kaḿsya or bharańa, not kaḿsa or kaḿsá.

paragraphs.text: The river that takes birth in Midnapore and whose waters are comparatively black is called Káliyághái (Keleghái). The Keleghái River merges in the Kánsái River slightly downstream from Midnapore. After joining together, their combined flow has been given the name Haldii. This Haldii River flows into the Bhagiirathii a little upstream from the mouth of the Bhagiirathii. The small village called Haldiyá that stood at that time at the place where these two rivers meet is not connected in any way with diyá or dviipa. The village was named Haldiyá because it was situated on the banks of the Haldii River.
summary: The river that takes birth in Midnapore and whose waters are comparatively black is called Káliyághái (Keleghái).
This Haldii River flows into the Bhagiirathii a little upstream from the mouth of the Bhagiirathii.
The village was named Haldiyá because it was situated on the banks of the Haldii River.

paragraphs.text: Qualities of villages
summary: Qualities of villages

paragraphs.text: Villages are often named for their qualities. There are many snakes in the villages and market centres of Bengal and there are a great many cobras in Ráŕh. Their name in Ráŕhi Bengali is kharis. The village that has a very huge number of snakes is called Sarpalehaná (Birbhum). Similarly, in Manbhum District there is Mańihárá, and in Bankura District there is Mukut́mańipur.
summary: Villages are often named for their qualities.
Their name in Ráŕhi Bengali is kharis.
Similarly, in Manbhum District there is Mańihárá, and in Bankura District there is Mukut́mańipur.

paragraphs.text: Formerly people were given names to signify manliness. At present there is a tendency towards giving sweet names. Formerly, girlsʼ names used to have six or seven syllables, for example, Viirendramohinii, and Shatad́álavásinii. Thereafter they were shortened to around four syllables, for example, Viińápáńii, and Saodámińii. Later on it became three syllables and nowadays just two, for example, Viińá, Riińá, and Rtá. Since the very long names of earlier times presented difficulty when calling people, a tendency arose to give nicknames. A woman whose name was Kirańashashii used to be called Kenná. Today short names are the custom, so there is no longer much need for nicknames. As names keep becoming shorter, perhaps one day they will become one syllable. However there are not many one-syllable names in our storeroom. Several come to mind – Áh, Uh, Ki, Chi, Thuh, Ca, Khá. I hope that in future many meaningful one-syllable words will be created in different languages of the world; then no one will laugh if these kinds of names are given.
summary: Formerly people were given names to signify manliness.
A woman whose name was Kirańashashii used to be called Kenná.
I hope that in future many meaningful one-syllable words will be created in different languages of the world; then no one will laugh if these kinds of names are given.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Chaŕá/Kándi
summary: Place-names ending in Chaŕá/Kándi

paragraphs.text: When many are taken together to make a single whole, then it is a guccha [bunch]. This guccha is called chaŕá in Bengali. What is spread about (chaŕiye deoyá) is also called chaŕá. Rural girls sprinkle (chaŕá dey) cow dung water in the threshold of the courtyard. Many guccha or chaŕá together make one kándi or káṋdi (the words chaŕá and káṋdi are pure native Bengali words), for example, a káṋdi of bananas, a káṋdi of palm fruit, a káṋdi of coconuts or a káṋdi of betel. There are many chaŕá in one káṋdi of bananas. Many villages forming a cluster in this fashion are also called chaŕá; in north Bengal it is called guŕi, for example, Lakśmiichaŕá, Durlabhchaŕá and Kaláchaŕá. As with chaŕá, villages are also given the name Kándi or Káṋdi for the very same reason, for example, Chátinákáṋdi, Káṋdi, Jemokáṋdi (Murshidabad), Pátharkáṋdi (former Sylhet District) and Háilákáṋdi (Kachar District).
summary: When many are taken together to make a single whole, then it is a guccha [bunch].

Many guccha or chaŕá together make one kándi or káṋdi (the words chaŕá and káṋdi are pure native Bengali words), for example, a káṋdi of bananas, a káṋdi of palm fruit, a káṋdi of coconuts or a káṋdi of betel.

As with chaŕá, villages are also given the name Kándi or Káṋdi for the very same reason, for example, Chátinákáṋdi, Káṋdi, Jemokáṋdi (Murshidabad), Pátharkáṋdi (former Sylhet District) and Háilákáṋdi (Kachar District).

paragraphs.text: Differences between Kándi and Káṋthi
summary: Differences between Kándi and Káṋthi

paragraphs.text: There is no relation between the names Kándi or Káṋdi and Káṋthi. The name Káṋthi comes from Kánthika, which means “shawl” [cádar] or “covering”. The word cádar, however, is Farsi. In Urdu cádar is feminine; that is, merii cádar rather than merá cádar. Since the British pronunciation of Kándi in Murshidabad District and Káṋthi in Midnapore are extremely similar, they used the word “Contai” for Káṋthi. There are two hidden reasons behind the origin of the name Káṋthi. One is the famous Káṋthi textile industry – [which produced] clothes and coverings. At one time, woven cloth was exported from Káṋthi outside India. The second reason is the renowned erudition (erudition is also a covering) of Káṋthi. At one time Káṋthi was one of the centres for the cultivation of knowledge. A good number of Sanskrit Pandits used to live there. Even though Sanskrit pandits are now few in number, Káṋthi has not completely lost its lustre.
summary: There is no relation between the names Kándi or Káṋdi and Káṋthi.
One is the famous Káṋthi textile industry – [which produced] clothes and coverings.
Even though Sanskrit pandits are now few in number, Káṋthi has not completely lost its lustre.

paragraphs.text: After government records were taken away from Leguyá, Káṋthi expanded. Today the city in many respects is more developed than other district cities. In those days, unlike many other district cities, Káṋthi had a college. I know many elderly people in Orissa who learned to read and write in Káṋthi College. Amongst the five districts in Orissa at that time (Cuttack, Puri, Baleshwar, Sambalpur and Aungul-Khondamahal), Cuttack alone had Ravenshaw College, so Káṋthiʼs educational importance must indeed be recognized.
summary: After government records were taken away from Leguyá, Káṋthi expanded.
In those days, unlike many other district cities, Káṋthi had a college.

Amongst the five districts in Orissa at that time (Cuttack, Puri, Baleshwar, Sambalpur and Aungul-Khondamahal), Cuttack alone had Ravenshaw College, so Káṋthiʼs educational importance must indeed be recognized.

paragraphs.text: I along with many of my friends were forced to go to college in Kolkata due to the scarcity of colleges in the provinces of Bihar and Orissa at that time. The Sanskritic and cultural importance of Káṋthi cannot be denied. It would not be a bad idea if a Sanskrit university were established there. It is my firm opinion that the poet Kalidas was a resident of Káṋthi region. The all-round development of Káṋthi would afford many opportunities and benefits. I would like to direct the attention of all concerned parties to [this region.]
summary: I along with many of my friends were forced to go to college in Kolkata due to the scarcity of colleges in the provinces of Bihar and Orissa at that time.
It is my firm opinion that the poet Kalidas was a resident of Káṋthi region.
I would like to direct the attention of all concerned parties to [this region.

paragraphs.text: It would be very good if a railway line were extended from Haldiyá to Dántan via Káṋthi-Diighá. ( 18 ) This would bring the luster of a new day to the city of Káṋthi and at the same time would foster the development of Haldiyá port. The sandy town of Diighá would become a favourite of the people and south Midnapore would be bathed in a new light. Not only that, it would enable the local fisher folk, banana farmers, betel farmers and flower farmers to expect a proper return for their commodities. If arokedia (Japanese tamarisk) trees are planted by the ocean, their lustrous growth would also assist matters by providing protection against ocean storms, since this tree species has the capacity to serve as an obstacle to cyclones. It would be even better if a marine drive were built along the ocean from Haldiyá to the mouth of the Suvarnarekha River. This would not only prove attractive to travellers, but would also foster the development of smaller and larger trade centres and towns on the roadside. It would promote the economic prosperity of the local people. Many sea-dependent industries should be developed in the region lying between Káṋthi [Contai] and Junput́. A small port should also be developed near Káṋthi at the mouth of the Rasulpur River. Since it could take advantage of natural amenities, the port would not entail much expenditure.
summary: It would be very good if a railway line were extended from Haldiyá to Dántan via Káṋthi-Diighá.
It would be even better if a marine drive were built along the ocean from Haldiyá to the mouth of the Suvarnarekha River.
Since it could take advantage of natural amenities, the port would not entail much expenditure.

paragraphs.text: Place-names ending in Talá/Talii/Banii
summary: Place-names ending in Talá/Talii/Banii

paragraphs.text: The area below any large tree is called talá or talii. Many places also have names that include talá or talii, for example, Nimtalá, Keoŕátalá, Táltalá (Kolkata), Ágartalá (Tripura) and Bádámtalá. Some examples of talii are Ámtalii, Kultalii, and Phultalii. If a particular place is used for some particular purpose or activity, in that case talá is used. Talii, however, is not used in such cases. Some examples are: Cańd́iitalá (Hooghly), Káliitalá, Paiṋcánantalá (Chandannagar), Mácántalá (Bankura), Poŕámátalá (Navadviipa), Śaśt́hiitalá (Krishnanagar) and Buŕo Shivatalá (Chandannagar). Besides this, many places have a Hát́talá and a Rathtalá.
summary: The area below any large tree is called talá or talii.
If a particular place is used for some particular purpose or activity, in that case talá is used.
Besides this, many places have a Hát́talá and a Rathtalá.

paragraphs.text: If large numbers of a certain object or certain tree are found spread over an extended area in a certain locality, then the villageʼs name is formed by adding vanii after the name of the tree or object, for example, Ásánvanii, Paláshvanii, Shálvanii (Midnapore) and Madhuvanii (Mithila).
summary: If large numbers of a certain object or certain tree are found spread over an extended area in a certain locality, then the villageʼs name is formed by adding vanii after the name of the tree or object, for example, Ásánvanii, Paláshvanii, Shálvanii (Midnapore) and Madhuvanii (Mithila).

paragraphs.text: Tales of Nayávasán

If new people make a settlement or are newly established in a place, then those places have the name Vasán attached to the end of the name, for example, Rájávasán, Nawábvasán, Mukundavasán and Nuyávasán. Many people mistakenly say Nayávasán, but this is incorrect. “New” is nuyá or noyá in southern Ráŕh and northern Orissa. Nayá is a Hindi word. Nayá-related words in the Bihar languages include nayká or navká. Nowadays many people mistakenly call the town of Noyágrám in Midnapore District as “Nayágrám”.
summary: If new people make a settlement or are newly established in a place, then those places have the name Vasán attached to the end of the name, for example, Rájávasán, Nawábvasán, Mukundavasán and Nuyávasán.
Nayá is a Hindi word.
Nowadays many people mistakenly call the town of Noyágrám in Midnapore District as “Nayágrám”.

paragraphs.text: When the British turned Mayurbhanj, Tripura and Coochbihar into native kingdoms, feudatory kingdoms or vassal kingdoms in accordance with their subsidiary alliance policy, they summarily included significant portions of them in British India. The former kings were thereafter considered as the zamindars of those areas and they would deposit their land revenue in the collectory. They were not considered native kings in those regions but instead became zamindars. In the remaining portions of their lands they were considered native kings.
summary: When the British turned Mayurbhanj, Tripura and Coochbihar into native kingdoms, feudatory kingdoms or vassal kingdoms in accordance with their subsidiary alliance policy, they summarily included significant portions of them in British India.
They were not considered native kings in those regions but instead became zamindars.
In the remaining portions of their lands they were considered native kings.

paragraphs.text: The British left the mountainous eastern portion of Tripura in the hands of the Maharaja. In that region the Maharaja of Tripura was a native king and he had his capital there. The densely populated, fertile areas in the western part of his kingdom were incorporated into British India. In this manner, they formed the Brahmanbaria Subdivision from part of the former Kingdom of Tripura and part of the former Sylhet District; along with this they formed British Tripura or Tipperah out of Chandpur and Comilla district headquarters. Since British Tripura or Tipperah District was densely populated, there was no need to colonize it anew, but the Maharaja of Tripura remained the zamindar of a substantial part of this district. He used to deposit the land revenue in the Comilla collectory. He remained the native king for the remaining portion, which was part of Tripura. The spoken Bengali of the Kingdom of Tripura is Sylheti Bengali in the north and Noyákháli Bengali in the south, which is a blending of Chittagong Bengali and Sylheti Bengali.
summary: The British left the mountainous eastern portion of Tripura in the hands of the Maharaja.
Since British Tripura or Tipperah District was densely populated, there was no need to colonize it anew, but the Maharaja of Tripura remained the zamindar of a substantial part of this district.
The spoken Bengali of the Kingdom of Tripura is Sylheti Bengali in the north and Noyákháli Bengali in the south, which is a blending of Chittagong Bengali and Sylheti Bengali.

paragraphs.text: Similarly, the British incorporated a vast region from the former kingdom of Coochbihar (its former name was also Kámtápur) into British Bengal. They left only eight thánás (Coochbihar, Máthábháuṋgá, Dinhát́á, Shiitalkuci, Haldibáŕi, Mekhligainj, Sitái and Tuphángainj) under control of the Maharaja. Rangpur District in the province of Bengal was formed from the areas taken over by the British. Since this region was also more or less densely populated, there was no need to make many new land leases. However, in the northern part of this region, private lands, or in a few cases leased lands, were appropriated for numerous tea plantations without paying loss compensation, or paying compensation in name only. Since the eastern part of Rangpur District was less populated, many farmers were brought in from outside and land tenures were drawn up. After Rangpur District grew very large, it was divided into three parts. The name of the southern portion remained Rangpur. The north was made into a new district, Jalpaiguri, and the northeast portion became Northeast Rangpur District. When the Province of Assam was created in 1912, Northeast Rangpur District was incorporated into it. Rangpur remained in Bengal Province and Northeast Rangpur was made part of Assam Province. Being somewhat incompatible, Northeast Rangpurʼs name was changed to Goyalpara. Dhubŕi was made the district headquarters. The spoken language of Dhubŕi is Rangpuri Bengali. The spoken language of Coochbihar and Jalpaiguri is also Rangpuri Bengali. However, in different parts of the two districts, different branches of Rangpuri Bengali are prevalent.
summary: Similarly, the British incorporated a vast region from the former kingdom of Coochbihar (its former name was also Kámtápur) into British Bengal.
The north was made into a new district, Jalpaiguri, and the northeast portion became Northeast Rangpur District.
However, in different parts of the two districts, different branches of Rangpuri Bengali are prevalent.

paragraphs.text: The mountainous regions in the western part of the Kingdom of Mayurbhanj were allowed to remain in the hands of the maharaja and the relatively level regions to the east were incorporated into British Bengal. The maharaja of this region became a zamindar of the British. His land revenue was deposited in the collectory at Midnapore. In the remaining areas he remained a native king. The capital of the kingdom was Báripadá. The portion incorporated into British Bengal was somewhat sparsely populated at that time. There was a small jungle but no mountains to speak of. The British brought in new tenants so the region became known as Nuyávasán, that is, “where tenants have been newly installed”. The spoken language of the western and southern parts of Mayurbhanj is northern Oriya, and the spoken language of the northeast part is Kerá Bengali.
summary: The mountainous regions in the western part of the Kingdom of Mayurbhanj were allowed to remain in the hands of the maharaja and the relatively level regions to the east were incorporated into British Bengal.
The capital of the kingdom was Báripadá.
The spoken language of the western and southern parts of Mayurbhanj is northern Oriya, and the spoken language of the northeast part is Kerá Bengali.

paragraphs.text: Kerá Bengali is a blending of Oriya and Bengali. Many people are aware of the fact that the Oriya and Bengali languages are extremely close cousins. To a great extent their history is also the same. Their social functions and community mores as well as their anthropological identities are almost the same. It is impossible to completely separate the two, thus it is meaningless to weary oneself trying to decide whether Kerá Bengali is a dialect of Bengali or of Oriya. No matter what the leaders or philologists say, I would affirm that since this dialect is equally related to both Bengali and Oriya, the people there can claim either Bengali or Oriya as their mother tongue, as they desire. It is only natural that they should do what appeals to them the most.
summary: Kerá Bengali is a blending of Oriya and Bengali.
Their social functions and community mores as well as their anthropological identities are almost the same.
It is only natural that they should do what appeals to them the most.

paragraphs.text: Another native kingdom situated in the far west of Bengal was Seráikelá. The spoken language of the southern portion of this kingdom (the south bank of the Saiṋjay River) is Kerá Bengali. The spoken language of the northern part (the areas of Ádityapur, Gámáriyá, Sini, and Kándrá) is Ráŕhii Bengali. There is scarcely any difference between it and the spoken language of Bankura.
summary: Another native kingdom situated in the far west of Bengal was Seráikelá.
The spoken language of the northern part (the areas of Ádityapur, Gámáriyá, Sini, and Kándrá) is Ráŕhii Bengali.
There is scarcely any difference between it and the spoken language of Bankura.

paragraphs.text: If a village has a well-known pond [pukur] or large tank [diighi], then it may also be named after that, for example, Tálpukur, Táldiighi (Táldiighi > Táldihi > Táldi), T́ungidiighi, Tapandiighi, ( 19 ) Bilvapuśkarińii (Belpukur – Nadia), Bámunpukur (Bráhmań-puśkarińii – Nadia), Pátrasáyer (Bankura), Ráńiibándh (Bankura), Rájbándh (Burdwan), Ságardiighi (Murshidabad) and Dattapukur (24 Parganas). chapters.title: Four Original Races
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Four races

There were originally four races on earth: Caucasian, Mongolian, Austric and Negroid. Many people, of course, do not wish to include the Semitic race among them. Like these races, the Semitic people are also a separate race, the people of the Middle East. In some peopleʼs opinion they are a mixture of the Caucasian and Negroid races.
summary: There were originally four races on earth: Caucasian, Mongolian, Austric and Negroid.
Like these races, the Semitic people are also a separate race, the people of the Middle East.
In some peopleʼs opinion they are a mixture of the Caucasian and Negroid races.

paragraphs.text: The Caucasian race has three branches – Nordic, Alpine and Mediterranean. The meaning of the word “Nordic” is “northern”; it comes from the Latin word nord. The Alpine people lived neither too far north nor too far south, that is, they were residents of central Europe, the table-lands of the Alps.
summary: The Caucasian race has three branches – Nordic, Alpine and Mediterranean.
The meaning of the word “Nordic” is “northern”; it comes from the Latin word nord.
The Alpine people lived neither too far north nor too far south, that is, they were residents of central Europe, the table-lands of the Alps.

paragraphs.text: Nordic people have high noses, blond hair, ruddy complexion and are tall in stature. Alpine people are relatively short in stature. They are not as ruddy in complexion, have bluish hair and blue eyes. Mediterranean people are fair-complexioned with black hair, black eyes and are somewhat shorter than Alpine people. The collective name for these three branches is “Aryan”. The English word “Aryan” comes from German and originally from the Vedic word árya. As far as can be determined, the word árya comes from the
summary: Nordic people have high noses, blond hair, ruddy complexion and are tall in stature.
Mediterranean people are fair-complexioned with black hair, black eyes and are somewhat shorter than Alpine people.
The English word “Aryan” comes from German and originally from the Vedic word árya.

paragraphs.text: Vedic verbal root r, which means “to cultivate” or “to plough”, so the meaning of the word árya becomes “that person or community whose culture thrives through husbandry”. The original homeland of the Aryans was Europe and the areas lying near the Caucasus Mountains in Central Russia. In northwest India and in Kashmir there are a good number of people of Aryan lineage; however, their population in the rest of India is quite insignificant. The few present are mostly of mixed blood. An attempt to search and locate them would be quite difficult.
summary: Vedic verbal root r, which means “to cultivate” or “to plough”, so the meaning of the word árya becomes “that person or community whose culture thrives through husbandry”.
In northwest India and in Kashmir there are a good number of people of Aryan lineage; however, their population in the rest of India is quite insignificant.
An attempt to search and locate them would be quite difficult.

paragraphs.text: As a result of [the prevalent] Caucasian-centred aristocracy of colour, an erroneous conception has become embedded in the mind which, if clearly pointed out, might cause many people to become uncomfortable. In other words, in order to avoid this uneasiness, short-statured people will have to be accepted as Aryan, dark-complexioned people will have to be accepted as having come from Aryan origins and flat-nosed people will have to be accepted as Aryan – what kind of situation is this? I will hearken back to my original remarks and reiterate that apart from Kashmir and the northwest areas, people in other parts of India are not of the Aryan race. The Caucasians came to India from far away. They belong to the Mediterranean branch, not the Alpine or Nordic. Many people consider them to be the original inhabitants of Kashmir, but that is not correct. The original inhabitants of Kashmir belong to the Kash or Khas clans. They were people with slightly earthen complexion, short stature and snub noses.
summary: As a result of [the prevalent] Caucasian-centred aristocracy of colour, an erroneous conception has become embedded in the mind which, if clearly pointed out, might cause many people to become uncomfortable.
They belong to the Mediterranean branch, not the Alpine or Nordic.
They were people with slightly earthen complexion, short stature and snub noses.

paragraphs.text: The word kashmir comes from the word kash or khas. In old Sanskrit the word meru was used to mean “country”; for example, ajeya meru > ajamiira. The original word is kashmeru. Kashmir means “the land or meru of the Kash people”. Many people write Káshmiir instead of Kashmiir.
summary: The word kashmir comes from the word kash or khas.
The original word is kashmeru.
Many people write Káshmiir instead of Kashmiir.

paragraphs.text: This is incorrect. The word káshmiir is derived by adding the suffix śńa to the word kashmiir, and it means “inhabitants of Kashmiir” or “concerning Kashmiir”. Saffron is produced in Kashmiir, thus saffron is also called káshmiir. The Hindi word keshriyá comes from the word káshmiir and it means “ochre colour”. We can call the Brahmans of Kashmir as Káshmiir Brahmans, not Káshmiirii Brahmans. Káshmiirii means “women from Kashmiir”. In the Rájataraunginii of Kalhan there is a description of the border of Kashmiir:
summary: The word káshmiir is derived by adding the suffix śńa to the word kashmiir, and it means “inhabitants of Kashmiir” or “concerning Kashmiir”.
The Hindi word keshriyá comes from the word káshmiir and it means “ochre colour”.
Káshmiirii means “women from Kashmiir”.

paragraphs.text: Sáradámat́hamárábhya kuḿkumádrtat́aḿtaka,
summary: Sáradámat́hamárábhya kuḿkumádrtat́aḿtaka,

paragraphs.text: Távat kashmiira deshasyád paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.
summary: Távat kashmiira deshasyád paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.

paragraphs.text: That is, Kashmiir is the land which measures fifty yojana [a distance measure ranging from four to ten miles] from Sáradámat́h to the Kumkum Mountains. India has a rich literature, especially in Sanskrit, but there is very little historical literature. Due to philosophical confusion, there was a particular apathy towards history among the people of India. It is due to this apathy that the inhabitants of India were averse to writing history. It has to be pondered by scholars to what extent, apart from the Rájatarauṋginii [Twelfth Century A.D.], can the Rájamálá of Tripura and the Assamese Buraiṋji be classified as history. The greater portion of what we consider to be the history of the Indian Middle Ages had to be collected from the diaries of foreign travellers. In order to write even a single page of history we had to look up Fá-Hiyen, Meghásthinis, Iuḿ, Chuyáḿ, or Ivanavatutá. During the Pathan and Mughal eras some history was recorded in the collections of different sovereigns, but it is difficult to say just how far they are authoritative. However, we can say that even if not all was lost, something certainly was.
summary: That is, Kashmiir is the land which measures fifty yojana [a distance measure ranging from four to ten miles] from Sáradámat́h to the Kumkum Mountains.
], can the Rájamálá of Tripura and the Assamese Buraiṋji be classified as history.
However, we can say that even if not all was lost, something certainly was.

paragraphs.text: The Negroid race has three branches: western, northern and southern. There are differences in their facial appearance and hair. Their hair is similar, but there are differences in the curls. The Mongolian race has five branches: Nippon (Japan), the original Chinese, Indo-Tibetan, Malaysian and Indo-Burmese. The script of the Chinese and Japanese branches is pictorial script. Each respective sound is represented by a particular picture. For example, instead of writing “tree” as we do, a mark is made to signify “tree”. Two of these marks mean “park”. A forest has many trees so three marks are used to mean “forest”. The framework of the Japanese alphabet is also fundamentally Chinese, that is, pictorial. Since the sun first rises over Japan, the name of the country is Nippon. The first syllable is ni and the second syllable is ppon and together they make nippon. Some people pronounce nippon as nihon. In this case they read the second picture hon instead of pon. In Chinese ni is pronounced ji and pon is pronounced pán, thus the pronunciation of nippon in Chinese became jipán. The distorted pronunciation of jipán in English gave rise to “Japan”. The people of the Nippon branch are large in size with flat noses and high jawbones. The Chinese branch is somewhat yellow in complexion and rather short in stature.
summary: The Negroid race has three branches: western, northern and southern.
The framework of the Japanese alphabet is also fundamentally Chinese, that is, pictorial.
The Chinese branch is somewhat yellow in complexion and rather short in stature.

paragraphs.text: The Caucasian alphabet is read from left to right. English, Latin and Greek, are all read from left to right. The Semitic alphabet is read from right to left as are the Arabic and Israeli alphabets. Negroid people do not have their own script. They use Roman script. The people we call Dravidian in India are a mixture of Austric and Negroid. The word támil comes from the word dráviŕa [dravid]. Their script is Indo-Aryan.
summary: The Caucasian alphabet is read from left to right.
They use Roman script.
Their script is Indo-Aryan.

paragraphs.text: The people of the Indo-Tibetan branch are somewhat earthen-coloured and medium in stature. Their script is also Indo-Aryan. In this group are found the Tibetans, Laddakhis,
summary: The people of the Indo-Tibetan branch are somewhat earthen-coloured and medium in stature.
Their script is also Indo-Aryan.

paragraphs.text: Bhutanese, Sherpas, Lepchas, Guruḿs, Newars and Thárus. The Gorkhas do not belong to this branch. The Gorkhas are a mixture of Aryan and Tibetan. Their language, Gorkháli, is not an Indo-Tibetan language; it is a Sanskrit-derived language. Nowadays many people call the Gorkháli language “Nepali”. Actually “Nepali” does not refer to any specific language, but rather to all the languages of Nepal. These languages are Gorkháli, Newári, Rái, Tháru, Guruḿ, Sherpa, Bhutanese, Lepcha, Magar, Limbu, Limpá, Bhojpurii (western Madeshii), Angika (Moráḿ), Maethilii (central Madeshii) and Bengali (Jháṋpá District). “Nepali” does not refer to a particular language any more than the word “Indian” does.
summary: Bhutanese, Sherpas, Lepchas, Guruḿs, Newars and Thárus.
Nowadays many people call the Gorkháli language “Nepali”.
“Nepali” does not refer to a particular language any more than the word “Indian” does.

paragraphs.text: The Gorkhas have adopted an Indo-Aryan script. Indo-Aryan scripts begin with a and end with kśa. The Indo-Aryan languages of Nepal are included in the same group as Bengali, and approximately twelve hundred years ago all of these languages were one and the same. The Caryápada or Caryácaryavinishcaya was written in this language. It should be remembered here that the Caryácaryavinishcaya was discovered in Nepal and it was written in the Bengali script of that time (Shriiharśa script). The language of the Caryácaryavinishcaya can just as well be called old Angika or old Maethilii as old Bengali. Their script was also the old Bengali script, or Shriiharśa. It should also be remembered here that during the time of the Newári kings, Maethilii, written in Shriiharśa script, was the court language of Nepal. Gorkháli gained acceptance as the court language of Nepal during the reign of the Gorkha kings (Prthviináráyańa Sháh), and it is this Gorkháli that is mistakenly called Nepali. Of course this is a partial error, not a complete error, because, like Nepalʼs other languages, Gorkháli is also a Nepali language. Gorkháliʼs old script is also Shriiharśa script. Later on Nágrii letters were introduced into Gorkháli. Old letters and records are all written in Bengali script (Shriiharśa). Thus the discovery of the old Bengali manuscript, the Caryápada, in Nepal is not at all surprising because Nepal is a land of Bengali script. When Lolitapat́t́an (Lolitapát́an), and Bhat́t́agrám (Bhát́gáon) were the capital of Nepal, they used Shriiharśa script exclusively.
summary: The Gorkhas have adopted an Indo-Aryan script.
It should also be remembered here that during the time of the Newári kings, Maethilii, written in Shriiharśa script, was the court language of Nepal.
When Lolitapat́t́an (Lolitapát́an), and Bhat́t́agrám (Bhát́gáon) were the capital of Nepal, they used Shriiharśa script exclusively.

paragraphs.text: The fourth branch is the Malay branch. Included within this branch are the Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia. Chinese, Kachin, Shan, Burmese and Arakan (Mag) fall within the Indo-Burmese branch. None of these languages use pictorial script. They use Indo-Aryan scripts, that is, they are written from left to right.
summary: The fourth branch is the Malay branch.
Chinese, Kachin, Shan, Burmese and Arakan (Mag) fall within the Indo-Burmese branch.
They use Indo-Aryan scripts, that is, they are written from left to right.

paragraphs.text: Next is the Austric branch. At one time there was one vast expanse of land which stretched from old Gondwanaland to Australia. The original inhabitants of this vast region were the ancient Austrics. They are black but not jet black. They are shorter in stature than Negroes and their hair is not as curly. Indiaʼs Kols, Bhiils, Muńd́as, Hars (Santhals) and Biirhoŕas, and the aborigines and Maoris of Australia and New Zealand all belong to the Austric branch; however, the native inhabitants of the Andaman Islands do not. They are a mixture of Austric and Mongolian. The Jarvadiis who live along the Bengal-Burma border are also more or less of the same blend.
summary: Next is the Austric branch.
They are shorter in stature than Negroes and their hair is not as curly.
The Jarvadiis who live along the Bengal-Burma border are also more or less of the same blend.

paragraphs.text: The Austric branch did not have its own script. They became familiar with Roman script when Christian missionaries came in contact with them while proselytizing. Indiaʼs Kols, Bhiils, Muńd́as, Santhals and Biirhoŕas also belong to the Austric branch; they do not have their own script. The “Ol” script that some Santhals like to use was invented by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, a man of modern times.
summary: The Austric branch did not have its own script.
Indiaʼs Kols, Bhiils, Muńd́as, Santhals and Biirhoŕas also belong to the Austric branch; they do not have their own script.
The “Ol” script that some Santhals like to use was invented by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, a man of modern times.

paragraphs.text: The script of the Dravidian group is Indo-Aryan; however, here and there they have an extra letter or two, or perhaps one or two less. For example, Tamil has fewer letters while Telegu has more. While it is true that the lack of those few letters in modern Tamil makes it difficult to write Sanskrit properly, it is even more true that the particular kind of Tamil script that Tamil pandits use for writing Sanskrit works perfectly fine. This script goes by the name of Granthalipi or Granthákśaram [book script]. The authorʼs professor in the Vedas, Pandit P. K. Ayar, was able to write very proper Sanskrit in this script. ( 1 ) The script has neither disappeared nor become completely obsolete today. In modern Tamil the numbers one and two are written alongside several letters to indicate a particular pronunciation. Others want to use certain Singhalese letters for this purpose, but there is no necessity. Tamil has its own closely related script. By using book script, Tamil will gain added respect.
summary: The script of the Dravidian group is Indo-Aryan; however, here and there they have an extra letter or two, or perhaps one or two less.
Ayar, was able to write very proper Sanskrit in this script.
By using book script, Tamil will gain added respect.

paragraphs.text: The Singhalese are a mixture of Aryan and Dravidian races. They are fair-complexioned and short in stature. Their language has a large number of Sanskrit words. It is also a mixture of Aryan and Dravidian and most likely originated from a blending of Tamil and Bengali in ancient times; however, more research into this issue is required. The Oráon sub-caste in the Chottanagpur area is also part of the Dravidian group, not the Austric group. Their language, which is called Kuruk, is a Dravidian language. However, Kuruk does not have its own script. The Oráons take their surnames from the names of different birds and animals, for example, Kacchap [tortoise], T́oppo and Miinz. Miinz means “fish” in Kuruk. In Tamil it is miinam. Many people think that miina is a Sanskrit word, but actually it is not. It is a Dravidian word that was absorbed into Sanskrit.
summary: The Singhalese are a mixture of Aryan and Dravidian races.
However, Kuruk does not have its own script.
It is a Dravidian word that was absorbed into Sanskrit.

paragraphs.text: In Bengal there is a mixture of Austric, Mongolian and Negroid stock. The further west and southwest you move, the greater the Dravidian (Austric-Negro) influence, and the further northeast you go, the greater the Mongolian influence. There is a great Mongolian influence seen in the Bengali Cákmás. The Cákmás live in the mountains of Chittagong, certain parts of Tripura and in the Demagiri region of the Lusái Hills (its modern name is Mizoram). The Mongolian influence is also pronounced in the far north of Bengal among the Bhutanese, Mech, Boŕo and Poliya communities. ( 2 )
summary: In Bengal there is a mixture of Austric, Mongolian and Negroid stock.
There is a great Mongolian influence seen in the Bengali Cákmás.
The Mongolian influence is also pronounced in the far north of Bengal among the Bhutanese, Mech, Boŕo and Poliya communities.

footnotes.text: Amongst the Tamil Brahmans, the Shaivites go by the name of Ayar and the Vaeśńavites go by the name of Ayengar. The Shaivites use a horizontal tilaka [decorative mark with religious significance] while the Vaeshnavites use a vertical tilaka.
The foregoing eighteen paragraphs are from the English edition of Varńa Vijiṋána, Discourse 9.

chapters.title: Semitic Languages and Scripts
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Hebrew and Arabic

Hebrew is a close contemporary of Latin. It is a Semitic language, that is, it is between an Aryan and non-Aryan language. The Semitic lands stretched from Eastern Europe to Western Asia, that is, from Turkey in the north to Eritrea in the south (ancient Abyssinia, modern-day northern Ethiopia). The crown jewel of this Semitic land was the Hebrew language. In subsequent times, Hebrew was divided into two branches. One was medieval Hebrew and the other was old Arabic. However, we do not have a modern Hebrew language developed from medieval Hebrew because, for certain reasons, those whose mother tongue was medieval Hebrew abandoned their homeland and scattered to various parts of the globe. For this reason, their original mother tongue disappeared. Their descendants, who returned to this Semitic land, have resuscitated medieval Hebrew and now use it in their everyday activities. They have also brought back to life the Semitic script [Hebrew] of that era. In addition, they have made significant strides towards the creation of a new literature. I was very happy to see these efforts to create a new literature when I was in Israel.
summary: Hebrew is a close contemporary of Latin.

However, we do not have a modern Hebrew language developed from medieval Hebrew because, for certain reasons, those whose mother tongue was medieval Hebrew abandoned their homeland and scattered to various parts of the globe.
I was very happy to see these efforts to create a new literature when I was in Israel.

paragraphs.text: Israelis are using the old Hebrew script. As with the language, the script is also Semitic. Arabic and Hebrew scripts belong to the same family, just as the two languages do. Moreover, the old Greek script and ancient Roman script were formerly used for Latin, which is indicative of the connection between the two. One difference is that the old Greek and Roman scripts are read from left to right, while the Semitic scripts are read from right to left. There is also similarity in the names of the letters. One says áliph and another says alpha. One says be and another says beta. Arabic script has diphthongs. In this system the diphthongs are written by joining the head of one letter to the tail of the other. Although this system remained in old Roman script, it is not found in modern Roman script.
summary: Israelis are using the old Hebrew script.
There is also similarity in the names of the letters.
Although this system remained in old Roman script, it is not found in modern Roman script.

paragraphs.text: I was speaking about the Arabic language. Arabic is a moderately developed language. At present, several states, especially Iraq and Egypt, are making full-fledged attempts to create a new Arabic literature. In Egypt one sees the clear influence of French literature over Arabic literature. Egypt was under French influence for quite some time. Thereafter British influence increased, and consequently it benefited from the constructive literary work of both the British and the French. Although Iraq did not have this opportunity, it is moving ahead rapidly.
summary: I was speaking about the Arabic language.
In Egypt one sees the clear influence of French literature over Arabic literature.
Although Iraq did not have this opportunity, it is moving ahead rapidly.

paragraphs.text: Farsi is written today in a changed and expanded version of Arabic script. In other words, it has increased the number of letters according to its needs. Old Farsi, however, was not written in Arabic script. This [custom] has only prevailed in the last one thousand years. Prior to that Farsi was written in the Bráhmii and Kharośt́hii scripts. Farsi is not a Semitic language. It is an Aryan language and a distorted form of the southern branch of Vedic. Some of the Indian languages belong to Vedicʼs southeastern branch and distortion, just as Latin is Vedicʼs western branch and distortion. Medieval Farsi was a developed language and its literature achieved significant development. While modern Farsi literature has also moved forward on the path of development, its speed is comparatively less than that of medieval Farsi.
summary: Farsi is written today in a changed and expanded version of Arabic script.
Farsi is not a Semitic language.
While modern Farsi literature has also moved forward on the path of development, its speed is comparatively less than that of medieval Farsi.

paragraphs.text: There is some Negroid influence and some Aryan influence in Semitic countries, but Vedic influence is negligible, though it cannot be altogether discounted. The Old Testament was first written in Hebrew. Later it was translated into Latin. ( 1 )
summary: There is some Negroid influence and some Aryan influence in Semitic countries, but Vedic influence is negligible, though it cannot be altogether discounted.
The Old Testament was first written in Hebrew.
Later it was translated into Latin.

paragraphs.text: Semitic script

Today Hebrew, Semitic is the official language of Israel, though it is not [completely] the day-to-day conversational language of the people. This language ceased to exist in Israel quite a few centuries ago. Since then, the Jews residing in different lands attempted to keep Hebrew alive as their language of religion and culture, but they could not revive it as their customary language. In recent times, converging from different lands, the Israelis are using Hebrew, the language of their culture, as the official language of their nation. After a long hibernation, the language has been resuscitated and is gradually turning into their customary conversational language. The three chief Semitic languages are (1) Ottoman Turkish, (2) Hebrew and (3) Ancient Arabic. A great similarity exists among these languages, with only a few disparities. Though the official Hebrew language has changed to some extent from the language of the Old Testament, the change is minimal. If the Hebrew language had remained alive for three thousand years and evolved accordingly, present Hebrew would certainly have changed substantially from the language of the Old Testament. However, that did not happen due to its long hibernation.
summary: Today Hebrew, Semitic is the official language of Israel, though it is not [completely] the day-to-day conversational language of the people.
The three chief Semitic languages are (1) Ottoman Turkish, (2) Hebrew and (3) Ancient Arabic.

When the Turks used Arabic scripts they did follow this rule. However, since the days of Kemal Ataturk, Turks have been using Roman script for their language. The context of their language has somehow deviated from the Semitic family and come closer to the Aryan family. Prior to their returning to Israel, the Jews living in any particular land would accept the local language of that land as their mother tongue. In some countries they used Iaáaáltiish [Yiddish] as their domestic language.

paragraphs.text: In synagogues, (places of Jewish worship) we saw that Hebrew was pronounced in its ancient intonation. Now that Hebrew has become the official Jewish language, or at least of those residing in Israel, there might be some impact of modern pronunciation on the language used in their synagogues. Jews have lived in the state of Kerala, India since very ancient times. They used Malayalam as their conversational language. Malayalam had a considerable impact on their pronunciation of the Hebrew language in the synagogues. Of course, a few of them attempted to pronounce Hebrew with the correct intonation. At one time in Armenian churches of Turkey, services were given in Hebrew instead of in Latin. Perhaps now they are offered in Latin or in Armenian Turkish. Even in Kolkata, there were once many Armenians. They had their own churches (perhaps they have them even now). I had no opportunity to know what language is used in their services today. Of course, the pronunciation of the first letter a in Armenian is very close to that of Greek, which is slightly different from that of Semitic. In Hebrew, Arabic, Ottoman and Iaáaáltiish [Yiddish] languages the first letter has two pronunciations – a and áya.

paragraphs.text: Hebrew and ancient Arabic were languages belonging to the same Semitic lineage – both were Semitic. Hebrew was uprooted from the land of Israel several centuries ago. Like ancient Arabic, it also died a natural death. Yet while ancient Arabic took on a new and transformed appearance, Hebrew did not, since the people speaking Hebrew were dispersed to many different lands. In certain parts of Europe, due to blending of Hebrew with local languages, Yiddish language took birth; however, it cannot be described as a transformation of the Hebrew language. After the establishment of the new state of Israel, Hebrew was made the state language and [at present] it is flourishing. If one looks at the revival of the Hebrew language in Israel, one has to wonder and reflect on the enormity of mental strength and stamina required to revive and resuscitate a language. Those conceited pundits who satisfy themselves by declaring that Sanskrit is a dead language should ponder and draw lessons therefrom. The time has come to reconsider the extent to which one is justified in declaring a language such as Sanskrit to be extinct. [Indians] not only borrow words several hundred times a day from Sanskrit but also borrow constantly from its style of expression, artistry and idioms.
summary: Hebrew and ancient Arabic were languages belonging to the same Semitic lineage – both were Semitic.
After the establishment of the new state of Israel, Hebrew was made the state language and [at present] it is flourishing.
[Indians] not only borrow words several hundred times a day from Sanskrit but also borrow constantly from its style of expression, artistry and idioms.

paragraphs.text: Hebrew and ancient Arabic belong to the same family and hence are sister languages. Thus the present author had the advantage of learning ancient Arabic while pursuing the Hebrew language. During my stay in Israel, I saw how nicely and commendably the Hebrew language was being cultivated. However, to my regret, I also noticed that ancient Arabic was not being pursued and cultivated with the same zeal in any country, even in comparatively developed countries such as Iraq, Lebanon and Egypt. Today, ancient Arabic not only lies veiled behind a dark curtain but is also in a mist of neglect and disregard. ( 3 )

chapters.title: History of Scripts
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Emanation also affects script and letters. I have already mentioned that a language survives approximately one thousand years. Individual scripts, however, last about two thousand years. Written script did not exist at the beginning of the Yajurvedic era. Written script was invented in India towards the end of that era, that is, about five thousand years ago. At the time when script was invented the sages thought that the creation was a composite of a-u-ma, that is, creation, preservation and destruction. However, the manifest universe is a result of the influence of the guńas of Prakrti over consciousness – the supremacy of the binding faculty over the cognitive faculty. In other words, Parama Puruśa comes within the jurisdiction of the binding power of Prakrti. This manifest universe is called saḿvrttibodhicitta in the Buddhist nomenclature and káryabrahma (expressed universe) in Aryan nomenclature. In order to indicate this state of Puruśa and Prakrti a vertical line is used for Puruśa and a horizontal line is used for Prakrti. Together the two form a cross (+) which signifies káryabrahma or the created universe. The biija [seed] mantra of káryabrahma is ka, so this cross became ka in the Bráhmii script. Through the process of writing the Bráhmii ka quickly it became transformed through distortion into todayʼs letter ka. For example:
summary: Emanation also affects script and letters.
However, the manifest universe is a result of the influence of the guńas of Prakrti over consciousness – the supremacy of the binding faculty over the cognitive faculty.
Through the process of writing the Bráhmii ka quickly it became transformed through distortion into todayʼs letter ka.

paragraphs.text: Hence we see that in the case of written script emanation also remains intact. The name of the first script invented by the people of India is Bráhmii or Kharośt́hii script. With the passage of time this Bráhmii-Kharośt́hii script evolved into three separate scripts. The name of the distorted script to the southwest of Allahabad is Náradá script. The distorted form to the northwest of Allahabad is Sáradá script. The script that arose in Allahabad and the lands east of there is known as Kut́ilá script.
summary: Hence we see that in the case of written script emanation also remains intact.
The name of the distorted script to the southwest of Allahabad is Náradá script.
The script that arose in Allahabad and the lands east of there is known as Kut́ilá script.

paragraphs.text: The area where Náradá script was used included the western areas of modern Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Sindhu, Gujarat and Maharashtra. The Nágar pandits of Gujarat wrote many Sanskrit compositions in Náradá script. Later the script was named Nágarii after them. When they wrote their local language in this script they used to call it Deshii Nágarii or Moŕi. When they wrote Sanskrit (devabháśá) they would write with conjuncts by joining the upper lines [mátrá]. Then they would call the script Devanágarii. Although the modern Gujarati script is Deshiinágarii and does not have mátrá, it does have conjuncts. Among the Moŕi scripts that were used to write the different languages of Rajasthan (Marwari, Mevárii, Háŕaoti, D́hund́háru, Meváti, etc.), western Madhya Pradesh (Málavii, Bundelii), and Maharashtra (Marathi, Varáŕi, Khándeshii, Koḿkanii), Maharashtraʼs Moŕi has conjuncts in certain circumstances. However the remaining Moŕi scripts did not and do not have conjuncts. Although modern Marathi books and so forth are printed in Devanágarii script, Devanágarii is not Maharashtraʼs script. The Moŕi scripts of Rajasthan (Curuwalii, Yodhpurii, Jhunjhunwalii, etc.) are still commonly used by the general public, especially by merchants. Sindhuʼs script is not used for printing modern-day books and so on. Books in Sindhi are now printed with Farsi script, however the old Sindhi script, or Láháńd́ei, is still prevalent among merchants.
summary: The area where Náradá script was used included the western areas of modern Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Sindhu, Gujarat and Maharashtra.
Among the Moŕi scripts that were used to write the different languages of Rajasthan (Marwari, Mevárii, Háŕaoti, D́hund́háru, Meváti, etc.
Books in Sindhi are now printed with Farsi script, however the old Sindhi script, or Láháńd́ei, is still prevalent among merchants.

paragraphs.text: The northwestern Sáradá script evolved into several branches. The T́ekŕi, T́egŕi or T́eḿŕei (this script is a close relative of Tibetan script) scripts of the Himalayan mountain regions, Laddaki script (it is also a close relative of Tibetan script), Kashmiri Sáradá (the script in which the modern-day Kashmir pandits write Sanskrit), and D́uggardeshii Sáradá (the script of Jammuʼs D́ogri language), etc. are all distortions of the ancient Sáradá script. The script in which modern-day Panjabi is written is known as Guŕmukhii script. It is not a natural distortion of Sáradá. The Sikh guru, Arjanadeva, introduced this script (there is some difference of opinion regarding this). This script does not have full conjuncts either, however if some effort is made conjuncts can be introduced. This will eliminate the need to write words such as skul, st́ap, st́eshan, etc. as sakul, satap, sat́eshan.
summary: The northwestern Sáradá script evolved into several branches.
It is not a natural distortion of Sáradá.
as sakul, satap, sat́eshan.

paragraphs.text: The pandits did not write down the Vedas for a long time, even after the invention of script. They used to believe that the Vedas should not be written down since their forefathers had not done so. Had they looked into it a little more deeply they would have realized that the Vedas were not written down in ancient times because written script did not exist. Later, when the Vedas could no longer be committed to memory, the Kashmir pandits were the first to write them down and they did so in this distorted Sáradá script. ( 1 )
summary: The pandits did not write down the Vedas for a long time, even after the invention of script.
Had they looked into it a little more deeply they would have realized that the Vedas were not written down in ancient times because written script did not exist.
Later, when the Vedas could no longer be committed to memory, the Kashmir pandits were the first to write them down and they did so in this distorted Sáradá script.

paragraphs.text: Although the scientific name of the script that arose in the lands east of Allahabad is Kut́ilá, it is better known as Shriiharśa in the annals of history. The gold coins of the emperor Harśavarddhan were inscribed with this script. It has been found in Kaoshámbi near Allahabad. Modern Bengali, Maethilii, Manipuri, Assamese and Oriya are written in this script. The scripts of Angika, Bhojpurii, Magahii, Chattisgarhii and Nagpurii are also Shriiharśa scripts, but since the people have forgotten their mother scripts and have not been able to create a developed literature of their own up until now, they do their writing and reading nowadays in Hindi. Since Hindi books are printed in Devanágarii script they are more familiar with Devanágarii script.
summary: Although the scientific name of the script that arose in the lands east of Allahabad is Kut́ilá, it is better known as Shriiharśa in the annals of history.
Modern Bengali, Maethilii, Manipuri, Assamese and Oriya are written in this script.
Since Hindi books are printed in Devanágarii script they are more familiar with Devanágarii script.

paragraphs.text: Oriya script is also Shriiharśa script but the people of those days used to write on palm leaves with a type of iron spud. In order to keep the palm leaves from being torn by the iron spud they rounded off the corners. Thus the modern-day Oriya script looks somewhat circular. Actually Bengali script and Oriya script are the same. The letters of Bengali script have corners, that is, they are angular, while Oriya script is circular. So in the olden days Bengali script used to be called the Gaod́iiya [Bengali] style of Kut́ilá script and Oriya used to be called the Od́ra style of Kut́ilá script.
summary: Oriya script is also Shriiharśa script but the people of those days used to write on palm leaves with a type of iron spud.

So in the olden days Bengali script used to be called the Gaod́iiya [Bengali] style of Kut́ilá script and Oriya used to be called the Od́ra style of Kut́ilá script.

paragraphs.text: The effect of emanation can also be seen in Bengali script. For example, in old Bengali ya used to be joined to the original letter in order to indicate a conjunct with ya. Formerly, all ya-conjuncts were written the way dya is written today (). In other words a kind of curved ya was written after the letter. This is no longer done in modern Bengali. Previously, kya, dya, tya, bhya, etc. used to be written:
summary: The effect of emanation can also be seen in Bengali script.
In other words a kind of curved ya was written after the letter.
Previously, kya, dya, tya, bhya, etc.

paragraphs.text: In old Bengali one ta was written underneath the other to indicate tta. Nowadays, however, the tail of the upper ta does not extend back up and the hem of the lower ta begins where the tail leaves off; the letter looks like the letter o. The difference is that tta has an upper line [mátrá] while the o does not. Similarly, the conjunct tra was written with a ra below the ta. Nowadays the tail of ta does not extend back up and the hem of the ra begins where it leaves off. The letter looks like the letter e, the difference being that the letter e does not have a mátrá while the conjunct tra does. If you look at any of the Bengali compound letters you will find that they are actually a proper blending of the original letters. This blending results from taking the path of emanation.
summary: In old Bengali one ta was written underneath the other to indicate tta.
Nowadays the tail of ta does not extend back up and the hem of the ra begins where it leaves off.
This blending results from taking the path of emanation.

paragraphs.text: We were talking about the Sáradá, Náradá and Kut́ilá scripts. The Sáradá script developed from the Bráhmii script; it achieved its full form about thirteen hundred years ago. Similarly, the Kut́ilá script achieved its maturity about eleven hundred years ago and the Nágarii script about eight hundred years ago. Thus very old Sanskrit manuscripts can be found in this Sáradá script. Moderately old manuscripts are found in Kut́ilá or Shriiharśa script. Nowadays those who are involved in deciphering obscure passages of old Sanskrit texts and reprinting those texts cannot avoid taking the help of scholars versed in the Sáradá and Shriiharśa scripts. During British rule, when arrangements were made for the study of Sanskrit in universities, there was a need felt to print the textbooks in a specific script so they began printing them in Devanágarii script. The use of Devanágarii script instead of Shriiharśa for Sanskrit in Varanasi, the then centre of Sanskrit study, became common at that time despite the fact that the local script was Shriiharśa and that Shriiharśa is found on stone engravings recovered there. However the pandits at Sanskrit schools in different parts of India used to write Sanskrit in their customary local script and still do so today. So no one should harbour the conception that Devanágarii is Sanskritʼs only script. Actually Sanskrit does not have its own script. Every script commonly used in different parts of India is Sanskritʼs script. Among these, the Sáradá, Shriiharśa and the south Indian scripts are older than Devanágarii. ( 2 )
summary: We were talking about the Sáradá, Náradá and Kut́ilá scripts.
