chapters.title: Shriiharśa and Other Scripts
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Shriiharśa Script

Many of you know that what passes for Bengali script today is traditionally known as Shriiharśa script. In ancient India, Saendhavii script was a bhávátmaka lipi [a script based on bháva, that is, ideas]. In the context of its lineage, it was somewhat related to Chinese pictorial script, though it did not belong exactly to the same family or type. In Saendhavii, one single idea was represented to a certain extent in the form of a single letter with the help of pictures. Bráhmii-Khorośt́hii ( 1 ) script was its metamorphosed form. Bráhmii script was prevalent in eastern India until the time of Ashoka, when the stone edicts of Ashoka were inscribed in Bráhmii letters. Now, is the oldest form of Bengali script, known thus far as Shriiharśa script, actually Shriiharśa script? Does Shriiharśa script in fact belong to the period of Emperor Shriiharśa? Did the script not exist before it came to be inscribed on the seals of King Harśavardhana? Has the Bengali first letter a or other letters of the present Bengali language come indirectly from Bráhmii script or directly from Shriiharśa script?
summary: Many of you know that what passes for Bengali script today is traditionally known as Shriiharśa script.
Bráhmii script was prevalent in eastern India until the time of Ashoka, when the stone edicts of Ashoka were inscribed in Bráhmii letters.
Has the Bengali first letter a or other letters of the present Bengali language come indirectly from Bráhmii script or directly from Shriiharśa script?

paragraphs.text: When examining the first Bengali letter a, one understands its indirect link with Bráhmii script as well as with Shriiharśa script. As a result, scholars came to the conclusion that the present Bengali resemblance to Shriiharśa script is about eleven hundred to twelve hundred years old. The appearance of Shushuniyá script in Bankura district (the deed of King Chandravarmaʼs gift, which is inscribed on the walls of Shushuniyá hills near Chatna police station in Bankura District) suggests that it is definitely the old Bengali script, and that this script is very close to Shriiharśa script. From the language and ideas revealed in that script, it can be understood that in Bengal (especially in Ráŕh) at that time, a new Hindu religion (not the ancient Puranic religion, that is, religion based on Bráhminism, and not the Vedic/Árśa religion or the Jain religion) was prevalent. So it is not difficult to surmise that the edict was inscribed during the Gupta age [from 320 A.D.] or some time later.
summary: When examining the first Bengali letter a, one understands its indirect link with Bráhmii script as well as with Shriiharśa script.

From the language and ideas revealed in that script, it can be understood that in Bengal (especially in Ráŕh) at that time, a new Hindu religion (not the ancient Puranic religion, that is, religion based on Bráhminism, and not the Vedic/Árśa religion or the Jain religion) was prevalent.
] or some time later.

paragraphs.text: When the people of Bengal, especially of Ráŕh, came into the realm of [recorded] history, they were devotees of Lord Shiva. This definitely occurred after the emergence of Sadáshiva – significantly less than seven thousand five hundred years ago. From this very period, it can be reasonably surmised that the people of Western Ráŕh were known as Máhátos. Today certain people claim that the Máhátos are descendants of Shivajii, since they introduced the system of agriculture in Western Ráŕh with the help of bullocks and ploughs. Others used to address them reverentially as Mahátman, which later turned into Máhátos. The Máháto civilization is at least seven thousand years old. They are the sons of the soil of Western Ráŕh. However, the emergence of Shivajii [1627] took place towards the end of the Mughal period. So by what logic could they be the descendants of Shivajii, who appeared only a few hundred years ago? How could more than fifty lakh [5,000,000] Máhátos be the descendants of Shivaji, who emerged only a few hundred years ago? The idea is antithetical to history and illogical. In reality, Máhátos are [among] the original Bengalis, such as Siḿmuŕá, Kháuṋgármuŕá, Kheriámuŕá, Ho-muŕá and Kushmet́muŕá of Western Ráŕh. They never originated from outside Bengal. Rather, the intellectual and wealthy people originated from within their own ranks. Attempting to pass themselves off as a distinct and separate race, they have turned themselves into so-called upper-caste Bengalis. Hence I have designated Máhátos as the ját báuṋgálii [original Bengalees], meaning that most communities of western Ráŕh have descended from this community.
summary: When the people of Bengal, especially of Ráŕh, came into the realm of [recorded] history, they were devotees of Lord Shiva.
So by what logic could they be the descendants of Shivajii, who appeared only a few hundred years ago?
Hence I have designated Máhátos as the ját báuṋgálii [original Bengalees], meaning that most communities of western Ráŕh have descended from this community.

paragraphs.text: This description is applicable not only to the Máhátos of western Ráŕh. Even the Kaevarta-Máhiśya of southern Ráŕh, Gope-Sadgopes of Central-North Ráŕh, Ráj-Baḿshii of North Bengal, Kot́ál-Namashúdras of Central Bengal and Cákmás (shákyamás) of Eastern Bengal are from this original Bengali community [Máhátos, Siḿmuŕa, etc.]. They did not originate from outside Bengal. Rather, they are the actual foundation of Bengali civilization and its upholder, its vehicle and nurturer. It is true that the so-called upper-castes have enhanced the glamour of Bengali society, but they are not its primary foundation. Since these original Bengalis have been neglected for so long (the pure Bengali equivalent for ‘so long’ is etadin, but we pronounce it ayáddin, according to the local Kolkata dialect of Bengali), the all-round development of Bengalis who followed Shaeva Dharma was not possible.
summary: This description is applicable not only to the Máhátos of western Ráŕh.
Rather, they are the actual foundation of Bengali civilization and its upholder, its vehicle and nurturer.

Since these original Bengalis have been neglected for so long (the pure Bengali equivalent for ‘so long’ is etadin, but we pronounce it ayáddin, according to the local Kolkata dialect of Bengali), the all-round development of Bengalis who followed Shaeva Dharma was not possible.

paragraphs.text: After a long period of time, that is, about two thousand five hundred years ago, Vardhaman Mahaviir, founder of the Jain religion, came to Astinagar with the goal of giving instruction on dharma. Earlier known as Atthinagar, the town was given its current name Vardhamán [Burdwan], in honour of Varddhaman [Vardhaman is also correct] Mahaviir. It was the central hub of activities of Ráŕh in those days. It is there that he preached his religious ideas. From that time onwards, the people of Ráŕh embraced the Jain religion, but they did not forget their ancient Deity, Lord Shiva. The situation was very much like that of the green plating on a golden ring. The gold was Shaeva Dharma, and the plating was that of the Digambar Jain religion.
summary: After a long period of time, that is, about two thousand five hundred years ago, Vardhaman Mahaviir, founder of the Jain religion, came to Astinagar with the goal of giving instruction on dharma.
It is there that he preached his religious ideas.
The gold was Shaeva Dharma, and the plating was that of the Digambar Jain religion.

paragraphs.text: Due to the impact of the Jain religion, the people of Ráŕh, though advanced in courage and valour, became averse to giving battle. They have silently [endured all sorts of] wrongs and injustices as they considered that to protest was an impious act. [However], the teachings of Shiva did not conform to this [ideology.] Even today, in the rural areas of Ráŕh, festivals like gájan, caŕak, jhṋápán and bolán [all local festivals related to Shiva], which have no relation to the Digambar Jain religion, are observed.
summary: Due to the impact of the Jain religion, the people of Ráŕh, though advanced in courage and valour, became averse to giving battle.
[However], the teachings of Shiva did not conform to this [ideology.

] Even today, in the rural areas of Ráŕh, festivals like gájan, caŕak, jhṋápán and bolán [all local festivals related to Shiva], which have no relation to the Digambar Jain religion, are observed.

paragraphs.text: By examining stone inscriptions, one could surmise that Shushuniyá script was about eleven hundred to twelve hundred years old, which tallies with the period of the new Hindu [Puranic] age. Yet prior to that in Ráŕh was Shaeva dharma or a blending of Shaeva dharma with Jainism. The symbol of Jain Shiva was the huge Shiva-liuṋga, known commonly as Jyotirliuṋga, and the gigantic Gaorii-pat́t́a, which is found in various ruins. The worship of these Shivas was not performed by Brahman priests of the new Hindu age but by native Bengalis known as láyá or Páńd́e-Brahmans. (They worked as priests amongst the tribals or so-called lower caste Hindus.) The priests of the D́om community still use the title of “Pandit” and the priests of the Sadgope community use “Deváḿshii” (deváḿshii > deáḿshii > deáshii) as their title. It may be that they use it even today. Traditionally, the stone idols of Lord Shiva, known as Jyotirliuṋga, have been found in Ráŕh in large numbers, especially in Western Ráŕh. Some time ago this Jain Shiva idol was found even in Burdwan, and is presently being worshipped as Vardhamáneshvar.
summary: By examining stone inscriptions, one could surmise that Shushuniyá script was about eleven hundred to twelve hundred years old, which tallies with the period of the new Hindu [Puranic] age.

paragraphs.text: Since the time of Harśavardhan, in Ráŕh as well as all of Bengal, there emerged the Maháyánii Buddhist religion. Due to the presence of Jainism in Ráŕh since early times, Buddhism could not strike as deep a root there as it could at Samatat́ [South Bengal], Davák [Dacca and adjacent districts of Bangladesh] and several other parts of Bengal. The Buddhist Shiva idols or Kúrma Shiva idols look somewhat like kúrmas [tortoise] or like the letter “zero,”which symbolizes the Buddhist concept of shunyaváda [nihilism.] Shankarácárya said, Yathá Shúnyavádináḿ sunyaḿ Brahma Brahmavidáḿstathá [“What Shúnya is for the followers of Shúnyaváda, Brahma is for the followers of Brahma.”]

paragraphs.text: When the Puranic religion was sweeping across Bengal, Kúrma Shiva was transformed into Dharmaráj or Dharmat́hákura, and elsewhere into Buŕoshiva. The priests for these deities were primarily native Bengalis. Some of these priests who followed the Puranic religion used threads of copper. Close to Kolkata (in the Shálkiyá area) is Dharmatalla, where the god Dharmat́hákur is also found. Dharmatalla Street of Kolkata is named after this Buddhist Shiva or Dharmat́hákur (I have already mentioned earlier and I say it again that by changing its name, a desecration of history has been perpetrated. I am certain that before committing this act, the wrongdoers did not consult any historian.) From the above-mentioned facts ( 2 ), it can be understood that before the existence of Shushuniyá script in Ráŕh or Bengal there existed Shaeva Dharma, Digambar Jainism influenced by Shaivism and Maháyánii Buddhism. However, Maháyánii Buddhism was prevalent throughout Bengal. Hinayánii Buddhism or sthavirváda (Theraváda) existed only in Chittagong, where it still persists to some extent.

Dharmatalla Street of Kolkata is named after this Buddhist Shiva or Dharmat́hákur (I have already mentioned earlier and I say it again that by changing its name, a desecration of history has been perpetrated.

paragraphs.text: Dálmá script – a new discovery
summary: Dálmá script – a new discovery

paragraphs.text: A good number of relics from the Jain period have been found recently in Bhulá-Pávanpur village of P. S. Patamda as well as in the adjoining Báiṋgurdá village of Kamalpur P. S. and Jáydá village of Chandil P.S. [in Singhbhum District – Ráŕh], to the southwest. Along with these relics, the Bengali script of that period has been found. That script must be seventeen hundred years old or more, because during that entire period Ráŕh witnessed the golden era of Jainism mingled with the Shaivite cult. The broken idols that can be found are all those of Digambar Jain gods. The script that has been discovered must be older than that of Shushuniyá script. It could even be older than the Shriiharśa script found in the seals of Harśavardhan. The script belongs to the family of Shriiharśa script, but it is far more ancient. It is probable that this script has evolved from Bráhmii script, or perhaps it has not; it might be the original eastern Indian script.
summary: A good number of relics from the Jain period have been found recently in Bhulá-Pávanpur village of P.
That script must be seventeen hundred years old or more, because during that entire period Ráŕh witnessed the golden era of Jainism mingled with the Shaivite cult.
It is probable that this script has evolved from Bráhmii script, or perhaps it has not; it might be the original eastern Indian script.

paragraphs.text: During the rule of Ashoka, Ráŕh was included in the Magadha Empire. Even after the demise of King Shasháuṋka, Ráŕh was part of the Tháneshvar (Harśavardhan) dynasty. It does not mean that the particular Shriiharśa script found in the seal of Harśavardhan, was also prevalent in the distant land of Ráŕh. Of course, it could be surmised that the script of Ráŕh, though similar to that of Shriiharśa script, is much older. Ashoka used Bráhmii script in his stone inscriptions, but no such stone inscription in Bráhmii script can be found in Ráŕh, and Ráŕh was under the rule of Ashoka. There was no dearth of hills, nor was there any scarcity of stone; in fact, many broken stone idols have been found. Then why did Ashoka not erect stone pillars bearing religious instructions in this region?
summary: During the rule of Ashoka, Ráŕh was included in the Magadha Empire.
Of course, it could be surmised that the script of Ráŕh, though similar to that of Shriiharśa script, is much older.
Then why did Ashoka not erect stone pillars bearing religious instructions in this region?

paragraphs.text: There are two strong possibilities. First, during the rule of Ashoka Ráŕh ceased to use Bráhmii script and introduced its own script and began using it. That is why Ashoka did not use Bráhmii script. The second possibility is that in Ráŕh, Buddhism was not as predominant as it was in Magadha during the rule of Ashoka or even later. At that time Jainism was the dominant influence in Ráŕh, and that is why no Buddhist edicts were inscribed on the rockwalls of Ráŕh. Consequently, the scripts found in the Bhulá-Pávanpur-Báiuṋgurdá-Jáydá areas were the relics of the Jain-cum-Shaeva golden age ruins. Based on these [considerations] one can conclude that Bengali script was at least seventeen hundred years old, if not more. After this discovery there is little doubt that Bengali script is not just eleven hundred years old. Rather, it is far older. It is the oldest among the [modern] Indian scripts. Since this discovery, the script called Shriiharśa script, which hitherto was considered the oldest Bengali script, is now proven to be more recent. Under these circumstances, it would not be possible to pretend that the Bengali script is Shriiharśa script, as Bengali script, though similar to Shriiharśa script, is in fact much older.
summary: There are two strong possibilities.
Based on these [considerations] one can conclude that Bengali script was at least seventeen hundred years old, if not more.
Under these circumstances, it would not be possible to pretend that the Bengali script is Shriiharśa script, as Bengali script, though similar to Shriiharśa script, is in fact much older.

paragraphs.text: Most of these scripts have been found in the river valleys surrounded by the Dálmá hills of Western Ráŕh (the southeastern part of the Vindhya mountains that end at Shavarbhúm). Hence, in my opinion this script should be called “Dálmá script”. There is ample scope to research whether Dálmá script originated from Bráhmii script. In other words, the Bengali language was written not in Shriiharśa script, but in the much older Dálmá script, which belongs to the Shriiharśa lineage.
summary: Most of these scripts have been found in the river valleys surrounded by the Dálmá hills of Western Ráŕh (the southeastern part of the Vindhya mountains that end at Shavarbhúm).
There is ample scope to research whether Dálmá script originated from Bráhmii script.
In other words, the Bengali language was written not in Shriiharśa script, but in the much older Dálmá script, which belongs to the Shriiharśa lineage.

paragraphs.text: It has taken a long time to discuss the history of the first letter a. There is a slight connection between the Bengali letter a and the Bráhmii letter a. It also has a strong similarity with the same letter in Shriiharśa script. In reality, it is the latest manifestation of the letter a in the Dálmá script. ( 3 )
summary: It has taken a long time to discuss the history of the first letter a.
It also has a strong similarity with the same letter in Shriiharśa script.
In reality, it is the latest manifestation of the letter a in the Dálmá script.

paragraphs.text: Footnotes

footnotes.text: The Aryans did not have their own script and thus were first introduced to the [written] alphabet after coming in contact with the Dravidians. The Dravidians of the Harappa and Mahenjodaro civilizations of India were already using a script, the Saendhavii script; after the Aryan migration into India, that script became transformed into the Bráhmii and Kharośt́hii scripts. – Shrii Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar, “Tantra and Indo-Aryan Civilization”, A Few Problems Solved Part 1.

uparyukta: it is to be noted that the Bengali equivalent of the word “above-mentioned” is upari-ukta; many people wrongly write the word as uparokta thinking that the word is upar + ukta = uparokta. In Sanskrit, while there is no word like upar, there is the word upari; thus, upari + ukta = uparyukta.
The foregoing fourteen paragraphs are from Varńa Vicitrá 2, Discourse 8.

chapters.title: The Alphabet – Mughal
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: The alphabet – Akśamálá
summary: The alphabet – Akśamálá

paragraphs.text: The word akśa has several meanings. The first letter of the alphabet is a and kśa is its last letter. Between a and kśa there are forty-eight other letters. The total number of letters is fifty. So akśa denotes the fifty letters of the [Sanskrit] alphabet. So in place of varńamálá [alphabet], the compound word akśamálá is also used. In the description of the goddess Bhadrakálii in the Atharvaveda, it has been said that Mahákálii or Bhadrakálii, the deity of time, holds these fifty letters. People of that era did not have any idea of scripts, but they had knowledge of letters or words. Disciples used to receive their mantra from the gurus by hearing them. In Sanskrit the ear is called shruti. Hence the Vedas learnt through the ears were called the shruti.
summary: The word akśa has several meanings.
So in place of varńamálá [alphabet], the compound word akśamálá is also used.
Hence the Vedas learnt through the ears were called the shruti.

paragraphs.text: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write. So in place of fifty letters, they used to imagine fifty faces. They would ideate that the first letter of creation a was in the hand of Bhadrakálii. They believed that the remaining letters were in her garland, although there was no distinct entity called Mahákála. Hence, in philosophical analysis the entities Mahákála or Mahákálii can find no logical support. Time is created at every moment from the mental measurement of the motivity of action. Yet the people of those days believed that [one day] there would be a calamity that would destroy everything. In the absence of adequate knowledge of science, they imagined a final cataclysm – that one day everything would be annihilated – this is the kind of fear that was expressed. During such a cataclysm (pralaya), it was believed that Bhadrakálii would save the letters, even though philosophical and scientific logic might be against the idea of a final cataclysm. There can be no thermal death of the universe. Perhaps a particular entity may undergo thermal death, but even in that case, entities transformed into hard, solid matter due to internal clash and cohesion would fragment in a fierce explosion, as a result of which immense thermal energy would be released from the broken structures, the fragments. This would prevent the thermal death of the universe from taking place. In any case, we are relating what the people of those days believed. They believed that Bhadrakálii would save the sounds [of the alphabet] during such a cataclysm. Since they had no knowledge of letters, they used human heads to represent the letters. That is why the people finally conceived of the alphabet as a wreath of human heads. By accepting Bhadrakálii as the symbol of welfare they gained peace of mind.
summary: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write.
During such a cataclysm (pralaya), it was believed that Bhadrakálii would save the letters, even though philosophical and scientific logic might be against the idea of a final cataclysm.
By accepting Bhadrakálii as the symbol of welfare they gained peace of mind.

paragraphs.text: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not write them. By orally creating the rks or shlokas of the Vedas, they taught their disciples by singing them out loud. That is why they contained melody, rhythm, grammar, kalpa, and nirukta; however, nothing existed in writing. The six parts of Vedic learning, such as chanda [science of rhythm], kalpa [explanation of religious rites], nirukta [etymology], vyákarańa (grammar; there are differences of opinion on this), jyotiiś [astrology] and ayurveda (medicine; there are even differences of opinion here; some say not ayurveda but dhanurveda) were called vedáuṋga. Vedáuṋga was unwritten, since humans at that time had no knowledge of script. In the absence of script, people of those days retained the Vedas as shruti (learnt through hearing; one name for ear is shruti). When people later learnt about scripts, even then they did not want to put the Vedas into written form. By that time they had piled up such mountainous superstitions in their heads that they believed the Vedas were not meant to be written! They did not carefully analyze that their ancestors did not write the Vedas only because they had no knowledge of script. Surely had they known a script, they would have put [the Vedas] in writing. ( 1 )
summary: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not write them.
In the absence of script, people of those days retained the Vedas as shruti (learnt through hearing; one name for ear is shruti).
Surely had they known a script, they would have put [the Vedas] in writing.

paragraphs.text: Mogul/Mughal

You have certainly heard about the word iyuichi, which is from the ancient Mongol language. You are probably familiar with the word ‘mongol’. It is the ancient language of the [northern] part of China, that is, Mongolia. Mongolians are residents of primarily inner and outer Mongolia. In ancient times, the people of both regions spoke in Mongol language. At present [that original language] has split into several regional languages. Mongolian is a mixture of Aryan-Vedic and Chinese languages. From “Mongol” has come the word “Mughal,” and through verbal transformation this word has become “Mogul”. The muglái parat́há [a special kind of flat bread containing spicy ingredients and fried in ghee or butter] is a speciality of this very area. In medieval India, there were several invasions originating from this region. Babar [1526–1530] was born from this ancient Mongol race, as was also Tamerlane [1336–1405]. The land of the Mongols was also the fatherland of the Shakas [A.D. 78]. The early habitation of the Huńas ( 2 ) was in the southwestern corner of the Mongol lands. (Mihirkul [Mihirgul – 505 A.D.] descended from this Huń dynasty.) Kujula Kadphises or Kujul Kadphises (he is not recognized as a king but rather as a leader in history) was the leader (sardár) of the Kushan sub-branch of the Iyucii branch of the Shakas [Sakas]. His successor (according to some, his son, and according to others, his son-in-law) Vimá Kadphises, or Wima Kadphises, was also a Kushan leader recognized in history. King Kanishka [A.D. 120], who belonged to the Kushan dynasty [A.D. 48–220], became the lord of a vast area of northwestern India. It is worth noting that Kujula Kadphises and Vimá Kadphises are two names that occur in the early Mongol language, but the name Kanishka belongs to Sanskrit. This change of language in Kanishkaʼs name took place when he came to India and embraced Buddhism. The names of the successors of Kanishka [Kańiśka], such as Vashishka, Huvishka and Vasudeva, are genuine Sanskrit names.
summary: You have certainly heard about the word iyuichi, which is from the ancient Mongol language.
The land of the Mongols was also the fatherland of the Shakas [A.
The names of the successors of Kanishka [Kańiśka], such as Vashishka, Huvishka and Vasudeva, are genuine Sanskrit names.

paragraphs.text: Hiuen Tsang (Yung Chuang) spoke in Chinese and was an ancient historian and traveler. According to most pundits, Mang-daring or Mang-daing Chinese was his vernacular mother language. Whether his vernacular language was Mang-daring, Cantonese or Sang Haiese Chinese, the present Chinese languages had not have appeared at that time. In addition, it is worth remembering that the letter r is hardly pronounced in Chinese. In ancient Chinese also, the same practice was observed. It can be emphatically asserted that during the last six thousand years, the letter r has been pronounced almost silently in Chinese. From my own knowledge of Chinese, I have no hesitation in making this statement. ( 3 )
summary: Hiuen Tsang (Yung Chuang) spoke in Chinese and was an ancient historian and traveler.
In addition, it is worth remembering that the letter r is hardly pronounced in Chinese.
From my own knowledge of Chinese, I have no hesitation in making this statement.

paragraphs.text: The Vedic word Naptá
summary: The Vedic word Naptá

paragraphs.text: Even today in northwestern India, Punjab and parts of Afghanistan, the daughterʼs son is called dohatar, which is derived from the Vedic word daohitrá. The Bengali word náti [grandson] is derived from the Vedic word naptá – the words nápit or nápte are derived from the same source. The word nápit [barber] is a pure Vedic word. The word naptá, meaning nápit, is also a Vedic word that stands for both náti and nápit. The true meaning of naptá is one who prevents downfall. A barber prevents the downfall of society through [personal] grooming; a grandson [according to Vedic belief] prevents downfall through offering of food to the manes. From this belief emerged the word napta. To a modern person it narrates a tale of ancient history.
summary: Even today in northwestern India, Punjab and parts of Afghanistan, the daughterʼs son is called dohatar, which is derived from the Vedic word daohitrá.
The true meaning of naptá is one who prevents downfall.
To a modern person it narrates a tale of ancient history.

paragraphs.text: Meaning of Prabara or sub-clan
summary: Meaning of Prabara or sub-clan

paragraphs.text: Pra – br + al/ac = prabara, meaning the best leader or the most respectable person. In certain regions of ancient India, along with the system of gotra there was the system of prabara. For instance, let us take the case of someone whose gotra was bharadváj. It indicates that the forefather of that person lived on a hill on which Bharadváj was the leader. I have mentioned in an earlier book that in ancient society, when matriarchal society and matrilineal order were in vogue, people used to identify themselves through their mother – through the name of the mother, through her mother, and again through her motherʼs mother. Identity was not determined through the fatherʼs side. The meaning of the word mátá [mother] is one through whom a family earns social respect. However, later on, due to certain unique needs of the extant social order, the patriarchal system was introduced. Amongst those special needs of the social structure, the primary one was that in the matriarchal system the mother had full responsibility towards the child and the father had very little responsibility. However, in the patriarchal system the motherʼs responsibility remained almost the same, but it was supplemented by the responsibility of the father. It created an advantage in raising children. Although the motherʼs responsibility persisted, she also received the aid of her husband. In this system, the social structure became much more solid.
summary: Pra – br + al/ac = prabara, meaning the best leader or the most respectable person.
The meaning of the word mátá [mother] is one through whom a family earns social respect.
In this system, the social structure became much more solid.

paragraphs.text: In any case, in the patrilineal system the gotra (clan) was determined by the name of the leader of the hill on which they lived. The meaning of the word gotra is “hill”. Now, a very large number of people used to take shelter on a big hill. Hence, under the leader of the gotra, there were also some local leaders. They received greater respect than anyone else. In fact they received the highest veneration, and from this evolved the word prabara. ( 4 )
summary: In any case, in the patrilineal system the gotra (clan) was determined by the name of the leader of the hill on which they lived.
Hence, under the leader of the gotra, there were also some local leaders.
In fact they received the highest veneration, and from this evolved the word prabara.

There is ńa in the pronunciation of the word huńa. So it is considered natural ńa.

chapters.title: Gondwanaland – Ráŕh – Asura
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Gondwana ( 1 )

About 8,000 million years ago, there was no solid structure in the world and the earth was a [ball of] glowing gas. The land mass was formed only about 2,330 million years ago. [Eventually] Gondwanaland was created. At that time, the middle portion of the earth was in a state of liquid composition.
summary: About 8,000 million years ago, there was no solid structure in the world and the earth was a [ball of] glowing gas.
[Eventually] Gondwanaland was created.
At that time, the middle portion of the earth was in a state of liquid composition.

paragraphs.text: In those days there was no Arabian Sea, no Bay of Bengal or its present islands, no Indonesia and no Australia. There was no North India, no Tibet and no Himalayas. There was only one contiguous land mass from what is now the eastern portion of Africa, including South India and Malaysia, up to Australia. This landmass – the oldest landmass in the world – consisted mainly of a long island in [the form of] an archipelago. What is now Canada and Argentina also existed at that time. The territory that covered what is presently the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, the Indonesian Archipelago, the Deccan Plateau, Southeast Asia and Oceania – has been named Gondwanaland by [geologists] because the Gond people of the Austric race lived in the central portion, although this portion was not the oldest part of the land. Even today the descendants of the Gond people still live in the [Chattisgarh region].
summary: In those days there was no Arabian Sea, no Bay of Bengal or its present islands, no Indonesia and no Australia.
This landmass – the oldest landmass in the world – consisted mainly of a long island in [the form of] an archipelago.
Even today the descendants of the Gond people still live in the [Chattisgarh region].

paragraphs.text: Ráŕh – the oldest part of Gondwanaland that has remained above the sea – was the birthplace of human beings. The hills of Ananda Nagar in Ráŕh are also at least 300 million years old. At that time there were no Himalayas.
summary: Ráŕh – the oldest part of Gondwanaland that has remained above the sea – was the birthplace of human beings.
The hills of Ananda Nagar in Ráŕh are also at least 300 million years old.
At that time there were no Himalayas.

paragraphs.text: Ancient Earthquake

At least 30 million years ago, a plutonic earthquake occurred. The land that presently comprises the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea was submerged under the ocean and the present North India emerged. In the same earthquake, those parts which were previously hills became islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea after the earthquake. In this way a group of 503 oceanic islands, comprising Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines islands, was also formed. All of this, including the emergence of the Himalayas, took place about 30 million years ago. The Himalayas are therefore approximately 30 million years old, but Gondwanaland and Ráŕh are far far older.
summary: At least 30 million years ago, a plutonic earthquake occurred.
In this way a group of 503 oceanic islands, comprising Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines islands, was also formed.
The Himalayas are therefore approximately 30 million years old, but Gondwanaland and Ráŕh are far far older.

paragraphs.text: The fossils of ocean creatures can be found in the Shivalik Range, which provides proof that at one time the Himalayan ranges were under water. The Indo-Gangetic plains were formed from the alluvial deposits of the Himalayas.
summary: The fossils of ocean creatures can be found in the Shivalik Range, which provides proof that at one time the Himalayan ranges were under water.
The Indo-Gangetic plains were formed from the alluvial deposits of the Himalayas.

paragraphs.text: The Sahara desert and Thar desert of Sind and Rajasthan were previously under the ocean, thus their sand dunes are of marine origin. These dunes provide proof that at one time these regions were under the ocean. ( 2 )
summary: The Sahara desert and Thar desert of Sind and Rajasthan were previously under the ocean, thus their sand dunes are of marine origin.
These dunes provide proof that at one time these regions were under the ocean.

paragraphs.text: Ancient land of Ráŕh
summary: Ancient land of Ráŕh

paragraphs.text: There was a great ocean, its surface agitated by rows of towering waves, an ocean which had neither name nor gotra [clan]. Who was there to name it, who was there to tell others about it? No one was there, since human beings had not yet emerged onto this earth. This was about 300 million years ago. ( 3 ) [And as regards the land mass,] there was no name yet on earth for that arid, mountainous terrain, nor even a single grove of trees to which a name could be given. ( 4 )
summary: There was a great ocean, its surface agitated by rows of towering waves, an ocean which had neither name nor gotra [clan].
No one was there, since human beings had not yet emerged onto this earth.
( 3 ) [And as regards the land mass,] there was no name yet on earth for that arid, mountainous terrain, nor even a single grove of trees to which a name could be given.

paragraphs.text: After a long time this very terrain, this nameless, mountainous terrain, was given the name Ráŕh. The word ráŕh originated in the ancient Austric language and means a land of red (laterite) soil. In the world of those days there was no Áryyávartta; ( 5 ) there were no plains of Bengal or of the Deccan, nor were there the deserts of Rajasthan and Gujarat. The northern part of the Arabian Sea did not exist either; what existed was its southern part, which linked the Deccan peninsula with Africa, the Andamans, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia. They were linked by [land] that lay sometimes a little above the water level, sometimes a little below. ( 6 ) In that world, uninhabited by human beings, the Ráŕh of those days was older than any other land. The snow-covered mountains of Ráŕh gave birth to numerous rivers. Those rivers, fed by melting snow, flowed some to the east and some to the southeast, towards the ocean.
summary: After a long time this very terrain, this nameless, mountainous terrain, was given the name Ráŕh.
They were linked by [land] that lay sometimes a little above the water level, sometimes a little below.
Those rivers, fed by melting snow, flowed some to the east and some to the southeast, towards the ocean.

paragraphs.text: Days passed, time passed, from beginninglessness to endlessness. Rainstorms and thunderbolts struck the mountains, and gradually the mountains diminished. Their snowy crowns fell off their heads, their height decreased. As the mountains became smaller and smaller through erosion, each river basin lying between two mountains became more elevated. The undulating red soil that we see today in western Ráŕh, the undulation that advances ahead of us till it mingles in the remote blue [horizon], the undulation that gives a hint of some lost address as it recedes behind us – that undulating land is our Ráŕh.
summary: Days passed, time passed, from beginninglessness to endlessness.
Their snowy crowns fell off their heads, their height decreased.

The undulating red soil that we see today in western Ráŕh, the undulation that advances ahead of us till it mingles in the remote blue [horizon], the undulation that gives a hint of some lost address as it recedes behind us – that undulating land is our Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: The mountains were gradually eroding and being transformed into sand and silt. The sand and silt, carried by the rivers of Ráŕh, formed eastern Ráŕh. This was lakhs and crores ( 7 ) of years ago.
summary: The mountains were gradually eroding and being transformed into sand and silt.
The sand and silt, carried by the rivers of Ráŕh, formed eastern Ráŕh.
This was lakhs and crores ( 7 ) of years ago.

paragraphs.text: The Himalayas were born many crores [tens of millions] of years after the birth of Ráŕh. ( 8 ) From the Himalayas came forth a daughter, the River Gauṋgá [Ganges], and a son, the River Brahamaputra. ( 9 ) The sand and silt their waters bore formed new soil; northern India and Báḿlá [Bengal] were formed. ( 10 ) The seabed that was east of Ráŕh rose higher and higher thanks to that sand and silt, and – after the formation of eastern Ráŕh – long after – many lakhs of years after – formed a vast plain (samatal). That plain [to the east of eastern Ráŕh] is known as Samatat́a in Sanskrit and Bágŕi in Bengali. Farther to the east, the sand and silt borne by the rivers of Ráŕh mingled with the sand and silt of the Brahmaputra and formed Vauṋga ( 11 ) or D́abák. The people of western Ráŕh migrated to eastern Ráŕh and established residence. This occurred lakhs [hundreds of thousands] of years ago. If human beings appeared one million years ago, then the inhabitants of western Ráŕh of a million years ago found eastern Ráŕh to be in a ripe state for them even before their birth. Even a portion of northern India arose before the origin of human beings. Samatat́ and D́abák, however, originated a little after the appearance of humans on earth. The people of western and eastern Ráŕh removed the forest cover and dwelt in Samatat́-Vauṋga-D́abák.
summary: The Himalayas were born many crores [tens of millions] of years after the birth of Ráŕh.
The people of western Ráŕh migrated to eastern Ráŕh and established residence.
The people of western and eastern Ráŕh removed the forest cover and dwelt in Samatat́-Vauṋga-D́abák.

paragraphs.text: Gauṋgá-rhid́i

In ancient Greek, the meaning of the word rhid́ is kingdom. However, the word Gauṋgá-rhid́i has come from the word Gauṋgá-Ráŕh, which means the land of Ráŕh that touches the Ganges. When Alexander invaded India, he heard admiration expressed for the prowess of the Bengalis of Ráŕh. ( 16 ) It is for this reason that the expression Gauṋgá-rhid́i first entered the Greek language. We can safely use the word Gauṋgá- Ráŕh in place of Gauṋgá-rhid́i. ( 17 )
summary: In ancient Greek, the meaning of the word rhid́ is kingdom.
When Alexander invaded India, he heard admiration expressed for the prowess of the Bengalis of Ráŕh.
We can safely use the word Gauṋgá- Ráŕh in place of Gauṋgá-rhid́i.

paragraphs.text: Gondwanaland

Geologists surmise that at one time regions such as North India and the Himalayas did not exist. Along with South India, there was Africa on one side, and on the other side was a vast expanse of land, comprising the Andamans, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia. This ancient land was named Gondwana after the ‘Gonds,’ who lived in the central region of this landmass. The people who lived in the western extremity of Gondwana were Negroid; those who lived in the Eastern extremity were Austric, and those who lived in the central part [of this landmass], meaning in the southern part of India, were Austrico-Negroid or of the Dravidian race. There is still a community of Gonds in Central India. The identity of the common people of the Gond community is to be found in the Dhuruva-gonds region. The place named Dhruwa near Ranchi can be mentioned in this connection. In this region, those belonging to the royal family were known as Rajgond. Later they gave up their old titles of Rajgond or Dhuruvagond and became assimilated with the Rajput and Thakur clans. ( 18 )
summary: Geologists surmise that at one time regions such as North India and the Himalayas did not exist.
There is still a community of Gonds in Central India.
Later they gave up their old titles of Rajgond or Dhuruvagond and became assimilated with the Rajput and Thakur clans.

paragraphs.text: Gondwanaland and Ráŕh
summary: Gondwanaland and Ráŕh

paragraphs.text: The region where we are now used to be the far eastern part of ancient Gondwanaland. I can not say it was the farthest eastern part because the farthest eastern part was that part of Gondwanaland that people nowadays call Ráŕh. The eastern mountains of Gondwanaland ran parallel from west to east. Only the Rajmahal Hills in the north ran northeast instead of due east, near Sahebganj and away from the Ganges. I say the Ganges although at that time the Ganges wasnʼt there – the ocean was. At that time the Himalayas had not been formed yet so where could the Ganges come from?
summary: The region where we are now used to be the far eastern part of ancient Gondwanaland.
Only the Rajmahal Hills in the north ran northeast instead of due east, near Sahebganj and away from the Ganges.
At that time the Himalayas had not been formed yet so where could the Ganges come from?

paragraphs.text: This was during the time before the breath of man had warmed the earthʼs air. All the way south, in the area near Meghasini peak, the mountains ran more or less southeast. The rest of the mountains ran from west to east and their last lofty peak was Sametashikhar, that today is known by the name of Pareshnáth. To the east of this Pareshnáth was the ancient land of Ráŕh and to the west was Jharkhanda. Of course this was before human beings came to the earth.
summary: This was during the time before the breath of man had warmed the earthʼs air.
The rest of the mountains ran from west to east and their last lofty peak was Sametashikhar, that today is known by the name of Pareshnáth.
Of course this was before human beings came to the earth.

paragraphs.text: Into the lowest portion of the valley, between these two mountain ranges, ran the melted ice water of Gondwanaland forming the Bánsh, Dváraká, Mayúrákśii, Hiḿlo, Ajaya, Dámodara, Dvárakeshvara, Kaḿsávatii, Shilávatii, Káliyághái, and Suvardarekhá rivers – these were all very large rivers. When human beings came and made the ancient soil of Ráŕh holy with the touch of their feet, they built their dwellings on the banks of these rivers. Not only humans – those prehistoric creatures who came hundreds of thousands of years before the advent of men also used to live on the banks of these rivers because all living beings need water.
summary: Into the lowest portion of the valley, between these two mountain ranges, ran the melted ice water of Gondwanaland forming the Bánsh, Dváraká, Mayúrákśii, Hiḿlo, Ajaya, Dámodara, Dvárakeshvara, Kaḿsávatii, Shilávatii, Káliyághái, and Suvardarekhá rivers – these were all very large rivers.
When human beings came and made the ancient soil of Ráŕh holy with the touch of their feet, they built their dwellings on the banks of these rivers.
Not only humans – those prehistoric creatures who came hundreds of thousands of years before the advent of men also used to live on the banks of these rivers because all living beings need water.

paragraphs.text: Do you know why Iʼm only talking about Ráŕh and not about any other part of Gondwanaland? Elsewhere it was extremely cold and rife with snowstorms. There was no proper environment there for human beings to evolve. Ráŕh had the living touch of warmth so humans came there first. They founded the worldʼs most ancient civilization and culture, which we can call the original Ráŕh culture. ( 19 )
summary: Do you know why Iʼm only talking about Ráŕh and not about any other part of Gondwanaland?
There was no proper environment there for human beings to evolve.
They founded the worldʼs most ancient civilization and culture, which we can call the original Ráŕh culture.

paragraphs.text: Nothing stops in this world, neither animate nor inanimate. It is not only that these rivers carried vital force for existence. They also led the irresistible attainment of civilization and culture swiftly toward union with the sea. That civilization that is founded upstream in the river reaches its fullness downstream. No two rivers carry identical civilizations. Thus, after two rivers merge, their combined flow carries yet a third civilization.
summary: Nothing stops in this world, neither animate nor inanimate.
That civilization that is founded upstream in the river reaches its fullness downstream.
Thus, after two rivers merge, their combined flow carries yet a third civilization.

paragraphs.text: Take, for instance, a small example. In our Birbhum there are two very small rivers: the Kopái and the Vakreshvara. The flow of these two civilizations and cultures is nearly the same. The spoken language of the people who live on their banks is also almost the same. But notice, I say ‘almost’ rather than 'the sameʼ because they are not identical. Afterwards, when they join each other in Melánpur near Indása village (the famous Indrahása from the Jain era) and become the Kuye river, then its accompanying civilization and culture becomes a little altered. The people who live on the banks of the Kuye river enjoy the blessings of both the Kopái and Vakreshvara rivers.
summary: Take, for instance, a small example.
The spoken language of the people who live on their banks is also almost the same.
The people who live on the banks of the Kuye river enjoy the blessings of both the Kopái and Vakreshvara rivers.

paragraphs.text: Dumka, Suri, Santhia, and Kandi – these four cities are in the Mayúrákśii valley. Their customs, behaviour, mode of living, and spoken language are the same but the Mandar hill, which is very near Dumka [Santhal Pargana], is situated on the Chandan river and thus the customs, comportment and language there is different than Dumkaʼs. Kandi is quite far from Dumka but they are alike in all ways. Moreover, Kándi is very close to Jangipur [Kándi and Jangipur are presently in Murshidabad district] but Jangipurʼs culture is different; its spoken language is Shershahabad Bengali. You will find this kind of history with all rivers. The rivers of Ráŕh did not simply carry sand and alluvium to the sea, thereby making the Bengali plains, they also brought the verdant riches of civilization and culture to Bengal.
summary: Dumka, Suri, Santhia, and Kandi – these four cities are in the Mayúrákśii valley.
Moreover, Kándi is very close to Jangipur [Kándi and Jangipur are presently in Murshidabad district] but Jangipurʼs culture is different; its spoken language is Shershahabad Bengali.
The rivers of Ráŕh did not simply carry sand and alluvium to the sea, thereby making the Bengali plains, they also brought the verdant riches of civilization and culture to Bengal.

paragraphs.text: After the rise of the Himalayas from the ocean, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra rivers brought the flow of civilization and culture with the current of their waters. The Ganges brought the Indo-Aryan culture, but near Sahebganj, where the Ganges turns south, the Gaod́iya [Gaod́a – a portion of Bengal] influence over the cultural life increased. Similarly, as the Brahmaputra reached the Assam valley near Sadiya there was a mixture of the Tibetan and Burmese civilizations. The triple mixture of these two with the Indo-Aryan gave rise to the Kamarupa civilization which a little downriver became transformed into the Bengali culture.
summary: After the rise of the Himalayas from the ocean, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra rivers brought the flow of civilization and culture with the current of their waters.
Similarly, as the Brahmaputra reached the Assam valley near Sadiya there was a mixture of the Tibetan and Burmese civilizations.
The triple mixture of these two with the Indo-Aryan gave rise to the Kamarupa civilization which a little downriver became transformed into the Bengali culture.

paragraphs.text: The lushness and artistry of the Bengali civilization and culture of today has been enriched by the civilization and culture carried by the many small rivers and tributaries of Ráŕh, and with the admixture of the Ganges and Brahmaputra civilizations the Bengali civilization has achieved its incomparable sweetness.
summary: The lushness and artistry of the Bengali civilization and culture of today has been enriched by the civilization and culture carried by the many small rivers and tributaries of Ráŕh, and with the admixture of the Ganges and Brahmaputra civilizations the Bengali civilization has achieved its incomparable sweetness.

paragraphs.text: [Speaking about] the different plants and wild animals of this area, in a word, the flora and fauna, in the laterite soil of this land you find mostly piyál (piyáshál), palásh, kuśum, shál, and kendu trees. You also come across wild jackfruit, wild mango and custard-apple trees. [Now a question] was the tree-life and different birds and beasts of this area the same during the end of the Pleiocene or beginning of the Meoiscene ages when ape-men first appeared?
summary: [Speaking about] the different plants and wild animals of this area, in a word, the flora and fauna, in the laterite soil of this land you find mostly piyál (piyáshál), palásh, kuśum, shál, and kendu trees.
You also come across wild jackfruit, wild mango and custard-apple trees.

paragraphs.text: The custard-apple trees [one will] find here in the wild were brought by the Portuguese about 450 years ago. [Now] about palásh.

paragraphs.text: Looking at the colour of the flower and its qualities, it seems that rather than the three varieties we have nowadays, white, red and yellow, there was only the red variety. The tree was ten times taller than the palásh trees of today. The flowers were bright red but very big in size, and the fruits were quite small but sweet and juicy.
summary: Looking at the colour of the flower and its qualities, it seems that rather than the three varieties we have nowadays, white, red and yellow, there was only the red variety.
The tree was ten times taller than the palásh trees of today.
The flowers were bright red but very big in size, and the fruits were quite small but sweet and juicy.

paragraphs.text: [It is] because there are more palásh trees in the eastern portion of Gondwanaland. Where rivers have more or less level land on both sides you get this red soil that the palásh tree favours. The interesting thing is that in all the river basins of that area, especially the Damodar, Ajaya,
summary: [It is] because there are more palásh trees in the eastern portion of Gondwanaland.
Where rivers have more or less level land on both sides you get this red soil that the palásh tree favours.

paragraphs.text: Ushri, Konar, Barakar, and the Mahanadiiʼs central river basin, you get ample amounts of coal – high quality coal. The primary source of material for this coal is decomposed palásh trees. Those palásh trees were not like the palásh trees of today but they were the forefathers of todayʼs palásh trees.
summary: Ushri, Konar, Barakar, and the Mahanadiiʼs central river basin, you get ample amounts of coal – high quality coal.
The primary source of material for this coal is decomposed palásh trees.
Those palásh trees were not like the palásh trees of today but they were the forefathers of todayʼs palásh trees.

paragraphs.text: The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel river. The difference between east and west is not only evidenced in the terrain, but also in the flora and fauna. I would guess that the western mountains that we now call the Vindhya and Sátpurá mountains were once much higher. They had peaks higher than the Himalayas. Flora and fauna could not evolve there in the ancient past due to excessive snowfall, but the eastern mountains, although very high and snow-capped, were not as high as the western mountains. It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhanda. In the west, the melted ice ran into the Arabian Sea. Although there was water, the soil was unfertile, so there was little flora and naturally little fauna as well. But in the east, where the water from the melted snows became rivers, the cold was not so severe. So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.
summary: The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel river.
It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhanda.
So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.

paragraphs.text: Thus we find an abundance of prehistoric fossils in the eastern portion of the Ramgarh Hills, the Dalmá Hills, the Meghásinii belt, and the southeast portion of the Rajmahal Hills (Pákuŕa and Rajmahal sub-divisions) ( 20 ). The small hills of Bankura District, especially the Shushuniyá Hills, are also an extension of this Ramgarh range. Fossils of various types of ancient animals have been found near these hills. Still, the greatest amount of fossils are lying in the areas closest to the Suvarńarehká, Kaḿsávatii, and Damodara rivers. It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region. Rhinoceroses also used to roam the extremely high grasses of this area. Just two hundred years ago rhinoceroses were living in Birbhum and Kandi sub-division. Only 125 years ago rhinoceroses were spotted in Rajmahal and Pákuŕ.
summary: Thus we find an abundance of prehistoric fossils in the eastern portion of the Ramgarh Hills, the Dalmá Hills, the Meghásinii belt, and the southeast portion of the Rajmahal Hills (Pákuŕa and Rajmahal sub-divisions) ( 20 ).
It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region.
Only 125 years ago rhinoceroses were spotted in Rajmahal and Pákuŕ.

paragraphs.text: There were also huge birds of the phiṋge [the drongo] variety with loose, hanging tails. I would guess that the size of a single bird was about five or six feet. Their tales used to trail on the ground and the sabre-toothed tigers of that day used to catch them easily by stepping on their tails with their paws. But when the sabre-toothed tiger disappeared from Ráŕh about 700,000 years ago, these large-bodied birds also became extinct. The descendants of these huge birds, the phiṋge and doyel birds of today, are much smaller in size. The hyena (govághá, hud́ál, hud́ár, or huńdár in rural Bengali; in Madhya Pradesh vighavá) of today is the descendant of this sabre-toothed tiger.
summary: There were also huge birds of the phiṋge [the drongo] variety with loose, hanging tails.
But when the sabre-toothed tiger disappeared from Ráŕh about 700,000 years ago, these large-bodied birds also became extinct.
The hyena (govághá, hud́ál, hud́ár, or huńdár in rural Bengali; in Madhya Pradesh vighavá) of today is the descendant of this sabre-toothed tiger.

paragraphs.text: Ape-men or man-apes first took birth in this part of the earth. There were some differences between the humans that evolved on either side of the Koyel river in terms of intelligence and other qualities. Such differences still exist today among their descendants. On the eastern side was the dwelling place of the Munda [Muńd́á] clan ( 21 )of that primitive age, and on the western side lived the Oráoṋ clan. The former belongs to the Austric group – their language also. Many Austric-family words are still used in modern Bengali, such as kurhi [twenty], dulál (from dulár [darling child]) and ghád́a [neck], among others.
summary: Ape-men or man-apes first took birth in this part of the earth.
On the eastern side was the dwelling place of the Munda [Muńd́á] clan ( 21 )of that primitive age, and on the western side lived the Oráoṋ clan.
Many Austric-family words are still used in modern Bengali, such as kurhi [twenty], dulál (from dulár [darling child]) and ghád́a [neck], among others.

paragraphs.text: The Oráoṋ family languages belong to the Dravidian group. ( 22 ) Although there are some words in Bengali that belong to the Dravidian family, they are much fewer by comparison than those of Austric origin. This family of words [Dravidian] includes pallii [hamlet], miin [fish], and tentul [tamarind] (tinturi > tenturi > tentur > tentul), among others.
summary: The Oráoṋ family languages belong to the Dravidian group.
( 22 ) Although there are some words in Bengali that belong to the Dravidian family, they are much fewer by comparison than those of Austric origin.
This family of words [Dravidian] includes pallii [hamlet], miin [fish], and tentul [tamarind] (tinturi > tenturi > tentur > tentul), among others.

paragraphs.text: The Biirhorh community also arose in this area in very ancient times. They are also part of the Austric family. The original home of the Málpáhárhiis is in the northeast part of this area. Later they were subdued by others and forced to take shelter in the forest at the far edge of the Rajmahal Hills.
summary: The Biirhorh community also arose in this area in very ancient times.
The original home of the Málpáhárhiis is in the northeast part of this area.
Later they were subdued by others and forced to take shelter in the forest at the far edge of the Rajmahal Hills.

paragraphs.text: In those ancient days there was a great deal of fighting between the ape-men and man-apes. The apes did not know the use of fire so they could not use it to burn their enemies. When men learned the use of fire, they started to burn to death their main enemies, the apes, and eat them. During the British era also, the Biirhoŕhs used to burn apes to death and eat them. They also had some attraction to cannibalism, however, there is no proof that they ever ate human beings. One can deduce from this that they used to kill the apes for the purpose of eating their enemies.
summary: In those ancient days there was a great deal of fighting between the ape-men and man-apes.
During the British era also, the Biirhoŕhs used to burn apes to death and eat them.
One can deduce from this that they used to kill the apes for the purpose of eating their enemies.

paragraphs.text: There is still another clan from this Koyel river basin – the Asuras. They originated here and developed their own separate culture. Later they left and headed northwest in the direction of Europe. A few words from their language can still be found among the Gypsies of central Asia and in the Romansch language of Europe.
summary: There is still another clan from this Koyel river basin – the Asuras.
Later they left and headed northwest in the direction of Europe.
A few words from their language can still be found among the Gypsies of central Asia and in the Romansch language of Europe.

paragraphs.text: Near the high mountains of this Gondwanaland there were many huge pits. With the passage of time the mountains eroded and became large hills, then smaller hills, knolls and mounds. Today also, Ráŕh and Jharkhanda are full of these hills, hillocks and knolls. Thus the land is undulating. What is today the lowest portion of this undulating land was at one time deep pits. And the upper portions were very tall mountains. Although many large pits have filled up, not all of them have. In Ráŕhii Bengali they are called káṋdara (kandara in Sanskrit). Still there are a few very large pits. You will also find large pits nearby wherever you find a coal yard with an open pit. ( 23 )
summary: Near the high mountains of this Gondwanaland there were many huge pits.
And the upper portions were very tall mountains.
You will also find large pits nearby wherever you find a coal yard with an open pit.

Each day I would go to one or two different spots in the Suvarnarekha River valley in search of archaeological artifacts of ancient Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: All day long I travelled like a whirlwind from village to village in Ranchi Districtʼs Silli area as well as the adjacent areas of Jhalda and Jaipur in what was then called Manbhum District. This region is also worthy of being recognized by archaeologists as the cradle of Ráŕhii civilization. Here the Suvarnarekha River valley, Kamsavati River valley and Damodar River valley (Alkushi, Kupai, Uttará or Chot́ki Guyai and Dakśińá or Baŕki Guyai) are all close to each other and I was able to discover many things there.

paragraphs.text: “I am extremely interested in the archaeology of Ráŕh,” he replied, “but I have never had an opportunity to meet anyone who was as interested in the subject as I am. I heard that you were in the area going around to different villages, and that you had managed to gather many facts. I also heard that you discovered in the house of a certain Siḿmuńd́á in the village of Mardu, an intact statue of the state goddess of Bengal, Dákśáyańii, from the beginning of the Shur dynasty. I went out to try to find you but you were moving so fast from village to village that it was impossible to catch up with you. I became tired and sat down under a mango tree near the Silli royal palace. Then it popped into my head that you were staying in the Jhalda dak bungalow, so I rushed here and managed to find you.”

paragraphs.text: “During the rule of the Shur dynasty,” he continued, “our Bengal extended from the Suvarnarekha River valley to the Naaf River valley. Although nowadays there are twelve dialects of Bengali spoken over this huge area, in those days there were even more because there was no proper transportation between the different areas. It was due to the impassability of traffic that so many dialects arose. Roughly speaking, the Bengali language of that time was a related version of Oriental Demi-Mágadhii. We can also call it old Bengali. We can find this Oriental Demi-Mágadhii form of Bengali in the Caryápada and the Caryácaryavinishcaya of the Buddhist era. From this we can easily conclude that the Bengali language is at least 1500 years old – not a bit less. There are older languages among the worldʼs modern living languages, but very few.

paragraphs.text: “In that era the influence of Shiva on the Bengali people was immense. Dákśáyańii, the daughter of King Dakśa and the wife of Shiva, was the state goddess of Bengal. Statues of Dákśáyańii have been found in a good number of villages in our Suvarnarekha River valley. Most of them have been carved from stone and some bear inscriptions in D́álma script. You went to the village of Mardu in the Silli area of Ranchi District – that village is very close to Jhalda; the Suvarnarekha River runs through it.

paragraphs.text: “During the Buddhist and Puranic eras, indeed, even during the Pathan era, the Dákrás ( 24 ) used to gather gold particles from the sand of this river, which they would then melt down to remove the base metals and extract the pure gold. During that time many archaeological artifacts made in Suvarnarekha valley were fashioned of pure gold, but they fell into the hands of thieves so they are no longer found today. During the time of Varddhamana Mahaviira, Jainism greatly influenced this region especially our Suvarnarekha and Kamsavati river valleys and to a lesser extent the Dhalkishore ( 25 ), Damodar, Ajay and Mayurakshi river valleys.

paragraphs.text: “You certainly must have discovered a large-sized Jain Shiva in the broken Shiva temple in Mardu village. This type of Shiva-liuṋga has been recovered in excavations elsewhere in Ráŕh and more will be in the future. Several of them can also be seen above ground, in some of the temple ruins. The names of these Jain Shivas ended with the word iishvara, not nátha. For example, Khadgeshvara [was used], and not Khadganátha. In Bengal the word iishvara was used at the end of Shivaʼs name from the end of the Buddhist era until the appearance of Shankaracharya. These Jain Shiva-liuṋgas were quite large in size and the gaorii pat́t́as were very large as well.

paragraphs.text: “The old Jain Shiva-liuṋgas had the same radius from top to bottom. Later, during the time of Shankaracharya, the people of Ráŕh who accepted Shankaraʼs Shaeva doctrine gave them the name jyotirliuṋga. But alongside the Jain religion, váńaliuṋgas were also prevalent in Bengal, chiefly in Buddhist Bengal. The váńaliuṋga has no relation to the Jain Shiva; thus, in olden times, the jyotirliuṋga and váńaliuṋga were worshipped with different mantras. Khadgeshvara of Birbhum, Jhaŕeshvara of Midnapore, and Tárakeshvara of Hoogly are all from the Jain era, but while some of their temples are quite old, many are less so and some are quite contemporary.

paragraphs.text: “If you go into the villages upland of the Suvarnarekha River valley region you will notice that the indigenous people of these areas (for example, the Singhmundas or Siḿmuńd́ás) are completely different from other Bengalees in their behaviour, practices, culture and womenʼs style of dress. Their spoken languages are the Páiṋc-Parganiya ( 26 ), Pátkumi or Golawári branches of Ráŕhii Bengali. Their skin colour is also not black; one can say that it is darkish. Light-skinned people are also found among them. This illustrates the fact that while the Bengali people are a blend of the Austric, Mongolian and Negroid races, the amount of Negroid blood in them is significantly less. There is also very little Negroid influence on body size and structure, though it cannot be denied that there is some influence.

This sentimentality has enabled the Bengalees to pass through many fiery ordeals and it will do so in future as well.”

paragraphs.text: Asuras are Assyrians

The spelling of sura is correct. In the absence of historical or linguistic knowledge, some people spell it as shura, which is wholly incorrect. The correct meaning of the word sura is “a good man.” The gods of mythology used to pass themselves off as honest and their enemies as dishonest, due to which they called themselves suras and their enemies asuras. In reality suras were people belonging to the Aryan race. Those belonging to the asura tribe can be found in significant number in Madhya Pradesh and in Palamau district of Bihar. I have seen these people in the vicinity of Mahuátáṋd́ in Palamau district. In ancient times, the Caucasian Aryans, that is the suras, were white complexioned or brown-coloured, and Ottomans [Turks] and asuras (Assyrians) of the Semitic group were dark-complexioned or copper-coloured. In those days the suras and asuras could be identified by their skin colour, but today this is no longer so simple. Especially in the Middle East and South Asia, large-scale racial blending occurred over the last three thousand years. ( 28 )
summary: The spelling of sura is correct.
Those belonging to the asura tribe can be found in significant number in Madhya Pradesh and in Palamau district of Bihar.

paragraphs.text: Gańa + náyiká = gańanáyiká. The meaning of the word náyiká is a woman who leads people to the right path. According to Puranic myth, at one time the battle between the devas [gods] or suras and asuras [demons] took on a violent form. Please remember that the devas or suras were of Caucasian or Aryan race – white-complexioned, tall and sharp-nosed. Their hair was golden, blue or black and was usually not curly. Their nose was neither flat nor broad, and their jaws were not raised. They had hair on their body, and their bodily complexion was neither pale, nor yellow nor deep dark. They were known as devas, suras or Aryans. Those who lived in ancient times in Assyria in Central Asia were no less civilized than the Aryans. They were of medium build and tall (not short-statured). Their bodily complexion was blue-black (shyámal) and their hair was slightly curly. They were never snub-nosed. Though slightly broad, their jaws were not raised. They were simpler in nature than the Aryans. They were more inclined towards the matriarchal system than the patriarchal system and were less conceited than the Aryans regarding their racial origins. In contrast to the Aryans, they were simple enough to trust others easily.
summary: Gańa + náyiká = gańanáyiká.
Those who lived in ancient times in Assyria in Central Asia were no less civilized than the Aryans.

paragraphs.text: In ancient Vedic language, the inhabitants of Assyria ( 29 ) were called asuras. For a long period there was a sanguinary battle between the suras and asuras. The Latin adjective for hope is sanguine, but the Latin adjective for blood is both sanguine and sanguinary. The guru of the suras or gods was Acarya Brhaspati and the guru of the asuras was Shukracáryá. Neither was less scholarly than the other. Brhaspati was a philosophically oriented person. At that time philosophy had not yet emerged; philosophy first emerged in Ráŕh during the time of Maharśi Kapil. Maharśi Shukrácárya was a scientist. He was the first to use solvent-related chemistry to manufacture wine or alcohol. Prior to that, people used to prepare fermented wine by using the herb somalatá, which was called somarasa. It was Shukracáryá who first produced distilled wine – Devásuraeryuddhakále shukreńa parinirmitam [During the war between devas and asuras the distilled wine was prepared by Shukrácárya].
summary: In ancient Vedic language, the inhabitants of Assyria ( 29 ) were called asuras.
Brhaspati was a philosophically oriented person.
It was Shukracáryá who first produced distilled wine – Devásuraeryuddhakále shukreńa parinirmitam [During the war between devas and asuras the distilled wine was prepared by Shukrácárya].

The name of the first part of the river is Dhalkishore. After it joins the Gandheshvari River in Bankura, the name of the combined flow is Dvarakeshvar. When this Dvarakeshvar River reaches the far border of Hoogly District it joins the Shilavati (Shilai) River coming from the west and thereafter flows towards the southwest under the name of the Rupanarayan River, dividing Midnapore and Howrah; thereafter it joins with the Bhagirathi. At its end, Howrah Districtʼs Shyampur area is on the left bank and Midnapore Districtʼs Tamluk is on the right bank.

The far western fringe of Rarh, where the Suvarnarekha, Kansavati and Damodar River-valleys come together, we can call the cradle of both Rarhii and human civilization. As regards the spoken language, the branch of Rarhii Bengali that is prevalent in the area lying on the right bank (south) of the Suvarnarekha River is called Páiṋc-Pargańiyá Bengali. The spoken language found on the left bank of the Suvarnarekha River and the right bank (south) of the Kansavati River is the Patkumi branch of Ráŕhii Bengali. And the language spoken on the left bank of the Kansavati and the right bank of the Damodar is the Golawárii branch of Ráŕhii Bengali. Gola is a famous place of this area from which the name Golawárii has come. The spoken language of the area lying on the left bank of the Damodar, that is, north and west of the Pareshanath Hills is called Dakśińii Khot́t́á Bengali. The closer one gets to the Pareshanath Hills the more the influence of Ráŕhii Bengali increases in this Dakśińii Khot́t́á Bengali and the nearer one gets to the Tilaiya Reservoir, the more the influence of southern Magahii or Gayáli Magahii increases. The Páiṋc-Pargańiyá branch of Ráŕhii Bengali is spoken in Ranchi Districtʼs Bundu, Arki, Tamar – 1, Tamar – 2, Sonahatu, the southern part of the Silli area, and the southern part of the Ángárá area. The Patkumi branch of Ráŕhi Bengali is prevalent in Purulia Districtʼs Jhalda and Tulin areas, the northern part of Ranchi Districtʼs Silli and Ángárá areas, and in certain parts of Hazaribag Districtʼs (now Giridi District) Kasmar and Petarwar areas. The Golawárii branch of Ráŕhii Bengali is spoken in Purulia Districtʼs Jaipur area, Dhanbad Districtʼs Chas, Chandankeyari, Bokaro Steel City and Jeridi, and in certain portions of Hazaribag Districtʼs (now Giridi District) Kasmar, Petarwar, Gola and Ramgarh areas. The spoken language of Hazaribag Districtʼs (now Giridi District) Gomoh, Nuyadi, Bermo, Dumri, Chandrapura and Bokaro (Thermal) areas is also a variety of this Golawárii Bengali.
