chapters.title: Vedas and Their Compositions
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Rgveda, Shruta and Shruti
summary: Rgveda, Shruta and Shruti

paragraphs.text: The Rgveda is very old. Moreover, it is certain that Krśńadvaepáyańa Vyása had divided the Vedas into three separate parts – the oldest portion, the middling portion, and the most recent portion – well before the Jain era. Here I use the words “well before the Jain era” because the Vedas are mentioned in the Jain scriptures, which were written in the Prákrta language. The propounder of the Jain religion, Varddhaman Mahaviir, was born a little over 2500 years ago, and the Prákrta language originated between four thousand and five thousand years ago. Thus, whatever portion of the Vedas is considered to be the most recent, it is certainly more than five thousand years old. And in regard to the Jain scriptures, certain portions of it were composed before the era of Varddhaman Mahaviir by various other Jain saints; still they are in no way more than five thousand years old. The time of the composition of the Rgveda was approximately between fifteen thousand years ago and ten thousand years ago, that of the Yajurveda between ten thousand years ago and seven thousand years ago, and that of the Atharvaveda between seven thousand years ago and five thousand years ago. The Sámaveda is not a Veda at all. The word sáma means “song”. The Sámaveda was made later on from the music portions of the three Vedas, that is, the Sámaveda is found within the Rgveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Vedas were first divided into the Rk, Yajuh, and Atharva – these three parts. However the Sámaveda is mentioned in the Jain scriptures, that is, the Vedas had already been divided into three parts at the time of the origin of the Jain scriptures, and the Sámaveda had already been created from the musical portions of the three Vedas. Just as the Vedas could not be written down due to lack of any written script, it may also be that the early Jain saints, however old they may have been, were not able to record their teachings through the medium of written script. Varddhaman Mahaviirʼs time was after the discovery of script, thus the Jain scriptures were written down and they were written in the Prákrta language of that time.
summary: The Rgveda is very old.
The Sámaveda is not a Veda at all.
Varddhaman Mahaviirʼs time was after the discovery of script, thus the Jain scriptures were written down and they were written in the Prákrta language of that time.

paragraphs.text: Varddhaman Mahaviirʼs birthplace was Vaeshali in eastern India. Magadha and Ráŕh are the lands of spiritual propagation. Thus, it is an easily discovered fact that whatever he spoke or wrote was in the prevalent Mágadhii Prákrta language of the day. So it will not be enough to say that the language of the Jain scriptures was Prákrta – there were seven main Prákrta languages. The language of the Jain scriptures was one among them, that is, Mágadhii Prákrta.
summary: Varddhaman Mahaviirʼs birthplace was Vaeshali in eastern India.
Thus, it is an easily discovered fact that whatever he spoke or wrote was in the prevalent Mágadhii Prákrta language of the day.
The language of the Jain scriptures was one among them, that is, Mágadhii Prákrta.

paragraphs.text: There was no script during the time of the Rgveda, so it was not written down. Nor was there any script during the time of the Yajurveda, so it also could not be written. Written script was invented during the time of the Atharvaveda. Yet since the Rk and Yajuh portions of the Vedas could not be written during the time of the composition of the Atharvaveda, that is, at the time of the composition of the last portion of the Vedas, people thought that perhaps the Vedas should not be written. Thus the Atharva portion remained unwritten like the Rk and Yajuh portions.
summary: There was no script during the time of the Rgveda, so it was not written down.
Written script was invented during the time of the Atharvaveda.
Thus the Atharva portion remained unwritten like the Rk and Yajuh portions.

paragraphs.text: The Atharvavedaʼs ádarsha puruśa (the first propounder or main propounder was called ádarsha puruśa at that time) was Brahmarśi Atharvá. He was most likely from Central Asia, but one cannot say for certain that he was not an original inhabitant of India. Still, there is no doubt that the propounders of the later portions of the Atharvaveda were inhabitants of India, especially Maharśi Vaedarbhi, because Vidarbha was the name of a settlement in the Central-Western portion of India.

paragraphs.text: Krśńadvaepáyańa Vyása is renowned as Vedavyása for having divided the Vedas into three main portions (Rk, Yajuh, and Atharva). There is a great difference of opinion about this word vyása. There are many historical figures named Vyása, however, careful observation shows us that Vyása is not a name; it is a hereditary title. Vádaráyańa Vyása, Saiṋjaya Vyása, Vivasvata Vyása – their titles were all Vyása, not their name.

paragraphs.text: The name of the Vyása who divided the Vedas was Krśńadvaepáyańa Vyása. He was born in a fishermanʼs family (Kaevarta [a fishing caste]) on a blackish island ( 1 ) that rose out of the waters of the confluence of the Ganges and the Yamuna at Prayag, and for this reason the people gave him the name Krśńadvaepáyańa. ( 2 ) Krśńadvaepáyańa or Vedavyása was the composer of the Mahábhárata. The Mahábhárata was composed long, long, long after the Vedas, but nonetheless it is undoubtedly more than three thousand years old.
summary: The name of the Vyása who divided the Vedas was Krśńadvaepáyańa Vyása.
( 2 ) Krśńadvaepáyańa or Vedavyása was the composer of the Mahábhárata.
The Mahábhárata was composed long, long, long after the Vedas, but nonetheless it is undoubtedly more than three thousand years old.

paragraphs.text: Although the Rgveda is mainly concerned with hymns, it also contains various tales and anecdotes. While not all of these stories and tales carry equal spiritual value, they are representative of the cultural heritage of those ancient human beings. They paint a portrait of the gradual advancement of human thinking and the structure of society. When considered from this point of view, the language, literature and expression of the Rgveda is of special value to the world. While it is true that there was no script during the Rgvedic age, phonemes and phonetic expression as well as the order of the sounds, interpolation and placement (the method of arranging the sounds) were in existence. The different Rgvedic styles of pronunciation for the various letters were in vogue, which the followers of the Rgveda would learn orally from the guru in subsequent times. I have talked about this to some extent here and there in our language books. If time permits I will discuss the subject further at a later date.
summary: Although the Rgveda is mainly concerned with hymns, it also contains various tales and anecdotes.

paragraphs.text: In the Vedas, especially in the Rgveda, a special rule can be seen for the naming of the rks (stanzas or mantras) and súktas (hymns). Normally the rk is named according to the name by which the Supreme Consciousness is addressed. Where the Supreme Consciousness is not addressed by any particular name, then that súkta, or in certain cases that rk also, is named with the help of the first word. The third characteristic is that in most cases the rks were composed in certain metres.
summary: In the Vedas, especially in the Rgveda, a special rule can be seen for the naming of the rks (stanzas or mantras) and súktas (hymns).
Where the Supreme Consciousness is not addressed by any particular name, then that súkta, or in certain cases that rk also, is named with the help of the first word.
The third characteristic is that in most cases the rks were composed in certain metres.

paragraphs.text: There are seven main metres: gáyattrii, uśńika, triśt́upa, anuśt́upa, brhatii, jagatii and paḿkti. Besides this, because there was no authoritative grammar in that language (that is, the Vedic language) whereby differences between the metre and the prevalent unwritten grammar of the day could be resolved according to rules, the custom was in vogue of violating the grammar according to oneʼs convenience by cutting, reducing, increasing or even changing sounds in order to keep the metre intact. One accepted name of the rk 310/62 that we generally call the gáyattrii mantra is savitr rk – not gáyattrii mantra. Gáyattrii is the name of a particular metre, not the name of a mantra or a rk. In the relevant rk, Parama Puruśa is addressed as “Savitá” (the word is derived by adding the suffix trń/trc to the verbal root sú). Thus the rkʼs name is “Savitr Rk”. At the beginning of one súkta [hymn] in the first mańd́ala [book] of the Rgveda we find:

paragraphs.text: By adding mahávyáhrti, the meaning of the “Savitr Rk” is strengthened. It was added for this reason. By adding the mahávyáhuti, the meaning of the mantra becomes clearer. “In the bhúr-bhuvah-svah, that is, crude, subtle and causal worlds, we are meditating on the excellent effulgence of Savitá, or the father, so that He might guide our dhii, or intellect, to the path of truth.” Awakening the inspiration to receive spiritual direction from Parama Puruśa with the help of this mantra is called “Vedic initiation”. Later on, when the person receives proper instructions in spiritual practice for moving on the spiritual path then that is called “Tantric initiation”.

paragraphs.text: The Rgveda was considered the chief Veda in ancient times, not only because of the value of its antiquity, but because Vedic initiation was more or less based on the “Savitr Rk” of the Rgveda, although as regards the adjustment between the spiritual world and the material world for a spiritual aspirant, the Yajurveda surpasses the Rgveda in importance. In terms of pronunciation and phonetics, the Yajurveda is quite different from the Rgveda. The Yajurveda had closer contact with Tantra, and the Atharva was mixed with Tantra at nearly every step. At one time the orthodox priests declared the followers of the Atharvaveda to be social outcasts; they said atharvánnaḿ má bhuiṋjiitháh, that is, the food of the followers of the Atharvaveda should not be accepted.

paragraphs.text: The verbal root rś has many meanings, one of which is “to rise upwards”. This verbal root rś is used for moving up from one floor of a house to the one above it. By adding the suffix in to the verbal root rś we obtain the word rśi, whose etymological meaning is “one who rises upwards”; its colloquial meaning is “a person of elevated mind, elevated intellect, elevated thought”. Although the feminine form of the word rśi is rśyá, the word rśi can also be used as common gender. That is, a woman can be called rśi just as a man can. And rśyá can also be used. Persons of elevated consciousness have been called rśi since Rgvedic times.
summary: The verbal root rś has many meanings, one of which is “to rise upwards”.
Although the feminine form of the word rśi is rśyá, the word rśi can also be used as common gender.
Persons of elevated consciousness have been called rśi since Rgvedic times.

paragraphs.text: Just as every mantra is composed in a certain metre, and just as most of the mantras address Parama Puruśa with a particular name, similarly each mantra had its draśt́á-rśi [seer-rśi] ( 3 ) who, after realizing the truth in his or her sádhaná, or meditation and concentration, would then teach it orally to his or her disciples.
summary: Just as every mantra is composed in a certain metre, and just as most of the mantras address Parama Puruśa with a particular name, similarly each mantra had its draśt́á-rśi [seer-rśi] ( 3 ) who, after realizing the truth in his or her sádhaná, or meditation and concentration, would then teach it orally to his or her disciples.

paragraphs.text: Since the Rgvedic age, rśis have been mainly divided into four categories: maharśi, devarśi, rájarśi and brahmarśi. Those persons who executed their worldly duties as required and at the same time cultivated meditation, concentration, sádhaná and philosophy (árańyak and upaniśad) in search of a higher world, and having attained perfection in that spiritual path, would do service to the world, were called maharśi (for example, Maharśi Vishvámitra).
summary: Since the Rgvedic age, rśis have been mainly divided into four categories: maharśi, devarśi, rájarśi and brahmarśi.

Those persons who executed their worldly duties as required and at the same time cultivated meditation, concentration, sádhaná and philosophy (árańyak and upaniśad) in search of a higher world, and having attained perfection in that spiritual path, would do service to the world, were called maharśi (for example, Maharśi Vishvámitra).

paragraphs.text: Those who, having taken birth in the race of devas (Nordic, Alpine and Mediterranean subraces and the Caucasian race), had established themselves in spiritual consciousness through sádhaná, were called devarśi (for example, Devarśi Nárada).
summary: Those who, having taken birth in the race of devas (Nordic, Alpine and Mediterranean subraces and the Caucasian race), had established themselves in spiritual consciousness through sádhaná, were called devarśi (for example, Devarśi Nárada).

paragraphs.text: Those who had to take care of great social responsibilities (as in the case of kings) but at the same time were able to saturate the urges of their heart and their intellect with spiritual consciousness were called rájarśi (for example, Rájarśi Janaka). ( 4 )
summary: Those who had to take care of great social responsibilities (as in the case of kings) but at the same time were able to saturate the urges of their heart and their intellect with spiritual consciousness were called rájarśi (for example, Rájarśi Janaka).

paragraphs.text: Those who infused their existence with a current of spiritual inspiration throughout their lives were called brahmarśi (for example, Brahmarśi Kańva, Brahmarśi Atharvá).
summary: Those who infused their existence with a current of spiritual inspiration throughout their lives were called brahmarśi (for example, Brahmarśi Kańva, Brahmarśi Atharvá).

paragraphs.text: During the time of the Atharvaveda, its propounder or originator (in the Vedic language ádarsha puruśa), Atharvá, was honoured as brahmarśi. A number of rśis were revered as maharśi, some of whom deserve special mention. They were Maharśis Atri, Auṋgirá, Auṋgirasa, Pulaha, Pulasta, Satyaváha, Vashiśt́ha and Vaedarbhi. Those who believe that the Vedas were composed entirely outside India cannot go unopposed, at least not in the case of the Atharvaveda. There is clear proof that the rśi named Vaedarbhi was a man of Vidarbha, that is, from the region of Nagpur and Amaravatii. It is hard to imagine Maharśi Vaedarbhi travelling all the way to Central Asia and remaining there to compose the Atharvaveda. On the other hand, it may well be that the entire Atharvaveda was not composed in India. Maharśi Atharvá was the ádarsha puruśa of the Atharvaveda. He was also respected as an elderly person. Even today we say about very aged people: “He has become Atharvá.”
summary: During the time of the Atharvaveda, its propounder or originator (in the Vedic language ádarsha puruśa), Atharvá, was honoured as brahmarśi.
It is hard to imagine Maharśi Vaedarbhi travelling all the way to Central Asia and remaining there to compose the Atharvaveda.

paragraphs.text: Bear in mind that rśi and muni are not the same thing. I have already spoken substantially about rśi. The word muni has two primary meanings. One meaning of muni is “contemplative entity” or “intellectual”. The second meaning of muni is “one who has dissolved oneʼs mind into Parama Puruśa”. Na munirdugdhabálakah munih saḿliinamánasah. (Muni does not mean “small child”; muni is one who has merged his or her mind in the Macrocosmic mind.) ( 5 )

paragraphs.text: The subject of Varśa – Bháratvarśa
summary: The subject of Varśa – Bháratvarśa

paragraphs.text: The verbal root tan means to expand – to extend. It is both subjective and objective. The verbal root bhr means to feed, to entertain, while the verbal root tan means to expand. The entity who feed and enhances growth in the physical, mental and spiritual spheres is called Bharata (bhr + ac = bhar, tan + d́a = ta). The country that nourishes its residents and helps in their all-round development is known as Bháratvarśa. In a colloquial sense it means three things. The word varśa means a country, for example, as in Bháratvarśa, Kimpuruśvarśa (Tibet) and Suvarńavarśa (Burma). The word khańd́a means “portion”. In ancient times, the learned ones divided the world into seven major portions. They are called saptadviipa [a land of seven islands, sapta meaning “seven” and dviipa meaning “island”] or sapta sandviipa [the word sandviipa also means island]. Certain parts of Asia and Southeast Asia constituted Jambudviipa. Certain varśas were denoted in each of these islands, and in each of these varśas were viśaya – called úraśa or úr in ancient Tamil. One portion of Jambudviipa was Bháratvarśa and Kimpuruśvarśa (Tibet). In Bháratvarśa there was Gaoraviśaya (Bengal), Auṋgaviśaya (Auṋga: the Bhagalpur-Purnea, etc. area), and Magadhaviśaya (Patna-Gaya, etc. area: Astimagadhaviśaya Pataliputtranámadheya nagarah), Mahiśaviśaya (the land of Karnataka; in old Tamil viśaya or varśa was called úr.) The Sanskrit name Mahishaviśya evolved into Mahiśa-úr > Mahiśúr > Myśore) in old Tamil. So you now understand Bháratavarśa or Bharatakhańd́a is a part of this Jambudviipa (Jambudvipae Bháratakhańd́e). ( 6 )
summary: The verbal root tan means to expand – to extend.
They are called saptadviipa [a land of seven islands, sapta meaning “seven” and dviipa meaning “island”] or sapta sandviipa [the word sandviipa also means island].
So you now understand Bháratavarśa or Bharatakhańd́a is a part of this Jambudviipa (Jambudvipae Bháratakhańd́e).

paragraphs.text: Footnotes

footnotes.text: The foregoing two paragraphs are from Shabda Cayaniká Part 16, Discourse 122.
The alluvial land of the Yamuna is a little blackish in colour and the alluvial land of the Ganges is yellowish.
Krśńadvaepáyańa means “coming from a black island” – Trans.

Originally there was no alphabet. Since there was no script, one did not say lekhaka-rśi [writer-sage] but rather draśt́á-rśi, that is, “that rśi who has seen the truth in his or her meditation”.
Hrdá maniiśá manasábhiklrptah [“Saturating the heart and mind in consciousness”].

chapters.title: River Valley Civilizations
chapters.partTitle: PART 2: Ancient Territories, Races, Languages, Scripts, and Civilizations

paragraphs.text: Gangetic civilizations and their stages
summary: Gangetic civilizations and their stages

paragraphs.text: The name of the city known as Allahabad, formerly it was called Prayága. It is true that Prayága is older than Konnagar. It was built towards the end of the Yajurvedic period six thousand years ago. But Burdwan is even more ancient than Prayága. During Pathan rule Prayága was renamed Allahabad (Abode of Allah). Since then its popularity has been increasing. The Shia Moslems named the city Illahabad, but during the Mughal period the prosperous growth of the city was checked. Thereafter, the city again began to flourish towards the end of British rule when it became the capital of the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short).
summary: The name of the city known as Allahabad, formerly it was called Prayága.
During Pathan rule Prayága was renamed Allahabad (Abode of Allah).
Thereafter, the city again began to flourish towards the end of British rule when it became the capital of the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short).

paragraphs.text: In the pre-Buddhist era Burdwan was the capital of Ráŕh. In the Buddhist and Jain era it remained Ráŕhʼs capital. During the Mughal period (during the reign of Akbar) Burdwan was the capital of Subá-Bángál. However, Konnagar had no similar royal glamour. It was just a highly cultured village of Burdwan District. (The district of Hooghly was not created then.) Iishan Chandra Ghosh, the renowned Bengali scholar of medieval Bengal; Rama Chandra Ghosh, the illustrious logician and author of scriptures; Práńatosá Biswas, the most erudite Sanskrit and scriptural scholar; and Dr. Krśńadhan Ghosh (father of Shrii Aurobindo), the first Bengali District Medical Officer (DMO) and Civil Surgeon, were all born in Konnagar.
summary: In the pre-Buddhist era Burdwan was the capital of Ráŕh.
It was just a highly cultured village of Burdwan District.
Krśńadhan Ghosh (father of Shrii Aurobindo), the first Bengali District Medical Officer (DMO) and Civil Surgeon, were all born in Konnagar.

paragraphs.text: We were travelling from west to east – from ancient Brahmávartta or Brahmarśidesh to the ancient Káshii kingdom. That part of the Gangetic valley is considered as the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. The Prayága area is considered as the upper part of the Ganges river civilization. The area stretching from Prayága to the confluence of the rivers Shone and Ganges is the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. And the area from the Shone-Ganges confluence to Sahebganj is considered as the Gaod́a part of the Ganges river civilization. The area from Sahebganj, where the Ganges starts flowing southward, to Gangasagar is known as the final part of the Ganges valley civilization or Gaod́iiya civilization. The Gaod́iiya civilization is most developed where the rivers of Ráŕh – carrying with them the local cultural specialities of Ráŕh civilization – and the Brahmaputra River, coming from the northeast and carrying with it the flow of Mongolian civilization, merge into the Ganges. The part of the Ganges valley civilization that was the homeland of the pre-Gaod́iiya and Gaod́iiya civilizations cannot be called an Aryan civilization in the proper sense of the term. Actually, it is the east India civilization or extended Ganges delta civilization.
summary: We were travelling from west to east – from ancient Brahmávartta or Brahmarśidesh to the ancient Káshii kingdom.
And the area from the Shone-Ganges confluence to Sahebganj is considered as the Gaod́a part of the Ganges river civilization.
Actually, it is the east India civilization or extended Ganges delta civilization.

paragraphs.text: Hence, the area from Allahabad to Káshii or Gańd́akii (here Gańd́akii means Náráyańii-Gańd́ak – not the Buŕi Gańd́ak of Muzaffarpur and Samastipur) is part of the pre-Gaod́iiya civilization. Burdwan can be considered as the nucleus of Ráŕhiiya civilization, and Konnagar as the main source of Gaod́iiya civilization, which itself is based on Ráŕhiiya civilization. ... Different species of plants, trees and animals and a unique human civilization have followed the Ganges downstream from its source in Gangottarii. Similarly, other species of plants, trees and animals as well as a different human civilization have followed the banks of the river Yamuna downstream from its source at Yamunottarii. What is the result of the merging of the two rivers, the Ganges and Yamuna, at Prayága?...
summary: Hence, the area from Allahabad to Káshii or Gańd́akii (here Gańd́akii means Náráyańii-Gańd́ak – not the Buŕi Gańd́ak of Muzaffarpur and Samastipur) is part of the pre-Gaod́iiya civilization.
Different species of plants, trees and animals and a unique human civilization have followed the Ganges downstream from its source in Gangottarii.
What is the result of the merging of the two rivers, the Ganges and Yamuna, at Prayága?...

paragraphs.text: Just as the river Ganges has brought with her saffron-coloured clay, special types of flora and fauna and its own alluvium, the river Yamuna has also carried her own distinct characteristics down from her source. A little further downstream, another river, the Charmanvatii or Chambal, carrying the special characteristics of the western Indian civilization of Málava and Bundelkhańd́a merges into the Yamuna. In this area a new mixed civilization occurred which can be called the Bághelii civilization. The Yamuna carried this mixed civilization, and merged its black waters into the Ganges at Prayága. Thus, the middle stage of the Gangetic valley civilization starts from Prayága.
summary: Just as the river Ganges has brought with her saffron-coloured clay, special types of flora and fauna and its own alluvium, the river Yamuna has also carried her own distinct characteristics down from her source.
In this area a new mixed civilization occurred which can be called the Bághelii civilization.
Thus, the middle stage of the Gangetic valley civilization starts from Prayága.

paragraphs.text: The Gangetic river valley civilizations upriver and downriver from Prayága are not the same. The middle stage lying to the south of the Ganges continues up to the Ganga-Shone confluence at Patna, and towards the north continues up to the Ganges-Náráyańii confluence near Hajipur. Thereafter the pre-Gaod́iiya civilization begins. Comparatively speaking, the Austric influence is less than the Mongol-Tantric influence. This area has been known since ancient times as Trihotriiya Bhúmi. On the south side of the Ganges, after the Ganga-Shone confluence, the Pre-Gaod́iiya civilization begins, no doubt, but there the Mongol-Tantric influence is less than the Gondwana influence.
summary: The Gangetic river valley civilizations upriver and downriver from Prayága are not the same.
Comparatively speaking, the Austric influence is less than the Mongol-Tantric influence.
On the south side of the Ganges, after the Ganga-Shone confluence, the Pre-Gaod́iiya civilization begins, no doubt, but there the Mongol-Tantric influence is less than the Gondwana influence.

paragraphs.text: From the ethnological point of view, there is a difference between Trihotriiya Bhúmi and Magadha Bhúmi. In the physical structure of the people of Trihotriiya Bhúmi [Mithila] the Austric influence is less than the Mongolian influence. Black people are few in number. From the complexion of the people in Magadha it is evident that the Mongolian influence is almost nil. Flat-nosed people are very few. There are many black-complexioned people but with aquiline noses.
summary: From the ethnological point of view, there is a difference between Trihotriiya Bhúmi and Magadha Bhúmi.
From the complexion of the people in Magadha it is evident that the Mongolian influence is almost nil.
There are many black-complexioned people but with aquiline noses.

paragraphs.text: Although Trihotriiya Bhúmi (Videha or Mithilá) and Magadha belong to the same language group, the Mágadhii Prákrta group; the Maethilii language belongs to the Eastern Demi-Mágadhii group, and the Magahii language belongs to the Western Demi-Mágadhii group. The difference in intonation of the languages is particularly discernible, although both languages belong to the pre-Gaod́iiya Gangetic Civilization. This becomes notable in Auṋga Bhúmi, where the Trihotriiya and Mágadhii cultural characteristics have blended into one. These characteristics came in contact with the Gaod́iiya civilization.
summary: Although Trihotriiya Bhúmi (Videha or Mithilá) and Magadha belong to the same language group, the Mágadhii Prákrta group; the Maethilii language belongs to the Eastern Demi-Mágadhii group, and the Magahii language belongs to the Western Demi-Mágadhii group.
This becomes notable in Auṋga Bhúmi, where the Trihotriiya and Mágadhii cultural characteristics have blended into one.
These characteristics came in contact with the Gaod́iiya civilization.

paragraphs.text: The Gangetic valley civilization has been transformed into pure Gaod́iiya civilization or deltaic civilization, where the River Ganges and the Vindhya Range have come closest to each other near Sahebganj in Angadesh, and from that point the Ganges flows southwards.
summary: The Gangetic valley civilization has been transformed into pure Gaod́iiya civilization or deltaic civilization, where the River Ganges and the Vindhya Range have come closest to each other near Sahebganj in Angadesh, and from that point the Ganges flows southwards.

paragraphs.text: As far as I understand, the land of Ráŕh is the land where Sanskrit originated. But the ancient language which we describe as the Vedic language came to India from the northwest along with the Aryans. The Aryans first migrated to the Sindhu-Saoviira, and the land of Sapta-Sindhu, the Seven Rivers (Sutlej or Shatadru, Bias or Vipásha, Ravi or Irávatii, Chenub or Candrabhágá, Jhelum or Vitastá, Kabul and Sind). These seven rivers together are known as the Sapta-Sindhu. Later on the land became known as the Punjab, that is, the land of five rivers. The names of two rivers have been dropped, so there remain only five.
summary: As far as I understand, the land of Ráŕh is the land where Sanskrit originated.
These seven rivers together are known as the Sapta-Sindhu.
The names of two rivers have been dropped, so there remain only five.

paragraphs.text: This is the first phase of the Vedic influence in India. In the second phase the Aryans moved further southeast: their influence pervaded in the northern part of the Yamuna valley. That area was known as Haritadhánya or the ‘Land of Green Vegetation’ (Haritadhánya > Hariahánna > Harihána > Hariyána).
summary: This is the first phase of the Vedic influence in India.
In the second phase the Aryans moved further southeast: their influence pervaded in the northern part of the Yamuna valley.
That area was known as Haritadhánya or the ‘Land of Green Vegetation’ (Haritadhánya > Hariahánna > Harihána > Hariyána).

paragraphs.text: Then, in the next phase, the Aryans reached Prayága around the Ganga-Yamuna valley. This we can describe as the third phase of the Vedic influence ( 1 ). Then they moved farther east, and their influence extended to the Gańd́akii River on the north and the Shone River on the south. This can be called the fourth phase of Vedic influence. The ancient Káshiirájya or Kingdom of Káshii was situated in this area. We are now journeying through the Káshiirájya. One thing to be noted here is that in the first phase, the Vedic language left two daughters behind: Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta. In the languages born from Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta (for example, Pashto and Punjabi) there is a multitude of words derived from the Vedic language. In the second phase, that is, in the Hariyánvii language, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is somewhat less. In the third stage, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less; for instance, in languages such as Máŕoyárii, Haŕaotii, Bundelii, Bághelii, Avadhii and Vrajabháśa. And in languages of the fourth stage, such as Bhojpurii, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less. But no one should misunderstand that in the fourth stage the Vedic influence was nil. No doubt direct Vedic influence in the fourth stage was nil, but the indirect influence in pre-Gaod́iiya and Gaod́iiya civilizations was tremendous, and that influence still persists even today.
summary: Then, in the next phase, the Aryans reached Prayága around the Ganga-Yamuna valley.
One thing to be noted here is that in the first phase, the Vedic language left two daughters behind: Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta.
No doubt direct Vedic influence in the fourth stage was nil, but the indirect influence in pre-Gaod́iiya and Gaod́iiya civilizations was tremendous, and that influence still persists even today.

paragraphs.text: The structure of the human skull of people in this area is different from that of the people of the area of pre-Gaod́iiya civilization. But the human skull of the people of Angadesh is almost the same as that of the people of the Gaod́iiya area; the difference is hardly discernible.
summary: The structure of the human skull of people in this area is different from that of the people of the area of pre-Gaod́iiya civilization.
But the human skull of the people of Angadesh is almost the same as that of the people of the Gaod́iiya area; the difference is hardly discernible.

paragraphs.text: Thames River valley civilizations and their stages
summary: Thames River valley civilizations and their stages

paragraphs.text: [Now let us see] how at different stages of rivers the patterns of civilizations vary.
summary: [Now let us see] how at different stages of rivers the patterns of civilizations vary.

paragraphs.text: Great Britain is a small country; the distance from any part of Britain to the ocean is not more than fifty miles. So naturally in that country there cannot be any large river: the distance between the source of a river and the ocean cannot be very great. Yet if we move along the banks of certain rivers, there is a difference between the civilization of the upper regions of the river and the lower ones, and there is also a variation in language.
summary: Great Britain is a small country; the distance from any part of Britain to the ocean is not more than fifty miles.
So naturally in that country there cannot be any large river: the distance between the source of a river and the ocean cannot be very great.
Yet if we move along the banks of certain rivers, there is a difference between the civilization of the upper regions of the river and the lower ones, and there is also a variation in language.

paragraphs.text: Take, for example, the case of the river Thames: it is not a big river, neither in width nor in breadth. The part of the river Thames where the ships sail is not really a river, it is only an estuary of the sea, just like the Mátlá river near Canning. Many people think that the Mátlá is perhaps a wide and large river. They may think that in olden days the southern branch of the river Yamuna (Vidyádharii) emerging from the Ganges at Trivenii, moved southwards. Then, after flowing separately for some distance, the Yamuna and the southeastern tributary of the Ganges (Piyálii) joined together to form the Mátlá river. Though this is a fact, yet the collective waters of these two combined rivers is quite small. In fact, the Mátlá River is nothing but the estuary of the sea entering into the land.
summary: Take, for example, the case of the river Thames: it is not a big river, neither in width nor in breadth.
They may think that in olden days the southern branch of the river Yamuna (Vidyádharii) emerging from the Ganges at Trivenii, moved southwards.
In fact, the Mátlá River is nothing but the estuary of the sea entering into the land.

paragraphs.text: The deltaic portion of the river Thames is somewhat similar. The more one proceeds down the river from the source of the Thames, the greater is the Anglo-Saxon and Norman influence. If one moves from the southern bank of the Thames towards the Straights of Dover, there is still a tremendous Norman influence, like a subterranean flow. If one moves from the northern side of the river towards the port of Grimsby on the delta at the coast, the Anglo-Saxon influence is greater than the Norman influence. If one moves towards the coast, the Norman influence becomes negligible. Where there is a Norman influence, there are large numbers of Latin derivations in the spoken language. Where the Anglo-Saxon influence is predominant, the number of Latin derivative words is comparatively small. The difference in intonation in the respective areas is also quite discernible.
summary: The deltaic portion of the river Thames is somewhat similar.
If one moves towards the coast, the Norman influence becomes negligible.
The difference in intonation in the respective areas is also quite discernible.

paragraphs.text: If one moves towards the opposite part of the Thames River, or towards Wales in the west, the ancient Briton influence becomes significant, even in the spoken language. This is the reason why, though Welsh is the language of a small country, yet it has certain specialities of its own. Even the difference in peopleʼs external appearance, though not very prominent, is significant as well.
summary: If one moves towards the opposite part of the Thames River, or towards Wales in the west, the ancient Briton influence becomes significant, even in the spoken language.
This is the reason why, though Welsh is the language of a small country, yet it has certain specialities of its own.
Even the difference in peopleʼs external appearance, though not very prominent, is significant as well.

paragraphs.text: Gangetic civilization – Gaod́-Ráŕh part
summary: Gangetic civilization – Gaod́-Ráŕh part

paragraphs.text: In our land of Ráŕh, on either bank of the Bakreshvar river in central Birbhum, there is a local civilization which, though small in area, has its own uniqueness, even in the style of its temples and also in its terracotta work. There is also a difference in the use of verbal forms in the spoken language of that area. Similarly, in southern Birbhum also, there is a small river called the Kopái (Kupita or ‘angry’) in whose valleys there is also some sort of local civilization. As far as I remember, someone once said that the water of the Bakreshvar valley is one of the best, for it is full of sulphur. But the water of Kopái valley, though it is as good as that of many places in Bengal, is not as good as that of the Bakreshvar valley. The two small rivers, with their own distinctive streams of water, flow from west to east, carrying the rhythmic songs of the most ancient human civilization, in cadence with the dancing rhythms of the land of Ráŕh. When the two rivers meet at Melánpur (meaning ‘meeting place’) at one end of the area under the jurisdiction of the Nanur police station, they are known as Kuye, and at that point both their local civilizations become blended. Actually, Melánpur merges the two rivers in all respects. If one listens intently to the local dialect, one will hear a particular drawled intonation that is lacking in western Birbhum. Aside from this, other local variations also came into being.
summary: In our land of Ráŕh, on either bank of the Bakreshvar river in central Birbhum, there is a local civilization which, though small in area, has its own uniqueness, even in the style of its temples and also in its terracotta work.

The two small rivers, with their own distinctive streams of water, flow from west to east, carrying the rhythmic songs of the most ancient human civilization, in cadence with the dancing rhythms of the land of Ráŕh.
Aside from this, other local variations also came into being.

paragraphs.text: The specialities of the river valley civilizations are very distinct in our Birbhum. In the upper reaches of Birbhum, the spoken language has no drawled intonation: it is one of the flawless branches of the Ráŕh language. But in the lower reaches of Birbhum, the same Ráŕh dialect has a local drawl.
summary: The specialities of the river valley civilizations are very distinct in our Birbhum.
In the upper reaches of Birbhum, the spoken language has no drawled intonation: it is one of the flawless branches of the Ráŕh language.
But in the lower reaches of Birbhum, the same Ráŕh dialect has a local drawl.

paragraphs.text: This subtle difference in intonation between the area of the Khayrásol police precinct and the Lábpur police precinct, and again between the Khayrásol police precinct and the Mayureshvar police precinct, be easily discerned simply by listening to it.
summary: This subtle difference in intonation between the area of the Khayrásol police precinct and the Lábpur police precinct, and again between the Khayrásol police precinct and the Mayureshvar police precinct, be easily discerned simply by listening to it.

paragraphs.text: At Khayrásol in the upper reaches of Birbhum, there is widespread use of poppy seed [as food], whereas in the lower reaches, the use of poppy seed is less by five to seven per cent. That is to say, in the upper reaches there is an empire of poppies, and in the lower reaches there is merely a kingdom of poppies!
summary: At Khayrásol in the upper reaches of Birbhum, there is widespread use of poppy seed [as food], whereas in the lower reaches, the use of poppy seed is less by five to seven per cent.
That is to say, in the upper reaches there is an empire of poppies, and in the lower reaches there is merely a kingdom of poppies!

paragraphs.text: The other symbols of Ráŕh culture – like d́iḿle [a type of pumpkin], kheŕo [another type of pumpkin], green gram and jhumur dance are equally popular in both the upper and lower reaches.
summary: The other symbols of Ráŕh culture – like d́iḿle [a type of pumpkin], kheŕo [another type of pumpkin], green gram and jhumur dance are equally popular in both the upper and lower reaches.

paragraphs.text: Gangetic civilization – Maethilii branch of pre-Gaod́iiya part
summary: Gangetic civilization – Maethilii branch of pre-Gaod́iiya part

paragraphs.text: [Now travelling] from the west to east across the border of the ancient Káshii state was the last area to come under Aryan influence. In the fourth phase of the Aryan invasion of India, Káshii can be regarded as a border state of northern India (Áryávartta). The River Sarayu not only carried the Aryan influence down its banks but also Mongol and to some extent Austric influence as well. That is why its eastern bank was considered as non-Aryan land. Later on, this boundary was further extended to the River Gańd́akii (Náráyańii Gańd́ak). The Kányakubja Brahmans of those days did not like to cross the River Sarayu. As the land on the other bank was non-Aryan it was considered unholy. They were afraid they would lose their Aryan purity. The Kányakubja Brahmans who dared to cross the river, being lured by the fertile land of the trans-Sarayu area, were declared outcastes. They lost their identity as Kányakubja Brahmans and became known as Sárayupárii Brahmans.
summary: [Now travelling] from the west to east across the border of the ancient Káshii state was the last area to come under Aryan influence.
The Kányakubja Brahmans of those days did not like to cross the River Sarayu.
They lost their identity as Kányakubja Brahmans and became known as Sárayupárii Brahmans.

paragraphs.text: During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District. In those days, northern India consisted of three Subás [administrative divisions]: Subá Bángál on the east, Subá Punjab on the northwest and Subá Hindostan between the two. Even today, the people of Bengal and the Punjab call the inhabitants of the central part of northern India “Hindustani”. Some people are of the opinion that Hindustan means the whole of India, and thus why should the inhabitants of a small part of India be called Hindustani. But this is wrong, because the term “Hindustani” is used for the people who were once the inhabitants of Subá Hindostan, and not in the sense of Hindustan as being the whole of India. During the Mughal period, when Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subás, the name of the northern part of Subá Hindostan was Oudh and the southern part was Subá Agra. Ghazipur District was the last boundary of Subá Agra. To the east of Ghazipur District lies Balia District. Previously it was only a subdivision of Ghazipur District. Similarly, there was no Deoria District in those days. It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.
summary: During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District.
During the Mughal period, when Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subás, the name of the northern part of Subá Hindostan was Oudh and the southern part was Subá Agra.
It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.

paragraphs.text: The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subás and created one administrative area from both – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short), with its capital at Allahabad. In the last part of British rule, the capital was moved to Lucknow. In any case, there was a marked influence of Mongol and Austric cultures on Aryan society inhabiting the Sarayu river valley. Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu River and declared the banks of the Gańd́akii as the boundary line of Áryávartta. The area lying to the west of the Gańd́akii valley was called Shákyárańya, and the area to the east was called Videha or Mithilá. The latter area was not considered an Aryan colony. I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaod́iiya Gangetic valley civilization.
summary: The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subás and created one administrative area from both – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short), with its capital at Allahabad.
Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu River and declared the banks of the Gańd́akii as the boundary line of Áryávartta.
I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaod́iiya Gangetic valley civilization.

paragraphs.text: King Mithi occupied Videha. To sanctify the land he held a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa [a large sacrifice presided over by three priests]. It was then declared sacred. The land sanctified by the performance of a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa was named Trihut. The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by Aryans, was respected by Buddhists. Lord Buddha visited it a couple of times. Later it became known as Shárańa (Shákyárańya > Shákyárańa > Shárańa). In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sháran.
summary: King Mithi occupied Videha.
The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by Aryans, was respected by Buddhists.
In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sháran.

paragraphs.text: To the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place called Champakárańya. Reference to it is made in the Rámáyańa [one of the two great Sanskrit epics] (Campakárańya > Campárańya > Camparań). Shákyárańya and Campakárańya are situated in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka valley. On the eastern bank is Videha, Mithilá or Trihut, the land occupied by King Mithi. Mithi + lá [holder] + d́a [suffix] + á [feminine suffix] = Mithilá. In the Buddhist period one of the famous villages of Shákyárańya was Hatthiigrám (Hastiigráma in Sanskrit). Buddha visited this place a couple of times. It is now known as Háthoyá. During British rule the Háthoyá estate was one of the largest estates in India. Then came the river Gańd́akii – Náráyańii Gańd́aka. The biggest cattle fair in India, known as the Hariharkśetra fair, is held once a year on the banks of this river. Nearby is the Shońpur railway station.
summary: To the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place called Champakárańya.
Buddha visited this place a couple of times.
Nearby is the Shońpur railway station.

paragraphs.text: During the Mughal period and the early part of British rule, the Mithilá division of Bengal Presidency consisted of three districts: Trihut, Champaran and Shárańa. The district headquarters of Champaran was Motihari, that of Shárań was Chapra, and that of Trihut was Muzaffarpur. The latter district was named after Muzaffar Shah. It covered a wide area and until the early part of the British period its fertile soils were thickly forested. The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, panthers and deer. The lake on the ancient river course of the river Lakhandei covered a larger area in those days and was surrounded by extensive forests full of abundant flora and fauna. A major part of the forest was part of the estate of King Darbhanga. Some of it was in the Shúraśańd́a kingdom, and other parts belonged to the estate of the Bettiah king. People today, due to necessity but also out of immense greed, have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.

The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, panthers and deer.
People today, due to necessity but also out of immense greed, have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.

paragraphs.text: At Vaeshali ( 2 ) in Trihut District, Vardhamána Maháviira was born into a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhártha and his mother was called Trishalá. Trihut District as well as Mithilá were located partly in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka valley and partly in the Buŕigańd́aka and Lakhandei valleys. There was greater Gaod́iiya influence prevalent here than in Aŕyávartta. Bengali script is used there. It is to be noted that both Buddha and Maháviira were born in a place where there was comparatively less Aryan influence.

paragraphs.text: Trihut District was quite a large area. The British divided it into two parts: Muzaffarpur District in the west, with its headquarters at Muzaffarpur, and Darbhanga District in the east, with its headquarters at Laheriasarai village which has since become so large that it almost touches the city of Darbhanga. The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hazipur). This is the same Muzaffarpur that once was considered one of the most cultured places in the whole of Subá Bángál. The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubanii (a place with an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga, named after the famous Dáŕibhángá Shah (in Maethilii the town is called “Daiŕbhángá” but spelt Daŕibhángá); and Samastipur, named after Samasti Náráyan Ray.

paragraphs.text: The Maethilii branch of the pre-Gaod́iiya valley civilization was enriched by the Mongol-Tantric civilization that flourished in the Náráyańii Ganges, Buri-Gańd́aka, Lakhandei, Bágmatii, Kamalábálán and Koshii valleys. King Prthvii Náráyan Shah established the Gorkha Empire in Nepal at this time. The Gorkhas occupied Tirhut District and advanced up to Hazipur. Thereafter they were defeated by the British and were forced to sign the Treaty of Sugaoli (Champaran District.) (The British commander-in-chief was General Octorloney in whose name the Englishmen living in Kolkata built a war memorial. In recent times, the [political] leaders, ignorant of history, have changed the name of the Octorloney Memorial to Shahiid Minar [Martyrsʼ Column].) According to the terms of the treaty, the British gained possession of Garhwal and Kumayun regions from Nepal, which was included in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and they also reclaimed a major portion of Champaran and Trihut Districts. Part of the northern portion of Trihut remained in Nepal and is still part of Nepalese territory. The former capital of Mithilá, Janakpur, is situated in that area. Many people of Bengal know the famous Janakpur catechu [Areca catechu] ( 3 )

“The oldest portion of the Vedas, that is, the Rgveda, was composed outside India. The remaining portions, that is, the Yajurveda and Atharvaveda, were partly Indian and partly non-Indian. Samaveda is not a separate Veda by itself but is the compilation of the lyrical and musical portions of the different Vedas. paragraphs.text: I have mentioned earlier that one meaning of the word khara is rákśasa. It seems that the Aryans of ancient times used to label people belonging to the Austric-Negroid group or Dravidian group as Rákśasas. Their own [Aryan] writings indicate that the Rákśasas had a developed civilization. They established large cities and towns, practiced dharma and were devotees of Lord Shiva. With the blessing of Shiva they came to possess enormous talents, power and wealth. Unwarranted comments have been made in a number of books so as to portray them in a poor light. It is true, of course, that they were antagonistic to the Aryan Vedas and their rituals, such as religious sacrifices – possibly because vital food supplies were wasted in these rituals. Wherever they saw such rituals being performed, they would storm the site and spoil the function. Ravana was described as a Rákśasa, most probably because he was opposed to the Vedas, although it was accepted that Ravana was a descendant of the sage Pulastya (according to some, a descendant of Vishvashravá). His mother Nikaśa, or Kaekesii, was born to a Rákśasa family. The character of Rama has been declared as the Maryádá Puruśottama, to signify that [according to the Puranic religion], if Puruśottama [Supreme Entity] Himself ever appeared on earth in human form, all the potential contributions He would have made have been portrayed in the Rámáyana text.

paragraphs.text: Why did a character like Maryádá Puruśottama [that is, Rama] want to assassinate an innocent man like Bali? In his plot to kill Bali, why did he seek the help of a weak person like Sugriva? Maryádá Puruśottamaʼs behaviour can be likened very much to that of present-day politicians – castigating someone when convenient, casting off another, but when in difficulty or in a tight corner, hobnobbing with them the very next moment, even secretly conspiring with those persons. Furthermore, both parties will have a clandestine agreement to criticize and blame each other in public but “would be very close like brothers with no division between them at all in private.”

paragraphs.text: Ramaʼs act of putting Sita through the ordeal of [walking through] fire can never be condoned. His desertion of a pregnant Sita by sending her to Valmikiʼs hermitage was another despicable deed. Finally, to ask that Sita undergo the ordeal of fire a second time was sheer inhumanity. In the Rámáyańa, there are three examples of truly developed characters – Sita, Urmila and Lakśańa. Jatáyu is another character who is illumined with sacrifice and nobility. In contrast, Rama again displays his vile nature when he indiscriminately slaughters the Rákśasas. According to the Rámáyańa, the reason why one of Ramaʼs Sanskrit names is Khardhvaisin or Kharadhvaḿsii is because he annihilated the Rákśas, also known as the Khars.

paragraphs.text: The word khara or rákśasas has a derogatory implication. It was used by the Aryans to indicate extreme cruelty or horror; it also signified ugliness in men. The condescending Aryans (indeed, their noses had high bridges) could not accept the Austric and Dravidian civilizations. They were reluctant to recognize them as civilized. They were accustomed to thinking that they alone had the capacity for good taste and culture. That was why they called themselves Aryans, which means 'progressive peopleʼ and ‘cultured ones.’

paragraphs.text: Since Buddhists and Jains were free to some extent from the influence of Aryans, they did not discriminate between Aryans and non-Aryans. Hence, they retained their respect for Ravana. You all know that although Valmiki was the official author of the Rámáyańa, earlier versions existed – the Buddhist Rámáyańa, the Jain Rámáyańa, the Cháyá Rámáyańa, the Giitá Rámáyańa and the Adhyátma Rámáyańa. The Válmikii Rámáyańa portrayed Aryan ideology. In those days, whoever opposed the Vedas or Árśa doctrine were considered by Aryans as Rákśasas, as barbarians and infidels. Perhaps due to the influence of Aryan superiority complex (evinced in the Páiṋcálii literature of Válmikii Rámáyańa and in the Rámcaritamánasa composed by Tulsidas), a differentiation was made between vipras and shúdras. Tulsidas called his Rámáyańa Rámcaritamánasa instead of Rámáyańa – meaning the character of Rama as conceived in his mind. He could not remove his prejudice against the shúdras. His Rámáyańa, albeit a treasure-house and a gem deserving of manifold praises, was not devoid of Aryan arrogance. Here too, the Rákśasas were denigrated. About the shúdras it was said:

paragraphs.text: Various writers of the Puranas maintained that the rákśasas and dánavas [so-called demons] practiced advanced meditation. They did not have yajiṋas, nor did they perform the ritual of offering haviih [butter-oil]. The nikumbhilá yajiṋa offered by Indrajit, the son of Ravana, was quite different from those offered by the Aryans. These writers also claimed that, blessed by Lord Shiva, many Rákśasas and dánavas became strong and powerful. It became clear from these stories and legends even if there was no similarity of thought or ideas between Aryans and so-called rákśasas and dánavas, the latter were in no way inferior to Aryans. So the name Kharadhvaḿsii for Rama did not reflect any worthy quality in him; rather, according to certain people, it reflected his intolerance.

paragraphs.text: Karkat́ii Rákśasii and cures for cancer and diabetes
summary: Karkat́ii Rákśasii and cures for cancer and diabetes

paragraphs.text: The word khasátmaja (khas + átman + jan = d́a) means the son of Rákśasii, who may not necessarily be a Rákśasa. There are many stories about this in the Puranas. According to the Puranas, Rákśasii women give birth to gods and to intelligent men. One such story is about Sutanuka, the son of Karkat́ii Rákśasii, Karkat́ii Rákśasii discovered the medicinal cure for cancer. Her husband Anuvasen was a human being. Sutanuka was an ideal character; he was a generous, caring physician. Although he was the son of a Rákśasii, Sutanuka was not a Rákśasa; he was a Khasátmája. In the scriptures, the word átmaja means the first child (a son or daughter); other children are called kámaja, not átmaja. Earlier it was mentioned that Karkat́ii Rákśasii had discovered the cure for cancer. Unfortunately, that medicine has been lost to posterity. In order to diagnose diseases and find their cures, Karkat́ii Rákśasii used to dissect [and examine] corpses. Since people in those days were very undeveloped, they concluded that she was a cannibal in search of human flesh. It is said that ungrateful men burnt Karkat́ii Rákśasii to death and that both a curse – the disease bisuciká (cholera) – and a blessing – the medicine madhumeha (for diabetes) – emanated from the burning flames. Bisuciká is the Sanskrit name for cholera. In Bengali it is called oláot́há, in English cholera, and in Farsi hyáyajá. The cure for cholera has been lost; administering saline is not an actual remedy. Humanity will have to rediscover the medicine for cholera. It is beyond human understanding how worship of the goddess Oláicańd́ii (Olábibi) can alleviate this disease. ( 2 )

paragraphs.text: Gandha + v – hval + ac. In the etymological sense, it means whoever moves or causes others to move because of a smell or at whose smell others move or stir. You know, the entire human race did not evolve at the same time in all parts of the world. Different human species with different skulls developed from tailless animals in various parts of the world. It is surmised that human beings first emerged from the western corner of Ráŕh and then from the central region of Gondwana. The first human species that appeared in Ráŕh, though belonging to the Austric race, had longer noses than those of the present-day Austric race. The first group of humans that originated from central Gondwana – Sumatra, Balidviip, Javadviip – were also Austrics, but their noses were slightly flat. It is difficult to say anything with certainty about their physical complexion. However, the land of Ráŕh was chiefly within the Karkatakranti [temperate] region. Hence it is believed that the physical complexion of these people of Ráŕh was dark blue or slightly dark. And since central Gondwana was situated in the equatorial region, the people of that area were comparatively dark-complexioned and slightly flat-nosed – but not entirely flat-nosed. It is surmised that later, people belonging to the Mongoloid group or Chinese race came there in great number in search of a livelihood, and due to the intermingling of these newcomers with the earlier Austric race, the Mongoloid-Malaysian branch of humanity was created.

paragraphs.text: There is a great amount of similarity between the skulls of the people of Ráŕh and those of the present-day Bengalis of Ráŕh. Though there is a blending of the blood of exotic Aryans or Caucasians therein, the Kayasthas of Ráŕh continue to bear a physical resemblance to their ancestors. As a result of Aryan genes, they are tall and have a brighter complexion. Nonetheless, the imprint of the ancient Ráŕhiian breed is clearly shown in their bodies. Other people of Ráŕh, especially original or native Bengalis, are bearers of that ancient skull. Amongst the Oráoṋs, due to the admixture of Negroid blood, substantial transformation has taken place in their skulls, akin to what happened among the Gońd́s and Satnámiis in Madhya Pradesh and among the Oriyás in Orissa However, in Ráŕh most of the native Bengalis – the Gopes, Sadgopes, Máhiiśyas and Kurmiis – have that ancient Ráŕhiian skull. The Brahmans, Kayasthas and Vaedyas of Ráŕh, no matter how much they consider themselves outsiders, are also the sons of the old land of Ráŕh.
summary: There is a great amount of similarity between the skulls of the people of Ráŕh and those of the present-day Bengalis of Ráŕh.
Nonetheless, the imprint of the ancient Ráŕhiian breed is clearly shown in their bodies.
The Brahmans, Kayasthas and Vaedyas of Ráŕh, no matter how much they consider themselves outsiders, are also the sons of the old land of Ráŕh.

paragraphs.text: Due to the blending of blood between Caucasians and Mongoloids, a definite change has come about in their physical complexion and features. Despite this, their appearance still indicates that they belong to Ráŕh. Using gold as an analogy, if the native Bengalis are pure gold, then the so-called upper caste people, especially the Kayasthas, are enameled gold. The Aryans who are known today as Caucasians originated from Switzerland. To escape from the snow in Switzerland, they turned eastwards to the Caucasus region to seek refuge in the first lap of their journey. The Negroid people made their first appearance in the central region of present-day Sahara. Due to earthquakes, the Sahara was elevated higher than sea-level; in its higher regions there was scarcity of water, though in the lower regions water was present – and could be brought up like fountains through artesian wells even today. The Sahara region appeared to lack water; hence, most of its inhabitants moved to the south. The remaining population migrated to the north and northeast. Through intermingling of this population with Caucasians, the Semitic population was born. Some of these Semitic people resemble Negroids and others Caucasians. Some have fair skin while others have brown skin; quite a number of them are curly-haired and an equally large number are straight-haired.
summary: Due to the blending of blood between Caucasians and Mongoloids, a definite change has come about in their physical complexion and features.

Due to earthquakes, the Sahara was elevated higher than sea-level; in its higher regions there was scarcity of water, though in the lower regions water was present – and could be brought up like fountains through artesian wells even today.
Some have fair skin while others have brown skin; quite a number of them are curly-haired and an equally large number are straight-haired.

paragraphs.text: The second home of the Caucasian Aryans was Caucasus Ural and part of the Volga River Basin of the Volga River. As the land was full of pebbles and excessively cold, these Aryans were forced to remain idle for the major part of the year. They constantly worried about where their next meal would come from, and were compelled to hunt wild animals for food. In order to survive, they had to leave in search of new lands and new horizons. This time they moved southwards. The branch of Caucasian Aryans that moved westwards are the Europeans or Euro-Aryans of today. Those who traveled southwards became the Aryo-Iranians or Aryan-Persians. They settled for some time in Persia. Owing to their physical proximity to the Caucasian branch [of Aryans], the Aryo-Iranians retained most of their Caucasian looks and appearance. Though the lustre in their physical complexion disappeared, it did not turn blue-black or dark. Another group of Caucasian Aryans traveled to the east. They went to the basins of Gauṋgá and Yamuna, to the Brahmaputra and Brahmariidesh via Gándhára [Afghanistan], Kashmir, Saptasindhu (Punjab) and Haritadhánya (Haryana). They continued moving eastward and left their physical imprint on the Kayasthas of Ráŕh. After crossing Padma, the kayasthas of Ráŕh became the Bauṋgaja Kayasthas and, after crossing the Mahananda, became the Barendra Kayasthas (kalitá). All the Kayasthas of Bengal are originally from Ráŕh, but possess a few genetic traits of Caucasian Aryans. If they consider themselves outsiders, they are wrong indeed.
summary: The second home of the Caucasian Aryans was Caucasus Ural and part of the Volga River Basin of the Volga River.
Owing to their physical proximity to the Caucasian branch [of Aryans], the Aryo-Iranians retained most of their Caucasian looks and appearance.
If they consider themselves outsiders, they are wrong indeed.

paragraphs.text: Let us come back to the original topic. The fatherland of Caucasian Aryans was a rocky and infertile region. When the Aryans learnt the art of cultivation, they grew oats and barley (bárlika) ( 3 ), albeit with difficulty. Besides eating oats and barley, they also killed animals and ate their livers, hearts and other parts for survival. Even lions, leopards and hyenas were not excluded from their diet (that region had a cold climate and was not hospitable for tigers, otherwise they would have eaten them as well.) When they came to Persia in search of food, they found paddy and wheat. Remember, the Sanskrit name for paddy is not dhánya but brhii. The word dhánya stands for green vegetation (shaśpa). The word brhii means staple food. After tasting paddy, would anyone choose oats and barley? The Aryans named paddy brhii.
summary: Let us come back to the original topic.
) When they came to Persia in search of food, they found paddy and wheat.
The Aryans named paddy brhii.

paragraphs.text: Later, brhii became riihi in Latin. Today, as a result of the oral translation of Scandinavian Anglo-Saxons, it is known as rice in English. Paddy is called brhii because different food dishes could be created from it: muŕi (puffed rice), huŕumba (or huŕumbu), rut́ii (rot́iká), cápát́i (carpat́kiá ), puri (somáliká), nuci (shakkulii or shauṋkulii), parot́á (priyarot́iká or pararot́iká), cṋŕe (cipit́akam), khae (láj or khadiká: khadiká > khaiyá > khae), madiká > maiyá > mae, suji (svádajit), cála ( 4 ) (tańd́ula) and bhát (odanam).
summary: Later, brhii became riihi in Latin.
Today, as a result of the oral translation of Scandinavian Anglo-Saxons, it is known as rice in English.

Paddy is called brhii because different food dishes could be created from it: muŕi (puffed rice), huŕumba (or huŕumbu), rut́ii (rot́iká), cápát́i (carpat́kiá ), puri (somáliká), nuci (shakkulii or shauṋkulii), parot́á (priyarot́iká or pararot́iká), cṋŕe (cipit́akam), khae (láj or khadiká: khadiká > khaiyá > khae), madiká > maiyá > mae, suji (svádajit), cála ( 4 ) (tańd́ula) and bhát (odanam).

paragraphs.text: Among you those who know grammar well must be aware of the fact that the kind of compound (samása) in which there are many ideas contained in is called bahuvrhii samása, that is, it is the ‘stock’ of many types (bahu) of foods (vrhii). There remains conjoining words (vyásvákya) like yáhár or yáháte in Bengali and yasys or yasmin in Sanskrit in bahuvrihii samása.
summary: Among you those who know grammar well must be aware of the fact that the kind of compound (samása) in which there are many ideas contained in is called bahuvrhii samása, that is, it is the ‘stock’ of many types (bahu) of foods (vrhii).
There remains conjoining words (vyásvákya) like yáhár or yáháte in Bengali and yasys or yasmin in Sanskrit in bahuvrihii samása.

paragraphs.text: The Aryans fell in love with the land of Persia. When do you love a country? When you find its environment pleasant, its weather congenial, its natural scenery beautiful, its land fertile and in addition there is excellent provision for a feast – is it not? Historians say that the name of the ancient capital of Ráŕh, Astiknagar, is Vardhaman, named after Vardhaman Mahavir; however, according to Khyát́andás Khásnobis [a voracious eater, as per the story of the author], it was given the name of Vardhaman [Burdwan] because of the abundance of food. You can patiently research this! In Persia or Iran, there are many such historical sources. They called this land Áryanya Vraja. The verb vraja means to move about with joy. Compare this with the words vrajabhúmi and vrajaparikrmá.
summary: The Aryans fell in love with the land of Persia.
You can patiently research this!
Compare this with the words vrajabhúmi and vrajaparikrmá.

paragraphs.text: Here, the Aryans found wheat. Many of you possibly know that one of the words for tongue is go. You must also be acquainted with the word dhumdhám. In North India, when any festival is celebrated with pomp and grandeur, it is said in northern India: baŕe dhumdhámse utsav mánáye gaye. In Bengali, we say: khuv dhumdhámer sauṋge jamidár bábu nátir biye dilen [the zamindar gave his daughter in marriage with pomp and grandeur.]
summary: Here, the Aryans found wheat.
You must also be acquainted with the word dhumdhám.
In Bengali, we say: khuv dhumdhámer sauṋge jamidár bábu nátir biye dilen [the zamindar gave his daughter in marriage with pomp and grandeur.

paragraphs.text: When the Aryans first ate wheat, their taste buds were filled with relish – mahádhum. That is why they called wheat godhum. The Tamil word godhumái comes from godhum. Due to its golden colour, wheat farmers in Punjab named it kańaka. In Urdu and Farsi, it is known as gondhum, also derived from godhum. In Saorasheni Prákrt it is called gehum, from which is derived the Hindi word gehu. In Mágadhii Prákrt it is called gahum. The ancient Bengali word goham originated from gahum. In present-day Ráŕhii Bengali it is called gaham. When this is quickly and briefly pronounced, it becomes gam.
summary: When the Aryans first ate wheat, their taste buds were filled with relish – mahádhum.
In Saorasheni Prákrt it is called gehum, from which is derived the Hindi word gehu.
When this is quickly and briefly pronounced, it becomes gam.

paragraphs.text: Should we conclude our discussion of wheat here? No, not yet. There is more – listen. Since there was no instrument for crushing wheat in those days, the Aryans used to crush the wheat with stones and, using their hands to knead the crushed wheat, they prepared cápát́i or carpat́iká (in Hindi cápát́i.) A special smell used to emerge from the crushed wheat while it was baking. They were very much drawn to it – just as bees are drawn to flowers and flies; just as bees are drawn to honey. Thus the Aryans of those days used to sit around the fire waiting for the bread to bake and, as the smell of the baking bread or capati wafted by, they felt thrills of joy and anticipation; they felt exhilarated at the thought that their Áryakanyá (the husbands of those days used to address their wives as Áryakanyá, and the wives used to address their husbands as Áryaputra) was going to put cápát́is with dates (always write kharjúra, not kharjura which means silver) on their plates for them to eat. In order to describe this smell of the [baking] wheat that so excited and exhilarated them, they created a word for it – gandhavihbal. ( 5 )
summary: Should we conclude our discussion of wheat here?
) A special smell used to emerge from the crushed wheat while it was baking.
In order to describe this smell of the [baking] wheat that so excited and exhilarated them, they created a word for it – gandhavihbal.
