chapters.title: Histories of Manipur, Arunachal, Haryana
chapters.partTitle: PART 5: Histories of Certain States in India along with Certain Important Places in Them

paragraphs.text: Manipur

The history of Manipur, the easternmost state of India, is decidedly old. Inhabitants of this region are Indo-Burmese stock. The land is rich in civilization, culture and heritage. Manipur is a beautiful plain surrounded by mountains on all four sides. In ancient times, a large lake existed in the centre of these mountains. Over the course of time, however, [the rains] carried stones, pebbles and alluvial soil down the mountains, until finally the lake was filled, resulting in the creation of an alluvial plain. The lake in miniature form is still present.
summary: The history of Manipur, the easternmost state of India, is decidedly old.
Manipur is a beautiful plain surrounded by mountains on all four sides.
The lake in miniature form is still present.

paragraphs.text: The state of Manipur is a very old one. Even in the Mahábhárata this state is mentioned. Some scholars believe that present-day Manipur is not the Manipur referred to in the Mahábhárata. Yet one hardly comes across any supportive arguments in favour of this belief. Unless we have grounds for doubt, we are compelled to accepts that Manipur belongs to the Mahábhárata [era.]
summary: The state of Manipur is a very old one.
Some scholars believe that present-day Manipur is not the Manipur referred to in the Mahábhárata.
Unless we have grounds for doubt, we are compelled to accepts that Manipur belongs to the Mahábhárata [era.

paragraphs.text: Up till the beginning of British rule, Manipur was a self-governing state. Imphal, its capital is also a very old city. After the downfall of Tikendrajit, the British brought the fertile ‘Kobe’ valley under its direct rule and returned the rest of the kingdom to the king. From that time onwards, Manipur became a native state of British India.
summary: Up till the beginning of British rule, Manipur was a self-governing state.
After the downfall of Tikendrajit, the British brought the fertile ‘Kobe’ valley under its direct rule and returned the rest of the kingdom to the king.
From that time onwards, Manipur became a native state of British India.

paragraphs.text: All of you know that once Burma (Brahmadesh) was considered to be a province of British India. The British incorporated the Kobe valley into Burma province. Even after the separation of Burma from India, the Kobe valley remained with Burma. After independence, Manipur – with the exception of the Kobe valley – became part of independent India. The people of Manipur have a special attraction for literature, art, dance and music. They are a peace-loving people and fond of entertainment. In ancient times, they were Theravadi Buddhists. Later, when Mahaprabhu Chaitanya Dev went there, he initiated them into Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion. On his way there, he preached Gaoŕiya Vaeśńavism in Tripura, and the local Tripura community likewise embraced Gaoŕiya Vaeśńavism. The Tipras gave up their Burmese names and adopted Sanskrit names. (The first Tipra leader was called Mu-Chang-fa.) From that time onwards, the king came to be called by the Sanskrit name “Máńikya Bahádur”.
summary: All of you know that once Burma (Brahmadesh) was considered to be a province of British India.
In ancient times, they were Theravadi Buddhists.
) From that time onwards, the king came to be called by the Sanskrit name “Máńikya Bahádur”.

paragraphs.text: After adopting the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion, the life of Manipur witnessed further cultural changes. The residents of Manipur opened new horizons in dance, music and the fine arts. Through their dances, they articulated specific subtle expressions of devotional themes relating to Radha and Krśńa of the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion. As many are aware, the Rása dance of Manipur is famous all over the world.
summary: After adopting the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion, the life of Manipur witnessed further cultural changes.
Through their dances, they articulated specific subtle expressions of devotional themes relating to Radha and Krśńa of the Gaoŕiya Vaeśńava religion.
As many are aware, the Rása dance of Manipur is famous all over the world.

paragraphs.text: The Manipuri language belongs to the Indo-Burmese group of languages, which does not signify any particular language, but rather a group of languages, of which the two main languages are Bishenpuria and Mithei. The Bishenpuria language is used by the Manipuris [the Manipuri people] in Bengalʼs Sylhet and in the Chittagong hills of the Tripura-Cachar region and Mizoram. The spoken language of [the capital] Imphal is Mithei, and this language is used in official transactions. In both these Manipuri languages, there is an abundance of Sanskrit words, and both use the Bengali alphabet.
summary: The Manipuri language belongs to the Indo-Burmese group of languages, which does not signify any particular language, but rather a group of languages, of which the two main languages are Bishenpuria and Mithei.
The spoken language of [the capital] Imphal is Mithei, and this language is used in official transactions.
In both these Manipuri languages, there is an abundance of Sanskrit words, and both use the Bengali alphabet.

paragraphs.text: Since Manipuris are adherents of the Gaod́iiya [Gaoŕiiya] Vaeśńava religion, their holiest of sacred sites is Navadvip [birthplace of Chaitanya.] They revere the Chaetanya Caritámrta as their holy scripture – a scripture written by Krishnadas Kaviraj, who resided in Jhamatpur village, Ketugram Police station in the Katwa subdivision of Burdwan district of Raoh.
summary: Since Manipuris are adherents of the Gaod́iiya [Gaoŕiiya] Vaeśńava religion, their holiest of sacred sites is Navadvip [birthplace of Chaitanya.

] They revere the Chaetanya Caritámrta as their holy scripture – a scripture written by Krishnadas Kaviraj, who resided in Jhamatpur village, Ketugram Police station in the Katwa subdivision of Burdwan district of Raoh.

paragraphs.text: There is no caste division amongst Manipuris. They are all considered as belonging to the same caste, that is, Kśatriyas. Those regarded as belonging to a different caste are all settlers from outside [Manipur.] The same practice exists among the Sindhis. There is no caste division among the people of Sindh. All are known as Sindhis. The Brahmans of Sindh all came from the Marwar region of Rajasthan. In the only Marwari-speaking district of Thar in Sindh province, they were comparatively in the majority.
summary: There is no caste division amongst Manipuris.
There is no caste division among the people of Sindh.
In the only Marwari-speaking district of Thar in Sindh province, they were comparatively in the majority.

paragraphs.text: The weaving industry of Manipur is world-renowned. The women of Manipur have complete freedom in their social life, and they also play a leading role in the work place. ( 1 )
summary: The weaving industry of Manipur is world-renowned.
The women of Manipur have complete freedom in their social life, and they also play a leading role in the work place.

paragraphs.text: Aruńácal/Arunachal

This name is a new one. During the rule of the Ahom kings, this area was known mostly as Baliapara. When the British conquered Assam, the district of Assam was known as Baliapara Border District. Yes, scholars do differ regarding the name “Assam.” In ancient times, this region was known as Prágjyotiśpur. In later times, with regard to spiritual thought and Tantra, it became known as Kamrup. The name Kamrup was in use only during the Buddhist era and during the era of the post-Buddhist Nátha religion. In a twelve-hundred year old Bengali poem, it is said:
summary: This name is a new one.
Yes, scholars do differ regarding the name “Assam.
The name Kamrup was in use only during the Buddhist era and during the era of the post-Buddhist Nátha religion.

paragraphs.text: Divasai bahuŕii kágai d́are bháy,
summary: Divasai bahuŕii kágai d́are bháy,

paragraphs.text: Ráti bhaele kámru jáy.
summary: Ráti bhaele kámru jáy.

paragraphs.text: The Sankrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a are transformed into a in Prákrta. Hence Kamrup became, “Kamrua,” “Kamru.” The superficial meaning of the poem is: “Our wife fears even the cry of the crow during the day. However, the same wife goes to distant Kamrup at night to practice Tantra.” In a later period, the storm between Shákta Tantra and Vaeśńava Tantra swept Kamrup. Just as this storm brought catastrophe to the social life of Kamrup, it also ushered an intellectual awakening through cultural conflict. In this context it could be correctly stated that nothing in this world is unmixed. If we look at the positive aspect of this Shákta-Vaeśńava tussle, leaving aside the pernicious aspect, it in fact resulted in the birth of a new civilization in the Brahmaputra valley, which, though it bore the impact of the past, also gave a new direction to the future. From that conflict emerged the present day cultural life of Kamrup. There was a pernicious side to this feud. On the one hand, Kamrup had to face disastrous consequences due to the Moghul invasion; on the other hand, it had to finally concede defeat when attacked by the Ahoms coming from Burma.
summary: The Sankrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a are transformed into a in Prákrta.
Just as this storm brought catastrophe to the social life of Kamrup, it also ushered an intellectual awakening through cultural conflict.
On the one hand, Kamrup had to face disastrous consequences due to the Moghul invasion; on the other hand, it had to finally concede defeat when attacked by the Ahoms coming from Burma.

paragraphs.text: Towards the end of this conflict, the Ahoms became the rulers of Assam. However, while many people say that from the name of the Ahoms came the subsequent name ‘Assom’ or 'Ahomʼ of Kamrup, this is not correct. This beautiful land of nature, formed due to a blending of rivers, plains and hills, came to be known as A-sama [A in Sanskrit stands for ‘not’ and sama means 'evenʼ] due to the rugged geography of its soil. It took the corrupted form of ‘Ássám’ in English. Following that distorted English pronunciation ‘Ássám,’ it is now called Ássám in Bengali. It should preferably be called ‘Asama.’ The Assamese language is the eastern borderland language belonging to the eastern Mágadhii group of languages. The style of its pronunciation is chiefly that of the Yajurveda. However, due to being under prolonged rule of the Ahom kings, and also due to the impact of Burmese pronunciation on the Ahoms, north Burmese pronunciation has certainly influenced the Assamese language.
summary: Towards the end of this conflict, the Ahoms became the rulers of Assam.
Following that distorted English pronunciation ‘Ássám,’ it is now called Ássám in Bengali.

However, due to being under prolonged rule of the Ahom kings, and also due to the impact of Burmese pronunciation on the Ahoms, north Burmese pronunciation has certainly influenced the Assamese language.

paragraphs.text: Yes, we were discussing Balipara District. Eventually, by separating Balipara from Assam, a separate province called North Eastern Frontier Agency (abbreviated as NEFA) was formed under the direct rule of the Governor General of India. As a result, its public life was cruelly separated from the mainstream of Assamese life. Thus, even today, [the people of Balipara] know Assamese as their natural second language. From cultural, economic and many other considerations, the relationship of this district (NEFA) with Assam is inseparable. In independent India, the name NEFA was changed to Arunachal. This name of this state [Aruńácal] should be spelled with cerebral ńa. ( 2 )
summary: Yes, we were discussing Balipara District.
Thus, even today, [the people of Balipara] know Assamese as their natural second language.
This name of this state [Aruńácal] should be spelled with cerebral ńa.

paragraphs.text: Haryana

Its Vedic name is Haritadhánya. In Vedic language, dhánya means green vegetation. When the Vedic Aryans came [to Haryana] after entering India, they were drawn to its green beauty and named it Haritadhánya. The Sanskrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a become a in Prákrta, dha becomes ha (for example, dadhi > dahi > dai – to write dae is incorrect; it is not bao which should be bau; similarly it is not maomáchi – the correct spelling should be maumáchi.) Thus, haritadhánya became hariahánan, and in Demi-Prákrta this became hariháná. In modern language this was transformed into Haryana. Similarly, lodhradhánya has become Ludhiana. In the spelling of dhánya there is the dental na. From that standpoint, it is proper to use the dental na in spelling Haryana and Ludhiana. However, here the vowel e follows the letter ra, after that there is ya, and beside it is a – these are all abádhak varńa [free letters unrestricted by the change of dental na into cerebral ńa.] According to this logic, it would be more reasonable to write it with cerebral ńa, that is haryańá. The local language of Haryana is Ját́t́u or Haryanvi.
summary: Its Vedic name is Haritadhánya.
Similarly, lodhradhánya has become Ludhiana.
The local language of Haryana is Ját́t́u or Haryanvi.

paragraphs.text: The combination of Haryanvi language, prevalent in the region of Delhi, with Persian and Turkish words gave birth to the Urdu language (Urddu) in the army cantonments. That very language which the men in uniform, that is, in varddii (wrongly pronounced urddi in Bengali) used to speak was called Urdu. Putting aside the history of the Urdu language, we incorrectly treat Urdu as a foreign language. Urdu is very much an Indian language spoken in the Delhi area. Its source is the Haryanvi language. Recently, teaching and studying in educational institutions are conducted to some extent in the Haryanvi language. Several films have also been produced in this language.
summary: The combination of Haryanvi language, prevalent in the region of Delhi, with Persian and Turkish words gave birth to the Urdu language (Urddu) in the army cantonments.
Urdu is very much an Indian language spoken in the Delhi area.
Several films have also been produced in this language.

paragraphs.text: The very old town of Haryana is “Merát́,” which in English and Bengali is wrongly pronounced ‘Meerut.’ The word Merát́ has come from the Sanskrit Mayráśt́ra. Mayráśt́ra → Mayrát́t́ha → Mayrát́ → Merát́. It was named after a certain non-Aryan king named Maydánava (dánava [demon] is not a creature of bizarre appearance. Aryans used to call a class of non-Aryans of India as dánavas). This Maydánava belongs to the era of the Mahábhárata. The present Harayana is fast advancing in the fields of education, culture and technology. It is a developed state of present-day India. Let various parts of India learn a valuable lesson from the present Haryana. Let me reiterate that the progress of Haryana is worth emulating. ( 3 )
summary: The very old town of Haryana is “Merát́,” which in English and Bengali is wrongly pronounced ‘Meerut.
This Maydánava belongs to the era of the Mahábhárata.
Let me reiterate that the progress of Haryana is worth emulating.

paragraphs.text: Utkal – Orissa

The word ut means to move upward; kul means sprout. The mass of sand and silt carried by multiple rivers into the ocean that has risen like a sprout (kal) from the seabed is utkala. The southern plains of Orissa are hence known as Utkal.
summary: The word ut means to move upward; kul means sprout.
The mass of sand and silt carried by multiple rivers into the ocean that has risen like a sprout (kal) from the seabed is utkala.
The southern plains of Orissa are hence known as Utkal.

paragraphs.text: One must remember that the northern part of Orissa is a hilly region. Its ancient name is not Utkal – it is Koshal or south Koshala. In those days, the Kanyakubja area was known partly as Koshala and partly as Shrávastii. This area is now part of Uttar Pradesh. The entire region is situated to the north of the Ganges; hence, it was also called north Koshala. During the rule of King Bimbisar, the king of Magadha, Prasenjit, was the king of north Koshala. Amongst the queens of King Bimbisar [546 B.C.] was Koshalkumarii, sister of Prasenjit. Ajatshatru [489–516 B.C.], an adherent of the Arya doctrine (the doctrine that follows the Vedas and the Rśis), became king by slaying Bimbisar, a follower of Buddha. Bimbisarʼs brother-in-law, Prasenjit, became angry and attacked Magadha to avenge the murder; however, he failed to win the battle. It should be remembered that Ajatshatru was without doubt the son of Bimbisar, but he was not the nephew of Prasenjit, that is, the son of Koshalkumarii.
summary: One must remember that the northern part of Orissa is a hilly region.
Amongst the queens of King Bimbisar [546 B.
It should be remembered that Ajatshatru was without doubt the son of Bimbisar, but he was not the nephew of Prasenjit, that is, the son of Koshalkumarii.

paragraphs.text: At an appreciable distance to the south of the Ganges was south Koshala or Mahákoshala. At one time the western part of south Koshala was divided into many small states. Each state had built up its own fortress or gaŕh. Thus, the western part of south Koshala later came to be known as Chattisgarh (a collection of thirty-six forts). Though there were a number of small and large states on the eastern side of south Koshala or Mahákoshala, this region was for a long time known simply as Koshala. It is situated in the northern region of Orissa. In those days the largest town of the Koshala region in Orissa was Sambalpur. Its spoken language is Koshalii, which is generally known as Sambalpurii Oriya [Oriya as spoken in the Sambalpur area]. This Koshala region of Orissa is considered a part of Áryávarta and the Utkal region as a part of the Deccan.
summary: At an appreciable distance to the south of the Ganges was south Koshala or Mahákoshala.
Though there were a number of small and large states on the eastern side of south Koshala or Mahákoshala, this region was for a long time known simply as Koshala.
This Koshala region of Orissa is considered a part of Áryávarta and the Utkal region as a part of the Deccan.

paragraphs.text: The fine arts of this area are highly developed; in that sense also, the word Utkal could be used.
summary: The fine arts of this area are highly developed; in that sense also, the word Utkal could be used.

paragraphs.text: The root verb od́ means to draw near, to caress, to embrace, to serve and care for. Od́ + rak = od́ra. The land that takes great care of its guests, drawing the far away people near, is called the land of Od́ra. The coastal area from the mouth of the River Mahánadi to the mouth of the River Subarnarekha is called Od́ra, and the area from the mouth of the river Mahánadi to the mouth of the river Godavari is known as Utkal. The entire coastal area from the mouth of the river Godavari to the mouth of the river Suvarnarekha is Kalinga – that is, the combined name of Utkal and Od́ra. Matters related to this land of Od́ra are called Od́ra, and the language is known as Odri/Aodri. From this Od́rii/Aod́rii has come the word Oriya. The mutated form of Od́rii/Aod́rii does not give rise to the word Uŕiyá – it gives rise to the word Oriya. Hence it is preferable that the word [Oriya] is used. ( 4 )
summary: The root verb od́ means to draw near, to caress, to embrace, to serve and care for.
Matters related to this land of Od́ra are called Od́ra, and the language is known as Odri/Aodri.
Hence it is preferable that the word [Oriya] is used.

paragraphs.text: The suffix rak is used when a person does something habitually. For example, the meaning of the verb ud́ is to entertain, to love and care for, to embrace mutually, to urge on, saying, ‘please eat this’, 'please eat that.ʼ Thus, by combining ud́ + rak we obtain the word Od́ra. Od́ra means one who knows how to love, how to show affection. In ancient times, Orissa was famous for its hospitality. That is why the northern part of Orissa, meaning the left bank of the Mahánadi, was called the land of Od́ra. From this word Od́ra has come the words Orissa, Oriya, and so forth. Even today, you will observe that the people of Orissa are very much accustomed to cooking, entertaining and taking care of people. If someone asks anything of them, they will certainly give it, if at all possible. In those days, the people of Od́ra land used to cultivate dance and fine arts, chiefly to entertain people, to please their minds. Even today, the people of Od́ra retain certain artistic skills, though it has declined to some extent. If their crippled economic status is ameliorated, we can expect them to regain their former artistic skills. The word Utkal means where there is a rise in the faculty of arts or where there is an upsurge of human creative skill (ud́ + kal + ac). ( 5 )
summary: The suffix rak is used when a person does something habitually.
From this word Od́ra has come the words Orissa, Oriya, and so forth.
The word Utkal means where there is a rise in the faculty of arts or where there is an upsurge of human creative skill (ud́ + kal + ac).

chapters.title: History of Himachal
chapters.partTitle: PART 5: Histories of Certain States in India along with Certain Important Places in Them

paragraphs.text: Himachal

Meghalay, Sikkim (Sukhim), and various other parts of the Himalayas are famous for orchids, or kákarúhá. I also once had the opportunity to become closely acquainted with the Himalayan kákarúhá.
summary: Meghalay, Sikkim (Sukhim), and various other parts of the Himalayas are famous for orchids, or kákarúhá.
I also once had the opportunity to become closely acquainted with the Himalayan kákarúhá.

paragraphs.text: Winter was on its way out and spring was fast approaching. I was on my way from Jammu to Bilaspur in Himachal Pradesh. We left at daybreak and would arrive in the evening, about eight at night. The entire journey was through the Himalayas and on the way I became acquainted with the Himalayas, the soul of the gods, its very essence filling every corner of the human mind, causing human beings to fall ardently in love with its icy crown.
summary: Winter was on its way out and spring was fast approaching.
We left at daybreak and would arrive in the evening, about eight at night.

The entire journey was through the Himalayas and on the way I became acquainted with the Himalayas, the soul of the gods, its very essence filling every corner of the human mind, causing human beings to fall ardently in love with its icy crown.

paragraphs.text: We started from Jammu at dawn. The road was up and down the whole way. This was the Jammu whose history stretches back to the Yajurvedic era. This was the first part of India that the Aryans colonized. One of its names is Jambushilá, or rose-apple coloured stone, for the particles of gold that are scattered here and there in this part of the Himalayas; they look a little like rose-apple, hence the name Jambushilá. From this comes the name of the region, Jambu (jambu > jammu), and from the name Jambu comes the name of all of India, from the ocean to the Himalayas – Jambudviipa.
summary: We started from Jammu at dawn.
This was the first part of India that the Aryans colonized.
From this comes the name of the region, Jambu (jambu > jammu), and from the name Jambu comes the name of all of India, from the ocean to the Himalayas – Jambudviipa.

paragraphs.text: The northernmost border of the territory of Jambu is the Pamir mountain range; to south, Kanyakumari; to the west, Iran; and to the east, Suvarńadviipa – the name of this vast land expanse is Jambudviipa. When the Aryans came here they chose this region as their first colony. Seeing the abundant potential for procuring food and clothes and so forth, the Aryans gave it the name Bháratakhańd́a. We live, and have been fed and clothed in Jambudviipaʼs Bháratakhańd́a.
summary: The northernmost border of the territory of Jambu is the Pamir mountain range; to south, Kanyakumari; to the west, Iran; and to the east, Suvarńadviipa – the name of this vast land expanse is Jambudviipa.
Seeing the abundant potential for procuring food and clothes and so forth, the Aryans gave it the name Bháratakhańd́a.
We live, and have been fed and clothed in Jambudviipaʼs Bháratakhańd́a.

paragraphs.text: We were journeying from Jammu to the central part of Himachal Pradesh, that is, Bilaspur. It was a rock-strewn landscape. In the middle of this rocky tract of land were two huge lakes, thus another name for the territory of Jammu was Dvigartabhúmi [land of two cavities], whose derived form in Bengali is Duggardesh (dvigarta > duiggara > duggar). Out of great respect, people have used the adjective D́ográ for the extremely courageous and straightforward people of Jammu, and their Paeshácii Prákrta-descended language has been given the name D́ogrii.
summary: We were journeying from Jammu to the central part of Himachal Pradesh, that is, Bilaspur.

In the middle of this rocky tract of land were two huge lakes, thus another name for the territory of Jammu was Dvigartabhúmi [land of two cavities], whose derived form in Bengali is Duggardesh (dvigarta > duiggara > duggar).

Out of great respect, people have used the adjective D́ográ for the extremely courageous and straightforward people of Jammu, and their Paeshácii Prákrta-descended language has been given the name D́ogrii.

paragraphs.text: The city of Jammu is quite ancient. There are several other places in India with the name Jammu, so in order to distinguish this Jammu from them the city is called Jammu-Tawi. Tawi is the name of a local river. The Aryans discovered gold in the sand particles of several rivers in this Jammu territory. Since they discovered gold in the rivers of Jammu, they also gave gold the name jámbunada [nada means “river”].
summary: The city of Jammu is quite ancient.
Tawi is the name of a local river.
Since they discovered gold in the rivers of Jammu, they also gave gold the name jámbunada [nada means “river”].

paragraphs.text: We had now started from this Jammu. Up until the pre-Pathan era, Jammu was an independent kingdom. In olden times Sanskrit, and after that, D́ogri, were its local languages. D́ogriʼs script is a central Indian form of Sáradá script. In ancient India, after the demise of both the Bráhmii and Kharośt́hii scripts, three different scripts sprang up in three different parts of India: (1) The Kut́ilá script in Allahabad and east of there; (2) Sáradá to the northwest of Allahabad; and (3) Náradá or Nágrii in the southwest. Sáradá means “Sarasvatii”, the goddess of knowledge. The Brahmans of this region are known as Sárasvata Brahmans – they are called this for their erudition. These Sárasvata Brahmans used to live principally in southern Russia, Afghanistan, Kashmiir, Jammu and the Saptanada Kingdom [Punjab]. The Sáradá script was prevalent in this territory. Just as there were three branches of Sárasvata Brahmans – Kashmiir Sárasvata, Dogri Sárasvata and Saptanada (Punjabi) Sárasvata – there were also three branches of Sáradá script – Kashmirii Sáradá, central Indian or D́ogri Sáradá, and southern Indian or Punjabi Sáradá. In all of these areas Sanskrit has been written, learned and taught in this Sáradá script since very ancient times.
summary: We had now started from this Jammu.
Sáradá means “Sarasvatii”, the goddess of knowledge.
In all of these areas Sanskrit has been written, learned and taught in this Sáradá script since very ancient times.

paragraphs.text: The British did not want to retain rule over Kashmir and Jammu themselves. Since the old royal house of Kashmiir had died out, it was not possible to return it to the descendants of that dynasty. Thus they sold Kashmiir and Jammu to a certain D́ográ chieftain – Golap Singh. After that Jammu became a native kingdom of India. The kingdomʼs name became Jammu and Kashmir; its summer capital was Srinagar and its winter capital was Jammu. The Kashmiir that is spoken about in Kalhanʼs Rájataraunginii is not the old land of Kashmiir. It is about Kashmiir without Jammu.
summary: The British did not want to retain rule over Kashmir and Jammu themselves.
After that Jammu became a native kingdom of India.
It is about Kashmiir without Jammu.

paragraphs.text: Sáradámat́hamárabhya kuṋkumádritat́ántakah
summary: Sáradámat́hamárabhya kuṋkumádritat́ántakah

paragraphs.text: Távat Kashmiiradeshasyat paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.
summary: Távat Kashmiiradeshasyat paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.

paragraphs.text: [The entire area, fifty yojanas in all, lying between the Sáradá Mát́ha and Kumkum Mountain was known as Kashmiira.]
summary: [The entire area, fifty yojanas in all, lying between the Sáradá Mát́ha and Kumkum Mountain was known as Kashmiira.

paragraphs.text: Maharaja Ranjit Singh made efforts to develop the Dogri language along with trying to make it the official government language. However, by that time Urdu and Farsi had become so thoroughly intertwined into the social fabric of Kashmiir and Jammu that it ended up being impossible to dislodge them and establish the D́ogri language and script.
summary: Maharaja Ranjit Singh made efforts to develop the Dogri language along with trying to make it the official government language.

However, by that time Urdu and Farsi had become so thoroughly intertwined into the social fabric of Kashmiir and Jammu that it ended up being impossible to dislodge them and establish the D́ogri language and script.

paragraphs.text: We were heading from west to east, the road passing through an almost completely mountainous area. However, that small portion of the Punjab that we passed through was more or less level. Two districts of the Punjab fell in that part of the road: Pathankot and Hoshiarpur.
summary: We were heading from west to east, the road passing through an almost completely mountainous area.
However, that small portion of the Punjab that we passed through was more or less level.
Two districts of the Punjab fell in that part of the road: Pathankot and Hoshiarpur.

paragraphs.text: We were travelling from west to east. From the land of sunset to the land of sunrise, taking the sunbeam particles of the evening radiance with us into the luminous presence of the rising sun, traveling, traveling, traveling.
summary: We were travelling from west to east.
From the land of sunset to the land of sunrise, taking the sunbeam particles of the evening radiance with us into the luminous presence of the rising sun, traveling, traveling, traveling.

paragraphs.text: Nowadays, both Jammu and Kashmiir are inhabited by people belonging to the Aryan community but their ancient inhabitants belonged to the Kash tribe. The meaning of the word kash/kaś is “those who move about or wander a lot”. The members of the Kash tribe never used to remain long in one place. They used to shift from place to place according to the severity of the cold, thus they were called Kash. There were greater numbers of Kash in the north, that is, Kashmiir, and less toward Jammu. In this sense the land of the Kash becomes kash + meru, Kashmeru – Kashmiir.
summary: Nowadays, both Jammu and Kashmiir are inhabited by people belonging to the Aryan community but their ancient inhabitants belonged to the Kash tribe.
They used to shift from place to place according to the severity of the cold, thus they were called Kash.
In this sense the land of the Kash becomes kash + meru, Kashmeru – Kashmiir.

paragraphs.text: Those people who were descended from the Aryans and made their home in Kashmiir belonged to the Mediterranean community. They have pale white skin, either black or blue eyes and hair, and are of medium stature. The people who made their home in the Jammu part were chiefly Alpine and secondarily Nordic. Their skin colour is pale reddish and they are rather tall. Their similarity to the Punjabi people in appearance, manners and language is especially noteworthy.
summary: Those people who were descended from the Aryans and made their home in Kashmiir belonged to the Mediterranean community.
The people who made their home in the Jammu part were chiefly Alpine and secondarily Nordic.
Their similarity to the Punjabi people in appearance, manners and language is especially noteworthy.

paragraphs.text: The D́ogra and Kashmiirii communities live nearer each other and in a much closer way in Doda District than around Banihal. The name of the common spoken language of this district is Bhádruvái; it is actually a mixed form of the Dogri and Kashmiri languages. However, Kashmiirii is also spoken in the part of the district which borders on Kashmiir; D́ogri is spoken as well in the remaining portion, near the province of Jammu. From the anthropological point of view, the people of this area are a blending of both. They possess a beautiful combination of valour and intellectuality – the radiance of the diamond with the fragrance of the campaka.
summary: The D́ogra and Kashmiirii communities live nearer each other and in a much closer way in Doda District than around Banihal.
However, Kashmiirii is also spoken in the part of the district which borders on Kashmiir; D́ogri is spoken as well in the remaining portion, near the province of Jammu.
They possess a beautiful combination of valour and intellectuality – the radiance of the diamond with the fragrance of the campaka.

paragraphs.text: The language of the first part of our journey was Dogri. The principal language of Himachal Pradeshʼs Kullu valley is D́ogri. The language of Himachal Pradeshʼs Kangra and the Punjabʼs Hoshiarpur and Pathankot is Punjabi. Just behind us lay western Punjabʼs Shialkot; its language, however, is Dogri.
summary: The language of the first part of our journey was Dogri.
The language of Himachal Pradeshʼs Kangra and the Punjabʼs Hoshiarpur and Pathankot is Punjabi.
Just behind us lay western Punjabʼs Shialkot; its language, however, is Dogri.

paragraphs.text: The language of western Punjabʼs Muzaffarbad is a mixture of Punjabi and Kashmiirii. The language of the region that our path took us through after passing the Kangra Valley is Páhaŕi. A little to our north on the left-hand side was Laddak. The language of Laddak is Laddákii. Laddákii is a western dialect of the Tibetan language. The Laddakii script, whose historical name is T́egŕii, is a local edition of Tibetan script. There is some resemblance between this script and Kut́ilá, or Bengali script. I have seen this script in the Buddhist temples in the mountainous regions of Sikkim and Darjeeling. The Buddhist priests recite mantras from scriptures written in this script.
summary: The language of western Punjabʼs Muzaffarbad is a mixture of Punjabi and Kashmiirii.
Laddákii is a western dialect of the Tibetan language.
The Buddhist priests recite mantras from scriptures written in this script.

paragraphs.text: During the time of Kashmiirʼs King Golap Singh [1839–1857], his commander-in-chief, Jarawar Singh, attacked the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, and finally, according to the stipulations of the treaty, Tibet (Kimpuruśavarśa) ceded the province of Laddak to the King of Kashmiir, and along with that madea pledge to send a yearly tribute of gold coins to the Kashmiirii court. From then on Laddak became a part of Kashmiir.
summary: During the time of Kashmiirʼs King Golap Singh [1839–1857], his commander-in-chief, Jarawar Singh, attacked the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, and finally, according to the stipulations of the treaty, Tibet (Kimpuruśavarśa) ceded the province of Laddak to the King of Kashmiir, and along with that madea pledge to send a yearly tribute of gold coins to the Kashmiirii court.
From then on Laddak became a part of Kashmiir.

paragraphs.text: Kimpuruśavarśa, or Tibet, starts a little to the east of Laddak. The area where Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar are today was part of Jambudviipaʼs Bháratakhańd́a at the time of the composition of the Viśńu Puráńa, that is, it was not Tibet or Kimpuruśavarśa. Later on, Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar were incorporated into Tibet. The relationship between India and Tibet has been quite cordial since very ancient times.
summary: Kimpuruśavarśa, or Tibet, starts a little to the east of Laddak.
Later on, Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar were incorporated into Tibet.
The relationship between India and Tibet has been quite cordial since very ancient times.

paragraphs.text: We were travelling from west to east. Sometimes our car practically passed right over the top of the mountains, sometimes alongside them, and sometimes it skirted the cultivated, furrow-serrated mountain fields. The driver of the car was Shrii Kuldip Sharma. Sharmajii was a child of the Saptasindhu. After the country was partitioned he came over here – the people of that country are refugees in this one. Such a twist of fate!
summary: We were travelling from west to east.
Sharmajii was a child of the Saptasindhu.
Such a twist of fate!

paragraphs.text: Driving a car through these serpentine mountain roads is not a trifling affair. Sharmajii was a skilful driver. He drove his vehicle beautifully.
summary: Driving a car through these serpentine mountain roads is not a trifling affair.
Sharmajii was a skilful driver.
He drove his vehicle beautifully.

paragraphs.text: The car kept on, sometimes passing through vast, verdant forests crowded with towering trees, sometimes disturbing the meditative tranquility of the sparsely wooded, rocky peaks, and sometimes making us completely losing track of our passage in the beautiful greenery.
summary: The car kept on, sometimes passing through vast, verdant forests crowded with towering trees, sometimes disturbing the meditative tranquility of the sparsely wooded, rocky peaks, and sometimes making us completely losing track of our passage in the beautiful greenery.

paragraphs.text: Between two mountains lay a deep, deep valley, thick with young, green grass. Through it ran a silvery small mountain stream, curved like a scimitar. Migratory birds were flying overhead; the time had come for them to return home. In winter, great flocks of migratory birds abandon the extreme cold of Siberia, Outer Mongolia, western China and Tibet, and head south, crossing over rivers and mountains, in search of warmth. Most of the birds that we could see there were from other countries. Although birds of the flamingo group were in the greatest number, there were also various other kinds of birds, such as dhanuśas, háŕgilás [Adjuntant stork], vultures, black swans, red swans, and eagles as well. Some of them had coloured tufts a little like the cockatoo.
summary: Between two mountains lay a deep, deep valley, thick with young, green grass.
In winter, great flocks of migratory birds abandon the extreme cold of Siberia, Outer Mongolia, western China and Tibet, and head south, crossing over rivers and mountains, in search of warmth.
Some of them had coloured tufts a little like the cockatoo.

paragraphs.text: There are crowds of these birds gathered round wherever there are lakes or ponds in the valley. One interesting thing I noticed is that the birds would not approach the edges of those mountain peaks around us that were covered in snow because they had left their own countries and come here in order to escape contact with the snow as well as the snowstorms.
summary: There are crowds of these birds gathered round wherever there are lakes or ponds in the valley.

One interesting thing I noticed is that the birds would not approach the edges of those mountain peaks around us that were covered in snow because they had left their own countries and come here in order to escape contact with the snow as well as the snowstorms.

paragraphs.text: These birds remain here for the winter; they build their nests, lay their eggs and wait for them to hatch, and then teach their young how to fly and how to gather food. Thereafter, when the winter ends and the warm spring breezes begin to blow, they return home along with their young that they have taught to fly. Although they do not have to face any botheration of passport and visa, they often fall into deep trouble as they travel while trying to protect themselves from the cruel clutches of human beings. Many meet an untimely death due to a cruel bullet or fall injured to the ground. Is this their fate! Is there no way to avoid this devilry! Is there no way that a little benevolence can awaken in the human mind! Does mankindʼs Neohumanism teach this!
summary: These birds remain here for the winter; they build their nests, lay their eggs and wait for them to hatch, and then teach their young how to fly and how to gather food.
Many meet an untimely death due to a cruel bullet or fall injured to the ground.
Does mankindʼs Neohumanism teach this!

paragraphs.text: We continued on. We still had far to go, crossing over the border of many former native kingdoms. Nearly the entire journey that we were making this day was through a former kingdom. The king of Jammu-Kashmiir was Hari Singh, the successor of its first D́ogra king, Golap Singh. His son, in turn, Karna Singh, was not able to become king. Officially he got the government post as Sadr-i-riyásat. The remaining parts thereafter were smaller or larger kingdoms. Our destination, Bilaspur, was also a middle-sized native kingdom. But Bilaspur was still quite far away – hanaoj Biláspura dúr ast. We continued on and on. It was like the lines: Pathik ámi pathei básá / Ámár jeman jáoyá temani ásá [“I am a traveler and the path is my home / It makes no difference whether I come or go”].
summary: We still had far to go, crossing over the border of many former native kingdoms.
The remaining parts thereafter were smaller or larger kingdoms.
It was like the lines: Pathik ámi pathei básá / Ámár jeman jáoyá temani ásá [“I am a traveler and the path is my home / It makes no difference whether I come or go”].

paragraphs.text: After going a little ways I suddenly noticed a change. Now there was an apple orchard beside us. This place was well above sea-level, but because there were apple orchards on both sides of us we could not tell how high we were. Here and there were some ciir and phár varieties of trees standing in the apple fields. In some trees I saw some rare birds – birds-of-paradise (Svarga vihauṋga). They rarely come into contact with people so they are not afraid of them. They do not know what cruel creatures human beings are. Seeing us, they were not afraid, rather they stared at us eagerly. Their simplicity made me feel uneasy and ashamed at the same time. I felt ashamed thinking that they do not realize how cruel we human beings are, how complex we are from the mental point of view, and how crooked.
summary: After going a little ways I suddenly noticed a change.
They rarely come into contact with people so they are not afraid of them.
I felt ashamed thinking that they do not realize how cruel we human beings are, how complex we are from the mental point of view, and how crooked.

paragraphs.text: After we passed by the apple orchards we came to yet another forest of towering trees. These trees were somewhat similar to oak trees. I noticed that numerous varieties of orchids (kákarúhá) were hanging in the trees. Some of their flowers were in bloom while others were about to bloom. Some of their buds were counting the moments, waiting for the arrival of spring. By judging the amount of warmth in the climate they had guessed that Holi [spring festival] was not far away.
summary: After we passed by the apple orchards we came to yet another forest of towering trees.
Some of their flowers were in bloom while others were about to bloom.
By judging the amount of warmth in the climate they had guessed that Holi [spring festival] was not far away.

paragraphs.text: I noticed that most of the orchids here bloomed in the months of Phálgun-Caetra. ( 1 ) It also appeared that there were a small number of orchid varieties that bloomed in the months of August-September. Some of the orchids looked identical to the orchids that grow uncared-for in the trees alongside the Burdwan-Guskara Road. I have seen these varieties of orchids in Birbhum on the way from Mámud Bazaar to Masháiṋjoŕ, and in areas near the Jonhá waterfall (Gaotamdhárá) on the Jhalda-Ranchi Road. I realized that they did not depend on the climate so much, so long as there was not snowfall.
summary: I noticed that most of the orchids here bloomed in the months of Phálgun-Caetra.
Some of the orchids looked identical to the orchids that grow uncared-for in the trees alongside the Burdwan-Guskara Road.
I realized that they did not depend on the climate so much, so long as there was not snowfall.

paragraphs.text: To the left of us, that is, to the north, at a good distance away was the kingdom of Kinnaur, renowned both in history and in the Puranas. This Kinnaur was situated in the northern extremity of India in the Sadáshiva mountain range. Some people may not be aware that the Himalayas, stretching from the west until the eastern horizon, are divided north and south into two parts. The Sanskrit name of the part of the Himalayas that touch the northern plains of India is Shivaliuṋga Parvatamálá (Shivalic Range). This part is high, but not so high. There is cultivation wherever there are green forested areas in the valleys lying between two mountains, cutting into the mountains with either step-farming or terracing. This Shivalic range is covered with snow in the wintertime, and its highest peaks remained snow-covered all year long. The fossils of prehistoric animals can be found in this part.
summary: To the left of us, that is, to the north, at a good distance away was the kingdom of Kinnaur, renowned both in history and in the Puranas.
This part is high, but not so high.
The fossils of prehistoric animals can be found in this part.

paragraphs.text: At one time the Himalayas were submerged in the bosom of the sea. Northern India was also then at the bottom of the sea. To the south, only Gondawanaland was above sea level. Approximately three million years ago the Himalayas rose up from the depths as a result of an earthquake. The skeletons of some of those animals who used to wander in these parts of the earth three million years ago can be found packed underneath the rocks in the Shivalic range. In later times when the hippopotamus and giraffe were living here, they used to live in these Lower Himalayas. Some of their fossils have also been found in the Lower Himalayas, and more are bound to be discovered in the future.
summary: At one time the Himalayas were submerged in the bosom of the sea.
Approximately three million years ago the Himalayas rose up from the depths as a result of an earthquake.
Some of their fossils have also been found in the Lower Himalayas, and more are bound to be discovered in the future.

paragraphs.text: The Sadáshiva range (Upper Himalayas) run west to east, directly parallel to the Lower Himalayas. We find this mountain range in Kashmir, Laddak, the northern part of Himachal Pradesh, Simla, Kinnaur, toward the north of Garhwal-Kumayun, the north of Nepal, northern Sikkim and Bhutan, and in southern Tibet. This part of the Himalayas is really quite high. The snow remains all year long but in winter it is really heavy. The highest Himalayan peaks are located in this part. The driest, coldest and most elevated area of the Upper Himalayas is Laddak and Kinnaur. During winter nights the temperature can fall below minus one-hundred degrees. While heating water it freezes and turns to ice.
summary: The Sadáshiva range (Upper Himalayas) run west to east, directly parallel to the Lower Himalayas.
The highest Himalayan peaks are located in this part.
While heating water it freezes and turns to ice.

paragraphs.text: In most parts of this barren mountain land there are snowstorms nearly twelve months of the year. There is virtually no green forest, and hardly any cultivation. I have seen a little barley being grown here in the summertime. Peopleʼs primary livelihood is raising livestock. The Indian cow cannot survive here; there are Yaks. Although the ancient land of Kinnaur was some ways from where we were it was not altogether that far. In olden days the people of this region were famed for their beauty, and to some extent they still are. Although their noses are slightly sloping, it does not detract from their loveliness. Seeing their beauty, the people of those days use to think and say that they were not people but angels. Erá ki nara? [Are they really human beings?] Kiḿ nara = kinnara.
summary: In most parts of this barren mountain land there are snowstorms nearly twelve months of the year.
Although the ancient land of Kinnaur was some ways from where we were it was not altogether that far.
] Kiḿ nara = kinnara.

paragraphs.text: The language of the people of Kinnaur is a southwestern dialect of Tibetan, just as Laddakii is a western dialect of Tibetan. The script of the Kinnauri language is also T́egrii or T́egrá (In Sanskrit, triguńii or triguńá script). Although the common religion of the Kinnauri people is the Lamabad branch of Maháyána Buddhism, it is clearly influenced by the Árśa doctrine. ( 2 ) Over the last two thousand years, Arśa-ism and Kinnaurʼs Maháyána Buddhism (centering around Avalokiteshvara) have coexisted peacefully because Buddhism has avoided clash. The common people revere both the Buddhist grottoes and the Árśa temples. During hours of worship, the Buddhist lamas place offerings of ground barley, roasted barley powder, etc. before the gods, and these return to the people as prasád [holy remains of the offerings which are then eaten]. In the Hindu [Árśa] temples the priests place offerings of fruits and vegetables. In the same house one person may be Hindu and another Buddhist, however those who wish to become renunciants generally adopt lamaism and cloister themselves in the Buddhist grottoes. Very few local people become Hindu renunciants.
summary: The language of the people of Kinnaur is a southwestern dialect of Tibetan, just as Laddakii is a western dialect of Tibetan.
During hours of worship, the Buddhist lamas place offerings of ground barley, roasted barley powder, etc.
Very few local people become Hindu renunciants.

paragraphs.text: In olden times the number of men in Kinnaur was much greater, by comparison, than the number of women, thus the practice of polygamy was current among women out of social necessity. Some traces of that may still remain today. Some people may consider this strange, but there is nothing to be astonished at, or to think odd. People build their social structure by effecting a suitable harmony between individual and collective necessity, so however this practice of Kinnaur may appear to others, it was perfectly natural.
summary: In olden times the number of men in Kinnaur was much greater, by comparison, than the number of women, thus the practice of polygamy was current among women out of social necessity.
Some people may consider this strange, but there is nothing to be astonished at, or to think odd.
People build their social structure by effecting a suitable harmony between individual and collective necessity, so however this practice of Kinnaur may appear to others, it was perfectly natural.

paragraphs.text: That is, “If one remembers these five ladies – Ahalyá, Draopadii, Kuntii, Tárá, and Mandodarii – then even the deadly sins are destroyed.” In the opinion of the old followers of certain schools, these five ladies just mentioned were sinners. Ahalyá was turned into stone for her wicked behaviour. ( 3 ) Draopadii had five husbands. Karńa was the son of unmarried Kuntii. Tárá, the wife of Bállii, married Sugriiva after Bálliiʼs death. Ravanaʼs wife, Mandodarii, married Vibhiiśań after Ravanaʼs death.
summary: That is, “If one remembers these five ladies – Ahalyá, Draopadii, Kuntii, Tárá, and Mandodarii – then even the deadly sins are destroyed.

paragraphs.text: The women of Kinnaur can rightfully say that if, despite the fact that she had five husbands, Draopadii is a memorable woman, and if, by remembering her, the deadly sins meet their demise, then what possible sin can there be in this ancient practice of their land. The logic is irrefutable.
summary: The women of Kinnaur can rightfully say that if, despite the fact that she had five husbands, Draopadii is a memorable woman, and if, by remembering her, the deadly sins meet their demise, then what possible sin can there be in this ancient practice of their land.
The logic is irrefutable.

paragraphs.text: It was past midday. We had left Jammu around seven in the morning, and I was starting to feel a bit drowsy. My driver, Kuldip Sharma, said: “Go ahead and lie down. I know the way quite well. It wonʼt be a problem.”
summary: We had left Jammu around seven in the morning, and I was starting to feel a bit drowsy.
I know the way quite well.
It wonʼt be a problem.

paragraphs.text: Sharmajii had just spent six months in Kolkata driving a taxi and he could speak good Bengali. I was riding in the car – now I started to feel as if I was floating, being pulled along by a distant, unknown music towards a faraway meridian. I was floating, crossing over rivers and mountains, forests and oceans and snow-covered peaks, on and on and on.
summary: Sharmajii had just spent six months in Kolkata driving a taxi and he could speak good Bengali.

I was floating, crossing over rivers and mountains, forests and oceans and snow-covered peaks, on and on and on.

paragraphs.text: Suddenly it seemed as if a silvery fountain was cascading down the side of a towering mountain. I felt the desire to get down and drink a palm-full of that sacred water.
summary: Suddenly it seemed as if a silvery fountain was cascading down the side of a towering mountain.
I felt the desire to get down and drink a palm-full of that sacred water.

paragraphs.text: [The spring is dancing along, painting with a silver line Flowing down the mountain, through the forest It recognizes no authority, it brooks no obstacle It rushes on down in a pleasant dream Shivaʼs wild matted locks rush passionately down Bursting with life along the way and begging for liberation in the delightful waters.]

paragraphs.text: So thought, so it was. Keeping the cascade at a little distance I extended my hands to take some water. Just then I heard someone speaking behind me. “Hold it a minute. Do not drink just yet. First put something in your stomach, then drink.”
summary: So thought, so it was.
Just then I heard someone speaking behind me.
First put something in your stomach, then drink.

paragraphs.text: What is this! Astonishing! What is a human voice doing here in this rough, difficult to access, thorny mountain ravine? I turned around to find a loving image of motherhood. In the womanʼs hands was brass tray with raised sides, and on it some yellow-coloured, puffed-up thing and some green curry. I looked at her questioningly. With a voice full of affection she said: “There wasnʼt anything in the house except apple bread so I rushed over here with it. Now, eat, eat, please. Donʼt drink on an empty stomach.”
summary: What is a human voice doing here in this rough, difficult to access, thorny mountain ravine?
I looked at her questioningly.
Donʼt drink on an empty stomach.

paragraphs.text: The woman was wearing the typical regional dress – an álkhálla [a kind of loose gown traditionally worn by Muslim women], an oŕńá [scarf] wrapped around her, and a great many earrings hanging from both ears. Her face was beaming with a radiant, affectionate humanity. It was like the last word on earthly beauty, the final essence of all human hearts.
summary: The woman was wearing the typical regional dress – an álkhálla [a kind of loose gown traditionally worn by Muslim women], an oŕńá [scarf] wrapped around her, and a great many earrings hanging from both ears.
Her face was beaming with a radiant, affectionate humanity.
It was like the last word on earthly beauty, the final essence of all human hearts.

paragraphs.text: The way the lady said it, it was as if she was doing me a great injustice by giving me apple bread, as if it was the kind of food one does not give a guest.
summary: The way the lady said it, it was as if she was doing me a great injustice by giving me apple bread, as if it was the kind of food one does not give a guest.

paragraphs.text: I ate it and greatly enjoyed it. When such a good person feeds you so eagerly you are sure to enjoy it. It was like the puláo and curry that the table servants serve in a wealthy household, better than anything the man of the house has ever seen. While I was eating I looked at some large trees standing here and there. The trees were full of orchids.
summary: I ate it and greatly enjoyed it.
It was like the puláo and curry that the table servants serve in a wealthy household, better than anything the man of the house has ever seen.
The trees were full of orchids.

paragraphs.text: In a bashful, modest voice the lady said: “I just received the news a short while ago that you were coming. I knew right then that you loved orchids and that threw me into a quandary. What should I do? Should I first prepare some bread and curry for you, or should I pluck some orchids from the trees? I decided that I should first prepare some bread, and then, if there was enough time, I would pluck some orchids for you from the tree. Iʼm very good at climbing trees.”
summary: In a bashful, modest voice the lady said: “I just received the news a short while ago that you were coming.
Should I first prepare some bread and curry for you, or should I pluck some orchids from the trees?
Iʼm very good at climbing trees.

paragraphs.text: “Why have I hardly seen any men in your village?” I asked.
summary: “Why have I hardly seen any men in your village?

paragraphs.text: The lady replied, “There is a great poverty now in our area. The men have all gone down to the plains in search of work. What little there is in the apple orchards the women are doing. Moreover, you well know that the men cannot do so much labour in the mountain areas. They fall sick if too great a burden is placed on their shoulders; they die before their time. So we donʼt let our men here work so much. We do much of the work in the apple orchards. We also go and sell in the markets. We only let the men do the packing for those apples which are exported to distant lands. They want to work, but we donʼt let them.”
summary: The lady replied, “There is a great poverty now in our area.
So we donʼt let our men here work so much.
They want to work, but we donʼt let them.

paragraphs.text: “You are really good people, indeed,” I said. “The boys here are just as good as the girls. I am really pleased to see it. Now then, how did you know that I was coming here? And how did you know that I love orchids?”
summary: “You are really good people, indeed,” I said.
I am really pleased to see it.
And how did you know that I love orchids?

paragraphs.text: “By the grace of Lord Shiva,” the lady replied.
summary: “By the grace of Lord Shiva,” the lady replied.

paragraphs.text: I noticed that the lady was standing with a glass of water from the spring. It was there for me should I want it or reach out my hands. I reached out my hands and she put the glass in my hand. What delicious water! As if drawn from a fountain of ambrosia falling from some immortal sphere. Suddenly I felt something push against my elbow. I saw that my right elbow was pressing lightly against the glass of the car window. Hey, where am I? I am inside the car. Had it been a dream all along? Ah yes, I had been dreaming. Kuldip Sharma was speeding along at the wheel, flying with the speed of a comet because there were not so many curves in the road here.
summary: I noticed that the lady was standing with a glass of water from the spring.
Suddenly I felt something push against my elbow.

The nymphs will spread their net of illusion and capture any person who comes along. Look over there, youʼll see a spring in the distance coming down that mountain.”

paragraphs.text: I looked and yes, in the distance, far away, very far away, the silvery line of a stream was descending from a tall mountain peak. We were traveling from west to east. There was still a little time remaining before we reached the former kingdom of Bilaspur. I asked Kuldip, “Well, can you tell me how this apple ( 5 ) bread is prepared?”

paragraphs.text: “Sure, Iʼll tell you,” he replied. “There is very little wheat grown here, however, the people here love wheat bread. It poses no difficulty or inconvenience for the rich people to buy wheat and eat bread made from wheat flour. But how much inconvenience the poor people face! In those years when the price of wheat is high or when there is an excess apple production and they fail to find good markets for their apples, then they dry the apples and grind them into a kind of flour. They spend a lot of time eating bread made from that apple flour. The people here consider serving guests to be an especially virtuous act. Those who donʼt serve guests properly are frowned on by society. No matter how much trouble it may bring them, they feed their guests wheat bread, either with ghee on it, or if not, then tandooris. Itʼs a troubling situation for them if they are ever forced to feed any guest apple bread; then there is no end to their shame. They will beg that guestʼs forgiveness over and over again. Remember this: the wealthy peopleʼs food here is wheat [gam ( 6 )] bread; the poor folkʼs food is apple bread.”
summary: “Sure, Iʼll tell you,” he replied.
The people here consider serving guests to be an especially virtuous act.
Remember this: the wealthy peopleʼs food here is wheat [gam ( 6 )] bread; the poor folkʼs food is apple bread.

paragraphs.text: “Well,” I asked, “is there any kind of green curry that the people here are especially fond of?”

paragraphs.text: “Yes,” Kuldip replied, “During the really cold times vegetables donʼt grow here. However, in the holes in the ice and in stone hollows clumps of a kind of spinach plant manage to grow. Its leaves are used as a vegetable. The wealthy never suffer any inconvenience. They have vegetables shipped in from outside. In the morning you will see maunds and maunds of milk also arriving here from the Punjab.”
summary: “Yes,” Kuldip replied, “During the really cold times vegetables donʼt grow here.
The wealthy never suffer any inconvenience.
In the morning you will see maunds and maunds of milk also arriving here from the Punjab.

paragraphs.text: I listened while Kuldip talked. We had come closer to that mountain with its spring but it was still far away. We were still passing through the land of the nymphs, and I began to think about Kinnaur and Tibet.

paragraphs.text: In the land of Kinnaur there was an unusual harmony between the Buddhist and Hindu religions. This kind of harmony is extremely rare in the annals of human history. The Buddhist religion arrived in Kinnaur and Laddak well after it arrived in the original Tibet, and Buddhism arrived in Laddak a little before it reached Kinnaur.
summary: In the land of Kinnaur there was an unusual harmony between the Buddhist and Hindu religions.
This kind of harmony is extremely rare in the annals of human history.
The Buddhist religion arrived in Kinnaur and Laddak well after it arrived in the original Tibet, and Buddhism arrived in Laddak a little before it reached Kinnaur.

paragraphs.text: The Kashmiri pundit, Kumáráyańa, was then world-famous. There is no greater scholar of Buddhist scriptures. He went to China at the invitation of the Chinese Emperor. Before going to China he strengthened the foundations of Buddhism in Laddak and the Kashmir valley. He propagated Buddhism in China and had some Maháyána scriptures translated into Chinese.
summary: The Kashmiri pundit, Kumáráyańa, was then world-famous.
He went to China at the invitation of the Chinese Emperor.
He propagated Buddhism in China and had some Maháyána scriptures translated into Chinese.

paragraphs.text: Kumáráyańaʼs wife was the Chinese royal princess, Jiivá. Kumáráyańaʼs son, Kumárajiiva [A.D. 344], spent the greater part of his life in China, but he went to Kashmiir for some time. He also composed some Maháyána scriptures in Sanskrit. He went to Laddak but he did not go to Kinnaur. Still, Buddhism was subsequently introduced into Kinnaur from Laddak. Buddhism was first propagated in the original territory of Tibet (whose name was then Kimpuruśavarśa) by the royal prince of Udayan, Padmasambhava. What we now call Garhwal-Kumayun was known as the kingdom of Udayan in olden times. The palms of the hands and the soles of the feet of the royal prince were bright red so he was given the name Padmasambhava. Due to his influence Tibet accepted Maháyána Buddhism. The religion of Tibet before that was Bonpa or Bonpa-ism. King Sáungt-sen-gámpo, a follower of the Bonpa religion, had two wives. One was the royal Chinese princess, Den Jing, and the other was Trikut́i, the daughter of the Nepali King at the time, Aḿshuvarmańa, who was a follower of Máháyána Buddhism. The influence of these two queens was considerable in the kingdom of Tibet. The king was inspired by them to accept the Buddhist religion.
summary: Kumáráyańaʼs wife was the Chinese royal princess, Jiivá.
What we now call Garhwal-Kumayun was known as the kingdom of Udayan in olden times.
The king was inspired by them to accept the Buddhist religion.

paragraphs.text: Sáungt-sen-gámpo was a historically renowned personality, a pious emperor. At that time, Magadha was resplendent for its erudition. The two best universities were then Magadhaʼs Nalanda and Taxila in the land of Kandahar. Taxila was famous for its philosophical thinking and for its spiritual community. Nalanda was successful in all spheres, and spiritually inspired. The chancellor of this Nalanda University was Dharmapála Diipauṋkar. Dharmapála Diipauṋkar came from Vikramańipur (its modern name is Vikrampur). Dhaka Districtʼs Vikrampur subdivision has been perched on the glorious golden summit of learning since very ancient times. In the Buddhist era, it became even more radiant in its keenness for learning and wisdom.
summary: Sáungt-sen-gámpo was a historically renowned personality, a pious emperor.
Nalanda was successful in all spheres, and spiritually inspired.
In the Buddhist era, it became even more radiant in its keenness for learning and wisdom.

paragraphs.text: At that time there was no other Buddhist pundit on earth as renowned as Dharmapála Diipauṋkar. Sáungt-sen-gámpo invited this Dharmapála Diipauṋkar to come to his kingdom, that is, Kimpuruśavarśa. While Diipauṋkar was there Buddhism became well established in Kimpuruśavarśa (after that time the name of Kimpuruśavarśa became Tibet). Buddhism became the common religion of the people of Laddak and Kinnaur at that time as well. The king gave Dharmapála Diipauṋkar the title of Shriijiṋána Atiisha as a reward for his recognized scholarship. After Dharmapála Diipauṋkar returned to Magadha, Buddhist pundits in good numbers came from Tibet and studied in Magadha, doing research in Buddhism and translating the Súttapit́aka, Vinayapit́aka and Abhidhammapit́aka into Tibetan.

paragraphs.text: Tibetʼs King Sáungt-sen-gámpo requested Dharmapála Diipauṋkar to come to Tibet once again to honour him. Since he could not avoid it, Dharmapála Diipauṋkar went one more time to Tibet. He was quite aged at the time and was not able to endure Tibetʼs cold dry climate. He passed away in Tibet, not very far from Lhasa.

paragraphs.text: Thus I have said that Indiaʼs, as well as Bengalʼs relationship with Tibet has always been cordial. No, no, no, it is not sufficient to say cordial – very cordial. In the middle of the Mughal era we see this cordiality carried over in the letters exchanged between the Maharaja of Coochbihar and the King of Tibet – in them runs the melody of this same heartfelt sincerity. The letters exchanged between the two of them were in Bengali. The king of Tibet (the then Dalai Lama) was bound to India by ties of affection. In the British administration as well, there were no great obstacles to intercourse between India and Tibet. Indian pilgrims used to go to Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar without any difficulty. Monks and renunciants used to sit and light the sacrificial fires on both sides of the Himalayas. The closest sea to Tibet was the Bay of Bengal and Kolkata was Tibetʼs seaport. Tibet used to export primarily wool, animal skins, precious stones, and medicinal ingredients, while Tibet used to import manufactured commodities and small amounts of foodstuffs. Several of Tibetʼs post-offices were under the supervision of Bengalʼs Postmaster-General.
summary: Thus I have said that Indiaʼs, as well as Bengalʼs relationship with Tibet has always been cordial.
In the British administration as well, there were no great obstacles to intercourse between India and Tibet.
Several of Tibetʼs post-offices were under the supervision of Bengalʼs Postmaster-General.

paragraphs.text: After Sáungt-sen-gámpo, that is, after Tibet accepted Buddhism, the Lamávád branch of Maháyána Buddhism replaced Bonpa as the state religion of Tibet. The Dalai Lama then came into the role of king. ( 7 ) The Tasi Lama and Panchen Lama ran Tibetʼs political and social machinery for a long time with a very friendly working relationship. From that time on the Dalai Lama used to be considered to be an incarnation of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, just as the king of Nepal used to be thought of as an incarnation of Viśńu from the time of Nepalʼs first Gorkha king, Prthviiráj Shah.

paragraphs.text: By now it seemed that we had come somewhat close to that mountain spring. However when one looks suddenly at a mountain it is never as close as it seems to be. In this case also, I experienced that fact once again. I told Kuldip Sharma, “We are still in that nymph kingdom.”

Over by the side I noticed a huge tree. Many orchids on broken branches had fallen to the ground below. The tree itself was also full of orchids. Up in the tree it seemed as if someone was moving. Yes, indeed there was. A boy about eighteen or nineteen quickly climbed down from the tree. When he got near the ground he jumped and when he landed he ran up to our car.

You met Dildar Singh in Náhán, in the kingdom of Sirmaor.

paragraphs.text: It was a long time ago. I was in Sirmaorʼs capital then, Náhán. Náhán is a small city, but I liked it very much. The kingdom of Sirmaor was at one time quite huge – nearly half of the present-day Himachal Pradesh was in Sirmaor. Moreover, Garhwal-Kumayun was once included within Sirmaor. Part of neighbouring Tibet was also within the borders of Sirmaor.
summary: It was a long time ago.
The kingdom of Sirmaor was at one time quite huge – nearly half of the present-day Himachal Pradesh was in Sirmaor.
Part of neighbouring Tibet was also within the borders of Sirmaor.

paragraphs.text: With the passage of time, many small and large kingdoms fell. A large part of present-day Himachal Pradesh left Sirmaor. In accordance with a verbal agreement between the Panchen Lama and the king of Sirmaor, part of Sirmaor came under the rule of the Dalai Lama. Nepalʼs Gorkha king took possession of Garhwal-Kumayun. Sirmaor became much smaller area-wise. Among all those native kingdoms who were assembled to make the present-day Himachal Pradesh, Sirmaor was not altogether insignificant as far as area goes.
summary: With the passage of time, many small and large kingdoms fell.
Nepalʼs Gorkha king took possession of Garhwal-Kumayun.
Among all those native kingdoms who were assembled to make the present-day Himachal Pradesh, Sirmaor was not altogether insignificant as far as area goes.

paragraphs.text: The language of Sirmaor is Sirmaorii (both language and script). It arose from a mixture of Paeshácii Prákrta and Shaorasenii Prákrta. Sirmaorii is closely related to the Páhári language of Simla.
summary: The language of Sirmaor is Sirmaorii (both language and script).
It arose from a mixture of Paeshácii Prákrta and Shaorasenii Prákrta.
Sirmaorii is closely related to the Páhári language of Simla.

paragraphs.text: Sirmaorii has its own script as well, but nowadays it is disappearing. If this situation continues Sirmaorii script will soon vanish behind the curtain of oblivion, just as Burmaʼs Sán-Kácin script has vanished. At one time these Sán-Kácins were close relatives of the Bengali Kukii community and their script was also Bengali script. However, in subsequent times they were ruined by northern Burmaʼs sub-script, but the Kukii script was unaffected. Sirmaori script is in that same situation. Archaeologists should make efforts to see that this script survives.

paragraphs.text: I got to thinking about that pre-Pathan era. At that time the influence of Shankaracharya over Sirmaor was quite high. The kings were making ongoing efforts with greater and lesser success to build a “learned society”; the relationship between Sirmaor and Bengal dates from that time. Garhwal-Kumayun was still a part of Sirmaor. Yes, Garhwal-Kumayun also left Sirmaorʼs control during Nepali rule. Afterwards, of course, when Nepal was defeated by General Octorloney, ( 9 ) Garhwal-Kumayun went back to the British in accordance with the treaty of Sugaolii (Champaran District) [1816]. The British kept Garhwal-Kumayun in their own hands, rather than return it to Sirmaor, and included it within the then United Province of Agra and Oudh (UP). Garhwal-Kumayun was lost to Sirmaor from then on.
summary: I got to thinking about that pre-Pathan era.
Yes, Garhwal-Kumayun also left Sirmaorʼs control during Nepali rule.
Garhwal-Kumayun was lost to Sirmaor from then on.

paragraphs.text: Let us return then to the subject at hand. The kings of Sirmaor brought some pundits from Bengal and Maharastra and settled them in their own kingdom (in Garhwal and Kumayun) with offers of rent-free land grants. The descendants of these pundits are still there today. They differ from the local Yoshi Brahmans in their manners, behaviours, ways of thinking. Among the sixteen branches of Brahmans in those areas, twelve branches have come from Bengal and four are from Maharastra, that is, they belong to the Maharastran Citpávan branch. Those whose forefathers came from Bengal continue to use such surnames as Bhat́t́a, Upádhyáya, Bahuguńá, and so forth.
summary: Let us return then to the subject at hand.
They differ from the local Yoshi Brahmans in their manners, behaviours, ways of thinking.
Those whose forefathers came from Bengal continue to use such surnames as Bhat́t́a, Upádhyáya, Bahuguńá, and so forth.

paragraphs.text: Maharastraʼs Citpávan Brahmans are mostly vegetarian – they do not eat meat or fish but they do not have so much aversion to onions. The Bengali Brahmans do not have any distaste for meat but they do for onions. Those who eat meat, or used to eat meat, used to cook their meat without onions. When they came to this mountainous region, however, the Bengali and Maharastri Brahmans came into close contact with one another. From the point of view of spiritual ideologies, there have been five acknowledged Tantras since ancient times – Shaeva, Shákta, Gáńapatya, Saora, and Vaeśńava. Shaeva Tantra was equally present in this mountain region and its nearby areas. It was a little stronger in the mountains because this area is called “Shivaʼs Field”. The name of the mountains is also the Shivalic Range. Shiva used to remain mostly in this area, also in the Mount Kailash region.
summary: Maharastraʼs Citpávan Brahmans are mostly vegetarian – they do not eat meat or fish but they do not have so much aversion to onions.
From the point of view of spiritual ideologies, there have been five acknowledged Tantras since ancient times – Shaeva, Shákta, Gáńapatya, Saora, and Vaeśńava.
Shiva used to remain mostly in this area, also in the Mount Kailash region.

paragraphs.text: Earlier I mentioned that until the time of the Viśńu Puráńa, Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar were part of Bharatakhańd́a. But from the Shákta and Gáńapatya Tantra point of view, we see that the successors of the Brahmans who came from Bengal principally accepted Shákta Tantra.
summary: Earlier I mentioned that until the time of the Viśńu Puráńa, Mount Kailash and Mánas Sarovar were part of Bharatakhańd́a.
But from the Shákta and Gáńapatya Tantra point of view, we see that the successors of the Brahmans who came from Bengal principally accepted Shákta Tantra.

paragraphs.text: And the successors of the Maharastra Citpávan Brahman community chiefly followed Gáńpatya Tantra. The influence of Shákta Tantra over the common people was greater, by comparison, than that of Gáńapatya Tantra. The Yoshii Brahmans are close to Shákta Tantra. For related reasons, Shiva and Shiva temples are pre-eminent in this region, but in important places Shákta Tantra, as well, is not neglected. The presiding goddess of the city of Simla is Tárá – Nayanatárá or Nayanadevii. Just near Simla is Kalka (Káliká). Delhi is in the nearby plains; the name of a large part of it is Kálkájii (Kálikájii). Chandigarh is a little to the west of Simla. ( 10 ) Its presiding goddess is Cańd́ii. The Cańd́ii temple of that place is also quite ancient.

Just near Simla is Kalka (Káliká).
The Cańd́ii temple of that place is also quite ancient.

paragraphs.text: Nihál Singh said to me: “I have a strong desire to go with you to Kolkata, but I am not able to.”

paragraphs.text: “Why canʼt you go?” I asked.

“We are going through a time of scarcity in our land. All the men have gone down to the plains in search of work. Iʼm the only man left in the entire village. Dildar Singh also went down to the plains, and my father, Bahadar Singh as well. The only people left in the village are the women. We donʼt have the wherewithal to buy wheat so now we are eating apple bread. If I go with you to Kolkata at this time then who will look after the village? Still, if my father returns and I get the opportunity, I will go and see Kolkata one time. But you know what? If the people in the village find out that I am going to Kolkata they will all cry when they see me.”
