chapters.title: History of Jammu and Kashmir
chapters.partTitle: PART 5: Histories of Certain States in India along with Certain Important Places in Them

paragraphs.text: Jammu and Kashmir

Khas + ac = khash. The root khas means to kill, to beat, to injure. To climb the high-peaked Himalayas in the northern part of India is quite dangerous and exhausting. That is why the girdle of the mountain range across northern India is called khash. The second meaning of the word khash is the group of very ancient, non-Aryan people living in the northern and Pamir regions of India.
summary: The root khas means to kill, to beat, to injure.
That is why the girdle of the mountain range across northern India is called khash.
The second meaning of the word khash is the group of very ancient, non-Aryan people living in the northern and Pamir regions of India.

paragraphs.text: When the Aryans came to northern India, they saw multiple rocks that looked like blackberries. Since those rocks were abundant, they gave that region the name Jambudvipa. In later times, Jambudvipa was used to denote the entirety of Southeast Asia, including India. India was a varśa of that Jambudvipa. The word varśa has three meanings: one is country, and the other two are rainy season and year. Kimpuruśavarśa or Tibet was a varśa in the central region of Jambudvipa. Later the word Jambu was transformed into Jammu. The Aryans first found traces of gold in the sands of the rivers there. Thus, one word for gold is jámbunada.
summary: When the Aryans came to northern India, they saw multiple rocks that looked like blackberries.
The word varśa has three meanings: one is country, and the other two are rainy season and year.
Thus, one word for gold is jámbunada.

paragraphs.text: Later, as they traveled further northward, the Aryans became involved in conflicts with the Khash group of people, conquered their land and named it Khashmeru. This word Khashmeru later mutated into the word Kashmir. One meaning of the word meru is land. So the meaning of the word Kashmir is the land of Kas or the Khash group of people. Similarly, Ajeyameru is the land which cannot be conquered (Ajeyameru > Ajmeru > Ajmir – both the words Ájmiir and Ajmiir are incorrect). So you understand that the name of the land is Kashmiir, not Káshmiir. The meaning of the word Káshmiir in the masculine gender is something related to Káshmiir, such as the men of the land of Kashmiir, or spice from the land of Kashmiir. Káshmiir also means saffron. From this word Káshmiir has come the Hindi word keshariyá. From the Persian word jáffrán has come the distorted English pronunciation saffron.
summary: Later, as they traveled further northward, the Aryans became involved in conflicts with the Khash group of people, conquered their land and named it Khashmeru.
So you understand that the name of the land is Kashmiir, not Káshmiir.
From the Persian word jáffrán has come the distorted English pronunciation saffron.

paragraphs.text: Do not, even by mistake, call any [male] a Káshmirii Brahman, because the meaning of the word “Káshmirii” is any object of Kashmiir in the feminine sense; for example, Káshmirii valley or Káshmiirii woman. “Káshmiirii Brahman” means a Brahman woman of the land of Kashmiir. Would it be proper to address any male in that way? In his book on the history of Kashmiir, Rájatarauṋginii, the royal poet, Kalhan, writes:

paragraphs.text: Sáradámat́hamárabhya kuṋkumádritat́ántakah,
summary: Sáradámat́hamárabhya kuṋkumádritat́ántakah,

paragraphs.text: Távat kashmiiradeshasyát paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.
summary: Távat kashmiiradeshasyát paiṋcáshat yojanátmakah.

paragraphs.text: In ancient times, in northern India the Kśatriyas living at the foothills of the Himalayas used to migrate to the Khas area and remain there. Kśatriyas live on wars. But those newly arrived Kśatriyas, after coming to the land [of Kashmiir], gave up battle in favour of tending animals. ( 1 )
summary: In ancient times, in northern India the Kśatriyas living at the foothills of the Himalayas used to migrate to the Khas area and remain there.
Kśatriyas live on wars.
But those newly arrived Kśatriyas, after coming to the land [of Kashmiir], gave up battle in favour of tending animals.

paragraphs.text: Khas + drń + elongated sound (prśi diirgha ( 2 )) + mr + rań + ṋiiś = kháshmarii. The etymological meaning of the word kháshmarii is the place where people have died at the hands of the Khash people, or where the people of Khash have died. Colloquially, one meaning of the word is the land of Kashmiir. The words khásmarii and káshmarii are synonymous. In ancient Vedic language, the country was called by both names – Kashmiir and Khashmiir. When the Aryans, with their Vedic language, early literature, Vedic lifestyle and spirituality, social wisdom, primary knowledge of contemporary science, economics, skill in archery, astrology and music, crossed over Aryańyavraja (Iran or Persia) to enter Gándhár, they did not meet any resistance on their journey. The area where they encountered the first opposition was the land of Kash or the people of Khas. They [Khas] also had a Mongoloid civilization blended with Dravidian. The people were flat-nosed. They had no intention to simply accept anything of the Vedic Aryans. A conflict of cultures ensued, leading to a bloody struggle. In this struggle, the Aryan invaders emerged victorious. They gradually occupied Baluchistan, Gunj, Chitral, Gilgit, Pamir and finally Kashmir, the main dwelling place of the Khas people, which in Aryan language was called “Kashmiir” or “Khashmiir”. The Khas people moved away to Laddakh [Ladakh] and Kimpuruśavarśa (Tibet). The land was occupied by the Aryans and it obtained a new identity in the name of Kashmeru or Kashmiir, Khashmeru or Khashmiir, Káshmarii or Kháshmarii.
summary: Khas + drń + elongated sound (prśi diirgha ( 2 )) + mr + rań + ṋiiś = kháshmarii.
They [Khas] also had a Mongoloid civilization blended with Dravidian.
The land was occupied by the Aryans and it obtained a new identity in the name of Kashmeru or Kashmiir, Khashmeru or Khashmiir, Káshmarii or Kháshmarii.

paragraphs.text: Beginning with the Vedic era, the Kśatriyas of Kashmir ruled over the kingdom for a long period, with the exception of one or two Pathan and Moghul invasions. During the rule of kings Lalitáditya Muktapiiŕ [724-760 A.D.], Jayápiir, Shankar Verma, et al, the name and fame of Kashmir reached its zenith. Kumarayańa and Kumarjiiva spread that fame to the eastern end of China. However, Queen Didda terminated that march of fame. For the sake of her own self-interest, she sought the help of Aryańyavraja (Iran or Persia), which led to the demise of Kashmir. It came under administrative control first of Persia and later of the Moghuls.
summary: Beginning with the Vedic era, the Kśatriyas of Kashmir ruled over the kingdom for a long period, with the exception of one or two Pathan and Moghul invasions.
Kumarayańa and Kumarjiiva spread that fame to the eastern end of China.
It came under administrative control first of Persia and later of the Moghuls.

paragraphs.text: The state of Kashmiir has now reached such a stage that its own Sáradá script, the script in which the Vedas were first written, is now being used only in writing the horoscope of the newly born among Kashmiir Brahmans. It is also the medium in which Sanskrit studies are being pursued in the chatuśpát́hiis [schools for teaching Sanskrit, especially the four Vedas]. In practical life, Sáradá script has been displaced by Persian script. At present, whatever little study and teaching are undertaken in Kashmiirʼs own language are being done in Persian script – not in its own Sáradá script.
summary: The state of Kashmiir has now reached such a stage that its own Sáradá script, the script in which the Vedas were first written, is now being used only in writing the horoscope of the newly born among Kashmiir Brahmans.
In practical life, Sáradá script has been displaced by Persian script.
At present, whatever little study and teaching are undertaken in Kashmiirʼs own language are being done in Persian script – not in its own Sáradá script.

paragraphs.text: Another meaning of the word kháshmarii is the plant whose original habitat is Kashmiir or which grows mainly in Kashmiir. The Sanskrit name of this plant is káshmiir, káshmarii or kháshmarii, which in Bengali we call jáffráń [saffron]. It is essentially a Persian word. [As told earlier], this word jáffráń is distortedly pronounced ‘saffron’ in English. Just as from ‘Káshmiir’ has come the Hindi word keshriyá, that which we call gaerik patáká or geruá patáká (saffron flag) in Bengali is called keshriyá jháńd́á in Hindi. ( 3 )
summary: Another meaning of the word kháshmarii is the plant whose original habitat is Kashmiir or which grows mainly in Kashmiir.

paragraphs.text: Bengal

Gań + al + ṋiiś = Gańd́álii. Both li and lii can be used in the spellings of the word. The suffix al is used to indicate an extended portion or extension, just as by adding al to the word bauṋga we obtain the word Bauṋgál, which means extended Bengal or expanded Bengal, Great Bengal. Vauṋga means a particular part of East Bengal. If Vauṋga is spelled in Sanskrit with the consonant ba, it would mean tin. In spelling ‘Vauṋga,’ meaning a specific part of Bengal, both consonantal ba and antahastha va can be used. That part of Bengal which we now consider to comprise parts of Dhaka, Mymensingh, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts was once called ‘Vauṋga’ or D́abák. Ráŕh, Samatat́, Cat́t́al or Upabauṋga, or according to a different view, Ráŕh, Samatat́, Barendra, Vauṋga and Mithila – these five constituted Paiṋca Gaod́ or Greater Bengal. Amongst them, ‘Vauṋga’ (that is, parts of Dhaka, Mymansingh, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts) was once renowned throughout the world for its knowledge, genius, wisdom, sacrifice and tolerance. By Paiṋca Gaoŕ people were more inclined to mean this Vauṋga. Hence, to indicate the entire Bengal or Paiṋca Gaoŕ, the word bauṋgál = bauṋga + al came to be used. Bengal was called Bauṋgál in Persian, Bauṋgálá in Turkish, Báiṋjál in Latin, Báiṋjálá in Chinese, Baḿlá and Báuṋglá in Bengali, Bengal in English, Bauṋgál in Urdu, and Bauṋgadesh, Gaoŕdesh or Paiṋca Gaoŕ and Bauṋgál in Sanskrit. ‘Bauṋgál’ did not mean only the diminutive Vauṋga but also the entire Bauṋgálistán. In Sanskrit and old Bengali, the word ‘Bauṋgál’ was widely prevalent, and finally it came to be used in unchanged form in Persian in the Pathan and Moghul royal courts – sometimes as Sube Bauṋgál [Bengal province].
summary: Gań + al + ṋiiś = Gańd́álii.

The plants that originally grew in India are known as plants of the indica group. Those plants whose origin is Bengal are known as belonging to the Byaiṋjalitis group. ( 4 )

paragraphs.text: The cultural specialties of Ráŕh are endless. Ráŕh sparkles in the lustre of her own characteristic features. Yet the attributes of East Bengal are the true Bengali characteristics. So when some people say that to see the real Bengal, to know the true look of Bengal, one must come in touch with the greenery of East Bengal, one must see Sylhet, Mymensingh, Dhaka and Chándpur, washed by the rivers Padma, Brahmaputra, Meghna and Kirtináshá, they are not incorrect. You must have noticed that even today, due to an abundance of Bengali traits, the people of East Bengal, even today, are jokingly called Báuṋgáls by the people of West Bengal. It is not so much a matter of fun or jest. Far more importantly, it conveys the truth of history. In a deeper sense, it is the expression of respect by the Bengalis of Ráŕh for the people of East Bengal. ( 5 )

paragraphs.text: Mahishur/Mysore

In present-day Sanskrit, the word viśaya, indicating a country, is hardly in use. However, in ancient and medieval Sanskrit, it was extensively used. The mythological name of Karnataka was Mahiśviśaya. According to legend, the battle between Cámuńd́á and Mahiśásur was fought on the Cámuńd́ii hills close to Mysore town. Hence, the country was called Mahiśaviśaya. In old Dravidian language, desh or viśaya was called úruś. Later, the words úruś/úr were used to denote the sense of locality: Bauṋgal + uru = Bauṋgaluru. It is incorrectly called Bangalore in English. Mauṋgal + uru = Mangaluru is likewise incorrectly called Mangalore in English. In some places in Kerala and South India, it is called Mangalapuram.
summary: In present-day Sanskrit, the word viśaya, indicating a country, is hardly in use.
In old Dravidian language, desh or viśaya was called úruś.
In some places in Kerala and South India, it is called Mangalapuram.

paragraphs.text: To conclude, let me say that in the sense of Mahiśaviśaya, Mahiśa + ur > Mahiśuru > Mahiśur is wrongly called Mysore in English. ( 6 )

chapters.title: Histories of Garwal-Kumaun, Kinnar, Traelanga, Vidarbha, Konkan, Kanauj.
chapters.partTitle: PART 6: Histories of Different Old Principalities

paragraphs.text: Udayan, Garwal, Kumaun
summary: Udayan, Garwal, Kumaun

paragraphs.text: The kingdom of Udayan (Uttarakhand): Two thousand five hundred years ago, the region that we now call Garhwal and Kumaun – this very area – was known as the kingdom of Udayan. Prince Padmasambhava first preached Buddhism in Tibet (then known as Kimpuruśavarśa). Befre that Bonpás religion (a local religion) was prevalent in Tibet. Tibetan King Sangat Sun Gumpo was initiated into Buddhism. Sangat Sun Gumpo had two wives. One was Denzing, a Chinese princess, and the other was Trikut́ii, the daughter of Aḿshuvarmańa, king of Nepal. Due to the efforts of these two wives of the Tibetan king, Buddhism spread throughout Nepal and China.
summary: The kingdom of Udayan (Uttarakhand): Two thousand five hundred years ago, the region that we now call Garhwal and Kumaun – this very area – was known as the kingdom of Udayan.
Tibetan King Sangat Sun Gumpo was initiated into Buddhism.
Due to the efforts of these two wives of the Tibetan king, Buddhism spread throughout Nepal and China.

paragraphs.text: The geographical configuration, water resources and forest resources of Udayan are much like those of Nepal. The developmental plans for this area should preferably emulate those of Switzerland. The same also holds true for Nepal. Udayan is part of present Uttar Pradesh [now a separate state of Uttarakhand.] While some people there belong to the Indo-Aryan community, other people, small in number, belong to the Indo-Tibetan community. There is excellent religious harmony amongst the inhabitants. The people of Udayan are now rapidly progressing in the spheres of education and culture. However if a drive for developmental activities is undertaken with proper planning, the speed of progress would be still greater. There are sixteen categories of Brahmans here. Of these, twelve are Bengali and four are Maharastrian Brahmins. Those belonging to the Bengali group migrated from West Bengal, especially from Burdwan district, during the Pathan and Moghul regimes, and particularly during the time of Aurangzeb. ( 1 )
summary: The geographical configuration, water resources and forest resources of Udayan are much like those of Nepal.
There is excellent religious harmony amongst the inhabitants.
Those belonging to the Bengali group migrated from West Bengal, especially from Burdwan district, during the Pathan and Moghul regimes, and particularly during the time of Aurangzeb.

paragraphs.text: Kinnar (Himachal Pradesh)
summary: Kinnar (Himachal Pradesh)

paragraphs.text: In very ancient times, Kinnar was an autonomous state. Later it turned into a native state [of British India.] Today it is a district of India. The people of [Kinnar] also belong to the Indo-Tibetan community. Their language belongs to the Tibetan family, with the alphabet being Indo-Aryan; that is a, á, ra, ka, kha – somewhat like the alphabet of Ladakh. The script is known as t́yáḿrá/t́egrá/t́egrii . In ancient India, the people of Kinnar were considered exquisitely beautiful. Hence if one happened to come across a strikingly handsome man, he used to be referred to as beautiful as the people of Kinnar. There is some Buddhist literature in the language of Kinnar. However, there is not much development with regard to modern [forms] of literature. ( 2 )
summary: In very ancient times, Kinnar was an autonomous state.
The script is known as t́yáḿrá/t́egrá/t́egrii .
However, there is not much development with regard to modern [forms] of literature.

paragraphs.text: Kiḿ + nr + ac = kiḿnar/kinnar. In the etymological sense, it means, “Is he really a man?” In the colloquial sense, it indicates “a group of people living on the Indo-Tibetan border.” Since these people were very good-looking, questions would haunt peopleʼs minds, “Are they men or gods”? The word kiḿnar/kinnar has emerged in this fashion. At present, Kinnar is a district of Himachal Pradesh, a region where the Himalayas reach a towering height. Most of the mountains are snow-clad.
summary: Kiḿ + nr + ac = kiḿnar/kinnar.
” Since these people were very good-looking, questions would haunt peopleʼs minds, “Are they men or gods”?
Most of the mountains are snow-clad.

paragraphs.text: People of the region are simple by nature. In terms of religious practices, they were Maháyánii Buddhists (of the Lama sect). Today, one can discern in them the influence of the Puranic religion. Even some time back, the practice of polygamy was prevalent among the women: however, it is now practically a defunct practice ( 3 )
summary: People of the region are simple by nature.
In terms of religious practices, they were Maháyánii Buddhists (of the Lama sect).
Today, one can discern in them the influence of the Puranic religion.

paragraphs.text: Though there is some impact of Mongoloid features on the appearance of the people there, they are quite good-looking. Hence they were called Kinnars and the region was called Kinnardesh. You all know that the ancient name of Tibet was Kimpuruśavarśa. One meaning of the word Varśa is “country”. For example, BhárataVarśa. The people of Tibet have scant hair. So, at times, there is difficulty in distinguishing the men from the women; the same difficulty is found to some extent in the case of the Bhutias. So, in ancient times people would wonder about the Tibetan men and ask themselves, “Are they males?” For this reason the country was venerably or fondly called Kimpuruśavarśa...
summary: Though there is some impact of Mongoloid features on the appearance of the people there, they are quite good-looking.
For example, BhárataVarśa.
” For this reason the country was venerably or fondly called Kimpuruśavarśa...

paragraphs.text: In any case, the word devayonii means an entity in whom certain divine qualities are manifested, that is, these are positive micŕovita. Suppose certain spiritual practitioners are good human beings, but have an innate attachment to worldly objects and are drawn to whatever they see; for example, money, jewelry, etc. Or, let us say we have a person who is a good sádhaka and is also is a good human being, but they beg Parama Puruśa for external beauty without desiring Him. They are meditating on Parama Puruśa, so they are human beings of a higher stature, but are seeking something ordinary from Parama Puruśa. After death, such persons will become devayonii [a being with ethereal, aerial, and luminous factors only] called kinnar. A kinnar is a devayoni, so it does not harm anyone. It does not have that disposition. People of ancient times used to seek the help of kinnars to become more beautiful. At one time, the pursuit of beauty or the art of cosmetics was called kinnar vidyá. “The person is extremely good-looking, like a kinnar”! In olden days, a beautiful dancing maiden was honoured with the epithet kinnarii. So you understand, this faculty is the positive microvitum related to the psychology of cosmetic art. Whatever theories exist regarding beauty enhancement, whatever skills exist for beautification, whatever art exists for aesthetic taste – all come under kinnar vidyá. ( 4 )
summary: In any case, the word devayonii means an entity in whom certain divine qualities are manifested, that is, these are positive micŕovita.
It does not have that disposition.
Whatever theories exist regarding beauty enhancement, whatever skills exist for beautification, whatever art exists for aesthetic taste – all come under kinnar vidyá.

paragraphs.text: Traelauṋga (Andhra Pradesh)
summary: Traelauṋga (Andhra Pradesh)

paragraphs.text: By adding the suffixes ań and byáiṋ to the word triliuṋga the words traelauṋga and traelauṋgya respectively are derived. In a particular locality in the northern part of South India, three special phallic images of Shiva were honoured with reverence. For this reason, the locality was named Traelauṋga or Traelauṋga Bhúmi. The language of this area is Telugu. In the prevalent spoken language, this land is called Telengana. The original name of the place in the southern part of Chandanagar, known as Telenipáŕá, was Teleuṋgiipárá. Since in those days workers coming from Telengana settled there, it was called Teleuṋgiipárá. The present name of Teleuṋgiipárá is Telenipáŕá. ( 5 )
summary: By adding the suffixes ań and byáiṋ to the word triliuṋga the words traelauṋga and traelauṋgya respectively are derived.
In the prevalent spoken language, this land is called Telengana.
The present name of Teleuṋgiipárá is Telenipáŕá.

paragraphs.text: Vidarbha/Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii (Maharastra)
summary: Vidarbha/Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii (Maharastra)

paragraphs.text: Vi-drbh + ghaiṋ gives us the word Vidarbha. Vidarbha + an gives vaedarbha. Vidarbha means that which cannot be conceived of or that which cannot be conquered. Vaedarbha means anything related to Vidarbha. Etymologically, Vidarbha indicates the eastern part of present-day Maharashtra; that is, the Nagpur-Akola region. In the prevailing language, Vidarbha is called Baráŕ (in English, Berar). In the Moghul era, Baráŕ belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad state. (The pronunciation of the word Nizam in English is [Naizam], not Nizam. However, in Persian and Arabic, the word is Nizam. The full word is Nizam-ul-mulk.) Later, the British occupied it and, to please the regal Nizam, they offered to address the prince of Hyderabad as the Prince of Berar, just as the prince of England is venerably called the Prince of Wales. Finding his own son compared with the prince of England, the Nizam was highly pleased.
summary: Vi-drbh + ghaiṋ gives us the word Vidarbha.
In the Moghul era, Baráŕ belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad state.
Finding his own son compared with the prince of England, the Nizam was highly pleased.

paragraphs.text: Baráŕii is one of the few living daughters of the Maharashtra Prákrit language. Like Marathi, Baráŕii has its own script, Moŕii. However, at present books in Marathi are printed in Devanagarii script. As a result, like people in other parts of Maharashtra, the people of Berar are close to forgetting their own Moŕii alphabet.
summary: Baráŕii is one of the few living daughters of the Maharashtra Prákrit language.
However, at present books in Marathi are printed in Devanagarii script.
As a result, like people in other parts of Maharashtra, the people of Berar are close to forgetting their own Moŕii alphabet.

paragraphs.text: The word Vidarbha has slightly more historical significance. Many of you might have heard the Puranic story of Nala and Damayanti. Nala was the king of this very Vidarbha. Even in the Vedic age, Vidarbha had some importance. The reason is that the name of Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii, the son of the soil of Vidarbha, is remembered along with those amongst the proponents of the Atharvaveda. These include the sages Atharva, Angira, Angiras and Satyavaha. As the great sage Atharva was the earliest of the sages of Atharvaveda, the word Atharva is used to indicate a very old person – “The man has become decrepit (Atharva)”. In this context, it must be mentioned that this Veda was named Atharvaveda after its chief proponent Atharva. For the sake of variation in reading, both the words Atharva and Atharvá can be used. ( 6 )
summary: The word Vidarbha has slightly more historical significance.
The reason is that the name of Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii, the son of the soil of Vidarbha, is remembered along with those amongst the proponents of the Atharvaveda.
For the sake of variation in reading, both the words Atharva and Atharvá can be used.

paragraphs.text: Koḿkań/Kouṋkań (Maharastra)
summary: Koḿkań/Kouṋkań (Maharastra)

paragraphs.text: The meaning of the root ku is “to create sound”, “to create high sound”, “ʼto cry loudly”. By adding the suffix ghaiṋ to the root ku, we obtain the word ko, which means “intense sound”. From kań + kac we derive the word kań, meaning “soft and sweet sound”. Kṋo + kań + ac = kouṋkań. In the etymological sense, it means a place where both sweet and strong sounds can be heard. Colloquially it stands for the northern part of the western coast of India. In the Indian sub-continent, there are, in total, six coasts. The coast of Kuch runs from the Indus valley to the Saurashtra. From Saurashtra to Gomantapurii (Goa) is the coast of Koḿkań or the Kouṋkań beach, while the Malabar Coast extends from Gomantapurii to Kannyakumarii. From Kannyakumarii to the valley of Godavari is the Coramandal coast and the Kaliuṋga coast extends from the Godavari valley to the mouth of Suvarnarekha. From the mouth of the Suvarnarekha to the river Naaf is the coast of Bengal. In this land of Kouṋkań, there are the western Ghats or Sahyadri mountains. Alongside them, across a stretch of land, is the Arabian Sea. Mingled with the vigorous roaring of the sea are the gentle murmurings of extensive forestlands. It is from these twin sounds kṋo and kań that the land came to be named Kouṋkań.
summary: The meaning of the root ku is “to create sound”, “to create high sound”, “ʼto cry loudly”.
The coast of Kuch runs from the Indus valley to the Saurashtra.
It is from these twin sounds kṋo and kań that the land came to be named Kouṋkań.

paragraphs.text: The language of Kouṋkań is derived from Maharastra Prákrit. Earlier, this language was called the Marathi version of Kouṋkań. Now the language of Kouṋkań is regarded as an independent language, and is prevalent from the south of Mumbai to Gomantapurii. The Chitpávan Brahmans of Maharashtra are slightly different from the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans of Kouṋkań. The Sárasvat Brahmans of India live in two different regions. Those living in Kashmir, Jammu and Punjab are known as north Sárasvat Brahmans or Káshimir Sárasvat Brahmans. Dogri and Punjabi Brahmans belong primarily to this group. The Brahmans of Kouṋkań are known as Gaoŕ Sárasvats. They are called thus because their ancestors came by land from Gaoŕ and settled there. Like the people of Bengal, they are also non-vegetarians. Hence, they do not care much for the vegetarian Brahmans in the rest of India. The customs and manners, practices and bearing of the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans are found to closely resemble those of the people of Bengal. They also have titles such as ‘Pái’ and 'Senoy.ʼ ( 7 )
summary: The language of Kouṋkań is derived from Maharastra Prákrit.
Dogri and Punjabi Brahmans belong primarily to this group.
They also have titles such as ‘Pái’ and 'Senoy.

paragraphs.text: The coast which resounds with this sound is called the Kouṋkań coast. Please do not identify Kouṋkań with kauṋkań. Kauṋkań is a type of bangle. Since very ancient times, women in most countries of the world have used these bangles. The earliest Sanskrit derivative form of kauṋkań was kań kań. It transformed into kaḿkań and with further metamorphosis became káḿgań. In North India, the word káṋgan is also prevalent. Once the word khágan was used in Bengali. In twelve hundred year old Bengali, it is said:
summary: The coast which resounds with this sound is called the Kouṋkań coast.
The earliest Sanskrit derivative form of kauṋkań was kań kań.
Once the word khágan was used in Bengali.

paragraphs.text: Háther káḿgań má leo dápań,
summary: Háther káḿgań má leo dápań,

paragraphs.text: Áppane appá bujhata nia man.
summary: Áppane appá bujhata nia man.

paragraphs.text: That is, to see the bangle you wear on your hand, do you require a mirror? So, to know what is the nature of your own mind, what is the need to ask someone else? You can yourself know your own mind through meditation. The meaning of the word kouṋkań is the Arabian Sea gale carried to the Sahyadris.
summary: That is, to see the bangle you wear on your hand, do you require a mirror?
You can yourself know your own mind through meditation.
The meaning of the word kouṋkań is the Arabian Sea gale carried to the Sahyadris.

paragraphs.text: People love to identify various sounds with others that are familiar. On an earlier occasion, you will remember I had told you about the movement of a train. When the driver blows the whistle indicating the train is starting, and it just begins to move, you hear its sound, and perhaps [you] think it is saying – gelum go-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o [Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving]. As the train accelerates somewhat, you seem to hear it making the sound – jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo [I am moving I must move, I am moving, I must move, I am moving I must move]. Then, as the train moves still more vigorously, you seem to hear the sound – jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo [I can take as much you can give, I can take as much as you can give, I can take as much you can give]. When the train accelerates still further, it appears to make the sound – káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul [“Raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind ripe tamarind”]. Then as the train moves closer to the next station, it suddenly decelerates and you seem to hear the train saying – esse gechi, esse gechi, esse gechi [I am home, I am home, I am home].
summary: People love to identify various sounds with others that are familiar.
As the train accelerates somewhat, you seem to hear it making the sound – jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo [I am moving I must move, I am moving, I must move, I am moving I must move].
Then as the train moves closer to the next station, it suddenly decelerates and you seem to hear the train saying – esse gechi, esse gechi, esse gechi [I am home, I am home, I am home].

paragraphs.text: Was the train really making all those sounds! No, not at all. You seemed to enjoy identifying those sounds with those the train was making. In any case, you must have now understood what the word kouṋkań means.
summary: Was the train really making all those sounds!
You seemed to enjoy identifying those sounds with those the train was making.
In any case, you must have now understood what the word kouṋkań means.

paragraphs.text: The spoken language of Kouṋkań is Kouṋkańii. This language is derived from the Maharastra Prákrta. Once it was considered a dialect of Marathi. Kouṋkańii has no alphabet of its own, and presently, in the area of Kouṋkań adjacent to Maharastra, it is written in Devanágariii letters. In Goa, it is written in Roman letters, and in Kouṋkańii-speaking areas of Karnataka, in Kannad́a script. To write a language in three different scripts is not convenient. From the days of the Portuguese, Kouṋkańii has come to be written in Roman script. Even its literary works have been composed in Roman script. However, only the people of Kouṋkań will decide in what script Kouṋkańii should be written – Kannad́a, Roman or Devanagáriii.
summary: The spoken language of Kouṋkań is Kouṋkańii.
In Goa, it is written in Roman letters, and in Kouṋkańii-speaking areas of Karnataka, in Kannad́a script.
However, only the people of Kouṋkań will decide in what script Kouṋkańii should be written – Kannad́a, Roman or Devanagáriii.

paragraphs.text: Prior to Post-Buddha period the Brahmans of Kouṋkań went there from Bengal by land.
summary: Prior to Post-Buddha period the Brahmans of Kouṋkań went there from Bengal by land.

paragraphs.text: Presently they are known as Gaoŕa Sárasvat and their surnames are Pai, Senoy, etc. Maharastra Brahmans are vegetarian whereas Kouṋkań Brahmans are used to eating fish. ( 8 )
summary: Presently they are known as Gaoŕa Sárasvat and their surnames are Pai, Senoy, etc.
Maharastra Brahmans are vegetarian whereas Kouṋkań Brahmans are used to eating fish.

paragraphs.text: Kányakubja – Kanauj (Uttar Pradesh)
summary: Kányakubja – Kanauj (Uttar Pradesh)

paragraphs.text: When there are calcium deposits in the joints of bones that compose the spine, they become stiff. The pliability of a childʼs spine is not to be found in that of grown-ups. If one works continuously for a long time stooping low, the upper part of the waist bones becomes slightly dislocated from those of the lower part. This increases the stiffness of the waist. Then one cannot stand erect; one tends to stoop or bend. The stiff part of the waist is perceived as burdensome. In Bengali, we call this weight of the waist kubjabhár or kujbhár or kuj [hump]. Manthara, the maidservant, whom the second queen Kaekeyii of king Dasharath brought from her parentʼs house, had a hump, as narrated in the Rámáyańa. So in the Bengali Rámáyańa, she had another name, Kṋujii. The story goes that the Aryans, after crossing Saptasindhu (Punjab), Haritdhánya (Haryana) and Brahmávarta (Brahmarśidesh or Doab,) advanced further to the east, that is, almost to the central region of the present Uttar Pradesh. They were not very familiar with the area. Seeing the Aryan warriors, the local people went into hiding; hence the Aryans had little opportunity to ask anyone for the name of that region. Along the way they happened to spot a woman with a hump. Since she had a hump, she could not run away quickly. The Aryan soldiers sought her help. They asked her, “Oh mother, what is the name of this land of yours?” Failing to understand them, she kept silent. Since they came across a woman with a hump in this land, the country came to be known as Kányakubja.From this [incident] we have derived the name of the historically renowned land of Kányakubja or Kanauj. Now Kanauj is a Tehsil [revenue district]. The Brahmans of Kányakubja are descended from a branch of the Paiṋcagouŕii Brahman community of northern India.
summary: When there are calcium deposits in the joints of bones that compose the spine, they become stiff.
They were not very familiar with the area.
The Brahmans of Kányakubja are descended from a branch of the Paiṋcagouŕii Brahman community of northern India.

paragraphs.text: If those who have to work for a long time by bending low from the waist regularly practice the Naokásana [boat posture], Pashchimottánásana [back-upwards posture] and Shalabhásana [locust posture], they will be least likely to develop a hump.
summary: If those who have to work for a long time by bending low from the waist regularly practice the Naokásana [boat posture], Pashchimottánásana [back-upwards posture] and Shalabhásana [locust posture], they will be least likely to develop a hump.

paragraphs.text: When a person has a bent waist, the raised part of the fallen waist is called kṋuj. In Bengali, the adjective of this word in masculine and neuter gender is kṋujo. We call the water pot, which somewhat looks like a hump, also kṋujo (the word suráhii is of foreign origin). The feminine gender of the word kṋujo is kṋujii. In chaste Bengali, it is kubja. The woman with a hump may be called kroŕii in standard Bengali or Sanskrit.
summary: When a person has a bent waist, the raised part of the fallen waist is called kṋuj.
The feminine gender of the word kṋujo is kṋujii.
The woman with a hump may be called kroŕii in standard Bengali or Sanskrit.

paragraphs.text: Next to Asansol of Ráŕh, there is a village inhabited by the Brahmans of Kányakubja. Its name is Kanyápur. This name too has come from Kányakubja. During the reign of King Gádhi, this was the capital of Kanauj. At that time the name of the town was Gadhipur. ( 9 )
summary: Next to Asansol of Ráŕh, there is a village inhabited by the Brahmans of Kányakubja.
This name too has come from Kányakubja.
At that time the name of the town was Gadhipur.
