points.body: When the people of Bengal, especially of Ráŕh, came into the realm of [recorded] history, they were devotees of Lord Shiva. This definitely occurred after the emergence of Sadáshiva – significantly less than seven thousand five hundred years ago. From this very period, it can be reasonably surmised that the people of Western Ráŕh were known as Máhátos. Today certain people claim that the Máhátos are descendants of Shivajii, since they introduced the system of agriculture in Western Ráŕh with the help of bullocks and ploughs. Others used to address them reverentially as Mahátman, which later turned into Máhátos. The Máháto civilization is at least seven thousand years old. They are the sons of the soil of Western Ráŕh. However, the emergence of Shivajii [1627] took place towards the end of the Mughal period. So by what logic could they be the descendants of Shivajii, who appeared only a few hundred years ago? How could more than fifty lakh [5,000,000] Máhátos be the descendants of Shivaji, who emerged only a few hundred years ago? The idea is antithetical to history and illogical. In reality, Máhátos are [among] the original Bengalis, such as Siḿmuŕá, Kháuṋgármuŕá, Kheriámuŕá, Ho-muŕá and Kushmet́muŕá of Western Ráŕh. They never originated from outside Bengal. Rather, the intellectual and wealthy people originated from within their own ranks. Attempting to pass themselves off as a distinct and separate race, they have turned themselves into so-called upper-caste Bengalis. Hence I have designated Máhátos as the ját báuṋgálii [original Bengalees], meaning that most communities of western Ráŕh have descended from this community.

points.body: This description is applicable not only to the Máhátos of western Ráŕh. Even the Kaevarta-Máhiśya of southern Ráŕh, Gope-Sadgopes of Central-North Ráŕh, Ráj-Baḿshii of North Bengal, Kot́ál-Namashúdras of Central Bengal and Cákmás (shákyamás) of Eastern Bengal are from this original Bengali community [Máhátos, Siḿmuŕa, etc.]. They did not originate from outside Bengal. Rather, they are the actual foundation of Bengali civilization and its upholder, its vehicle and nurturer. It is true that the so-called upper-castes have enhanced the glamour of Bengali society, but they are not its primary foundation. Since these original Bengalis have been neglected for so long (the pure Bengali equivalent for ‘so long’ is etadin, but we pronounce it ayáddin, according to the local Kolkata dialect of Bengali), the all-round development of Bengalis who followed Shaeva Dharma was not possible.

points.body: After a long period of time, that is, about two thousand five hundred years ago, Vardhaman Mahaviir, founder of the Jain religion, came to Astinagar with the goal of giving instruction on dharma. Earlier known as Atthinagar, the town was given its current name Vardhamán [Burdwan], in honour of Varddhaman [Vardhaman is also correct] Mahaviir. It was the central hub of activities of Ráŕh in those days. It is there that he preached his religious ideas. From that time onwards, the people of Ráŕh embraced the Jain religion, but they did not forget their ancient Deity, Lord Shiva. The situation was very much like that of the green plating on a golden ring. The gold was Shaeva Dharma, and the plating was that of the Digambar Jain religion.

Yet prior to that in Ráŕh was Shaeva dharma or a blending of Shaeva dharma with Jainism. The symbol of Jain Shiva was the huge Shiva-liuṋga, known commonly as Jyotirliuṋga, and the gigantic Gaorii-pat́t́a, which is found in various ruins. The worship of these Shivas was not performed by Brahman priests of the new Hindu age but by native Bengalis known as láyá or Páńd́e-Brahmans. (They worked as priests amongst the tribals or so-called lower caste Hindus.) The priests of the D́om community still use the title of “Pandit” and the priests of the Sadgope community use “Deváḿshii” (deváḿshii > deáḿshii > deáshii) as their title. It may be that they use it even today. Traditionally, the stone idols of Lord Shiva, known as Jyotirliuṋga, have been found in Ráŕh in large numbers, especially in Western Ráŕh. Some time ago this Jain Shiva idol was found even in Burdwan, and is presently being worshipped as Vardhamáneshvar.

points.body: When the Puranic religion was sweeping across Bengal, Kúrma Shiva was transformed into Dharmaráj or Dharmat́hákura, and elsewhere into Buŕoshiva. The priests for these deities were primarily native Bengalis. Some of these priests who followed the Puranic religion used threads of copper. Close to Kolkata (in the Shálkiyá area) is Dharmatalla, where the god Dharmat́hákur is also found. Dharmatalla Street of Kolkata is named after this Buddhist Shiva or Dharmat́hákur (I have already mentioned earlier and I say it again that by changing its name, a desecration of history has been perpetrated. I am certain that before committing this act, the wrongdoers did not consult any historian.) From the above-mentioned facts ( 2 ), it can be understood that before the existence of Shushuniyá script in Ráŕh or Bengal there existed Shaeva Dharma, Digambar Jainism influenced by Shaivism and Maháyánii Buddhism. However, Maháyánii Buddhism was prevalent throughout Bengal. Hinayánii Buddhism or sthavirváda (Theraváda) existed only in Chittagong, where it still persists to some extent.

points.body: A good number of relics from the Jain period have been found recently in Bhulá-Pávanpur village of P. S. Patamda as well as in the adjoining Báiṋgurdá village of Kamalpur P. S. and Jáydá village of Chandil P.S. [in Singhbhum District – Ráŕh], to the southwest. Along with these relics, the Bengali script of that period has been found. That script must be seventeen hundred years old or more, because during that entire period Ráŕh witnessed the golden era of Jainism mingled with the Shaivite cult. The broken idols that can be found are all those of Digambar Jain gods. The script that has been discovered must be older than that of Shushuniyá script. It could even be older than the Shriiharśa script found in the seals of Harśavardhan. The script belongs to the family of Shriiharśa script, but it is far more ancient. It is probable that this script has evolved from Bráhmii script, or perhaps it has not; it might be the original eastern Indian script.

points.body: During the rule of Ashoka, Ráŕh was included in the Magadha Empire. Even after the demise of King Shasháuṋka, Ráŕh was part of the Tháneshvar (Harśavardhan) dynasty. It does not mean that the particular Shriiharśa script found in the seal of Harśavardhan, was also prevalent in the distant land of Ráŕh. Of course, it could be surmised that the script of Ráŕh, though similar to that of Shriiharśa script, is much older. Ashoka used Bráhmii script in his stone inscriptions, but no such stone inscription in Bráhmii script can be found in Ráŕh, and Ráŕh was under the rule of Ashoka. There was no dearth of hills, nor was there any scarcity of stone; in fact, many broken stone idols have been found. Then why did Ashoka not erect stone pillars bearing religious instructions in this region?

points.body: There are two strong possibilities. First, during the rule of Ashoka Ráŕh ceased to use Bráhmii script and introduced its own script and began using it. That is why Ashoka did not use Bráhmii script. The second possibility is that in Ráŕh, Buddhism was not as predominant as it was in Magadha during the rule of Ashoka or even later. At that time Jainism was the dominant influence in Ráŕh, and that is why no Buddhist edicts were inscribed on the rockwalls of Ráŕh. Consequently, the scripts found in the Bhulá-Pávanpur-Báiuṋgurdá-Jáydá areas were the relics of the Jain-cum-Shaeva golden age ruins. Based on these [considerations] one can conclude that Bengali script was at least seventeen hundred years old, if not more. After this discovery there is little doubt that Bengali script is not just eleven hundred years old. Rather, it is far older. It is the oldest among the [modern] Indian scripts. Since this discovery, the script called Shriiharśa script, which hitherto was considered the oldest Bengali script, is now proven to be more recent. Under these circumstances, it would not be possible to pretend that the Bengali script is Shriiharśa script, as Bengali script, though similar to Shriiharśa script, is in fact much older.

In other words, the Bengali language was written not in Shriiharśa script, but in the much older Dálmá script, which belongs to the Shriiharśa lineage.

So in place of varńamálá [alphabet], the compound word akśamálá is also used.

points.body: The word akśa has several meanings. The first letter of the alphabet is a and kśa is its last letter. Between a and kśa there are forty-eight other letters. The total number of letters is fifty. So akśa denotes the fifty letters of the [Sanskrit] alphabet. So in place of varńamálá [alphabet], the compound word akśamálá is also used. In the description of the goddess Bhadrakálii in the Atharvaveda, it has been said that Mahákálii or Bhadrakálii, the deity of time, holds these fifty letters. People of that era did not have any idea of scripts, but they had knowledge of letters or words. Disciples used to receive their mantra from the gurus by hearing them. In Sanskrit the ear is called shruti. Hence the Vedas learnt through the ears were called the shruti.

points.title: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write
summary: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write.
During such a cataclysm (pralaya), it was believed that Bhadrakálii would save the letters, even though philosophical and scientific logic might be against the idea of a final cataclysm.
By accepting Bhadrakálii as the symbol of welfare they gained peace of mind.
points.body: Indeed, the people of those days did not know how to write. So in place of fifty letters, they used to imagine fifty faces. They would ideate that the first letter of creation a was in the hand of Bhadrakálii. They believed that the remaining letters were in her garland, although there was no distinct entity called Mahákála. Hence, in philosophical analysis the entities Mahákála or Mahákálii can find no logical support. Time is created at every moment from the mental measurement of the motivity of action. Yet the people of those days believed that [one day] there would be a calamity that would destroy everything. In the absence of adequate knowledge of science, they imagined a final cataclysm – that one day everything would be annihilated – this is the kind of fear that was expressed. During such a cataclysm (pralaya), it was believed that Bhadrakálii would save the letters, even though philosophical and scientific logic might be against the idea of a final cataclysm. There can be no thermal death of the universe. Perhaps a particular entity may undergo thermal death, but even in that case, entities transformed into hard, solid matter due to internal clash and cohesion would fragment in a fierce explosion, as a result of which immense thermal energy would be released from the broken structures, the fragments. This would prevent the thermal death of the universe from taking place. In any case, we are relating what the people of those days believed. They believed that Bhadrakálii would save the sounds [of the alphabet] during such a cataclysm. Since they had no knowledge of letters, they used human heads to represent the letters. That is why the people finally conceived of the alphabet as a wreath of human heads. By accepting Bhadrakálii as the symbol of welfare they gained peace of mind.

points.title: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not writ…
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not writ…
summary: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not write them.
In the absence of script, people of those days retained the Vedas as shruti (learnt through hearing; one name for ear is shruti).
Surely had they known a script, they would have put [the Vedas] in writing.
points.body: In this connection it is worth mentioning that those who created the Vedas did not write them. By orally creating the rks or shlokas of the Vedas, they taught their disciples by singing them out loud. That is why they contained melody, rhythm, grammar, kalpa, and nirukta; however, nothing existed in writing. The six parts of Vedic learning, such as chanda [science of rhythm], kalpa [explanation of religious rites], nirukta [etymology], vyákarańa (grammar; there are differences of opinion on this), jyotiiś [astrology] and ayurveda (medicine; there are even differences of opinion here; some say not ayurveda but dhanurveda) were called vedáuṋga. Vedáuṋga was unwritten, since humans at that time had no knowledge of script. In the absence of script, people of those days retained the Vedas as shruti (learnt through hearing; one name for ear is shruti). When people later learnt about scripts, even then they did not want to put the Vedas into written form. By that time they had piled up such mountainous superstitions in their heads that they believed the Vedas were not meant to be written! They did not carefully analyze that their ancestors did not write the Vedas only because they had no knowledge of script. Surely had they known a script, they would have put [the Vedas] in writing. ( 1 )

points.body: You have certainly heard about the word iyuichi, which is from the ancient Mongol language. You are probably familiar with the word ‘mongol’. It is the ancient language of the [northern] part of China, that is, Mongolia. Mongolians are residents of primarily inner and outer Mongolia. In ancient times, the people of both regions spoke in Mongol language. At present [that original language] has split into several regional languages. Mongolian is a mixture of Aryan-Vedic and Chinese languages. From “Mongol” has come the word “Mughal,” and through verbal transformation this word has become “Mogul”. The muglái parat́há [a special kind of flat bread containing spicy ingredients and fried in ghee or butter] is a speciality of this very area. In medieval India, there were several invasions originating from this region. Babar [1526–1530] was born from this ancient Mongol race, as was also Tamerlane [1336–1405]. The land of the Mongols was also the fatherland of the Shakas [A.D. 78]. The early habitation of the Huńas ( 2 ) was in the southwestern corner of the Mongol lands. (Mihirkul [Mihirgul – 505 A.D.] descended from this Huń dynasty.) Kujula Kadphises or Kujul Kadphises (he is not recognized as a king but rather as a leader in history) was the leader (sardár) of the Kushan sub-branch of the Iyucii branch of the Shakas [Sakas]. His successor (according to some, his son, and according to others, his son-in-law) Vimá Kadphises, or Wima Kadphises, was also a Kushan leader recognized in history. King Kanishka [A.D. 120], who belonged to the Kushan dynasty [A.D. 48–220], became the lord of a vast area of northwestern India. It is worth noting that Kujula Kadphises and Vimá Kadphises are two names that occur in the early Mongol language, but the name Kanishka belongs to Sanskrit. This change of language in Kanishkaʼs name took place when he came to India and embraced Buddhism. The names of the successors of Kanishka [Kańiśka], such as Vashishka, Huvishka and Vasudeva, are genuine Sanskrit names.

points.body: Even today in northwestern India, Punjab and parts of Afghanistan, the daughterʼs son is called dohatar, which is derived from the Vedic word daohitrá. The Bengali word náti [grandson] is derived from the Vedic word naptá – the words nápit or nápte are derived from the same source. The word nápit [barber] is a pure Vedic word. The word naptá, meaning nápit, is also a Vedic word that stands for both náti and nápit. The true meaning of naptá is one who prevents downfall. A barber prevents the downfall of society through [personal] grooming; a grandson [according to Vedic belief] prevents downfall through offering of food to the manes. From this belief emerged the word napta. To a modern person it narrates a tale of ancient history.

points.body: Pra – br + al/ac = prabara, meaning the best leader or the most respectable person. In certain regions of ancient India, along with the system of gotra there was the system of prabara. For instance, let us take the case of someone whose gotra was bharadváj. It indicates that the forefather of that person lived on a hill on which Bharadváj was the leader. I have mentioned in an earlier book that in ancient society, when matriarchal society and matrilineal order were in vogue, people used to identify themselves through their mother – through the name of the mother, through her mother, and again through her motherʼs mother. Identity was not determined through the fatherʼs side. The meaning of the word mátá [mother] is one through whom a family earns social respect. However, later on, due to certain unique needs of the extant social order, the patriarchal system was introduced. Amongst those special needs of the social structure, the primary one was that in the matriarchal system the mother had full responsibility towards the child and the father had very little responsibility. However, in the patriarchal system the motherʼs responsibility remained almost the same, but it was supplemented by the responsibility of the father. It created an advantage in raising children. Although the motherʼs responsibility persisted, she also received the aid of her husband. In this system, the social structure became much more solid.

points.body: In any case, in the patrilineal system the gotra (clan) was determined by the name of the leader of the hill on which they lived. The meaning of the word gotra is “hill”. Now, a very large number of people used to take shelter on a big hill. Hence, under the leader of the gotra, there were also some local leaders. They received greater respect than anyone else. In fact they received the highest veneration, and from this evolved the word prabara. ( 4 )

points.body: In those days there was no Arabian Sea, no Bay of Bengal or its present islands, no Indonesia and no Australia. There was no North India, no Tibet and no Himalayas. There was only one contiguous land mass from what is now the eastern portion of Africa, including South India and Malaysia, up to Australia. This landmass – the oldest landmass in the world – consisted mainly of a long island in [the form of] an archipelago. What is now Canada and Argentina also existed at that time. The territory that covered what is presently the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, the Indonesian Archipelago, the Deccan Plateau, Southeast Asia and Oceania – has been named Gondwanaland by [geologists] because the Gond people of the Austric race lived in the central portion, although this portion was not the oldest part of the land. Even today the descendants of the Gond people still live in the [Chattisgarh region].

points.body: At least 30 million years ago, a plutonic earthquake occurred. The land that presently comprises the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea was submerged under the ocean and the present North India emerged. In the same earthquake, those parts which were previously hills became islands in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea after the earthquake. In this way a group of 503 oceanic islands, comprising Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines islands, was also formed. All of this, including the emergence of the Himalayas, took place about 30 million years ago. The Himalayas are therefore approximately 30 million years old, but Gondwanaland and Ráŕh are far far older.

points.body: After a long time this very terrain, this nameless, mountainous terrain, was given the name Ráŕh. The word ráŕh originated in the ancient Austric language and means a land of red (laterite) soil. In the world of those days there was no Áryyávartta; ( 5 ) there were no plains of Bengal or of the Deccan, nor were there the deserts of Rajasthan and Gujarat. The northern part of the Arabian Sea did not exist either; what existed was its southern part, which linked the Deccan peninsula with Africa, the Andamans, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia. They were linked by [land] that lay sometimes a little above the water level, sometimes a little below. ( 6 ) In that world, uninhabited by human beings, the Ráŕh of those days was older than any other land. The snow-covered mountains of Ráŕh gave birth to numerous rivers. Those rivers, fed by melting snow, flowed some to the east and some to the southeast, towards the ocean.

points.body: The Himalayas were born many crores [tens of millions] of years after the birth of Ráŕh. ( 8 ) From the Himalayas came forth a daughter, the River Gauṋgá [Ganges], and a son, the River Brahamaputra. ( 9 ) The sand and silt their waters bore formed new soil; northern India and Báḿlá [Bengal] were formed. ( 10 ) The seabed that was east of Ráŕh rose higher and higher thanks to that sand and silt, and – after the formation of eastern Ráŕh – long after – many lakhs of years after – formed a vast plain (samatal). That plain [to the east of eastern Ráŕh] is known as Samatat́a in Sanskrit and Bágŕi in Bengali. Farther to the east, the sand and silt borne by the rivers of Ráŕh mingled with the sand and silt of the Brahmaputra and formed Vauṋga ( 11 ) or D́abák. The people of western Ráŕh migrated to eastern Ráŕh and established residence. This occurred lakhs [hundreds of thousands] of years ago. If human beings appeared one million years ago, then the inhabitants of western Ráŕh of a million years ago found eastern Ráŕh to be in a ripe state for them even before their birth. Even a portion of northern India arose before the origin of human beings. Samatat́ and D́abák, however, originated a little after the appearance of humans on earth. The people of western and eastern Ráŕh removed the forest cover and dwelt in Samatat́-Vauṋga-D́abák.

points.body: Geologists surmise that at one time regions such as North India and the Himalayas did not exist. Along with South India, there was Africa on one side, and on the other side was a vast expanse of land, comprising the Andamans, Malaysia, Indonesia and Australia. This ancient land was named Gondwana after the ‘Gonds,’ who lived in the central region of this landmass. The people who lived in the western extremity of Gondwana were Negroid; those who lived in the Eastern extremity were Austric, and those who lived in the central part [of this landmass], meaning in the southern part of India, were Austrico-Negroid or of the Dravidian race. There is still a community of Gonds in Central India. The identity of the common people of the Gond community is to be found in the Dhuruva-gonds region. The place named Dhruwa near Ranchi can be mentioned in this connection. In this region, those belonging to the royal family were known as Rajgond. Later they gave up their old titles of Rajgond or Dhuruvagond and became assimilated with the Rajput and Thakur clans. ( 18 )

points.body: The part of Gondwanaland in which we are now is more or less divided into east and west by the Koyel river. The difference between east and west is not only evidenced in the terrain, but also in the flora and fauna. I would guess that the western mountains that we now call the Vindhya and Sátpurá mountains were once much higher. They had peaks higher than the Himalayas. Flora and fauna could not evolve there in the ancient past due to excessive snowfall, but the eastern mountains, although very high and snow-capped, were not as high as the western mountains. It is likely that the first appearance in the world of both flora and fauna was here, in this area where we find our ancient Ráŕh and Jharkhanda. In the west, the melted ice ran into the Arabian Sea. Although there was water, the soil was unfertile, so there was little flora and naturally little fauna as well. But in the east, where the water from the melted snows became rivers, the cold was not so severe. So the first expression of developed life was in the land of Ráŕh – this we can be certain of.

The small hills of Bankura District, especially the Shushuniyá Hills, are also an extension of this Ramgarh range. Fossils of various types of ancient animals have been found near these hills. Still, the greatest amount of fossils are lying in the areas closest to the Suvarńarehká, Kaḿsávatii, and Damodara rivers. It is quite clear that the brontosaurus and other dinosaurs lived in this region. Rhinoceroses also used to roam the extremely high grasses of this area. Please remember that the devas or suras were of Caucasian or Aryan race – white-complexioned, tall and sharp-nosed. Their hair was golden, blue or black and was usually not curly. Their nose was neither flat nor broad, and their jaws were not raised. They had hair on their body, and their bodily complexion was neither pale, nor yellow nor deep dark. They were known as devas, suras or Aryans. Those who lived in ancient times in Assyria in Central Asia were no less civilized than the Aryans. They were of medium build and tall (not short-statured). Their bodily complexion was blue-black (shyámal) and their hair was slightly curly. They were never snub-nosed. Though slightly broad, their jaws were not raised. They were simpler in nature than the Aryans. They were more inclined towards the matriarchal system than the patriarchal system and were less conceited than the Aryans regarding their racial origins. points.body: The Rgveda is very old. Moreover, it is certain that Krśńadvaepáyańa Vyása had divided the Vedas into three separate parts – the oldest portion, the middling portion, and the most recent portion – well before the Jain era. Here I use the words “well before the Jain era” because the Vedas are mentioned in the Jain scriptures, which were written in the Prákrta language. The propounder of the Jain religion, Varddhaman Mahaviir, was born a little over 2500 years ago, and the Prákrta language originated between four thousand and five thousand years ago. Thus, whatever portion of the Vedas is considered to be the most recent, it is certainly more than five thousand years old. And in regard to the Jain scriptures, certain portions of it were composed before the era of Varddhaman Mahaviir by various other Jain saints; still they are in no way more than five thousand years old. The time of the composition of the Rgveda was approximately between fifteen thousand years ago and ten thousand years ago, that of the Yajurveda between ten thousand years ago and seven thousand years ago, and that of the Atharvaveda between seven thousand years ago and five thousand years ago. The Sámaveda is not a Veda at all. The word sáma means “song”. The Sámaveda was made later on from the music portions of the three Vedas, that is, the Sámaveda is found within the Rgveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. The Vedas were first divided into the Rk, Yajuh, and Atharva – these three parts. However the Sámaveda is mentioned in the Jain scriptures, that is, the Vedas had already been divided into three parts at the time of the origin of the Jain scriptures, and the Sámaveda had already been created from the musical portions of the three Vedas. Just as the Vedas could not be written down due to lack of any written script, it may also be that the early Jain saints, however old they may have been, were not able to record their teachings through the medium of written script. Varddhaman Mahaviirʼs time was after the discovery of script, thus the Jain scriptures were written down and they were written in the Prákrta language of that time.

points.body: Although the Rgveda is mainly concerned with hymns, it also contains various tales and anecdotes. While not all of these stories and tales carry equal spiritual value, they are representative of the cultural heritage of those ancient human beings. They paint a portrait of the gradual advancement of human thinking and the structure of society. When considered from this point of view, the language, literature and expression of the Rgveda is of special value to the world. While it is true that there was no script during the Rgvedic age, phonemes and phonetic expression as well as the order of the sounds, interpolation and placement (the method of arranging the sounds) were in existence. The different Rgvedic styles of pronunciation for the various letters were in vogue, which the followers of the Rgveda would learn orally from the guru in subsequent times. I have talked about this to some extent here and there in our language books. If time permits I will discuss the subject further at a later date.

A number of rśis were revered as maharśi, some of whom deserve special mention. They were Maharśis Atri, Auṋgirá, Auṋgirasa, Pulaha, Pulasta, Satyaváha, Vashiśt́ha and Vaedarbhi. points.body: The verbal root tan means to expand – to extend. It is both subjective and objective. The verbal root bhr means to feed, to entertain, while the verbal root tan means to expand. The entity who feed and enhances growth in the physical, mental and spiritual spheres is called Bharata (bhr + ac = bhar, tan + d́a = ta). The country that nourishes its residents and helps in their all-round development is known as Bháratvarśa. In a colloquial sense it means three things. The word varśa means a country, for example, as in Bháratvarśa, Kimpuruśvarśa (Tibet) and Suvarńavarśa (Burma). The word khańd́a means “portion”. In ancient times, the learned ones divided the world into seven major portions. They are called saptadviipa [a land of seven islands, sapta meaning “seven” and dviipa meaning “island”] or sapta sandviipa [the word sandviipa also means island]. Certain parts of Asia and Southeast Asia constituted Jambudviipa. Certain varśas were denoted in each of these islands, and in each of these varśas were viśaya – called úraśa or úr in ancient Tamil. One portion of Jambudviipa was Bháratvarśa and Kimpuruśvarśa (Tibet). In Bháratvarśa there was Gaoraviśaya (Bengal), Auṋgaviśaya (Auṋga: the Bhagalpur-Purnea, etc. area), and Magadhaviśaya (Patna-Gaya, etc. area: Astimagadhaviśaya Pataliputtranámadheya nagarah), Mahiśaviśaya (the land of Karnataka; in old Tamil viśaya or varśa was called úr.) The Sanskrit name Mahishaviśya evolved into Mahiśa-úr > Mahiśúr > Myśore) in old Tamil. So you now understand Bháratavarśa or Bharatakhańd́a is a part of this Jambudviipa (Jambudvipae Bháratakhańd́e). ( 6 )

That part of the Gangetic valley is considered as the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. The Prayága area is considered as the upper part of the Ganges river civilization. The area stretching from Prayága to the confluence of the rivers Shone and Ganges is the middle part of the Ganges river civilization. And the area from the Shone-Ganges confluence to Sahebganj is considered as the Gaod́a part of the Ganges river civilization. The area from Sahebganj, where the Ganges starts flowing southward, to Gangasagar is known as the final part of the Ganges valley civilization or Gaod́iiya civilization. The Gaod́iiya civilization is most developed where the rivers of Ráŕh – carrying with them the local cultural specialities of Ráŕh civilization – and the Brahmaputra River, coming from the northeast and carrying with it the flow of Mongolian civilization, merge into the Ganges. points.body: Then, in the next phase, the Aryans reached Prayága around the Ganga-Yamuna valley. This we can describe as the third phase of the Vedic influence ( 1 ). Then they moved farther east, and their influence extended to the Gańd́akii River on the north and the Shone River on the south. This can be called the fourth phase of Vedic influence. The ancient Káshiirájya or Kingdom of Káshii was situated in this area. We are now journeying through the Káshiirájya. One thing to be noted here is that in the first phase, the Vedic language left two daughters behind: Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta. In the languages born from Páshcáttya and Paeshácii Prákrta (for example, Pashto and Punjabi) there is a multitude of words derived from the Vedic language. In the second phase, that is, in the Hariyánvii language, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is somewhat less. In the third stage, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less; for instance, in languages such as Máŕoyárii, Haŕaotii, Bundelii, Bághelii, Avadhii and Vrajabháśa. And in languages of the fourth stage, such as Bhojpurii, the percentage of Vedic-derived words is still less. But no one should misunderstand that in the fourth stage the Vedic influence was nil. No doubt direct Vedic influence in the fourth stage was nil, but the indirect influence in pre-Gaod́iiya and Gaod́iiya civilizations was tremendous, and that influence still persists even today.

points.body: Take, for example, the case of the river Thames: it is not a big river, neither in width nor in breadth. The part of the river Thames where the ships sail is not really a river, it is only an estuary of the sea, just like the Mátlá river near Canning. Many people think that the Mátlá is perhaps a wide and large river. They may think that in olden days the southern branch of the river Yamuna (Vidyádharii) emerging from the Ganges at Trivenii, moved southwards. Then, after flowing separately for some distance, the Yamuna and the southeastern tributary of the Ganges (Piyálii) joined together to form the Mátlá river. Though this is a fact, yet the collective waters of these two combined rivers is quite small. In fact, the Mátlá River is nothing but the estuary of the sea entering into the land.

points.body: In our land of Ráŕh, on either bank of the Bakreshvar river in central Birbhum, there is a local civilization which, though small in area, has its own uniqueness, even in the style of its temples and also in its terracotta work. There is also a difference in the use of verbal forms in the spoken language of that area. Similarly, in southern Birbhum also, there is a small river called the Kopái (Kupita or ‘angry’) in whose valleys there is also some sort of local civilization. As far as I remember, someone once said that the water of the Bakreshvar valley is one of the best, for it is full of sulphur. But the water of Kopái valley, though it is as good as that of many places in Bengal, is not as good as that of the Bakreshvar valley. The two small rivers, with their own distinctive streams of water, flow from west to east, carrying the rhythmic songs of the most ancient human civilization, in cadence with the dancing rhythms of the land of Ráŕh. When the two rivers meet at Melánpur (meaning ‘meeting place’) at one end of the area under the jurisdiction of the Nanur police station, they are known as Kuye, and at that point both their local civilizations become blended. Actually, Melánpur merges the two rivers in all respects. If one listens intently to the local dialect, one will hear a particular drawled intonation that is lacking in western Birbhum. Aside from this, other local variations also came into being.

points.body: [Now travelling] from the west to east across the border of the ancient Káshii state was the last area to come under Aryan influence. In the fourth phase of the Aryan invasion of India, Káshii can be regarded as a border state of northern India (Áryávartta). The River Sarayu not only carried the Aryan influence down its banks but also Mongol and to some extent Austric influence as well. That is why its eastern bank was considered as non-Aryan land. Later on, this boundary was further extended to the River Gańd́akii (Náráyańii Gańd́ak). The Kányakubja Brahmans of those days did not like to cross the River Sarayu. As the land on the other bank was non-Aryan it was considered unholy. They were afraid they would lose their Aryan purity. The Kányakubja Brahmans who dared to cross the river, being lured by the fertile land of the trans-Sarayu area, were declared outcastes. They lost their identity as Kányakubja Brahmans and became known as Sárayupárii Brahmans.

points.body: During Pathan rule, the last boundary of Áryávartta was the present Ghazipur District. In those days, northern India consisted of three Subás [administrative divisions]: Subá Bángál on the east, Subá Punjab on the northwest and Subá Hindostan between the two. Even today, the people of Bengal and the Punjab call the inhabitants of the central part of northern India “Hindustani”. Some people are of the opinion that Hindustan means the whole of India, and thus why should the inhabitants of a small part of India be called Hindustani. But this is wrong, because the term “Hindustani” is used for the people who were once the inhabitants of Subá Hindostan, and not in the sense of Hindustan as being the whole of India. During the Mughal period, when Akbar divided his empire into fifteen subás, the name of the northern part of Subá Hindostan was Oudh and the southern part was Subá Agra. Ghazipur District was the last boundary of Subá Agra. To the east of Ghazipur District lies Balia District. Previously it was only a subdivision of Ghazipur District. Similarly, there was no Deoria District in those days. It was only a subdivision of Gorakhpur District.

points.body: The British occupied both Agra and Oudh Subás and created one administrative area from both – the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh (UP for short), with its capital at Allahabad. In the last part of British rule, the capital was moved to Lucknow. In any case, there was a marked influence of Mongol and Austric cultures on Aryan society inhabiting the Sarayu river valley. Later on many Aryans crossed the Sarayu River and declared the banks of the Gańd́akii as the boundary line of Áryávartta. The area lying to the west of the Gańd́akii valley was called Shákyárańya, and the area to the east was called Videha or Mithilá. The latter area was not considered an Aryan colony. I personally consider it as part of the area covered by the pre-Gaod́iiya Gangetic valley civilization.

points.body: King Mithi occupied Videha. To sanctify the land he held a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa [a large sacrifice presided over by three priests]. It was then declared sacred. The land sanctified by the performance of a Trihotriiya Yajiṋa was named Trihut. The land of Shákyárańya, although not widely valued by Aryans, was respected by Buddhists. Lord Buddha visited it a couple of times. Later it became known as Shárańa (Shákyárańya > Shákyárańa > Shárańa). In later years it was wrongly spelt as Sháran.

points.title: To the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place called Champakárańya

points.body: To the north of Shákyárańya was the ancient and famous place called Champakárańya. Reference to it is made in the Rámáyańa [one of the two great Sanskrit epics] (Campakárańya > Campárańya > Camparań). Shákyárańya and Campakárańya are situated in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka valley. On the eastern bank is Videha, Mithilá or Trihut, the land occupied by King Mithi. Mithi + lá [holder] + d́a [suffix] + á [feminine suffix] = Mithilá. In the Buddhist period one of the famous villages of Shákyárańya was Hatthiigrám (Hastiigráma in Sanskrit). Buddha visited this place a couple of times. It is now known as Háthoyá. During British rule the Háthoyá estate was one of the largest estates in India. Then came the river Gańd́akii – Náráyańii Gańd́aka. The biggest cattle fair in India, known as the Hariharkśetra fair, is held once a year on the banks of this river. Nearby is the Shońpur railway station.

points.body: During the Mughal period and the early part of British rule, the Mithilá division of Bengal Presidency consisted of three districts: Trihut, Champaran and Shárańa. The district headquarters of Champaran was Motihari, that of Shárań was Chapra, and that of Trihut was Muzaffarpur. The latter district was named after Muzaffar Shah. It covered a wide area and until the early part of the British period its fertile soils were thickly forested. The forests contained an abundance of numerous species of flora and fauna, notably tigers, antelopes, crocodiles, panthers and deer. The lake on the ancient river course of the river Lakhandei covered a larger area in those days and was surrounded by extensive forests full of abundant flora and fauna. A major part of the forest was part of the estate of King Darbhanga. Some of it was in the Shúraśańd́a kingdom, and other parts belonged to the estate of the Bettiah king. People today, due to necessity but also out of immense greed, have destroyed most of the forest, particularly in Trihut District.

points.body: At Vaeshali ( 2 ) in Trihut District, Vardhamána Maháviira was born into a Vaeshya family. His fatherʼs name was Siddhártha and his mother was called Trishalá. Trihut District as well as Mithilá were located partly in the Náráyańii-Gańd́aka valley and partly in the Buŕigańd́aka and Lakhandei valleys. There was greater Gaod́iiya influence prevalent here than in Aŕyávartta. Bengali script is used there. It is to be noted that both Buddha and Maháviira were born in a place where there was comparatively less Aryan influence.

The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hazipur).

The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubanii (a place with an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga, named after the famous Dáŕibhángá Shah (in Maethilii the town is called “Daiŕbhángá” but spelt Daŕibhángá); and Samastipur, named after Samasti Náráyan Ray.
points.body: Trihut District was quite a large area. The British divided it into two parts: Muzaffarpur District in the west, with its headquarters at Muzaffarpur, and Darbhanga District in the east, with its headquarters at Laheriasarai village which has since become so large that it almost touches the city of Darbhanga. The old Muzaffarpur District is now divided into three districts: Sitamarhi, Muzaffarpur and Vaeshali (Hazipur). This is the same Muzaffarpur that once was considered one of the most cultured places in the whole of Subá Bángál. The old Darbhanga District has since also been divided into three districts: Madhubanii (a place with an abundance of forest honey); Darbhanga, named after the famous Dáŕibhángá Shah (in Maethilii the town is called “Daiŕbhángá” but spelt Daŕibhángá); and Samastipur, named after Samasti Náráyan Ray.

points.body: The Maethilii branch of the pre-Gaod́iiya valley civilization was enriched by the Mongol-Tantric civilization that flourished in the Náráyańii Ganges, Buri-Gańd́aka, Lakhandei, Bágmatii, Kamalábálán and Koshii valleys. King Prthvii Náráyan Shah established the Gorkha Empire in Nepal at this time. The Gorkhas occupied Tirhut District and advanced up to Hazipur. Thereafter they were defeated by the British and were forced to sign the Treaty of Sugaoli (Champaran District.) (The British commander-in-chief was General Octorloney in whose name the Englishmen living in Kolkata built a war memorial. In recent times, the [political] leaders, ignorant of history, have changed the name of the Octorloney Memorial to Shahiid Minar [Martyrsʼ Column].) According to the terms of the treaty, the British gained possession of Garhwal and Kumayun regions from Nepal, which was included in the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh, and they also reclaimed a major portion of Champaran and Trihut Districts. Part of the northern portion of Trihut remained in Nepal and is still part of Nepalese territory. The former capital of Mithilá, Janakpur, is situated in that area. Many people of Bengal know the famous Janakpur catechu [Areca catechu] ( 3 )

points.body: I have mentioned earlier that one meaning of the word khara is rákśasa. It seems that the Aryans of ancient times used to label people belonging to the Austric-Negroid group or Dravidian group as Rákśasas. Their own [Aryan] writings indicate that the Rákśasas had a developed civilization. They established large cities and towns, practiced dharma and were devotees of Lord Shiva. With the blessing of Shiva they came to possess enormous talents, power and wealth. Unwarranted comments have been made in a number of books so as to portray them in a poor light. points.body: The word khasátmaja (khas + átman + jan = d́a) means the son of Rákśasii, who may not necessarily be a Rákśasa. There are many stories about this in the Puranas. According to the Puranas, Rákśasii women give birth to gods and to intelligent men. One such story is about Sutanuka, the son of Karkat́ii Rákśasii, Karkat́ii Rákśasii discovered the medicinal cure for cancer. Her husband Anuvasen was a human being. Sutanuka was an ideal character; he was a generous, caring physician. Although he was the son of a Rákśasii, Sutanuka was not a Rákśasa; he was a Khasátmája. In the scriptures, the word átmaja means the first child (a son or daughter); other children are called kámaja, not átmaja. Earlier it was mentioned that Karkat́ii Rákśasii had discovered the cure for cancer. Unfortunately, that medicine has been lost to posterity. In order to diagnose diseases and find their cures, Karkat́ii Rákśasii used to dissect [and examine] corpses. Since people in those days were very undeveloped, they concluded that she was a cannibal in search of human flesh. It is said that ungrateful men burnt Karkat́ii Rákśasii to death and that both a curse – the disease bisuciká (cholera) – and a blessing – the medicine madhumeha (for diabetes) – emanated from the burning flames. Bisuciká is the Sanskrit name for cholera. In Bengali it is called oláot́há, in English cholera, and in Farsi hyáyajá. The cure for cholera has been lost; administering saline is not an actual remedy. Humanity will have to rediscover the medicine for cholera. It is beyond human understanding how worship of the goddess Oláicańd́ii (Olábibi) can alleviate this disease. ( 2 )

You know, the entire human race did not evolve at the same time in all parts of the world. Different human species with different skulls developed from tailless animals in various parts of the world. It is surmised that human beings first emerged from the western corner of Ráŕh and then from the central region of Gondwana. The first human species that appeared in Ráŕh, though belonging to the Austric race, had longer noses than those of the present-day Austric race. The first group of humans that originated from central Gondwana – Sumatra, Balidviip, Javadviip – were also Austrics, but their noses were slightly flat. It is difficult to say anything with certainty about their physical complexion. However, the land of Ráŕh was chiefly within the Karkatakranti [temperate] region. Hence it is believed that the physical complexion of these people of Ráŕh was dark blue or slightly dark. And since central Gondwana was situated in the equatorial region, the people of that area were comparatively dark-complexioned and slightly flat-nosed – but not entirely flat-nosed. It is surmised that later, people belonging to the Mongoloid group or Chinese race came there in great number in search of a livelihood, and due to the intermingling of these newcomers with the earlier Austric race, the Mongoloid-Malaysian branch of humanity was created.

points.body: There is a great amount of similarity between the skulls of the people of Ráŕh and those of the present-day Bengalis of Ráŕh. Though there is a blending of the blood of exotic Aryans or Caucasians therein, the Kayasthas of Ráŕh continue to bear a physical resemblance to their ancestors. As a result of Aryan genes, they are tall and have a brighter complexion. Nonetheless, the imprint of the ancient Ráŕhiian breed is clearly shown in their bodies. Other people of Ráŕh, especially original or native Bengalis, are bearers of that ancient skull. Amongst the Oráoṋs, due to the admixture of Negroid blood, substantial transformation has taken place in their skulls, akin to what happened among the Gońd́s and Satnámiis in Madhya Pradesh and among the Oriyás in Orissa However, in Ráŕh most of the native Bengalis – the Gopes, Sadgopes, Máhiiśyas and Kurmiis – have that ancient Ráŕhiian skull. The Brahmans, Kayasthas and Vaedyas of Ráŕh, no matter how much they consider themselves outsiders, are also the sons of the old land of Ráŕh.

points.body: Due to the blending of blood between Caucasians and Mongoloids, a definite change has come about in their physical complexion and features. Despite this, their appearance still indicates that they belong to Ráŕh. Using gold as an analogy, if the native Bengalis are pure gold, then the so-called upper caste people, especially the Kayasthas, are enameled gold. The Aryans who are known today as Caucasians originated from Switzerland. To escape from the snow in Switzerland, they turned eastwards to the Caucasus region to seek refuge in the first lap of their journey. The Negroid people made their first appearance in the central region of present-day Sahara. Due to earthquakes, the Sahara was elevated higher than sea-level; in its higher regions there was scarcity of water, though in the lower regions water was present – and could be brought up like fountains through artesian wells even today. The Sahara region appeared to lack water; hence, most of its inhabitants moved to the south. The remaining population migrated to the north and northeast. Through intermingling of this population with Caucasians, the Semitic population was born. Some of these Semitic people resemble Negroids and others Caucasians. Some have fair skin while others have brown skin; quite a number of them are curly-haired and an equally large number are straight-haired.

points.body: The second home of the Caucasian Aryans was Caucasus Ural and part of the Volga River Basin of the Volga River. As the land was full of pebbles and excessively cold, these Aryans were forced to remain idle for the major part of the year. They constantly worried about where their next meal would come from, and were compelled to hunt wild animals for food. In order to survive, they had to leave in search of new lands and new horizons. This time they moved southwards. The branch of Caucasian Aryans that moved westwards are the Europeans or Euro-Aryans of today. Those who traveled southwards became the Aryo-Iranians or Aryan-Persians. They settled for some time in Persia. Owing to their physical proximity to the Caucasian branch [of Aryans], the Aryo-Iranians retained most of their Caucasian looks and appearance. Though the lustre in their physical complexion disappeared, it did not turn blue-black or dark. Another group of Caucasian Aryans traveled to the east. They went to the basins of Gauṋgá and Yamuna, to the Brahmaputra and Brahmariidesh via Gándhára [Afghanistan], Kashmir, Saptasindhu (Punjab) and Haritadhánya (Haryana). They continued moving eastward and left their physical imprint on the Kayasthas of Ráŕh. After crossing Padma, the kayasthas of Ráŕh became the Bauṋgaja Kayasthas and, after crossing the Mahananda, became the Barendra Kayasthas (kalitá). All the Kayasthas of Bengal are originally from Ráŕh, but possess a few genetic traits of Caucasian Aryans. If they consider themselves outsiders, they are wrong indeed.

The word brhii means staple food. After tasting paddy, would anyone choose oats and barley? The Aryans named paddy brhii.

points.body: Should we conclude our discussion of wheat here? No, not yet. There is more – listen. Since there was no instrument for crushing wheat in those days, the Aryans used to crush the wheat with stones and, using their hands to knead the crushed wheat, they prepared cápát́i or carpat́iká (in Hindi cápát́i.) A special smell used to emerge from the crushed wheat while it was baking. They were very much drawn to it – just as bees are drawn to flowers and flies; just as bees are drawn to honey. Thus the Aryans of those days used to sit around the fire waiting for the bread to bake and, as the smell of the baking bread or capati wafted by, they felt thrills of joy and anticipation; they felt exhilarated at the thought that their Áryakanyá (the husbands of those days used to address their wives as Áryakanyá, and the wives used to address their husbands as Áryaputra) was going to put cápát́is with dates (always write kharjúra, not kharjura which means silver) on their plates for them to eat. points.body: It is worth mentioning here that chillies are not indigenous to India or Bengal. Before chillies were available in India, long peppers (pippali in Sanskrit) and black peppers (kat́ubiijam) were used. When the Portuguese brought chilli [lauṋká] to India, people had a problem naming it. In order to differentiate between chilli and black pepper, they gave it the name gáchmaric and called the other golmaric. (Before the arrival of chillies, black pepper was simply called maric [pepper]). Black pepper is a creeper while chilli is an upright plant; accordingly the name gácmaric was given [gách means “plant” or “tree”]. In old Bengali lauṋká used to refer to any expanse of land enclosed by water, that is, it did not refer only to Sri Lanka or Ceylon. The word viláyet, prevalent in Arabic and Farsi, also means “an enclosed island territory” or “foreign land”. Some people think that perhaps Viláyet or Vilet means “Britain”, but this conception is incorrect. In Urdu and Farsi, Britain is called “Varttániyá”. The British government is called “Hukumate Varttániyá”. Anyhow, lauṋkámaric or chili-pepper came from a foreign land, that is, it came from Lauṋká.

points.body: Nepal is an independent kingdom situated on the border of India and Tibet. In ancient times, Nepal was split into small states. In those days the rulers were the kings of the Newar dynasty. [Today] these Newars reside primarily in the Kathmandu valley of central Nepal. Though there is some Tibetan influence on their language, the influence of Sanskrit is immense. Their own letters are in Shriiharśa script (Bengali). The Gorkha leader, Prithvinaryan Shah, built a single state by conquering the neighbouring fragmented states. That was probably in 1773. The Gorkhas also conquered the kingdom of Udayan and present-day Tarái Aiṋcal of Northeast Himalayas, adjacent to Bihar and Jhapa District of Cooch Behar. Later there were several battles between Nepal and British India over these lands. At last General Ochterlony of British India defeated Nepal. A permanent agreement known as the Sugouli Pact was made between Nepal and British India. Sugouli is a small town in Champaran district. According to this pact, the kingdom of Udayan (present-day Garwal and Kumaon) was ceded to British India, whereupon it became part of Uttar Pradesh (a state that then included Audh and Agra). The southern part of Tarái Aiṋcal in Bihar was surrendered to the British, and the northern part of Tarái (Sattari, Mahattari, Rajbiraj, Morang, Jháṋpá [Jhapa] and Birgaiṋja districts) remained with Nepal. This part of North Tarái Aiṋcal in Nepal is presently known as Madhesha (Madhya desha) and the people are called Madheshiis. Relations between India and Nepal have been very good for a long time. Both countries are culturally linked. As long as it was under the rule of the Newar dynasty, Maethilii written in Shriiharśa script was the state language of Nepal.

Apart from these, there are regional Madheshi languages, such as Bhojpurii, Maethilii, Auṋgiká (Morang) and Bengali (Jhapa). [Nepal has now abolished the monarchy and become a full-fledged democratic republic.] Historically, Nepal was a land of Maháyánii Buddhism. Why are there so many verbs for movement? The reason is that the Vedic Aryans were nomads before they learnt how to cultivate crops. The Vedic Aryans were not the only nomads; people of all races were initially nomads. Whenever food supplies in a particular region were exhausted, people used to migrate to other regions in search of food. In their quest for food, they roamed the entire world. Those who have this habit of moving are called nomads. In snowbound and desert areas, these nomadic habits are maximally prevalent. The stretch of land between Asia and Europe is called mishrabhúmi in Sanskrit due to its blending of western dynamism and oriental humanism. The expression mishar or mish originates therefrom. Mishar is the symbol of western and oriental synthesis. In the past, this gándhára style was welcomed all over the world. In those days there was the famous Taxila University (near present-day Peshawar). points.body: In fact, Kalidas [probably third or fourth century] in his literature has secured a place for this malayánila [soothing breeze]. Kalidas was a man of Bengal. He was an inhabitant of the Contai area in Midnapur district, so his comments on Malaya sprang from his own experience. People used to think that there might be a mountain in the south on the other side of the Indian Ocean. [According to legend] there was a sandalwood forest on that mountain, from whence the soothing pleasant breeze wafted by. By adding the suffix ań to the word malaya we get the word málaya, that is, the land of the malaya breeze is Malaya. To the south of Burma-Martaban is the land of Malaya. Perhaps this southerly breeze comes from that very land of Malaya. Most likely there was once a sandalwood forest there, because the climate is congenial for the cultivation of sandalwood. It may be that since rubber plantations fetch a better profit, cultivation of sandalwood disappeared from this area over the course of time. The word girisára also indicates the [legendary] Malaya Mountain. It is as if the quintessence of all the fragrances on different mountains have converged in this Malay Mountain. points.body: The fairly old city of Dhaka has got two Sanskrit names – D́hakkánagarii and D́ákánagarii. This city must be older than 1500 years; it could be even older. As praises of [Dhaka] once resounded across distant lands and countries, it was given the name D́hakkánagarii. The origin of this name does not refer to the demarcation of the boundary of the city by drumbeats. However, it was more widely known as D́ákánagarii. The word D́áká [Dacca] has come from the word d́abák. The root verb d́ab means to go under water. So d́abák means lowland. Since there were lowlands surrounding the city, Bauáṋgabhukti [Eastern Bengal] was called D́abák in those days. Other bhuktis [bhukti means a district] of Bengal were Burdwan bhukti and Dańd́abhukti of Ráŕh, Samatat́bhukti of Samatat́, Kámtápur and Paońd́ravardhanbhukti of Barendra, Bauṋgabhukti of Bauṋga (Bauṋgabhukti primarily meant Mymensingh, Dhaka, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts of undivided Bengal) and Upabauṋga or Shribhúmi (this Upabauṋga stands for Sylhet, Cachar, Tripura, British Tripura, that is, Comilla, Bhulua, that is, Noakhali, etc.). Chittagong was usually known as Chat́t́ala. Most of the time, this Chat́t́ala was part of Upabauṋga or Shriibhúmi. But on occasion the king of Arakan would occupy, and during other periods Arakan would be absorbed into Chat́t́ala. The relationship between Arakan and Chat́t́ala was quite intimate. For a long time the state language of Arakan was Bengali. Every educated man is aware of the name Syed Muhammad Alwal, the medieval court poet of Arakan. The complete works of this great poet, so well-versed in Sanskrit, have not yet been properly compiled. During the British regime, Arakan was made a permanent part of Burma. At that time the Kobe valley of Manipur also became a part of Burma.

points.body: In the Rámáyańa, two sons of Rama are mentioned – Lava and Kusha. According to various and sundry stories, Rama had one son named Lava. According to many people the Lavapura town which is presently called Lahore was set up by Lava. When Sita was living in the hermitage of Valmikii, it is said that Lava once got lost. Sita was utterly stricken with grief. The sage Valmikii, was unable to bear this sight. So by the grace of Brahmá, the Lord of creation, he created another boy like Lava sprinkling the kushodaka ( 5 ) [mythological sacred water.] Since he was created out of kushodaka, he was given the name Kusha. Later, when Lava returned, Sitá did not want to part with Kusha under any circumstances. From that time onwards, Sitá came to be the mother of two sons – Lava and Kusha. ( 6 )

It was the practice of the Buddhist age for the ashes collected from the funeral pyre of great men to be kept in a stone urn (sometimes even in a clay pot). These preserved ashes were called dhátu. Viháras and Saḿgháráms were built over this dhátu. (Saḿghárám is a Prákrta word which has come from the Sanskrit word Saḿgraham. From the word Saḿghárám has come the word Saḿgha, that is, organization. Saḿgháráms were places where many people used to gather together for meditation, to discuss dharma and philosophy. It has to be remembered that both the words Saḿghárám and Saḿgha are Prákrta words; they are not original Sanskrit words. Those who sometimes say, saḿghe shakti kalao yuge, that is, in the age of kali strength lies with the organization, are possibly not aware that this is not a Sanskrit utterance. ( 7 )) In memory of the ashes of funeral pyres, the Viháras and Saḿgháráms were called Caityas. According to many people, in ancient times, due to the presence of several Caityas, one town of Bengal was called Caityagrám, which in the course of time became Chattagram.

(In those days, in the spoken language of the ancient people of Chattagram, cát́i/sát́i meant lamps). That is why the place came to be called Cát́igáoṋ or Cát́gáoṋ. Before reaching the shore of Chattagram, from a ship in the Bay of Bengal, one could see this port from a distance decorated with strings of lamps; hence it was so named. Of course, the Portuguese did not use any of these words, that is, Caetyagrám, Chattagram or Cát́igáoṋ. They gave the place the name Porte-de-Báuṋgálá. When the Portuguese came to [India], there were large big ports in Bengal. In the East there was Cát́gáon or Porte-de-Báuṋgálá and in the west Saptagrám or Sátgáon of Hooghly district. Probably to differentiate Cát́gáon from Sátgáon, they did not use those names but called one Porte-de-Báuṋgálá and the other Porte-de-gráṋdi. ( 8 )

points.body: Potaka means port. Similarly, the banks of the river where boats rest are also called nadiipotaka [river port], and the places where carts and horses gather are known as sthalapotaka [land port]. In the beginning, the spelling of ‘port’ in English was incorrect. The original spelling was porte – its pronunciation should be porte. Still today the spelling porte is the standard spelling in languages of Latin origin. The port Rome is called Porte-de-Romá. The Portuguese named Saptagrám port as Porte-de-gráṋdis and Chittagong port as Porte-de-Báuṋgálá. As per French grammatical rules, if a vowel is not used after the letter t, then t will lose its pronunciation, that is, t will become mute. So if we write porte instead of port, the pronunciation would be ‘port’, but if we write 'portʼ, its pronunciation would be por, just as táṋte is pronounced as táṋt (aunt). However, if we write tant, its pronunciation would be tṋá. In this case t will lose its sound. The French pronunciation for tea is te. Here the pronunciation is correct because the vowel e comes after t. However, vant is pronounced as váṋ whereas vante is pronounced as váṋt – one is the masculine form of selling and the other is its feminine form. Now you understand why in languages of Latin origin, in the sense of potaka one has to write porte for port for the sake of pronunciation. In English there is no need to use the vowel e after t. For this reason, they mistakenly removed the letter e from porte. Today the spelling of “port” is quite normal. The similarity of the two words potaka and porte is significant.

points.body: Potaka has another meaning. When the commencement of five kinds of actions; namely, the construction of houses, excavation of ponds, planting of trees, building of temples and donation of goods for a righteous cause, are done with the chanting of guru mantra and with the ideation of dedicating these acts for the welfare of the people, then this is called pratiśt́há [firm establishment], and the land where this is done is also called potaka. Presently, the word potaka means ‘compound’ in English. In Bengali it is called hátá; the hát́a of Rambabuʼs house means the compound of Rambabuʼs house; the hátá of the garden means the compound of the garden, the garden compound of Rambabu. The word hátá means compound. Today the word is widely prevalent in Ráŕh. However, this word has come from Hindustani or, according to another source, from the Persian word áhátá. In the course of time á disappeared and the hátá (kalchul) remains. ( 9 )

points.body: In the Buddhist era in India, there was a famous Vihára [Buddhist monastery] called Gandhakut́ivihára or Mulagandhakut́ivihára. Around that Vihára were muláguru trees. ( 10 ) That is why it was named Mulagandhakut́i vihára. Vi – hr + ghaiṋ, thus we attain the word Vihára [Bihar]. Vihára means the place where a spiritual aspirant remains merged in bliss with Parama Puruśa. Lord Buddha used the word Brahmavihára to describe these Viháras. In a later period, the Buddhist sádhakas preferred to use the word Baoddhavihára instead of the expression Brahmavihára. Vihára is an ordinary word used to describe the Baoddhaviháras – structures built on sites where the remains of ashes of Buddhist sages were kept. These Baoddhaviháras were called Caityas or Caityaviháras. Though there was a Vihára called Baoddhavihára, they were all Viháras.

points.body: In reality, even Gandhakut́i was a Vihára. At one time in Bengal, especially, in East Bengal, Buddhism was firmly rooted. However, since, along with religious firmness, there was no solidarity in [developing] social bonds, Buddhism perished. Casteism was the main reason for this debacle. Though Jainism existed alongside Buddhism in Ráŕh, Jainism was the more vigorous of the two. However, in one part of present day Hooghly district, Buddhism was strong. It was a kind of triangle, one corner of which was Baṋeci, another corner Mahánád and another Dvárvásinii. Baeṋci was a Baoddha prajiṋávihára. From Baoddha prajiṋávihára has come the word Baeṋci – not from the type of sour and sweet fruit called baeṋci. In a later period, this triangle of Buddhist cities was buried under the sands due to flooding of the Damodar River. The capital of Ráŕh was moved from Mahánád. Pandua, its earlier capital, had also perished under the sands. By excavating the layers of sand, traces of Pandua can still be found today. ( 11 )

The Farsi language, and after that the Urdu language, were introduced here at the time of Queen Didda. Earlier I mentioned that Jammu had been an independent, autonomous kingdom since ancient times. It is true that at the time of Kashmiirʼs King Shauḿkarvarmá, and at the time of Lalitáditya Muktapiid́a ( 13 ), that is, every once in a while, Jammu was incorporated into Kashmiir. During the time of Akbar, Jammu and Kashmiir were under the sovereignty of the Mughal court, but in name only. Kashmiir, along with Jammu and Afghanistan, fell under the control of the Punjabi chief, Ranjit Singh. After the last Sikh war, that is, after the fall of Queen Jhindan when Punjab came under British control, the British did not take upon themselves the burden of ruling all of Afghanistan. Rather they kept some part of Afghanistan in their own hands for military reasons. That portion they joined to India and gave it the name Northwest Frontier Territory with its capital at Peshawar (its old name was Puruśapura). The major portion of Afghanistan, however, they returned to the local Muslim Kings of that time; for example, they returned the kingdom of Mahiishúra [Mysore] to the descendants of the former king of that region. As this seat was used for preparing food and eating, it was called pińd́ika. Pińd́a means food. So, that which was used as a seat for cooking and eating food was called pińd́ika or pińd́iká. Shatadru, Bipáshá, Irávati, Candrabhágá, (Candra and Bhágá are two separate rivers. They later combined and their united flow of waters came to be known as Candrabhágá. To the Europeans of medieval times it was known as the Cenáb), Bitastá, Kabul and Sindhu – they together formed Saptasindhu. Later during the Pathan era, the province came to be known as the Punjab. In Persian, paiṋj means five, ab means water. points.body: Upon migrating to Saptasindhu they became slowly habituated to agricultural life. At that time, the spots of agricultural land where they used to sit and have their lunch were called pińd́ika or places for taking food (pińd́a). In later times, in Paeshácii Prákrta, the meaning of the word pińd́i became the “village” where people ate and drank. Even today, in Punjabi language the word is used in that particular sense. Rawalpindi means the village of the Ráwáls. During that time, the Brahmans of South India were called Ráwáls. Shankaracharya took along with him several pundits from South India who were well-versed in scriptures to that area. Those pundits came to be known as Ráwáls.

points.title: People used to sit on mats or piŕis to eat food served in metal dishes, banana leaves,…

points.body: People used to sit on mats or piŕis to eat food served in metal dishes, banana leaves, sál leaves or the leaves of lotus plants. Prosperous people, wealthy tradesmen, kings and their officials used to take food either like common people, by sitting on raised wooden seats or across tables [called kaśt́hakośa in Bengali], on normal food plates or on plates of their own choice. On the dining table, they used darbii, srak, d́imbaká, kańt́akapatra and kośasháyiká. D́imbaká means small spoon (teaspoon) and srak means large spoon (tablespoon), darbii means ladle, kańt́akapatra means fork, and kośasháyiká means table knives. Kośasháyiká was known in Central Europe or France as kanif. There was no system of using table knives in England until the reign of King Henry VIII. During the reign of King Henry VIII, table knives made their way into British dining tables. Prior to that, knives were to be found in the hands of attendants only. King Henry VIII was very much a gourmet. He frequently used to stay in Paris, the capital of France, for good wine and food. While returning home, he would carry with him not only tasty food items but also French etiquette and vocabulary. He imported French kanif to Britain. In English the word was transformed into ‘knife’. Because of the presence of the letter “k” in the French kanif, the letter “k” has been retained in the English word “knife”, though it is not pronounced. The Sanskrit word for knife is koshasháyiká. One could very well use this word even in Bengali.

They come out victorious in evolutionary advancement. One who lags behind is a vikránta [counter-evolutionary] – the seed of counter-evolution lies in this lagging behind. points.body: Scholars are divided over the name Mymensingh. According to some, the entire region was known as Momensháhi; however, during the Pathan era, no trace of the name Momensháhi can be found. Even during the Moghul period this name was not commonly used. The name came to be used only during the last one hundred years. It is said that the area came to be called Mymensingh after the name of a Rajput general, Mumin Singh of Isha Khan, one of the twelve Bhuiṋás [feudal princes governing Bengal during the Moghul regime]. In the pre-Pathan era, prior to its being named Mymensingh or Mumensingh, the area was known as Barabauṋga, or the best of Bengal (bara means the “best”). Mymensingh is not a very old town. It came into existence during the end of Pathan rule or in the early Moghul period. The town was founded in the name of a self-sacrificing, religious emperor of Delhi, Nasiruddin, and called Násirábád. To bridge the gulf between Mymensingh district and its headquarters, Násirábád, people named the headquarters also as Mymensingh. For example, if the name of the district was Rajshahi, and the headquarters was called Rampur-Boalia, for the sake of convenience, the people would give also the headquarters the name Rajshahii. Similarly if the name of the district was Jessore, and the district headquarters was called Kasba, then for convenience the people called the headquarters also Jessore; and if the name of the district was Bakhargaunge, and its headquarters was Barishál [Barisal], again, for their convenience, people named the district Barisal (“Where do you live?” “In Baeshál [colloquial for ‘Barishál’] District.”).

In 1912 when Vauṋgabhauṋga [partition of Bengal] was radd [modified] Mymensingh was included in the province of Bangla. Had the Garo Hills been within Mymensingh district, the Házangs and the Garos would have revived the embers of a renewed vitality, which they had already initiated. Upon separation from Mymensingh, they were deprived of this opportunity. Even today the Bengali dialect, which the original residents of the Garo Hills – the Garos, Házongs and Koches – generally use among themselves, is the dialect of Mymensingh. The sweet cultural link that evolved between Mymensingh and Garo Hills, even after change in the political situation, is inseparably tied, even today, in an eternal bond of gold. ( 1 )

The valley of the Mekong River in Southeast Asia and the Bauṋgálistán region of India and Bangladesh are examples of such a Maháśt́hán. To the north of Bauṋgálistán are the impenetrable Himalayas, and to the south is the Bay of Bengal, in the west the Ramgarh Hills, which are part of the Vindhya Mountain range, in the east lies the Arakan-Iyomá [mountain range], and in the center is the land of alluvial soil carried by the ever-flowing Gauṋgá, Brahmaputra and the rivers of Ráŕh, including the Damodar River, surrounded by its tributaries. Possibly for these reasons, during the Vedic age, Báuṋglá was called both Vauṋga and Maháśt́hán. In the Buddhist age, Paiṋca Gaoŕ was clearly identified as Ráŕh, Samatat́, Vauṋga, Barendra and Mithila. They were more clearly defined by Maháśt́hángaŕh, the name of the capital of Paiṋca Gaoŕ in that period. points.body: In this context, it is good to remember that Matsyendranath returned from Nepal by ratha [chariot]. That was the first chariot of Bengal or of eastern India. In commemoration of that chariot, the residents of Dharmarájiká Vihára, a vast center of Mantrayán Buddhism of Bengal, introduced the rathajátrá festival. In Nepal a wooden chariot (sojá ratha) was built for the onward journey of Matsyendranath, and an iron chariot (ult́o ratha) was built for his return journey. In those days, Dharmarájiká Vihára was renowned in for craftsmanship. The people there, utilizing all their expert craftsmanship, constructed a bamboo chariot for Matsyendranath, and then eagerly waited for the return of their dear prince by road. That chariot of Dharmarájiká is the oldest ratha of Bengal or eastern India. The current name of Dharmarájiká is Dhámrái (Dharmarájiká > Dharmarájiá > Dhámrái). There are very few people who have not heard of the rathajátrá festival of Dhámrái in Dhaka district.

points.body: Matsyendranath ( 3 ) was the prince of Bengal. His capital in the beginning was Rampal and towards the end it was Maynámati. Maynámati was part of Tripura district during British rule and not far from Comilla. Maynámati was one of the centers of Buddhist yogic practices (baoddha yogácára). Though it was included in the former Tripura district, its distance to the border of Dhaka district was not much. Dhaka district, the Comilla sub-division and the Brahmanberia sub-division of British Tripura district, along with its contiguous areas of the Habiganj sub-division of Sylhet, were once the centre of Buddhist practices. With Buddhism as its focal point, a highly learned society evolved in this area over the last 1500 to 2000 years. This society controlled Bengalʼs cultural life for several hundred years. The sense of civility and courtesy of Dhaka and Tripura, their knowledge and wisdom, culinary arts and social norms, have long inspired Báuṋgálistán. And this was not all! The widely acknowledged center of Sanskrit studies in Bengal, Vikrampur was also situated in this area. Dharmapál Dipauṋkar [981 A.D.], the chancellor of Nalanda University and head of the institution of Tibetan Buddhism, who was known in Tibet as Sriijiṋána Atiish, was also the affectionate scion of Vikrampur. Today that Vikrampur may be gone, but a genuine search might lead to the recovery of its ruins, its skeletal remains. ( 4 )

The word la is derived as lá (root verb) + d́a (suffix), meaning one that holds or one that is held. Something that holds ker, that is, coconut, is Kerala. Then the capital of Ráŕh was Siḿhapur (presently Singur of Hooghly district). The port was in an area close to Siḿhapur, and later the port came to be known as Siḿhalpát́an (which is close to Singur). Vijay Siḿha conquered Lanka and, along with his followers, permanently settled there. They are the ancestors of the present-day Sinhalese people. These Sinhalese are very similar to Bengalis in their ways and manners, their customs and behaviour. Their facial appearance bears a close resemblance to that of Bengalis. Until they speak it is difficult to differentiate a Bengali from a Sinhalese. The Sinhalese language is similar to the Bengali language of the Indo-Aryan group, even in its script. Though most Sinhalese are today Hinayánii Buddhists, their traditional styles and practices remain very close to those of Bengal. The Sinhalese have such titles as Senánáyaka, Jayavardhana, Guńatilaka, Bháńd́arnáyaka (many people incorrectly say Bandarnayaka.
