points.body: In the Pathan era, there were three provinces (subá) in India – the Punjab, Hindustan and Bengal. Akbar broke up these provinces and created a few more provinces. He split Hindustan province into Agra and Oudh provinces (it should have been Avadh; but, in history, it is written in English as Oudh). And Bengal province was split up into Bihar and Orissa provinces. During Pathan regime Orissa was practically independent. But during Moghul era Orissa changed hands quite frequently. Sometimes it was in the hands of Moghuls, sometimes in the hands of Bhoṋsle Marathas, sometimes in the hands of local Hindu kings. In fact, after the Royal Kesari dynasty (in which there were great kings like Ananta Keshari, Jajáti Kesari) the history of Orissa fell into uncertainty. During the rule of Akbar [1556–1605] when the province of Behar was created, then its name was written with the Persian letter Be, it was written as Behar. Later the province of Behar lost its separate identity and was included into Bengal province.

points.body: During the Buddhist age in Bihar, especially in Magadha, Buddhism had a firm foothold – there were a large number of Buddhist Vihára which were also called Brahmaviháras. I have said a little earlier that in the local pronunciation there was only ba. When during Shahjahanʼs rule [1628–1658], Urdu was made the state language of the Moghuls in place of Persian, then the Munsis (who worked as clerks in small courts) of Behar, alongside with Persian script, used to write Urdu in a somewhat transformed form of Nágarii script. Although in official works and in the upper levels of the big and small courts, Urdu written in Persian script was in practice, but at the ordinary level Urdu written in changed Nágarii script was more widely used. Even during British era when English came to replace Urdu as the official language in the law courts and at the state level, at the ordinary level that very Urdu in mutated Nágarii script was in use. Since most of these court clerks were Kayasthas by caste, this transformed Nágarii script came to be known as káyethi lipi [a script used mostly by Kayastha scribes]. During our boyhood days, in the court documents and police records that script was in use and it was meant to be learnt compulsorily by the officers. After independence, that script was removed and in its place, the Devanágarii script was installed. In the káyethi lipi there is only one va which should serve both as vargiiya ba and antahstha va. Hence, to write correctly, it must be written as “Vihár”.

points.body: Campakárańya, described in the Rámáyańa, turned into Mágadhii Prákrta Campárań; in Occidental demi-Mágadhii it became Campáranya. Campakaranya constituted the present East Champaran (Matihari), West Champaran (Bettia) and the adjacent Madeshii [central region] areas of Nepal. (For a short period a Tehshil [sub-district] of Gorakhpur was within Campakaranya.) Important places like Lumbini, Kushinagar (Kashiya), Nandangarh, Lauria and even Kapilavastu were once part of Champaran. The historically famous Lumbini – the Lumbini script was used to write the history of India – also belonged to the western part of Champaran. The Bráhmii letters of the Lauriyá script, in which the history of Buddhist India was recorded, also had their origin near Bettia of Champaran.

In my historical search, I went to Lauria. The locals revere this place as sacred. They call it Lor Bábá. It is Champaran which, by an inevitable decree of history, today is in fragments. The major rivers of Champaran, the Rápti (which flows alongside the city of Gorakhpur), Narayańii, Gańd́aka and Dhanavatii (Dhanauti) once kept the land green with plentiful corn, flowers and fruits. Champaka [magnolia] trees are seen in abundance in the area even today. Its natural beauty and forest resources are incomparable.

The language of the northeastern part of this district is Paiṋcakroshii Maethilii, and of its southwestern part, Baijiká Maethilii. Even during British rule, Tirhut was a large district. Its headquarters was Muzaffarpur (named after Muzaffar Shah). During the early part of British rule, extensive stretches of forest prevailed in this district. Where many tigers, niilgái [antelope] and even rhinoceros existed, today the forest has vanished, and the wild animals have [consequently] become extinct. The sub-divisional town of Zehanabad in Gaya district belongs to the Pathan era; hence, the town is quite old. In those days, Bengal province had two sub-divisional towns, one in Gaya district and the other in Hooghly district. It led to some difficulties in the discharge of official work. Since there was confusion between the Kanthi of Midnapur and the Kandi of Murshidabad [two very similar sounding names], the British used the name Contai for Káṋthi, and for the same reason contemplated changing the name of Zehanabad. As Zehanabad of Gaya district is an old and large town, they thought it wiser to change the name of Zehanabad in Hooghly district. Thus, in accordance with the name of the adjoining administrative division, the town Zehanabad of Hooghly district was renamed Arambag. Today the people of Arambag have forgotten that the original name of their town was Zehanabad.

points.body: During the early part of British rule, the governor of Purnea was Shaukat Jung or Shaukat Ali [1756]. This part of Indian history is not at all ancient; however, its details are murky and somewhat clouded. Most likely certain opportunists, to serve their own interests, have deliberately distorted that history. Yet, as far as can be ascertained, the wife of Shaukat Jung/Shaukat Ali was Maimuna Begum, the Khala Amma (maternal aunt) of Siraj-ud-daula. According to some people, Shaukat Jung/Shaukat Ali was the maternal uncle of the only married wife of Siraj Bubbujan (not the mother of Ummat Jahura). But many people do not support this view. Many believe that Maimuna Begum was in fact the maternal aunt of Siraj, but was not the daughter of Nawab Alibardi. She was the daughter of Begum Sharfunnisa through her first marriage. According to others, however, Begum Sharfunnisa married only once; hence, the question of her first or second marriage does not arise. Regarding Begum Sharfunnisa it is said that Alibardi Khan, when doing each and every noble deed, used to consult her. However, he carried out all his dishonest deeds (many thought Nawab Alibardi was highly reputed in this regard) without her knowledge. Be that as it may, Mirza Muhammad (who later became Siraj-Ud-Daula) was made the heir to the throne in consultation with Begum Sharfunissa. After Siraj became the Nawab, his maternal aunt became filled with vengeance. She wanted her own son to become the Nawab. At her instigation, Shaukat Jung (Shaukat Ali) advanced with an army towards Murshidabad to teach Siraj a lesson. Coming to the southern part of Purnea, the two armies were almost face to face. The water of Purnea did not suit the soldiers of Shaukat Jung. In search of water for them, he dug a huge diirghiká [tank.] Then a fierce battle began between the two armies. In this battle, Shaukat Ali was badly defeated. The local people gave this site the name Diighikát́ihára, meaning, the defeat that was due to the digging of the tank.

points.body: From the Sanskrit word mudgagiri has come the word Muṋgir. The word Muṋgir was transformed into the present Mongher. Mongher is a very ancient town. Even during the time of Rashtrakutas, Mongher was famous. This Mungher town was also the last capital of Moghul Bengal. Mir Kashim was its Nawab. The fort of those days still stands in Mungher. There remains still today the Topkhana Bazar (the cannon manufacturing center), the maidan [large field] for army drills (the Kareya maidan), the Kashim Bazar and the Sujighat. Suja, the son of Shahjahan, went into this ghat́ [river bank used as a boat station] to Arakan via Bhagalpur by waterway to seek refuge with their king. The Sujagang of Bhagalpur was named after him. During the Pal regime, for just a few days, this town was the second capital of Bengal. The major capital was Gaoŕ. The Rashtrakutas [753–973 A.D.] repeatedly attacked Monghyr, probably during the time of Mahendra Pal. Unfolding extensively along the northeast of the Ganges, this district was one of the most important districts of Bihar. The language of northwestern Mongher was Maethilii, in the southwest it was Magahii, while in most parts of Mungher, it was Angika. There is no Maethilii-speaking area in the present, small district of Mungher. Those areas have gone partly to Begusarai and partly to Saharsa district. The British bifurcated this district and called the eastern part Bhagalpur, and the western part Mungher.

It was jokingly said that the highest government official of Saharsa was the local police officer (daphádár). However if you are browbeaten, with bloodshot eyes, moving even a short distance then it cannot be described as vihára. One whose mind always moves in Parama Brahma is Brahmabihárii. One whose mind is always ensconced in the beauty of Krśńaʼs play, is Krśńabihárii – Brajabihárii. One of my devotees was a great devotee of Tagore. He named his son Rabindrabihárii. points.body: Its Vedic name is Haritadhánya. In Vedic language, dhánya means green vegetation. When the Vedic Aryans came [to Haryana] after entering India, they were drawn to its green beauty and named it Haritadhánya. The Sanskrit letters ka, ta, pa, d́a become a in Prákrta, dha becomes ha (for example, dadhi > dahi > dai – to write dae is incorrect; it is not bao which should be bau; similarly it is not maomáchi – the correct spelling should be maumáchi.) Thus, haritadhánya became hariahánan, and in Demi-Prákrta this became hariháná. In modern language this was transformed into Haryana. Similarly, lodhradhánya has become Ludhiana. In the spelling of dhánya there is the dental na. From that standpoint, it is proper to use the dental na in spelling Haryana and Ludhiana. However, here the vowel e follows the letter ra, after that there is ya, and beside it is a – these are all abádhak varńa [free letters unrestricted by the change of dental na into cerebral ńa.] According to this logic, it would be more reasonable to write it with cerebral ńa, that is haryańá. The local language of Haryana is Ját́t́u or Haryanvi.

points.body: The root verb od́ means to draw near, to caress, to embrace, to serve and care for. Od́ + rak = od́ra. The land that takes great care of its guests, drawing the far away people near, is called the land of Od́ra. The coastal area from the mouth of the River Mahánadi to the mouth of the River Subarnarekha is called Od́ra, and the area from the mouth of the river Mahánadi to the mouth of the river Godavari is known as Utkal. The entire coastal area from the mouth of the river Godavari to the mouth of the river Suvarnarekha is Kalinga – that is, the combined name of Utkal and Od́ra. Matters related to this land of Od́ra are called Od́ra, and the language is known as Odri/Aodri. From this Od́rii/Aod́rii has come the word Oriya. points.body: The suffix rak is used when a person does something habitually. For example, the meaning of the verb ud́ is to entertain, to love and care for, to embrace mutually, to urge on, saying, ‘please eat this’, 'please eat that.ʼ Thus, by combining ud́ + rak we obtain the word Od́ra. Od́ra means one who knows how to love, how to show affection. In ancient times, Orissa was famous for its hospitality. That is why the northern part of Orissa, meaning the left bank of the Mahánadi, was called the land of Od́ra. From this word Od́ra has come the words Orissa, Oriya, and so forth. Even today, you will observe that the people of Orissa are very much accustomed to cooking, entertaining and taking care of people. If someone asks anything of them, they will certainly give it, if at all possible. In those days, the people of Od́ra land used to cultivate dance and fine arts, chiefly to entertain people, to please their minds. Even today, the people of Od́ra retain certain artistic skills, though it has declined to some extent. If their crippled economic status is ameliorated, we can expect them to regain their former artistic skills. The word Utkal means where there is a rise in the faculty of arts or where there is an upsurge of human creative skill (ud́ + kal + ac). ( 5 )

Tawi is the name of a local river. The Aryans discovered gold in the sand particles of several rivers in this Jammu territory. Since they discovered gold in the rivers of Jammu, they also gave gold the name jámbunada [nada means “river”].

points.body: We had now started from this Jammu. Up until the pre-Pathan era, Jammu was an independent kingdom. In olden times Sanskrit, and after that, D́ogri, were its local languages. D́ogriʼs script is a central Indian form of Sáradá script. In ancient India, after the demise of both the Bráhmii and Kharośt́hii scripts, three different scripts sprang up in three different parts of India: (1) The Kut́ilá script in Allahabad and east of there; (2) Sáradá to the northwest of Allahabad; and (3) Náradá or Nágrii in the southwest. Sáradá means “Sarasvatii”, the goddess of knowledge. The Brahmans of this region are known as Sárasvata Brahmans – they are called this for their erudition. These Sárasvata Brahmans used to live principally in southern Russia, Afghanistan, Kashmiir, Jammu and the Saptanada Kingdom [Punjab]. The Sáradá script was prevalent in this territory. Just as there were three branches of Sárasvata Brahmans – Kashmiir Sárasvata, Dogri Sárasvata and Saptanada (Punjabi) Sárasvata – there were also three branches of Sáradá script – Kashmirii Sáradá, central Indian or D́ogri Sáradá, and southern Indian or Punjabi Sáradá. In all of these areas Sanskrit has been written, learned and taught in this Sáradá script since very ancient times.

points.body: The British did not want to retain rule over Kashmir and Jammu themselves. Since the old royal house of Kashmiir had died out, it was not possible to return it to the descendants of that dynasty. Thus they sold Kashmiir and Jammu to a certain D́ográ chieftain – Golap Singh. After that Jammu became a native kingdom of India. The kingdomʼs name became Jammu and Kashmir; its summer capital was Srinagar and its winter capital was Jammu. The Kashmiir that is spoken about in Kalhanʼs Rájataraunginii is not the old land of Kashmiir. It is about Kashmiir without Jammu.

They used to shift from place to place according to the severity of the cold, thus they were called Kash. There were greater numbers of Kash in the north, that is, Kashmiir, and less toward Jammu. In this sense the land of the Kash becomes kash + meru, Kashmeru – Kashmiir.

From the anthropological point of view, the people of this area are a blending of both. They possess a beautiful combination of valour and intellectuality – the radiance of the diamond with the fragrance of the campaka.

The Laddakii script, whose historical name is T́egŕii, is a local edition of Tibetan script. There is some resemblance between this script and Kut́ilá, or Bengali script. I have seen this script in the Buddhist temples in the mountainous regions of Sikkim and Darjeeling. The Buddhist priests recite mantras from scriptures written in this script.

In winter, great flocks of migratory birds abandon the extreme cold of Siberia, Outer Mongolia, western China and Tibet, and head south, crossing over rivers and mountains, in search of warmth. Most of the birds that we could see there were from other countries. Although birds of the flamingo group were in the greatest number, there were also various other kinds of birds, such as dhanuśas, háŕgilás [Adjuntant stork], vultures, black swans, red swans, and eagles as well. The king of Jammu-Kashmiir was Hari Singh, the successor of its first D́ogra king, Golap Singh. His son, in turn, Karna Singh, was not able to become king. points.body: After going a little ways I suddenly noticed a change. Now there was an apple orchard beside us. This place was well above sea-level, but because there were apple orchards on both sides of us we could not tell how high we were. Here and there were some ciir and phár varieties of trees standing in the apple fields. In some trees I saw some rare birds – birds-of-paradise (Svarga vihauṋga). They rarely come into contact with people so they are not afraid of them. They do not know what cruel creatures human beings are. Seeing us, they were not afraid, rather they stared at us eagerly. Their simplicity made me feel uneasy and ashamed at the same time. I felt ashamed thinking that they do not realize how cruel we human beings are, how complex we are from the mental point of view, and how crooked.

Some of their buds were counting the moments, waiting for the arrival of spring. By judging the amount of warmth in the climate they had guessed that Holi [spring festival] was not far away.

I have seen these varieties of orchids in Birbhum on the way from Mámud Bazaar to Masháiṋjoŕ, and in areas near the Jonhá waterfall (Gaotamdhárá) on the Jhalda-Ranchi Road. points.body: To the left of us, that is, to the north, at a good distance away was the kingdom of Kinnaur, renowned both in history and in the Puranas. This Kinnaur was situated in the northern extremity of India in the Sadáshiva mountain range. Some people may not be aware that the Himalayas, stretching from the west until the eastern horizon, are divided north and south into two parts. The Sanskrit name of the part of the Himalayas that touch the northern plains of India is Shivaliuṋga Parvatamálá (Shivalic Range). This part is high, but not so high. There is cultivation wherever there are green forested areas in the valleys lying between two mountains, cutting into the mountains with either step-farming or terracing. This Shivalic range is covered with snow in the wintertime, and its highest peaks remained snow-covered all year long. The fossils of prehistoric animals can be found in this part.

points.body: At one time the Himalayas were submerged in the bosom of the sea. Northern India was also then at the bottom of the sea. To the south, only Gondawanaland was above sea level. Approximately three million years ago the Himalayas rose up from the depths as a result of an earthquake. The skeletons of some of those animals who used to wander in these parts of the earth three million years ago can be found packed underneath the rocks in the Shivalic range. In later times when the hippopotamus and giraffe were living here, they used to live in these Lower Himalayas. Some of their fossils have also been found in the Lower Himalayas, and more are bound to be discovered in the future.

points.body: The Sadáshiva range (Upper Himalayas) run west to east, directly parallel to the Lower Himalayas. We find this mountain range in Kashmir, Laddak, the northern part of Himachal Pradesh, Simla, Kinnaur, toward the north of Garhwal-Kumayun, the north of Nepal, northern Sikkim and Bhutan, and in southern Tibet. This part of the Himalayas is really quite high. The snow remains all year long but in winter it is really heavy. The highest Himalayan peaks are located in this part. The driest, coldest and most elevated area of the Upper Himalayas is Laddak and Kinnaur. During winter nights the temperature can fall below minus one-hundred degrees. While heating water it freezes and turns to ice.

points.body: In most parts of this barren mountain land there are snowstorms nearly twelve months of the year. There is virtually no green forest, and hardly any cultivation. I have seen a little barley being grown here in the summertime. Peopleʼs primary livelihood is raising livestock. The Indian cow cannot survive here; there are Yaks. Although the ancient land of Kinnaur was some ways from where we were it was not altogether that far. In olden days the people of this region were famed for their beauty, and to some extent they still are. Although their noses are slightly sloping, it does not detract from their loveliness. Seeing their beauty, the people of those days use to think and say that they were not people but angels. Erá ki nara? [Are they really human beings?] Kiḿ nara = kinnara.

points.body: The language of the people of Kinnaur is a southwestern dialect of Tibetan, just as Laddakii is a western dialect of Tibetan. The script of the Kinnauri language is also T́egrii or T́egrá (In Sanskrit, triguńii or triguńá script). Although the common religion of the Kinnauri people is the Lamabad branch of Maháyána Buddhism, it is clearly influenced by the Árśa doctrine. ( 2 ) Over the last two thousand years, Arśa-ism and Kinnaurʼs Maháyána Buddhism (centering around Avalokiteshvara) have coexisted peacefully because Buddhism has avoided clash. The common people revere both the Buddhist grottoes and the Árśa temples. During hours of worship, the Buddhist lamas place offerings of ground barley, roasted barley powder, etc. before the gods, and these return to the people as prasád [holy remains of the offerings which are then eaten]. In the Hindu [Árśa] temples the priests place offerings of fruits and vegetables. In the same house one person may be Hindu and another Buddhist, however those who wish to become renunciants generally adopt lamaism and cloister themselves in the Buddhist grottoes. Very few local people become Hindu renunciants.

points.body: The lady replied, “There is a great poverty now in our area. The men have all gone down to the plains in search of work. What little there is in the apple orchards the women are doing. Moreover, you well know that the men cannot do so much labour in the mountain areas. They fall sick if too great a burden is placed on their shoulders; they die before their time. So we donʼt let our men here work so much. We do much of the work in the apple orchards. We also go and sell in the markets. We only let the men do the packing for those apples which are exported to distant lands. They want to work, but we donʼt let them.”

points.body: “Sure, Iʼll tell you,” he replied. “There is very little wheat grown here, however, the people here love wheat bread. It poses no difficulty or inconvenience for the rich people to buy wheat and eat bread made from wheat flour. But how much inconvenience the poor people face! In those years when the price of wheat is high or when there is an excess apple production and they fail to find good markets for their apples, then they dry the apples and grind them into a kind of flour. They spend a lot of time eating bread made from that apple flour. The people here consider serving guests to be an especially virtuous act. Those who donʼt serve guests properly are frowned on by society. No matter how much trouble it may bring them, they feed their guests wheat bread, either with ghee on it, or if not, then tandooris. Itʼs a troubling situation for them if they are ever forced to feed any guest apple bread; then there is no end to their shame. They will beg that guestʼs forgiveness over and over again. Remember this: the wealthy peopleʼs food here is wheat [gam ( 6 )] bread; the poor folkʼs food is apple bread.”

Before going to China he strengthened the foundations of Buddhism in Laddak and the Kashmir valley. He propagated Buddhism in China and had some Maháyána scriptures translated into Chinese.

points.body: Kumáráyańaʼs wife was the Chinese royal princess, Jiivá. Kumáráyańaʼs son, Kumárajiiva [A.D. 344], spent the greater part of his life in China, but he went to Kashmiir for some time. He also composed some Maháyána scriptures in Sanskrit. He went to Laddak but he did not go to Kinnaur. Still, Buddhism was subsequently introduced into Kinnaur from Laddak. Buddhism was first propagated in the original territory of Tibet (whose name was then Kimpuruśavarśa) by the royal prince of Udayan, Padmasambhava. What we now call Garhwal-Kumayun was known as the kingdom of Udayan in olden times. The palms of the hands and the soles of the feet of the royal prince were bright red so he was given the name Padmasambhava. Due to his influence Tibet accepted Maháyána Buddhism. The religion of Tibet before that was Bonpa or Bonpa-ism. King Sáungt-sen-gámpo, a follower of the Bonpa religion, had two wives. One was the royal Chinese princess, Den Jing, and the other was Trikut́i, the daughter of the Nepali King at the time, Aḿshuvarmańa, who was a follower of Máháyána Buddhism. The influence of these two queens was considerable in the kingdom of Tibet. The king was inspired by them to accept the Buddhist religion.

points.body: Sáungt-sen-gámpo was a historically renowned personality, a pious emperor. At that time, Magadha was resplendent for its erudition. The two best universities were then Magadhaʼs Nalanda and Taxila in the land of Kandahar. Taxila was famous for its philosophical thinking and for its spiritual community. Nalanda was successful in all spheres, and spiritually inspired. The chancellor of this Nalanda University was Dharmapála Diipauṋkar. Dharmapála Diipauṋkar came from Vikramańipur (its modern name is Vikrampur). Dhaka Districtʼs Vikrampur subdivision has been perched on the glorious golden summit of learning since very ancient times. In the Buddhist era, it became even more radiant in its keenness for learning and wisdom.

points.title: At that time there was no other Buddhist pundit on earth as renowned as Dharmapála Dii…

Buddhism became the common religion of the people of Laddak and Kinnaur at that time as well.

After Dharmapála Diipauṋkar returned to Magadha, Buddhist pundits in good numbers came from Tibet and studied in Magadha, doing research in Buddhism and translating the Súttapit́aka, Vinayapit́aka and Abhidhammapit́aka into Tibetan.
points.body: At that time there was no other Buddhist pundit on earth as renowned as Dharmapála Diipauṋkar. Sáungt-sen-gámpo invited this Dharmapála Diipauṋkar to come to his kingdom, that is, Kimpuruśavarśa. While Diipauṋkar was there Buddhism became well established in Kimpuruśavarśa (after that time the name of Kimpuruśavarśa became Tibet). Buddhism became the common religion of the people of Laddak and Kinnaur at that time as well. The king gave Dharmapála Diipauṋkar the title of Shriijiṋána Atiisha as a reward for his recognized scholarship. After Dharmapála Diipauṋkar returned to Magadha, Buddhist pundits in good numbers came from Tibet and studied in Magadha, doing research in Buddhism and translating the Súttapit́aka, Vinayapit́aka and Abhidhammapit́aka into Tibetan.

points.body: When the Aryans came to northern India, they saw multiple rocks that looked like blackberries. Since those rocks were abundant, they gave that region the name Jambudvipa. In later times, Jambudvipa was used to denote the entirety of Southeast Asia, including India. India was a varśa of that Jambudvipa. The word varśa has three meanings: one is country, and the other two are rainy season and year. Kimpuruśavarśa or Tibet was a varśa in the central region of Jambudvipa. Later the word Jambu was transformed into Jammu. The Aryans first found traces of gold in the sands of the rivers there. Thus, one word for gold is jámbunada.

points.body: Later, as they traveled further northward, the Aryans became involved in conflicts with the Khash group of people, conquered their land and named it Khashmeru. This word Khashmeru later mutated into the word Kashmir. One meaning of the word meru is land. So the meaning of the word Kashmir is the land of Kas or the Khash group of people. Similarly, Ajeyameru is the land which cannot be conquered (Ajeyameru > Ajmeru > Ajmir – both the words Ájmiir and Ajmiir are incorrect). So you understand that the name of the land is Kashmiir, not Káshmiir. The meaning of the word Káshmiir in the masculine gender is something related to Káshmiir, such as the men of the land of Kashmiir, or spice from the land of Kashmiir. Káshmiir also means saffron. From this word Káshmiir has come the Hindi word keshariyá. From the Persian word jáffrán has come the distorted English pronunciation saffron.

points.body: Khas + drń + elongated sound (prśi diirgha ( 2 )) + mr + rań + ṋiiś = kháshmarii. The etymological meaning of the word kháshmarii is the place where people have died at the hands of the Khash people, or where the people of Khash have died. Colloquially, one meaning of the word is the land of Kashmiir. The words khásmarii and káshmarii are synonymous. In ancient Vedic language, the country was called by both names – Kashmiir and Khashmiir. When the Aryans, with their Vedic language, early literature, Vedic lifestyle and spirituality, social wisdom, primary knowledge of contemporary science, economics, skill in archery, astrology and music, crossed over Aryańyavraja (Iran or Persia) to enter Gándhár, they did not meet any resistance on their journey. The area where they encountered the first opposition was the land of Kash or the people of Khas. They [Khas] also had a Mongoloid civilization blended with Dravidian. The people were flat-nosed. They had no intention to simply accept anything of the Vedic Aryans. A conflict of cultures ensued, leading to a bloody struggle. In this struggle, the Aryan invaders emerged victorious. They gradually occupied Baluchistan, Gunj, Chitral, Gilgit, Pamir and finally Kashmir, the main dwelling place of the Khas people, which in Aryan language was called “Kashmiir” or “Khashmiir”. The Khas people moved away to Laddakh [Ladakh] and Kimpuruśavarśa (Tibet). The land was occupied by the Aryans and it obtained a new identity in the name of Kashmeru or Kashmiir, Khashmeru or Khashmiir, Káshmarii or Kháshmarii.

points.body: Beginning with the Vedic era, the Kśatriyas of Kashmir ruled over the kingdom for a long period, with the exception of one or two Pathan and Moghul invasions. During the rule of kings Lalitáditya Muktapiiŕ [724-760 A.D.], Jayápiir, Shankar Verma, et al, the name and fame of Kashmir reached its zenith. Kumarayańa and Kumarjiiva spread that fame to the eastern end of China. However, Queen Didda terminated that march of fame. For the sake of her own self-interest, she sought the help of Aryańyavraja (Iran or Persia), which led to the demise of Kashmir. It came under administrative control first of Persia and later of the Moghuls.

In Sanskrit and old Bengali, the word ‘Bauṋgál’ was widely prevalent, and finally it came to be used in unchanged form in Persian in the Pathan and Moghul royal courts – sometimes as Sube Bauṋgál [Bengal province].
points.body: Gań + al + ṋiiś = Gańd́álii. Both li and lii can be used in the spellings of the word. The suffix al is used to indicate an extended portion or extension, just as by adding al to the word bauṋga we obtain the word Bauṋgál, which means extended Bengal or expanded Bengal, Great Bengal. Vauṋga means a particular part of East Bengal. If Vauṋga is spelled in Sanskrit with the consonant ba, it would mean tin. In spelling ‘Vauṋga,’ meaning a specific part of Bengal, both consonantal ba and antahastha va can be used. That part of Bengal which we now consider to comprise parts of Dhaka, Mymensingh, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts was once called ‘Vauṋga’ or D́abák. Ráŕh, Samatat́, Cat́t́al or Upabauṋga, or according to a different view, Ráŕh, Samatat́, Barendra, Vauṋga and Mithila – these five constituted Paiṋca Gaod́ or Greater Bengal. Amongst them, ‘Vauṋga’ (that is, parts of Dhaka, Mymansingh, Faridpur and Bakharganj districts) was once renowned throughout the world for its knowledge, genius, wisdom, sacrifice and tolerance. By Paiṋca Gaoŕ people were more inclined to mean this Vauṋga. Hence, to indicate the entire Bengal or Paiṋca Gaoŕ, the word bauṋgál = bauṋga + al came to be used. Bengal was called Bauṋgál in Persian, Bauṋgálá in Turkish, Báiṋjál in Latin, Báiṋjálá in Chinese, Baḿlá and Báuṋglá in Bengali, Bengal in English, Bauṋgál in Urdu, and Bauṋgadesh, Gaoŕdesh or Paiṋca Gaoŕ and Bauṋgál in Sanskrit. ‘Bauṋgál’ did not mean only the diminutive Vauṋga but also the entire Bauṋgálistán. In Sanskrit and old Bengali, the word ‘Bauṋgál’ was widely prevalent, and finally it came to be used in unchanged form in Persian in the Pathan and Moghul royal courts – sometimes as Sube Bauṋgál [Bengal province].

points.body: In any case, the word devayonii means an entity in whom certain divine qualities are manifested, that is, these are positive micŕovita. Suppose certain spiritual practitioners are good human beings, but have an innate attachment to worldly objects and are drawn to whatever they see; for example, money, jewelry, etc. Or, let us say we have a person who is a good sádhaka and is also is a good human being, but they beg Parama Puruśa for external beauty without desiring Him. They are meditating on Parama Puruśa, so they are human beings of a higher stature, but are seeking something ordinary from Parama Puruśa. After death, such persons will become devayonii [a being with ethereal, aerial, and luminous factors only] called kinnar. A kinnar is a devayoni, so it does not harm anyone. It does not have that disposition. People of ancient times used to seek the help of kinnars to become more beautiful. At one time, the pursuit of beauty or the art of cosmetics was called kinnar vidyá. “The person is extremely good-looking, like a kinnar”! In olden days, a beautiful dancing maiden was honoured with the epithet kinnarii. So you understand, this faculty is the positive microvitum related to the psychology of cosmetic art. Whatever theories exist regarding beauty enhancement, whatever skills exist for beautification, whatever art exists for aesthetic taste – all come under kinnar vidyá. ( 4 )

points.body: Vi-drbh + ghaiṋ gives us the word Vidarbha. Vidarbha + an gives vaedarbha. Vidarbha means that which cannot be conceived of or that which cannot be conquered. Vaedarbha means anything related to Vidarbha. Etymologically, Vidarbha indicates the eastern part of present-day Maharashtra; that is, the Nagpur-Akola region. In the prevailing language, Vidarbha is called Baráŕ (in English, Berar). In the Moghul era, Baráŕ belonged to the Nizam of Hyderabad state. (The pronunciation of the word Nizam in English is [Naizam], not Nizam. However, in Persian and Arabic, the word is Nizam. The full word is Nizam-ul-mulk.) Later, the British occupied it and, to please the regal Nizam, they offered to address the prince of Hyderabad as the Prince of Berar, just as the prince of England is venerably called the Prince of Wales. Finding his own son compared with the prince of England, the Nizam was highly pleased.

points.body: The word Vidarbha has slightly more historical significance. Many of you might have heard the Puranic story of Nala and Damayanti. Nala was the king of this very Vidarbha. Even in the Vedic age, Vidarbha had some importance. The reason is that the name of Vaedarbhi/Vaedarbhii, the son of the soil of Vidarbha, is remembered along with those amongst the proponents of the Atharvaveda. These include the sages Atharva, Angira, Angiras and Satyavaha. As the great sage Atharva was the earliest of the sages of Atharvaveda, the word Atharva is used to indicate a very old person – “The man has become decrepit (Atharva)”. In this context, it must be mentioned that this Veda was named Atharvaveda after its chief proponent Atharva. For the sake of variation in reading, both the words Atharva and Atharvá can be used. points.body: The meaning of the root ku is “to create sound”, “to create high sound”, “ʼto cry loudly”. By adding the suffix ghaiṋ to the root ku, we obtain the word ko, which means “intense sound”. From kań + kac we derive the word kań, meaning “soft and sweet sound”. Kṋo + kań + ac = kouṋkań. In the etymological sense, it means a place where both sweet and strong sounds can be heard. Colloquially it stands for the northern part of the western coast of India. In the Indian sub-continent, there are, in total, six coasts. The coast of Kuch runs from the Indus valley to the Saurashtra. From Saurashtra to Gomantapurii (Goa) is the coast of Koḿkań or the Kouṋkań beach, while the Malabar Coast extends from Gomantapurii to Kannyakumarii. From Kannyakumarii to the valley of Godavari is the Coramandal coast and the Kaliuṋga coast extends from the Godavari valley to the mouth of Suvarnarekha. From the mouth of the Suvarnarekha to the river Naaf is the coast of Bengal. In this land of Kouṋkań, there are the western Ghats or Sahyadri mountains. Alongside them, across a stretch of land, is the Arabian Sea. Mingled with the vigorous roaring of the sea are the gentle murmurings of extensive forestlands. It is from these twin sounds kṋo and kań that the land came to be named Kouṋkań.

points.body: The language of Kouṋkań is derived from Maharastra Prákrit. Earlier, this language was called the Marathi version of Kouṋkań. Now the language of Kouṋkań is regarded as an independent language, and is prevalent from the south of Mumbai to Gomantapurii. The Chitpávan Brahmans of Maharashtra are slightly different from the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans of Kouṋkań. The Sárasvat Brahmans of India live in two different regions. Those living in Kashmir, Jammu and Punjab are known as north Sárasvat Brahmans or Káshimir Sárasvat Brahmans. Dogri and Punjabi Brahmans belong primarily to this group. The Brahmans of Kouṋkań are known as Gaoŕ Sárasvats. They are called thus because their ancestors came by land from Gaoŕ and settled there. Like the people of Bengal, they are also non-vegetarians. Hence, they do not care much for the vegetarian Brahmans in the rest of India. The customs and manners, practices and bearing of the Gaoŕ Sárasvat Brahmans are found to closely resemble those of the people of Bengal. They also have titles such as ‘Pái’ and 'Senoy.ʼ ( 7 )

points.body: People love to identify various sounds with others that are familiar. On an earlier occasion, you will remember I had told you about the movement of a train. When the driver blows the whistle indicating the train is starting, and it just begins to move, you hear its sound, and perhaps [you] think it is saying – gelum go-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o, gelum g-o-o-o [Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving, Oh friend, I am leaving]. As the train accelerates somewhat, you seem to hear it making the sound – jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo, jácchi jábo [I am moving I must move, I am moving, I must move, I am moving I must move]. Then, as the train moves still more vigorously, you seem to hear the sound – jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo, jata debe tata nobo [I can take as much you can give, I can take as much as you can give, I can take as much you can give]. When the train accelerates still further, it appears to make the sound – káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul, káṋcá teṋtul páká teṋtul [“Raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind, ripe tamarind, raw tamarind ripe tamarind”]. points.body: The spoken language of Kouṋkań is Kouṋkańii. This language is derived from the Maharastra Prákrta. Once it was considered a dialect of Marathi. Kouṋkańii has no alphabet of its own, and presently, in the area of Kouṋkań adjacent to Maharastra, it is written in Devanágariii letters. In Goa, it is written in Roman letters, and in Kouṋkańii-speaking areas of Karnataka, in Kannad́a script. To write a language in three different scripts is not convenient. From the days of the Portuguese, Kouṋkańii has come to be written in Roman script. Even its literary works have been composed in Roman script. However, only the people of Kouṋkań will decide in what script Kouṋkańii should be written – Kannad́a, Roman or Devanagáriii.

points.body: When there are calcium deposits in the joints of bones that compose the spine, they become stiff. The pliability of a childʼs spine is not to be found in that of grown-ups. If one works continuously for a long time stooping low, the upper part of the waist bones becomes slightly dislocated from those of the lower part. This increases the stiffness of the waist. Then one cannot stand erect; one tends to stoop or bend. The stiff part of the waist is perceived as burdensome. In Bengali, we call this weight of the waist kubjabhár or kujbhár or kuj [hump]. Manthara, the maidservant, whom the second queen Kaekeyii of king Dasharath brought from her parentʼs house, had a hump, as narrated in the Rámáyańa. So in the Bengali Rámáyańa, she had another name, Kṋujii. The story goes that the Aryans, after crossing Saptasindhu (Punjab), Haritdhánya (Haryana) and Brahmávarta (Brahmarśidesh or Doab,) advanced further to the east, that is, almost to the central region of the present Uttar Pradesh. They were not very familiar with the area. Seeing the Aryan warriors, the local people went into hiding; hence the Aryans had little opportunity to ask anyone for the name of that region. Along the way they happened to spot a woman with a hump. Since she had a hump, she could not run away quickly. The Aryan soldiers sought her help. They asked her, “Oh mother, what is the name of this land of yours?” Failing to understand them, she kept silent. Since they came across a woman with a hump in this land, the country came to be known as Kányakubja.From this [incident] we have derived the name of the historically renowned land of Kányakubja or Kanauj. Now Kanauj is a Tehsil [revenue district]. The Brahmans of Kányakubja are descended from a branch of the Paiṋcagouŕii Brahman community of northern India.

points.body: During the time of the Mahábhárata, when Angadesh was first accepted as an independent kingdom, Duryodhana made Karna the king of Angadesh and rather than consider him a vassal, he allowed him to wear the crown of a sovereign king. Since ancient times the Anga region was not considered part of northern India. Neither Anga, Vauṋga, nor Kaliuṋga were considered part of northern India. Starting from this time, Anga was declared an appendix or Auṋga of northern India and hence its name became Angadesh. Vauṋga remained outside of northern India. Kalinga gained acceptance as a part of southern India. Thus, even today, Oriya Brahmans are sometimes known as Dakśińátya Vedic Brahmans in Bengal. At the time of Karna the capital of Angadesh was Champakanagar. ( 1 ) Karna also founded an auxiliary capital in Mudgagiri, on the western border of the kingdom of Anga. Hence Monghyr has a tradition as a capital. ( 2 )

Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without there being any communication problems as such.
points.body: When Gujaratʼs Rastrakuts [a royal dynasty] defeated eastern India then Angadesh came under their jurisdiction. The Khirkhiriya Hills that we are sitting on were the eastern boundary of the Rastrakut kingdom. Thus they established a capital in their border city of Mungagiri. So we see that Monghyr became a capital more than once. At that time the road system of Bengal, as well as India, was not at all developed. The long highway Shershah built that extended from Suvarnagram in Dhaka District to the city of At́t́ak in western Punjab via Teota (Mańikganj subdivision) and Howrah-Burdwan, and passing by Kolkata, did not afford much convenience to Murshidabad, Monghyr or Patna but Monghyrʼs water-route transport system was good. The waterway worked well all the way from Dhaka to Benares/Allahabad passing via Narayanganj, Teota, Rampur, Boyaliya (Rajsahii), Lalagola Ghat, Godagarii Ghat, Chapaghati, Rajmahal (at one time Rajmahal was the capital of Bengal), Bhagalpur, Monghyr, and Azimabad. Benares and Allahabad used to be helped out by the Shershah-built Badshahii road. Thus, since Monghyr was marked as an important centre of water transport, the capital could be established there without there being any communication problems as such.

points.body: Miirkashim accepted Vireshvijayʼs reasoning and moved the capital to Monghyr. On Vireshvijayʼs advice, the nawab set out preparing the capital in Monghyr with great speed and began constructing his armoury. A great fortress was built in Monghyr as well as a munitions factory, heavy-weapons arsenal, huge parade grounds (Karheya Maidan or Kora Maidan), and a new cultural centre, Kasimbazar. The East India Company recognized the danger. Seizing on various small pretexts they declared war against Miirkashim. They had economic power and were prepared for war – the nawab had nothing. He had just begun organizing. On the other side, the East India Company had concentrated their power at Fort William in Kolkata and in Alinagar (present-day Alipur, now a part of Kolkata).

points.body: The first battle was a trifling affair; it took place in Katwa and the nawab was defeated. The second battle took place in Gheriya and there also the nawab was defeated. The third took place in Udhuyá or in the Udhuyánálá. The East India Company advanced along the Ganges in the direction of Monghyr. A great battle took place in the Dakra canal. With his finger my visitor pointed out to me the Dakra canal which originated on the western border of the Khirkhiriya Hills and joined the Ganges a little to the west of Monghyr. In reality, the Dakra was not a canal but a river. In the East India Company records it is mistakenly called a canal. At the time of the monsoon deluge, the water of the Ganges goes upstream through the Dakra River and floods a wide area in Monghyr District.

points.body: [Now] something about the history of Angadeshʼs terrain. In Karnaʼs time the north of Angadesh bordered on the Himalayas. ( 3 ) The southern border was the source of the Chandan river, a little to the north of Deoghar. On the western border was Ramdiri and Shamhodira (Samidha), near Beguserai, and the eastern border was the Rajmahal Hills near Sahebganj where they approach the Ganges. The Rajmahal Hills range occupy a large area in eastern Angadesh. Their eastern branch stops abruptly near Sahebganj and the Ganges; its western branch ends near Monghyr by the side of the Ganges. The western branchʼs Sanskrit name is the Kśirakśiriká Hills. In Angika they are called Khirkhiriya Hills and in English the Kharagpur Hills. These Kharagpur Hills are a branch of the Rajmahal Hills.

points.body: The Angika language has three chief dialects: Dharamapuriya, Champanagarii or Chekachekii, and Mangeriya. The Dharamapuriya dialect is spoken on the north bank of the Ganges. The Chekachekii dialect is spoken in far eastern region where the Rajmahal Hills approach the Ganges near Sahebganj, and in the western border area where the Khirkhiriya Hills stop near the Ganges. Miirzachauki, near Sahebganj, was at the border of the provinces of Bengal and Bihar during the time of Akbar. Miirzachauki was a busy checkpost. It occupied a narrow strip of land between the Ganges and the mountains and thus was an ideal spot for a checkpost. The Mongeriyá dialect is prevalent to the west of the Khirkhiriya Hills in the Dakra River basin.

points.body: Besides these, there are also two mixed sub-dialects of Angika: The first is the Shriipuriyá sub-dialect which is used in the region lying between Purnea and Kisanganj. Purneaʼs language is Angika, and Bengali is the language of Kisanganj. The Shriipuriyá language that is spoken in the interlying areas is a mixture of Angika and Rauṋapurii Bengali (Súryapurii). The second sub-dialect is the Northern Khat́t́á dialect which is used in the region between Katihar and Malda. The language of Katihar is Angika, and in Malda, Bengali. In certain places between the two one can find this Northern Khat́t́á sub-dialect. It is a mixture of Angika and Shershahabad Bengali. In Mungeriyá Angika one can find some influence of Magahii. Similarly, in the Magahii of the Kiul River basin there is some influence of Angika.

During the Mughal era, certain districts in the Province of Bengal were extremely large (Monghyr, Sylhet, Birbhum, Mymensingh, Purnea, etc.). In many districts the district administrator was called the Jilá Hákim but in Birbhum and Purnea he was called the Baŕá Hakim or governor. The governor of Birbhum used to live in Rajnagar. The last governor, Alinakhii Khan II, only ruled Birbhum for a short time, and Purneaʼs last governor, Shaokatjang, ( 6 ) after being defeated in the Katihar war by Siraj-ud-Daola, was removed from the post of Purneaʼs Baŕá Hákim.

Various cultural artifacts are scattered throughout our Angadesh but who is there to point them out? Angadeshʼs condition is like that of an orphaned child. What to speak of Angadesh, a great part of India is in the same condition today. Where will the historical materials come from if we continue to neglect these cultural artifacts? points.body: In the Lachmiipur jungle area by the eastern border of the Khirkhiriya (Kśiirkśiriká) Hills, there [are] many cave paintings from the Buddhist era. [There are] some artifacts that dated back to the beginning of humankindʼs history in old Angadesh. In these hills humankind depicted its existence through many different varieties of drawings. From these it can be understood just how far back Angadeshʼs history goes. If Karna is accepted as Angaʼs first king, then Angaʼs political history is over 3500 years old, but these cave paintings are signs of the first stage of prehistoric humansʼ ascension through the annals of history. They are approximately twelve thousand to fifteen thousand years old. No writings are found with them because at that time humankind had not yet invented script.

points.title: The meaning of the word ka is water
points.prompt: Recall and explain from memory: The meaning of the word ka is water
summary: The meaning of the word ka is water.
Ka + chad + d́a = kaccha.
Here Kaccha means “surrounded by water”.
points.body: The meaning of the word ka is water. That which lies extended in ka is kalambii or kalmii leaves. Ka also means the expressed universe. One who nurtures the universe is a kápálika. Kaḿ saḿvrttibodhicittaḿ pályatiiti kápálikah. [One who protects the created universe, one who is engaged in the pálana kriyá of the expressed universe, is kápálika.] Another meaning of the word is the chief deity of the expressed universe, about whom it has been said in the Vedas, Kasmae deváya haviśá bidhema. It means “I propitiate this god, whose acoustic root is ka, by offering havih” [fire-sacrifice]. Here kasmae does not mean “whom” it indicates the god having the form of ka. Ka + chad + d́a = kaccha. Generally after a, á or a-ending word or vowels, and before the form of kta or d́a of the root verb with aspirates, the related non-aspirate is used. For example, in the case of the word kaccha, there is an a sound in the letter ka. Therefore, instead ofka+ cha = kacha, it will be kaccha. Etymologically, kaccha means the land surrounded or covered by water. On one side is the Gulf of Kuch, the Arabian sea, and the Raan of Kuch, which is surrounded by water. Hence the place is called Kuch. At the farthest tip of South India, near the Mannar Gulf, there lies a small island named Kacchatibhu, midway between India and Sri Lanka. The word comes from the expression Kucchadviipa. Here Kaccha means “surrounded by water”. ( 10 )

points.body: Often when writing or engraving the name of an object on paper, hoardings, clips and ornaments, one is faced with the problem of space. However a symbol which bears the identity of an organization can easily be denoted. For example, in the ancient Bhanjabhúm kingdom, there used to be the symbol of a peacock on everything – even on the ornaments of the daughters and brides of the family. Thus, the name of the state came to be Mayurbhanj [Mayur means “peacock”]. Situated on the extremities of Ráŕh, Utkal and Koshal, this state has been known as Mayurbhanj for quite a long time. Likewise all official documents of the state of Darbhanga [in Bihar] carried the symbol of a fish. Mithila [Darbhanga is within the Mithila area] is a fish-eating and fish-loving land. Possibly because of this, in all the state affairs of Darbhanga, the symbol of fish was used. That is the reason why Darbhanga was called Miinaketana. Once in an area near the city of Madras, there was an abundance of fish. Fish symbolized the place. That is why in chaste language it was called Miinaketanam. The name of the Madras airport is still Miinambakam. ( 11 )

points.body: Today the rivers of Magadha have all but dried up, but it was not always so. At one time the source of its rivers was in the deep forest. There was a great deal of rainfall in those days and the rivers used to flow twelve months a year. Today, as a result of senseless destruction of the forest, Magadha is gradually being turned into a desert. The village where we met was a little outside the Kiul valley. It falls within the jurisdiction of the Ksuri valley. Today the Kśuri river ( 13 ) has dried up but at one time it was a very big river. This can be ascertained by measuring the width of its source.

points.body: It is true that, at that time, the Maháyánii Buddhist god Máriici was popular among the people. Some people used to do Máriici pújá [worship] and others used to throw sand in the idolʼs face to get the god to leave the village. Háriiti was also popular in Magadha but one would not usually see both Máŕiici and Háriiti in the same place. At one spot in the Kśuri valley we found idols of both Máriici and Háriiti.

Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.
points.body: Háriiti was also a Maháyána Buddhist goddess. The difference between Máriici and Háriiti was that Háriiti was worshipped by both the Maháyána Buddhists and the Shvetámbara Jains. We found both Háriiti and Máriici in the Kśuri river basin. One can deduce from this that in this part of Magadha both Buddhism and Jainism existed side by side. Whether as enemies or friends, they lived together.

points.body: It may also be, moreover, that this river basin was the original centre of Maháyána Buddhism. It should not be forgotten that Rajagir-Nalanda, Barhgaon, Mahabihar (Biharsharif), Paharhiya (the village of Maharsi Saiṋjaya, the philosophy teacher of Lord Buddha), and Pavapurii (the place where Varddhaman Mahaviira died) are all in the Kśuri river valley. points.body: Our Magadha is situated in the northeast corner of the prehistoric Gondwanaland. Since Gondwanaland is the oldest land on earth, it is also the original home of human beings, the birthplace of human civilization. Ráŕh is in eastern Gondwanaland. In the prehistoric era, human beings came from Ráŕh to make their home in Magadha and they brought with them the current of their civilization and culture. Just as the geography of Magadha slopes downwards from north to south and the rivers flow from north to south, similarly the culture and civilization flowed from south to north. Thus the people of Ráŕh and Magadha are fundamentally one. Like the people of Ráŕh, the common people of Magadha are dark-skinned. Magadha borders Ráŕh along its south-east border. The skin and bodily structure of the people of Ráŕh and Magadha are identical. There is also a noticeable similarity between their languages.

points.body: In those days Magadha was full of forests and had abundant rainfall, so there was no need of irrigation. The pre-Aryan people of Magadha used to believe that their land received rainfall due to the grace of the sun-god. Thus they used to worship the sun-god according to their ancient local customs, once during the autumn paddy harvest and again during the spring sun harvest (chaetii harvest). This sun-worship of pre-Aryan Magadha is known today as chat́ pújá. This worship was not performed according to Aryan rules. It was a completely local Magadha practice. The people of Magadha did not bow their heads and submissively accept any of the Aryan practices. For that reason the Aryans called the land magadha. They were afraid of Magadha and used to pay it respect. Thus, to satisfy their grudge and vent their spite, they declared Magadha an unholy land. They said that if a man died there he would not go to heaven and they made efforts to forcibly impose their language, culture and civilization on Magadha. It is up to the historians and social scientists to consider just how successful they were in their efforts.

The caste system in Magadha came much later due to the influence of the Aryans. He practised austerities for a long time in Magadha in the areas of the Barábar, Brahmayoni and Grdhrakút́a mountains. His Guru in Sáḿkhya philosophy, Ácárya Saiṋjaya (Nawada district), was also from Magadha. Although what is called avidyá in his philosophy is not the same as pradhána or prakrti in Sáḿkhya, there is some similarity between the Buddhaʼs concept of avidyá and the Sáḿkhya concept of pradhána.

Haŕsavarddhana did not let this opportunity go by and struck a powerful blow against Ráŕh. War ensued and after two sanguinary battles at Nalhát́i and Parkat́iipur (Pákuŕ), Ráŕh fell under Harśavarddhanaʼs control. The same Harśavarddhana who has achieved everlasting fame in India, who, as legend has it, was known for his generosity and who, in some peopleʼs opinion, was the founder of the Kumbhamelá and the Mághamelá, also killed Ráŕhʼs Queen Jayashankarii and her under-age son, Mrgánkashekhara, with his own hand, and utterly exploited Magadha, tossing it aside like a worn-out banana peel. According to the scriptures, the elderly, women, the sick, the disabled, conscientious dissenters, under-age men, and emissaries must not be killed. Harśavarddhana blatantly violated this scriptural injunction. Both the people of Bengal and the people of Magadha condemned and censured him for this.

points.body: As long as Shasháuṋka was alive he did not allow the Buddhist religion into Ráŕh. After the defeat of Bengal by Harśavarddhana, Buddhism, despite not enjoying his open support, became predominant, due to the tremendous indirect support he gave it. In their hearts the people remained Shaivites but on the outside they became Buddhists. Later on, during the time of Shankaracharya, a small number of Ráŕhʼs Jains and large numbers of Buddhists throughout Bengal accepted the Puranic religion. This may have been because in Ráŕh there was some similarity between the traditions of the Puranic religion and the Digambar Jain doctrine of that time. So Harśavarddhana dealt a strong blow to the religious thought of Ráŕh, as well as Bengal, and by exploiting Magadha brought it to its lowest point.

points.body: Gamadha. The word gam means road. The root dhá+ d́a gives the word, dha which means “something that holds something”. You know that in ancient times those who defied the Vedas were called Mags. The etymological meaning of the word mag is to live a fast life [wantonness]; that is, taking food without restraint, moving recklessly, and doing things without any restraint. In the Vedas, activities such as eating, moving and carrying out actions were bound by certain regulations. Therefore, those who did not obey the Vedas were called Mags.

points.title: In the popular sense, the Hinayánii Buddhists of Arakan were called Mags

points.body: In the popular sense, the Hinayánii Buddhists of Arakan were called Mags. In the broader sense, any Buddhist was called a Mag. The land that followed the path of those who were opposed to the Vedas was called Magadha (maga + dha + d́a = magadha). That is, the land that was treading the path of the Mags. When Caucasian Aryans entered India from the northwest, they were not amenable to crossing the border north of the Shone River in eastern India. Hence, they gave the name Magadha to that border region. Later, during the age of Lord Buddha and Vardhaman Mahaviir, the people of that land accepted Buddhism with an open heart. However, because of Mahaviiraʼs implicit support of nudism, they did not accept Mahaviira so readily, although both the doctrines of Buddha and Vardhaman Mahaviira were anti-Vedic. Buddha had denounced the fire ritual but did not explicitly decry the Vedas. Vardhaman Mahaviira also criticized the Vedas. He utterly disapproved of animal slaughter. Most Vedic sacrificial rites were centered around animal slaughter; hence, he indirectly censured religious sacrifice. In any case, both these anti-Vedic doctrines were first preached from Magadha. Thus the name Magadha became more firmly established in [the history of] logic.

points.body: Vardhaman Mahaviira did not receive much support from Magadha. So he moved away to the then capital of Ráŕh, Ástiknagar (Atthinagar). The people there were followers of Tantra since ancient times. Although they did not lend much support to Vardhaman Mahaviiraʼs doctrine of non-violence, they did not oppose nudism, since Tantric practices include instructions to be free of shame and other bondages. This is corroborated especially by the Jain statues of western Ráŕh. Most of the old idols of Shiva found in Ráŕh are of Jain Shiva. Usually, by the addition of ‘Nátha’ to the name of Jain Shiva, the name of the lord of a holy place is determined – just like Baidyanath, Taraknath, Beharinath, et al. The Jain religion that was established in western Ráŕh was closely related to Tantra – it was Digambarváda. In eastern Ráŕh, Buddhism and Jainism flourished side by side. The Digambar doctrine of western Ráŕh ultimately led to naming even Sadashiva as Digambara. In a song of Ráŕh, it is said:

points.body: However, the Jainism of Ráŕh is centered on Tantra and is saturated with Shaivism. Though the followers of the Vedas did not like Ráŕh, they dared not affront the land of Ráŕh by naming it Magadha. There was only one reason for this; the followers of the Vedas did not encounter any major resistance while entering the land of Magadha. The resistance they faced was ideological in nature. (It was differences in cult and ideology and not any political enmity.) However, in Ráŕh, the situation was quite different. The conflict between the followers of the Vedas with those of Tantra already existed. Furthermore, Ráŕh accepted neither the Vedic caste system nor any discrimination on the grounds of skin complexion. The religious social order was solely based on occupation; not on casteism. During that era, in the battle against the Aryans in Ráŕh, intellectual leadership was provided by Vaedyas (The Vaedyas were not a caste, but practitioners of Vaedyaka medicine – which was not the same as the ayurveda of the Vedas). And, with the help of powerful weapons, the Kayasthas of Ráŕh provided the requisite leadership to resist the Aryans. They did not allow the Vedic religion to gain easy access to Ráŕh, and later they likewise resisted Buddhism. Their final efforts failed with the death of Shasháuṋka, the king of Ráŕh. At that point in time, Buddhism managed to enter Ráŕh through the royal dynasty of Thaneshvar.

points.body: At the fag end of the Vedic age, the Aryans courageously crossed the river Saraju. Before that they had crossed over Saptasindhu (Punjab), Haritdhánya (Haryana), Brahmavarta, Brahmaśidesh (with Surasen and later Doab); the Aryans halted for some time at Prayág. It could be said that it was like a mark of colon in their journey. More fertile and greener lands beckoned them. In the east they founded the kingdom of Káshii. They brought the kingdom of Káshii within the fold of Aryan customs and manners. In the south of Ganges there was a non-Vedic land, Magadha (Maga menas anti-Vedic; magadha means the land which is anti-Vedic in its inclinations). In the east of Káshii, in the north of Ganges remained Videha, (one of the names of Sita, daughter of Janaka, is Vaedehi). They saw that to proceed to Magadha (non-Aryan land) they would have to cross the Shońaka river (Shone River) and to go to Videha in the north they would be required to cross the river Saraju. So they refrained from crossing the river Shone and Saraju and declared that those were non-Aryan lands. Advancing on the eastern side a little they would have reached Gaúṋgá-Ráŕh (Gaúṋgá-Ridi).

points.body: Gal + lá + d́a = galla. The root lá means “to contain” or “to be contained”. The word la is derived from the root lá + d́a [suffix]. The land that possesses ker, that is, narikel or naliker, is ker+lá+d́a= Kerala. The land that was controlled by King Mithi or the land that upheld King Mithi is Mithila. You must have heard of King Mithi. In ancient times, the river Gandaka (Narayani Gandakii) used to be treated as the eastern boundary of that portion of Áryávarta situated to the north of the Ganges. And the Shońaka or Shone River was taken to be the eastern border of the portion situated to the south of the Ganges. On the eastern side of Narayani Gandakii, north of the Ganges, is Mithila or Videha. South of the Ganges, on the eastern side of the Shone, is Magadha. The land of Magadha is on the eastern border of Aryavarta. That is why Magadha is belittled as non-Aryan or Mags. In the sense that it was ruled by Mags, the land was therefore called Magadha. The Aryans used to treat this land with contempt. They thought that if one dies in this land of non-Aryans, one would have to be reborn as a donkey in the next life. Hence, in normal situations, no one in those days wanted to go to farther east, crossing the River Shone and coming to Anga, Vauṋga, or Kaliuṋga. Similarly, they did not like to encounter Videha, Anga, Vauṋga and Prágjyotiśpur [Assam] by crossing the river Narayanii Gandaka to the north. Even now, the people of Magadha, Videha (Mithila), and Bengal firmly believe that if one dies in Káshii, one will go to heaven. For a long time, the old people of Bengal thought it best to live in Káshii, so as to count their days till death. Giving up their land and property to their descendants, they used to settle down in Káshii. Another reason for doing this, they thought, was that Káshii, though not exactly on the eastern border of Áryávarta, was somewhat close to the border. A little walk further to the east of Káshii would find one in the land of non-Aryans.

While a little paler in complexion than the Bengalis of Ráŕh, with somewhat flatter noses, they were very cultured, gracious and simple human beings. At that very point in time, we obtained the original Bengali Kaevartas of Barendrabhúmi as vital resources for the Bengali race. I have mentioned elsewhere that originally every Bengali was a Kaevarta. Just as the Kaevartas moved from Ráŕh to Samatat́, they also migrated northwards from Ráŕh to Barendra. The Namashudras, who are the essence of the Bengalis of central Bengal, were merely an ornament of the Kaevartas. The people of Barendra have likewise descended from the Kaevartas. The subterranean flow of Kaevarta culture mingled together with Máhiśya culture of south Bengal or Midnapur, meaning that their bloodstream reverberates with the tender and adamantine traits of the original Bengalis. In the last phase of the Buddhist era, the Kaevartas of Barendra became vocal against the tyranny of King Devapal II. In the history of the world, such a well-organized peopleʼs resistance movement is rare – it may be that there has not been any other [comparable movement in history.] The Kaevarta rebellion [Eleventh century] ushered a unique renaissance of the Bengali race – it infused in them an intense consciousness to discover new horizons of ideas.

points.body: These very Kaevartas moved to the north and northwest. Those who moved northwest settled down in Mithila and initiated a new way of life. Even today, thousands of original Bengali Kaevartas live in the Purnea – Saharsa region. Those who went northeast advanced throughout the entirety of the region of Bengal. In Kaevarta society, men slightly outnumbered women. Those who went towards the northeast corner, were compelled to marry Mongolian women in order to preserve their society, thus creating a new branch of Bengali ethnicity. These very people, moving gradually northwards, advanced near the peaks of the Himalayas. They settled down on both sides of the River Saiṋkoch, which originated from Bhutan. This new generation of Bengalis came to be named Koch after the river Saiṋkoch. In their days of woes, when Bengali life was battered by the impact of the descent and explosion of gigantic meteors, the Kaevartas were the greatest refuge and asset of Bengal. That is why they were named Koch, not only after the River Saiṋkoch, but also due to their characteristic of providing shelter to the shelterless. When an idealistic youth of the Koch race saw that the social life of Bengal was heading towards disaster, and had degenerated in its cultural life, he came forward as the living symbol of the sceptre of Bengalʼs revival. This Bengali youth of the Mech dynasty established Kámtápur state in the Saiṋkoch valley with the help of only two hundred dedicated young men. (According to another opinion, the Mech people had not yet been recognized as a branch of the Koch society; they were treated as part of the Koch race.) The name of that youth was Haridas Mondal [Thirtteenth century]. (There is, of course, some difference of opinion on this question.)

points.body: Since the pre-Buddhist era, Bengal had remained divided into five parts for reasons of geographical diversity and administrative convenience: (1) Ráŕh, to the west of the Bhagirathi River, (2) the central region, comprising the Bhagirathi and Madhumati Rivers (Bágŕii), (3) Barendra, to the north of the Padma River, (4) Vauṋga, on the eastern side of the river Madhumati, and (5) Mithila, to the north of Padma and west of the river Koshii (Kaoshikii). Compared to other regions, Ráŕh and Barendra were slightly larger in area. The other parts each had a bhukti [administrative district]; that is, Bágŕii bhukti comprised the entire Samatat́. The entire Vauṋga area constituted Vauṋga bhukti, and the entire Mithila formed Tirhut bhukti. Yet Ráŕh and Barendra, being comparatively larger in size, each had two bhuktis. The northern part of Ráŕh (north of where the Damodar River used to flow but no longer does today), meaning the present Dhanbad, Burdwan, Birbhúm, Deoghar, Dumka, Gad́d́á, Sahebganj, Ráŕh and Murshidabad, comprised Burdwan bhukti. (In those days Hooghly and Howrah were included in Burdwan.) Medinipur, Bankura, Manbhum, East Ranchi, Singbhum and Bhanjabhúm comprised Dańd́abhukti (Medinipur). Similarly, in the southern part of Barendrabhúmi was Paondrabardhan bhukti, and its northern part formed Kámtápur bhukti. The Bengali Kaevartas of those days, infused with vitality, selected Haridas Mondal as their leader and at the same time made him the king of Kámtápur. From the time of Haridas Mondal, the Kaevartas of this region came to be called Koch. In the course of time the Koch people came to be divided into four characteristic branches: (1) Mech, (2) Rajbaḿshii, (3) Rájguń, and (4) Koliá (Kolliká – Koliá). Needless to say, all four branches were the original Bengalis, and they accepted as the quintessence of their existence the task of upholding, conveying and nourishing the original Bengali culture, and continued to provide evidence of their worthiness as “the shelter or koch of Bengali culture”.

points.body: In ancient times in India and even today, certain metals like copper and tin are very much in demand, even though they are not as valuable as gold, and also not as useful. However, since copper is somewhat scarce in India, it is valued. At one time in Ráŕh, there were copper mines and copious quantities were extracted. The copper was exported abroad from Tamralipta Port (Tamralipta engaged in exporting támra, that is, copper – madhyapadalopi karmadháráya samása [a mode of framing compound words in Bengali grammar by deleting the word in between two other words]). Those mines today are practically extinct. In the copper mines of Manbhum (Purulia), there is hardly any copper today. The copper of Musabani Moubháńd́ár of Singhbhum is also nearly exhausted. At present it is available to some extent in Bankura and in Rajasthan. Hence, since it was much in demand, although not like gold in quality, it was, like brass, called svarńetar [more scarce than gold]. In the Buddhist period, bronze was also called svarńetar. Similarly, a Sanskrit name for tin is rajatetar. Its pure Bengali name is ráuṋg, [derived from] the pure Sanskrit name of bauṋga. Due to its scarcity tin is called rajatetar. points.body: Thus you understand that if the name of the country is written in English, it should be written as Vauṋga and not Bauṋga. The Vedic name for this land is Vauṋga, in popular Sanskrit Gaoŕdesha or Vauṋgál. In ancient Bengali, words like Gaoŕdesha, Ráŕhdesha, Vauṋga and Vauṋgál were used to describe Bengal. In Latin, it is called Báiṋjálá; anything related to Bengal is called Banjalitis, in Chinese it is Báiṋál, in Turkish Báuṋgálá, in Persian and Urdu Bauṋgál, and in Bengalʼs own language Váuṋgálá or Váuṋglá [Báḿlá/Báuṋglá /Báuṋlá]. In ancient literature it was called Váuṋgálá using the letter a, and in spoken language Vauṋgála. For example, Bhu su ku áji tu Váṋgálii bhaelii [“Bhu su ku, today you have become a Bengali”], Vauṋge nilo jáyá, Ámi jái Vauṋge, kapál jáy sauṋge [“I go to Bengal and my destiny follows me”], Anuṋga-Vauṋga-Kaliuṋgesu Saoráśt́re Magadheśu ca [“Also in Aungadesh, Bengal, Kaliuṋga and in Saoráśt́ra”]. Remember, in all cases, antahstha va is to be used; if consonantal ba is used, it would mean “tin.” In certain Sanskrit dictionaries, for the word Vauṋga, both Bauṋga and Vauṋga are used in the sense of territory. It is said that both kinds of ba-s are acceptable. No, they are not. Only Vauṋga is acceptable. Respected historian Ramesh Chandra Mazumdar was in favour of using anthastha va when spelling the word Vauṋga. This was appropriate.

points.body: In Buddhist literature, it is said that in the palace of Kapilavastu, Shakyasingha, the son of Shuddhodhan, learnt Bengali in his childhood. From this it is not surprising to say that the Bengali language was not directly the daughter or granddaughter of Mágadhii Prákrt. Still, there was a tremendous impact of Mágadhii Prákrt on Bengali. Buddha came more than two thousand five hundred years ago, and if for this reason he had learnt Bengali, then it must be even older than two thousand five hundred years. Mágadhii Prákrt was alive from 3000 B.C to 1200 A.C. That is, from such estimations it can be said that more than eighteen hundred to nineteen hundred years from today, the Mágadhii language existed. Then came Avahat́t́a, its corrupted form. Ancient Maethilii pundits thought Maethilii was related to Avahat́t́a. Amongst the dialects of Bengali language, as far as we can tell, the most ancient is the Mymensingh dialect, and next to it comes the dialect of Central Ráŕh (the spoken language of Bankura-Purulia). So it could be compellingly stated that Bengali has not descended directly from Mágadhii Prákrta.

points.body: South Koshala means the southeastern part of the present-day Madhya Pradesh and the northern part of the present-day Orissa. South Koshala was also known as Mahákoshala. The western part of Mahákoshala is known today as Chattisgarh (Raipur, Durg, Bastar, Balaghat, Raigarh, Bilaspur, Sarguja, etc.), and the eastern side is known as Koshala and Sambalpur (Sambalpur, Bolangir, Sundargarh, Keonjhar, etc.). Evolving from Saorasenii Prákrta, the present language of North Koshala is Avadhi (the language in which Tulsidas wrote his [version of the] Rámáyańa or Rámcharitamánasa), the language of Chattisgarh in South Koshala [its western part] is born from Mágadhii Prákrta, and the spoken language of east Koshala in Sambalpur area is Oriya (Sambalpurii Oriyá). What is known today as Oriya language has three dialects: (1) that of north Oriya, which is the spoken language of the Cuttuck-Balasore region and also the language used in books. This dialect is very close to Bengali; (2) that of south Oriya, which is prevalent in a large area of Puri district, as well as in Koraput, Ganjam and other areas. It has been impacted by Telugu in its pronunciation and vocabulary. Some words correspond exactly with those of Telugu; (3) that of Koshala and Sambalpur areas of Orissa. Though it is close to Bengali and Nagpuria languages, there exists also the influence of Chattisgarhii language. In addition, it includes a significant number of north Indian words. Bimbisara was killed by his son, Ajátshatru. However Ajátshatru was not the son of Koshalkumarii. In protest against the murder of Bimbisara, Prasenjit attacked Magadha. Later, at the request of other Indian kings, he halted the battle. The other kings convinced Prasenjit that Bimbisara had forsaken his own religion, revolted against it and become a follower of Buddha. Ajátshatru was a defender of the Aryan religion and was opposed to Buddha. Therefore, disturbing Ajátshatru would not be the right thing to do for any follower of the Aryan religion. Later, of course, Prasenjit even paid obeisance to Buddha. The ashes of Lord Buddha are still preserved in metal urns in various renowned places in India. Prasenjit then took a portion of Buddhaʼs ashes to Koshala. He alleged that, though he had differences with Buddha with regard to religion, yet in one way, they were of the same mold. Buddha was a Kśatriya [warriorclass] and so was he. Thus, ultimately, a compromise was reached between the king of Koshala and Buddha or Buddhism. ( 5 )

points.body: Many of you know that the king of all mountains, the Himalayas, while very extensive in the east and the west, is no less extensive in the north and the south. The branch of the Himalayas situated on its northern border, which grazes the Tibetan plateau, is snow-covered all year round. These northern Himalayas or upper Himalayas are called Himgiri. Most of the holy mountainous sites in India are located in the Himgiri region. The part of the Himalayas somewhat to the south is covered with forests. However, in the winter season it also becomes covered with snow. This lower Himalaya range is known by its three different segments – in the western, central and eastern parts of India. The ancient name of the westernmost part of the lower Himalayas that extends up to Kashmir, Kimpuruśavarśa (Tibet) and Prameru adhityaká (Pamir plateaux: In very ancient times, the Pamir plateau was part of Kashmiir. Later, it was considered part of Kimpuruśavarśa) was Akśay Cihna [literally “eternal” symbol]. The Rgvedic pronunciation of this mountain was Akśay Ci-h-n, and the Yajurvedic pronunciation was Ak-khay Cihna. The Rgvedic Aryans lived in the region comprising the Akśay Cihna mountain. Later, through oral transmutation, the name of the mountain became distorted and was called Áksái Chin. On further corruption, the word cihna turned into cin. Let this not mislead anyone to consider it as China. The ancient name of the central part of the lower Himalayas was Shivaliuṋga parvamálá (Shivalik range). In Himachal Pradesh, Garhwal and Kumaon regions, this is known as the 'lower Himalayan Shivaliuṋga mountain rangeʼ.
